learning_objectives: Introduce a Database Management System (DBMS) with its aspects.
State the advantages of using a DBMS.
Define Data Definition Language (DDL) and Data Manipulation Language (DML).
Introduce and use the database model.
State the concept of normalization.
Compare between centralized and distributed databases.
Introduce database security and apply it.

blocks.text: Data and database technology are having a major impact on the growing use of computers. The database plays a critical role in almost all areas where computers are used, including education, business, engineering, law, medicine, and science and technology.

A database management system (DBMS) is a collection of programs that enables users to create and maintain a database. The objective of a DBMS is to provide a convenient and effective method for defining, storing or constructing, and retrieving or manipulating databases for various applications. Defining a database involves specifying the data types, structures, and constraints for the data to be stored. Manipulating a database includes functions such as querying the database to retrieve specific data, and updating the database among multiple applications or users.

blocks.caption: Block diagram showing the DBMS, the database, end users and their connections.

blocks.text: The figure illustrates that the DBMS stands between the database and the number of users. In effect, the DBMS serves as the intermediate between the user and the database by translating user requests into the complex code required to fulfil those requests. The DBMS hides much of the database's internal complexity from the application programs that use the database.
Data and information

Data is a collection of raw facts and figures which is isolated, un-interpreted, unrelated and unorganized, but able to be organized into useful information. Data can be manipulated to produce output. Data are the raw facts from which we start to get information. Example: 1, Ram, Kathmandu.

Information is the processed data — after processing the data we get information. Information of one thing may be the data of another. Hence information is data arranged in an order that is useful to the people who receive it.
A raw list '1, Ram, Kathmandu' is data. Put into a labelled table — S.No. 1, Name Ram, Address Kathmandu; S.No. 2, Name Hari, Address Pokhara — it becomes the information 'Address of the Students'.
Database, database system and DBMS

A database is a collection of related information about a subject organized in a useful manner that provides a base or foundation for procedures such as retrieving information, concluding and making a decision. It is a collection of interrelated data of a certain place, person or things in such a way that it can be easily accessed by an application program like a DBMS. Examples: banking records of customers, result sheets, payroll sheets and product records of a shopping centre.
A database system consists of a collection of interrelated data and a set of application programs to access, update and manage the data.

A DBMS is a set of programs that manages the database files. It allows accessing the files, updating the records and retrieving data as requested, and acts as an interface between the application program and the data in the database. Examples of DBMS software: Microsoft Access, Oracle, MySQL, SQL Server, dBase, Clipper, FoxPro.
Why a database?

Traditional file systems have been used from the beginning for managing data in a computer. In a traditional file system data can be duplicated, they cannot be shared, and security and integrity cannot be maintained very well. It is also very difficult to search for data. So it is not easy to work on a file system where everything is kept in a file.
Problems with file processing

items: Data duplication: independent data files include a lot of duplicated copies of the same data — for example a student's name and address stored in several files. This data duplication (data redundancy) causes problems when data have to be updated, since separate file maintenance programs have to be developed and coordinated to ensure each file is properly updated. In practice this proves difficult, so inconsistency occurs among the separate files.

Data dependence: in traditional file processing, data are dependent on a particular application program, so any change in data organization or format requires a change in all the programs associated with those files.

Lack of data integration: having data in independent files makes it difficult to provide end users with information for ad hoc (unplanned) requests that require accessing data stored in several different files. Special programs have to be written to retrieve data from each independent file — difficult, time-consuming and expensive.

blocks.text: Objectives of a DBMS

items: To provide a storage area for the mass amount of relevant data.
To make access to the data easy for the end user.
To provide prompt response to the user's request for data.
To make the latest modification to the database available immediately.
To eliminate data redundancy (duplication of data).
To allow multiple users to be active at one time.
To allow the growth of the database.
To protect the data from physical harm and unauthorized access.

blocks.text: Short Answer Question 3 asks: 'Define DBMS. List out the objectives of DBMS.' The 8 objectives above are the answer — teach them as a numbered list, not prose.

blocks.caption: Data storage hierarchy — components of a file, from bit up to database.

blocks.text: The data storage hierarchy

items: Bit: the smallest unit of memory. It can be either 0 or 1.
Character: a collection of 8 bits. It represents an alphabet, number, or any sign or symbol. E.g. in ASCII-8 bits, 01000001 is equal to 'A'.
Field (data item / data element): holds a single fact or attribute of an entity. It is often referred to as an attribute. E.g. Pratap, Anusha, 90.
Record: a collection of related fields which represents a complete unit of information.
File: a collection of related records or identical records in an entity set, labelled to identify the entity set.
Database: a collection of integrated files.

blocks.text: Information stored in a database is maintained in the form of tables, each with rows and columns. Tables have unique names. Each row represents a relationship among values, and each column must have similar data types. A field is the data value at the intersection of a row and column, and all values in a field must be of the same data type. Common data types include numeric, character/string, integer, float, date and logical. To distinguish rows, columns must have unique values, ensuring no two rows are identical. Keys are used to identify these unique attributes and to distinguish relationships between rows.
Table, field, record and object
In a relational database a table is a structured collection of data organized into rows and columns. Tables store related data, making it easy to retrieve, update and manage information.

items: Field (column or domain): the smallest unit of data in a table, representing a single piece of information within a record. Each column represents a specific data attribute and defines the type of data stored in that column. For example, in a 'student' table fields might include studentID, Name, Age, Mark and Email; a domain for the attribute 'Age' might be integers between 0 and 120. The stored value of an attribute is referred to as an attribute value, stored field, or simply field — for example, Gopal is a field of the attribute student_name.

Record (row or tuple): a collection of fields that represents a single entity within a table. It includes all the fields for one item. For example: Edu_1, Gopal, gopal@gmail.com is one row of the student table.
Object: in a DBMS, objects are database components that store data or perform specific functions related to data management.

blocks.caption: Relationship between field, record and file.

blocks.text: Components of an object in a DBMS

items: Tables: store data, each representing an entity with attributes.
Views: virtual tables from queries, used for data presentation without storage.
Indexes: enhance data retrieval speed.
Sequences: generate unique numeric values, often for primary keys.
Stored procedures: precompiled SQL tasks.
Triggers: automatically execute procedures on table or view events.
Constraints: enforce data integrity rules on columns (e.g. primary key, foreign key, uniqueness).

blocks.text: Keys
A key is an attribute that is used to identify a particular record in a database. A key may be composed of more than one attribute. Any attribute that is part of a key is known as a key attribute.

items: Candidate key: any field or combination of fields that can uniquely identify a record in a table. A table can have multiple candidate keys, but only one can be chosen as the primary key. Example: in the 'student' table both studentID and the combination of Name + Email could serve as candidate keys.
Alternate key: a candidate key which is not used as the primary key. It can still uniquely identify records.

Primary key: a candidate key chosen by the database designer to identify the entity from the entity set. Primary keys are unique identifiers for each record; they must contain unique values and cannot be NULL.

Foreign key: a key attribute whose value is derived from the primary key of another table. It establishes a relationship between two tables by referencing the primary key or a unique key in another table.
Super key: a set of one or more attributes that, taken collectively, allows us to identify uniquely an entity in the entity set.

blocks.text: Keynotes on the primary key

items: In the relational model, the attribute that uniquely identifies each record in a table is the primary key.
A primary key is one or more columns in a table that uniquely identifies each row.
It is the foundation for maintaining data integrity and enforcing relationships between tables.
It ensures each row has a distinct identifier, allowing efficient retrieval and management of data.
Just as a bank or government department asks for an ID (account number, member number, tax file number), the primary key uniquely identifies records even when other data change.

blocks.text: Keynotes on the foreign key

items: A foreign key establishes a relationship between two tables and references the primary key of another table.
When data is inserted or updated in the foreign key column, the database ensures the referenced value exists in the related table's primary key column.
This maintains consistency and data integrity in database management systems.
A foreign key can be unique or null, making it flexible for modelling relationships between tables.

sections.title: Advantages and Disadvantages of Using a DBMS

blocks.text: Advantages of a DBMS

items: Data can be shared (concurrent access of data): data stored in a database can be shared among several different users, including concurrent access — access to the same data simultaneously by more than one user. With a DBMS the data for the entire company is effectively made available to all managers and end users who need them.
Reduce data redundancy: in traditional file processing the same data may be duplicated many times or in many places. A DBMS reduces duplication of data with the help of a primary key.

Integrity can be maintained: integrity ensures that the data stored in a database is correct or accurate. Inconsistency between two entries is an example of a lack of integrity. A DBMS avoids the data inconsistency problem, so it improves data integrity.

Data independence: the DBMS keeps the description of data separate from the applications that use the data, so changes in the data definition can occur without changing every application program. This reduces maintenance cost and makes the database independent of the storage media.

Data availability: in a traditional file processing system data is scattered in many files, and because of non-uniformity in file design the same data may have different identification, making it difficult to obtain the relevant data. A DBMS overcomes this problem.

Standards can be enforced: with central control of the database the DBA can ensure that all applicable standards are followed in the representation of data — company, installation, department, industry, national and international standards.
Security can be improved: certain restrictions can be applied by giving different authority to different users, so confidential data is not available to everyone.

Inconsistency can be avoided: when the same data are duplicated and a change is made at one site but not another, data inconsistency results. A DBMS reduces inconsistency by eliminating two entries regarding the same data.

Providing multiple user interfaces: a DBMS provides query language interfaces, forms and command interfaces, and in some cases menu-driven interfaces. Forms and menu-driven interfaces are collectively called a GUI (Graphical User Interface).
Providing backup and recovery: a DBMS must provide facilities for recovering from hardware or software failures. The backup and recovery subsystem of the DBMS is responsible for recovery.

blocks.text: Disadvantages of a DBMS

items: The initial investment is high for implementing hardware, software (DBMS software) and training.
Proper training is required for staff to work properly in the database system, year after year.
When a fault occurs in one part of the database it affects the other parts as well.
It is complex to understand and implement.
There is the overhead cost of providing security, recovery and integrity functions.
There is the cost of hardware upgrade to allow for the extensive program, plus maintenance of hardware, software, backup and recovery which remain forever.
Problems arise if the database is not properly designed, or if the database application system is not properly implemented.
There is an additional cost for migration from a traditionally separate application environment to an integrated one.

blocks.title: Exam pattern
blocks.text: Questions on this chapter very often ask for 'advantages and disadvantages of DBMS'. Give 10 advantages and 8 disadvantages, each with a one-line explanation.

sections.title: Structured Query Language (SQL) and DBMS Languages

blocks.text: In order to provide various facilities to different types of users, a DBMS provides one or more specialized programming languages called database languages. A language called SQL has recently been taken as the standard database language. SQL is the relational language for the end user and offers a mechanism of universal database access. A query language allows users to retrieve data from the database without having detailed information about the structure of the records and without being concerned about the DBMS processes. SQL is used as an intermediary and a standard in accessing a large number of different types of database systems, and contains the statements that describe the data contained in the database.
Types of DBMS language

Used by database designers and programmers to specify the content and structure of the database, and to define the physical characteristics of records. It is a link between the logical and physical structures of the database. The logical structure of the database is called the schema; a sub-schema is the way a particular application views the data from the database that the application uses.

Provides the techniques for processing the database, such as retrieval, sorting, display and deletion of data or records. It lets a user query a database and receive summary reports, and is integrated with other programming languages to implement sophisticated database functions. Two types exist: (i) Procedural DML — the user must specify what data are needed AND how to get them; (ii) Non-procedural DML — the user specifies what data are needed without specifying how to get them.
Differences between DDL and DML

blocks.caption: DDL vs DML
head: Data Definition Language (DDL)
Data Manipulation Language (DML)
rows: DDL is declarative and is used to define database structures
DML is imperative and is used to perform operations on the data stored in the database
DDL commands create or define the database schema and manage structure and constraints, providing the ability to define, create and modify database objects such as tables, views, indexes and users
DML commands add, retrieve or update data, allowing manipulation of data in a database such as inserting, updating and deleting records
The structure of the database is affected by changes made using DDL
The data stored in the database is affected by changes made using DML
DDL statements are typically used during the design and setup phase of the database
DML statements are used during the normal operation of the database
Some DDL commands: CREATE, DROP, ALTER, TRUNCATE, RENAME
Some DML commands: SELECT, INSERT, UPDATE, DELETE

blocks.text: A data dictionary is a file that contains metadata ('data about data'). It is consulted before actual data are read or modified in the database system. The language used to define the data dictionary is called the data dictionary language. A comprehensive dictionary also includes cross-references — which user requires which report, which user requires which form, and so on.
Short Answer Question 13 asks for definitions of DDL and DML. Give the definition plus the 5-point difference table.
The database model describes the structure of a database. It is a collection of conceptual tools for describing data, relationships, etc. It defines how the data are stored and accessed.
Characteristics of a good data model

items: Simplicity: the model should be easy to understand and use.
Accuracy: the model should accurately represent the real-world scenario and must capture all necessary details to avoid data redundancy.
Security: the model should incorporate security features to protect data.
Scalability: it should support the growth of the database in terms of volume of data and number of users without degrading performance.
Consistency, flexibility and extensibility as required.

blocks.text: Types of database model

items: Hierarchical database model
Network database model
Relational database model

blocks.text: 1. Hierarchical database model

In a hierarchical database model, records are logically organized into a hierarchy of relationships. A hierarchically structured database is arranged logically in an inverted tree pattern. All records in the hierarchy are called nodes. Each node is related to the others in a parent-child relationship: each parent record may have one or more child records, and each child can have only one parent. The top-level record in the hierarchy is called the root record.

blocks.caption: Hierarchical database model — an inverted tree of parent and child nodes.
Hierarchical model — advantages and disadvantages
head: Advantages
Disadvantages
rows: It is the easiest model of the database
It is an old-fashioned, outdated database model
A database owner is more secure because nobody else can see and modify a child without consulting its parent
It is a non-flexible model — modification or addition of a child without consulting the parent is impossible or very complex
Searching is fast and easy if the parent is known
It is very efficient in handling 'one-to-many' relationships
It increases data redundancy as the same data can be saved in different places
It helps to build complex systems from simple components
When a parent node is deleted, all the child nodes are deleted automatically

blocks.text: 2. Network database model

The network database model is a modified version of the hierarchical database. In a network database structure each node may have several parents, and the model views all records in sets. It has a higher level of flexibility than the hierarchical model. It is easier to restructure the information stored in this structure, since the path of relationship enables member records to be stored in an arbitrary manner. However, operation and maintenance become complicated as the number of points in the network increases, and it is less user-friendly than the hierarchical structure.

blocks.caption: Network database model — a node may have several parents.
Network model — advantages and disadvantages
head: Advantages
Disadvantages
rows: It is more flexible than the hierarchical model because it accepts 'many-to-many' relationships
It is one of the complex database models
It reduces redundancy because data should not be repeated if the same data is needed
It needs larger programs to handle the relationships
Searching is fast because of multidirectional pointers
Pointers needed in this model increase the overhead of storage
It is less secure compared to the hierarchical model, as it is open to all

blocks.text: 3. Relational database model

In a relational database model data are arranged in two-dimensional tables, which are easy for a user to develop and understand. This type of model can also be described mathematically. Because many managers often work with data in tabular form, it is easy for most of them to understand the structure used in a relational database. The name 'relational' is derived from the fact that each table represents a relation and each row of the table corresponds to a single record of the database. It is highly flexible to program and retrieve data and can be used efficiently even on a computer with limited memory and processing capability. Its processing efficiency is comparatively low; no processing can be done without establishing the data relationships.

A relational database consists of a collection of tables, each assigned a unique name. A row in a table represents a relationship among a set of values. Relations represent facts describing a set of real-world entities. In a relation we represent one entity per row and one attribute per column. Table names and column names help to interpret the meaning of the values in each row of the relation.

Table1 holds Name, Address, House no, City and Department no for Barsha, Samjhana, Apsara, Asha and Kalpana. Table2 holds Name, Profession and Income for Nirmal, Rohit, Samjhana, Lautan and Barsha. A JOIN on Name combines the two; a PROJECT on City and Department no extracts just those columns.
Features of a relation

items: Attributes: the name of a column in a relation. The attributes of the relation STUDENT are Roll_Number, Student_Name, DOB, Class and Year; of COURSE they are CourseNumber, CourseName, Room, Day and Hr. No two attributes in a relation can have the same name.

Domain: the set of all values that an attribute takes on. The domain of Roll_Number is the set of all roll numbers in the class. A domain can be viewed as a data type — possibly a simple system-defined type such as integer or character, or more generally a user-defined data type. Several attributes in a relationship can share the same domain.
NULL value: indicates that the value for the corresponding attribute is either not available or not applicable. An attribute used as the primary key should not have a NULL value.

Tuple: every row of a relation is called a tuple, so a relation is a set of tuples. Each tuple contains exactly one value for each attribute. There cannot be two identical tuples in a relation, because a set cannot have duplicate elements. A tuple is also called a record.

blocks.caption: Advantages and disadvantages of the relational model
head: Advantages
Disadvantages
rows: Since one table is linked with another, common fields and rules implemented on one table can easily be implemented on another
It is more complex than other models
Too many rules make the database non-user-friendly
Normalization of the database is possible
Rapid processing of the database is possible
New data can be added without redesigning the database afresh — a new table can be added and related to existing tables

blocks.text: Long Answer Questions 2, 3, 4 and 11 all ask about database models. Practise drawing the hierarchical inverted tree and the network graph side by side, then list 5 + 5 points for each model.

Many early database applications and some current low-end applications could access and manipulate only one table at a time. Each table was stored in its own file, so there was no reason to use the term 'table' — the table and the database were one and the same, and the table was simply called a file or just the database. This type of database using a single file for a table is called a flat-file database.

A flat-file database is useful for a single user and a small system. When the system is large, the flat-file database is very difficult to maintain, because when adding, deleting or editing any field we have to make changes in every file that contains the same field. To eliminate these drawbacks, a relational database management system was developed. In an RDBMS the database is made up of a set of tables, and the data of one table is related to other tables through a common field.
Advantages of a DBMS / RDBMS over a flat-file system

items: The database system is easier to access, update, manage and retrieve data than the flat-file system.
Data redundancy is low in a database system.
Data sharing is easier in a database system.
The physical and logical links required between different files to cope with complex multiple-key queries on multiple files are not possible in the flat-file system.
Searching and sharing of data are easier than in the flat-file system.
A database system is secure and integrity can be maintained very well.
A database system executes data operations much faster than the flat-file system.

blocks.text: An entity is the name of a 'thing', 'person' or 'object' in the real world that is distinguishable from all other objects — an existing thing in the system used in the database. Examples: student, employee, book, loan, zone, account. An entity set is a set of entities of the same type that share the same properties or attributes, for example the set of all loans (house loan, car loan, personal loan) provided by a particular bank.

The properties that characterize an entity set. They are the descriptive properties possessed by each member of an entity set. For example the attributes of the customer entity can be Customer_id, Customer_name, Customer_street, Customer_city, Customer_telno and Customer_email. The values for each attribute are defined in terms of: data type (what type of data can be stored, such as integer, text or picture), domain (the set of permitted values — for example the mark of a subject cannot be greater than the full marks), and default value (the value recorded if the user does not specify one, such as 0 as the default mark).
The association between entities. For example, a student takes a class, a professor teaches a class, a department employs a professor.
Types of relationship
For a binary relationship set R between entity sets A and B, the relationship may be of four types: one-to-one, one-to-many, many-to-one and many-to-many.

items: One-to-one: an entity in A is associated with at most one entity in B, and an entity in B is associated with at most one entity in A. Example: the relationship between husband and wife.

One-to-many: an entity in A is associated with any number of entities in B; an entity in B, however, can be associated with at most one entity in A. Example: the relationship between teacher and course.

Many-to-one: an entity in A is associated with at most one entity in B; an entity in B, however, can be associated with any number of entities in A. Example: fire chief, police chief, mayor and minister reporting to one authority.
Many-to-many: an entity in A is associated with any number of entities in B, and an entity in B is associated with any number of entities in A. Example: the relationship between student and course.

blocks.caption: Relationship: one to one (husband — wife).
Relationship: one to many (teacher — courses).
Relationship: many to one (several officials — one authority).
Relationship: many to many (students — courses).

blocks.text: Teach the four relationship types with the same picture changing only the arrows: 1↔1, 1→many, many→1, many↔many. Students then only need to memorise the four arrows, not four paragraphs.

The E-R model is based on a perception of the real world that consists of a collection of basic objects called entities and the relationships among these objects. An E-R diagram is a graphical representation of different entities and their relationships — a graphical representation of the database. The overall logical structure of a database can be expressed graphically by an E-R diagram.
Symbols used in an E-R diagram

blocks.caption: E-R diagram symbols
head: S.No.
Symbol
Function / meaning
rows: It represents the entity. It contains objects used in relational databases.
It represents the relationship among entities.
It is used to link attributes to entity sets and entity sets to the relationship, and vice versa.

blocks.caption: E-R diagram: a customer deposits an amount in his account.
E-R diagram: a writer writes a book.

blocks.text: An entity set usually has some attributes whose values are distinct for each individual entity — this is called a key. A key allows us to identify a set of attributes that suffice to distinguish entities from each other. No two entities are allowed to have exactly the same value for all attributes.
Advantages of the E-R diagram in system design

items: It provides a visual representation of the database design.
It is simple and easier to understand.
It allows designers to effectively communicate the features of the database.
It is highly flexible to use, as additional relationships can be added as per need.
It supports physical database creation.
It provides a higher-level description of the system.
It can be generalized or specialized based on needs.

blocks.text: Long Answer Questions 5 and 6 ask for the E-R symbols with meanings and examples. Short Answer Question 6 asks for the advantages of the E-R diagram — there are exactly 7.

Data normalization is a process to present a database in a normal form to avoid undesirable things such as repetition of information, inability to represent information, and loss of information. It improves performance by reducing data redundancy to a large extent.
Advantages of normalization

items: It reduces data redundancy.
It improves faster sorting and index creation.
It creates a few indexes and nulls.
It ignores the repetition of information.
It simplifies the structure of tables.
It improves the performance of a system.
It avoids the loss of information.

blocks.text: Normal forms
The most important and widely used normal forms are: First Normal Form (1NF), Second Normal Form (2NF), Third Normal Form (3NF), Boyce-Codd Normal Form (BCNF) and Fourth Normal Form (4NF).
Need for normalization

The table is the basic building block in the database design process, so the structure of the table is of great interest in relational database design. A poor table structure degrades the performance of the RDBMS. Recognizing a poor table structure and producing a good table is based on normalization, which is a process for assigning attributes to entities. Normalization reduces data redundancies and helps to eliminate data anomalies. It does not eliminate redundancy outright; instead it produces a controlled mechanism to reduce repetition of data that lets us link database tables.
Normalization is the process of decomposing a big table into much smaller and simpler tables so that the following are ensured:

items: Dependence between the data is identified.
Redundancy in the database is minimized.
The data model is made more flexible and easier to maintain.
Database design is improved.
Anomalies are removed for database activities.
Data is protected from unauthorized users and secured in the database.

blocks.text: Normalization works through a series of stages called normal forms. The first three stages are 1NF, 2NF and 3NF. A relation is said to be in a particular normal form if it satisfies a prescribed set of rules. From a structural point of view 2NF is better than 1NF and 3NF is better than 2NF. For most database designs 3NF is as high as we need to go, although some very specialized applications may require higher-level normalization. De-normalization produces a lower normal form — for example, a third normal form would be converted to a second normal form through de-normalization.
First Normal Form (1NF)

A relation or table is said to be in 1NF if all its attributes are atomic — that is, there should not be any repeating groups of an attribute. The purpose of 1NF is to eliminate repeating groups of attributes in an entity. If any characteristic is repeated again and again in the same table or row, such attributes are removed either into a separate table or decomposed into different rows.

blocks.text: Second Normal Form (2NF)

A relation is in second normal form if it is in first normal form and each attribute is functionally dependent on the entire primary key. The purpose of 2NF is to eliminate partial key dependencies — each attribute in the table must depend on the whole key, not just part of it.

In the table above the primary key is the combination of Roll_No + Class. Name depends on Roll_No and Class; Subject depends only on Class, not on Roll_No; Marks depends on Subject and Name. So the table is decomposed into three tables: Student (Name, Roll_No, Class), Subjects (Subject, Class) and Marks (Name, Subject, Marks).

blocks.text: Third Normal Form (3NF)

A relation is in third normal form if it is in second normal form and it does not contain any transitive dependency on the primary key. All attributes that are not dependent upon the primary key must be eliminated. A transitive dependency is one in which, among three attributes A, B and C, if A → B and B → C then C → A. A relation in 3NF should not contain such a transitive dependency.

Centralized database system

Centralized database systems are those that run on a single computer system. A computer system may be single-user or multiuser; a database system designed for a single-user system does not provide many of the facilities that a multiuser database system provides. In this system users have access to computer resources via hundreds of remote communication devices, including online terminals used to input data and printers to obtain reports. Highly skilled, technically trained specialists are required for this processing. This processing mode offers control of data processing expenses and also better security, control and protection of data.

Disadvantages

It has a low cost of implementation and operation

It is suitable for a small organization with limited data and users
It is not appropriate for big organizations with a large number of users and computers

blocks.text: Distributed database system

In a distributed database system the database is stored on several computers. Distributed databases are databases located at different places; they facilitate easy access to data from any location. There is the problem of control of security, increased problems of control of the database, and a need for more computer resources. It can manage people with functional knowledge. This mode of processing incurs more expense with limited security, control and protection of data.

blocks.text: Database Administrator (DBA)

The data administrator is the person who makes the strategic and policy decisions regarding the data of the enterprise, and the database administrator (DBA) is the person who provides the necessary technical support for implementing those decisions. The DBA is responsible for the overall control of the system at a technical level.
Functions of the DBA

items: Defining the internal schema: the DBA must define how the data is to be represented in the stored database — usually referred to as physical database design.
Defining the external schema: the DBA must decide exactly what information is to be stored in the database — usually called logical (sometimes conceptual) database design.
Liaising with users: it is the business of the DBA to liaise with users to ensure that the data they require is available, and to write the necessary external schemas.
Defining security and integrity rules: the DBA must define security rules for the protection of data against unauthorized users, and integrity rules for checking the accuracy or validity of data.
Defining backup and recovery procedures: necessary because damage to any portion of the system causes an error.
Monitoring performance and responding to changing requirements: the DBA must monitor performance and make appropriate adjustments as requirements change.

blocks.text: Data integrity

Data integrity, or an integrity constraint, is a rule that restricts the values that may be present in the database. Integrity constraints ensure that changes made to the database by authorized users do not result in a loss of data consistency, and guard against accidental damage to the database.

items: Entity integrity: the rule that no column that is part of the primary key may accept null values. It guarantees that each record will indeed have its own identity and that one record can be distinguished from another.

Referential integrity: if table A contains a foreign key that matches the primary key of table B, then the values of this foreign key either must match the value of the primary key for some row in table B, or must be null. It keeps us from making data-entry mistakes — essentially all the information in the two fields should match.

Domain integrity: domain constraints specify the set of possible values that may be associated with an attribute, and may allow the use of null values for particular attributes. They are the most elementary form of integrity constraint and are tested easily by the system whenever a new data item is entered into a database.

blocks.text: Short Answer Question 9 and Long Answer Question 9 cover data security and the DBA. Short Answer Question 10 asks for the types of data integrity — there are exactly 3.

Data security is the means of ensuring that data is kept safe from corruption and that access to it is suitably controlled. Thus data security helps to ensure privacy, and helps in protecting personal data and in preventing data theft, loss of data privacy and data corruption from the database. Security refers to the protection of data against unauthorized access — not every user of the database system should be able to access all the data.

In a banking system, payroll personnel need to see only that part of the database that has information about the various bank employees. They do not need access to information about customer accounts. The security mechanism of a DBMS makes sure that only authorized users are given access to the data in the database.

A database very often keeps sensitive data about the users of the database. The data are placed in the files of the database, which should be kept in a secure room, but there is no guarantee that the disk drives cannot be stolen by an organized group of intruders. Sensitive data such as credit card numbers, addresses and health status can be misused. Databases are constructed to use many hard disk drives that can be placed on different disks, but the following guidelines apply to all databases and ensure more reliable and more cost-effective backups.
Rollback, backup and recovery

items: Rollback is a technique that allows reverting a database to a previous state. It is useful for undoing unintended changes or recovering from errors during transactions.
Regular database backups are essential for data protection. Backups create copies of the database at specific points in time, allowing recovery in case of data loss, corruption or system failures.

Recovery techniques ensure that the database remains consistent after a failure such as a system crash. Recovery mechanisms include redo logs, undo logs and checkpoints to bring the database back to a consistent state.

Firewalls are security systems designed to prevent unauthorized access to private networks, but these are not directly related to database protection. Database security involves multiple layers including access controls, encryption and monitoring, in addition to these techniques.

blocks.text: How data may be lost

blocks.caption: Accidental and intentional loss of data
head: Accidental loss may result from
Intentional loss may result from
rows: Distribution of data over several computers

blocks.text: Five levels at which security measures must be taken

items: Physical level: the place or site containing the computer systems must be physically secure against external intruders. Software security is not enough — physical security is a must.
Human: users must be authorized carefully to reduce the chance of such users giving access to an intruder.
Operating system: even though the database system is highly secured, weakness in the operating system may provide the pathway for unauthorized access.
Network: since almost all database systems allow access through terminals or networks, software-level security within the network software is as important as physical security.

Database system: security should also be provided by the database system itself — some database users may be authorized to access only a limited portion of the database, for example allowed to issue queries but forbidden to modify data.

blocks.text: Main guidelines for database backup and security

items: Always maintain a log of your backup schedule.
Occasionally store backups in a separate location.
Spread your database across several disks.
Always consider your existing hardware configuration and system workload.
Determine the volatility and value of your data.
Verify the integrity of your database regularly.
Verify the integrity of your backup media after each backup.

blocks.text: Techniques used to achieve security

items: Cryptographic tools can be used to defend data in transit between systems, reducing the probability that data can be intercepted or modified in between.
Strong authentication techniques can be employed to ensure that the two end-points taking part in a transaction are who they say they are.
Secure crypto-processors can be used to leverage physical security techniques into protecting the security of the computer system.
Chain of trust techniques can be used to attempt to ensure that all software loaded has been certified as authentic by the system designers.
Mandatory access control can be used to ensure that privileged access is withdrawn when privileges are retracted.
Capability and access control list techniques can be used to ensure privilege separation.
Anti-virus software deletes or disables viruses on the computer, protecting against them.
Firewalls — hardware and/or software components — protect the computer system from intruders, not allowing anything to enter without correct markings.
An intrusion-detection system is used to detect people who are on the network but doing things that can be hazardous to the whole system.
Backups are a way of securing the information by keeping another copy of all required files and documents.

sections.title: Lab Work in SQL — MySQL, XAMPP and phpMyAdmin

blocks.text: SQL stands for Structured Query Language. It is a database language used to access and manipulate databases. SQL statements can instruct the server to perform certain operations:

items: Data query: requesting specific information from the existing database.
Data manipulation: adding, deleting, changing, sorting and other operations that modify the data, the values or the visuals.
Data identity: defining data types, e.g. changing numerical data to integers. This also includes defining a schema or the relationship of each table in the database.
Data access control: providing security techniques to protect data, including deciding who can view or use any information stored in the database.

blocks.text: MySQL

MySQL is one of the most popular RDBMS software packages. It implements a client-server model: MySQL creates a database for storing and manipulating data and defines the relationship of each table. Clients make requests by typing specific SQL statements on MySQL, and the server application responds with the requested information, which appears on the client's side. MySQL is popular because it is flexible and easy to use, high performance, an industry standard, and secure.

MySQL and related tools can be installed separately, but developers have made all-in-one setup packages that automatically install and set up MySQL and PHP environments on Windows, Linux or Mac machines:

items: XAMPP — Windows / Linux / Mac, Apache, MySQL, PHP (used in this chapter)
WAMP — Windows, Apache, MySQL, PHP
LAMP — Linux, Apache, MySQL, PHP
MAMP — Mac, Apache, MySQL, PHP

blocks.text: The DISTINCT keyword
DISTINCT is used with the SELECT statement to retrieve unique values from a table. It removes all duplicate records while retrieving from the database.
The LIKE clause

The LIKE clause is used as a condition in an SQL query. It compares data with an expression using wildcard operators and is used to find similar data from the table. There are two wildcard operators: the percent sign %, which represents zero, one or more than one character; and the underscore _, which represents only one character.

SELECT * from Student where s_name like 'A%';   -- starts with 'A'
SELECT * from Student where s_name like '_d%';  -- 'd' as the second character
SELECT * from Student where s_name like '%x';   -- 'x' as the last character
GROUP BY and HAVING

GROUP BY groups the results of a SELECT query based on one or more columns, and is used with aggregate functions to group the result set. HAVING is used because the WHERE keyword cannot be used with an aggregate function.

SELECT column_name, function(column_name)
FROM table_name
WHERE condition
GROUP BY column_name;

-- example
Select count(sid), lastname
from student
group by lastname having count(sid) < 5;

blocks.text: BETWEEN is inclusive — it includes both the starting and the ending value. It works with numbers, text and dates.

sections.title: SQL — CASE, LIMIT, ROUND and Joins

blocks.text: CASE
CASE statements are used to create different outputs, usually in the SELECT statement. It is SQL's way of handling if-then logic.

SELECT column_name,
  CASE
    WHEN condition THEN 'Result_1'
    WHEN condition THEN 'Result_2'
    ELSE 'Result_3'
  END
FROM table_name;
LIMIT
LIMIT is a clause that lets you specify the maximum number of rows the result set will have.
ROUND()
ROUND() takes a column name and an integer as arguments, and rounds the values in the column to the number of decimal places specified by the integer.

SELECT ROUND(column_name, integer)
FROM table_name;
Joins
An inner join combines rows from different tables if the join condition is true.

SELECT column_name(s)
FROM table_1
JOIN table_2
ON table_1.column_name = table_2.column_name;

An outer join combines rows from different tables even if the join condition is not met. Every row in the left table is returned in the result set, and if the join condition is not met then NULL values are used to fill in the columns from the right table.

SELECT column_name(s)
FROM table_1
LEFT JOIN table_2
ON table_1.column_name = table_2.column_name;

Transaction Control Language is a subset of SQL that deals with managing transactions within a database. A transaction is a sequence of one or more SQL statements executed as a single unit of work. The primary purpose of TCL is to ensure data consistency and integrity during database operations.

short.q: What is a database? List the major uses of database application software.
short.a:
A database is an organised collection of interrelated data stored so that it can be accessed, managed and updated easily. Instead of scattering facts across unrelated files, a database keeps them once, in a structured form, and lets many programs and users share them.

Major uses of database application software:

  • Banking — customer accounts, loans, transactions and ATM activity.
  • Airlines and railways — reservations, seat availability and schedules.
  • Universities — student records, course registration, marks and fees.
  • Sales and inventory — stock levels, orders, billing and suppliers.
  • Human resources — employee records, payroll, leave and appraisals.
  • Health care — patient history, tests, prescriptions and billing.
  • Government and e-governance — citizenship, tax, land and licence records.

short.q: Differentiate between Database and DBMS.
short.a:
DatabaseDBMS
A collection of related data stored in an organised way. The software that creates, maintains and controls access to that data.
It is passive — it is the data itself. It is active — it is the set of programs that work on the data.
Does not provide security, backup or concurrency control by itself. Provides security, backup, recovery, concurrency and integrity control.
Users cannot easily retrieve or update it without writing their own code. Provides a query language (SQL) so users can retrieve and update easily.
Examples: the student table, the marks table. Examples: MySQL, Oracle, PostgreSQL, SQL Server, MS Access.

In short, the database is the warehouse and the DBMS is the warehouse manager.

short.q: Define DBMS. List out the objectives of DBMS.
short.a:
A DBMS (Database Management System) is a collection of programs that enables users to create and maintain a database. It is the interface between the physical data stored on disk and the application programs or users who need it, and it hides the internal complexity of storage from them.

The main objectives of a DBMS are to:

  • store data in an organised, structured form;
  • provide easy and flexible access to the data;
  • answer queries with a prompt response;
  • update data immediately so every user sees the current value;
  • remove redundancy so the same fact is not duplicated;
  • allow many users to work on the data at the same time;
  • allow the database to grow as the organisation grows;
  • protect the data against loss, theft and unauthorised access.

short.q: Give two advantages of using a database rather than a number of separate files.
short.a:
Two advantages of keeping one database instead of a number of separate files:
  • No duplication (reduced redundancy). In a file system the same customer's address may be stored in the sales file, the accounts file and the dispatch file, and all three copies must be updated together — if one is missed the data becomes inconsistent. In a database the address is stored once and every application reads that one value, so inconsistency cannot arise.
  • Data independence and sharing. The description of the data is stored separately from the applications, so the structure can change (a new column, a longer field) without rewriting every program. Data is also shared by all authorised users at the same time under the DBMS's concurrency and security control, which separate files cannot do safely.

Other gains follow from the same idea: better security, integrated access, backup and recovery, and far less wasted storage space.

short.q: What are Domains and Tuples? What are the characteristics of a good data model?
short.a:
Domain — the complete set of permitted values that an attribute may take. It acts like a data type with rules attached: the domain of age might be whole numbers from 0 to 120, and the domain of standing might be the fixed list {'First', 'Second', 'Third', 'Fourth'}. A value outside its domain is rejected.

Tuple — one row of a relation. A tuple is a single, complete record: it holds exactly one value for every attribute of the table. For the relation Student(snum, sname, major, standing, age), the row (1, 'Ram', 'CS', 'First', 18) is one tuple.

Characteristics of a good data model:

  • it describes the real world closely enough for users to understand it;
  • it is simple and easy to change as requirements change;
  • it keeps the data structure independent of the applications that use it;
  • it supports the constraints the data must obey (domains, keys, relationships);
  • it avoids redundancy and the inconsistency that comes with it;
  • it can be implemented efficiently on the available DBMS.

short.q: What is an E-R diagram? Explain the advantages of the E-R diagram in system design.
short.a:
An E-R (Entity-Relationship) diagram is a graphical model of a database: it shows the entities (things about which data is kept), their attributes, and the relationships that connect them. The usual notation is a rectangle for an entity, an oval for an attribute, a diamond for a relationship, and lines linking them, with 1 and N marking one-to-one, one-to-many or many-to-many.

Advantages in system design:

  • it gives designers and users one simple picture to agree on before any table is built;
  • it is independent of any particular DBMS, so the model survives a change of technology;
  • it maps directly onto relational tables, making the conversion mechanical;
  • it exposes redundancy, missing entities and wrong relationship types early, when they are still cheap to fix;
  • it documents the system for everyone who maintains it later.

short.q: What is normalization? Explain 1NF, 2NF and 3NF.
short.a:
Normalization is the process of organising the columns and tables of a relational database to remove redundancy and the update anomalies it causes. It works by decomposing large, badly designed relations into smaller, well-structured ones that are joined back together by keys.

1NF (First Normal Form) — the table has no repeating groups and every cell holds a single atomic value; each row is identified by a primary key.

2NF (Second Normal Form) — the table is in 1NF and every non-key column depends on the whole primary key, not just part of it. This removes partial dependency, which only matters when the key is composite.

3NF (Third Normal Form) — the table is in 2NF and no non-key column depends on another non-key column. This removes transitive dependency. For example, storing student → department → head_of_department in one table is not in 3NF, because head_of_department depends on department, not on the student; the department belongs in its own table.

short.q: Explain the benefits of a Centralized Database.
short.a:
A centralized database is one in which all the data is stored and managed at a single site, and every user reaches it from that one place.

Its benefits are:

  • Consistency — there is only one copy, so every user always sees the same, current data and no conflicting versions can appear.
  • Simple control — security, backup, recovery and concurrency are all handled in one place instead of being duplicated across sites.
  • Lower cost — one set of hardware, one licence and one administrator rather than many.
  • Easier integrity — constraints and validation rules are enforced once, uniformly.
  • Straightforward querying — a query never has to be split across sites and reassembled.

The trade-off is that a single site becomes a single point of failure, and remote users suffer delay and are cut off entirely if the link goes down.

short.q: What is data security? How it can be implemented?
short.a:
Data security is the protection of data against accidental or deliberate loss, corruption, theft and unauthorised access, while still making it available to everyone who is entitled to use it.

It can be implemented by:

  • Authentication — user names and strong passwords, and increasingly two-factor authentication, so only real users get in.
  • Authorization — the DBA grants each user only the privileges the job needs (SELECT, INSERT, UPDATE, DELETE) on only the tables it needs.
  • Views — giving a user a view that exposes only the permitted columns and rows, hiding everything else.
  • Encryption — encrypting stored data and data on the network so it is unreadable if intercepted.
  • Backup and recovery — regular backups kept off-site, plus transaction logs so the database can be rolled back or rolled forward after a failure.
  • Auditing — keeping a log of who read or changed what, so misuse can be traced.
  • Physical controls — locking the server room, firewalls, and restricting removable media.

short.q: State and describe different types of data integrity.
short.a:
Data integrity means the data in the database is accurate, consistent and trustworthy. A DBMS enforces it with constraints, so bad data is rejected at entry instead of being discovered months later. The main types are:
  • Entity integrity — every table has a primary key, and the primary key is never NULL and never duplicated, so every row is uniquely identifiable.
  • Domain integrity — every value must come from the permitted set for its column: the right data type, the right length, and any CHECK or NOT NULL rule (age between 0 and 120, standing from a fixed list).
  • Referential integrity — a foreign key must either match an existing primary key value in the parent table or be NULL. You cannot record a marks row for a snum that does not exist in Student.
  • User-defined integrity — the business rules that no general constraint covers, e.g. a student may enrol in at most six courses.

short.q: What is a database? List out the advantages of a Database Management System.
short.a:
A database is a shared collection of logically related data, organised so that it can be stored once, retrieved quickly and updated safely.

The advantages of using a DBMS to manage it are:

  • Reduced redundancy — data is stored once instead of being duplicated in every application's file.
  • Consistency — with one copy there is one value, so the database cannot contradict itself.
  • Data sharing — many users and applications work on the same data at the same time.
  • Data independence — the structure can change without rewriting every application.
  • Security — the DBA controls who may see or change what.
  • Integrity — the DBMS enforces the rules automatically.
  • Backup and recovery — the DBMS restores the data after a crash.
  • Concurrency control — simultaneous updates are serialised so they cannot corrupt each other.
  • Easy access — a non-procedural language (SQL) lets users state what they want, not how to get it.

short.q: What is RDBMS? List out the function of RDBMS.
short.a:
An RDBMS (Relational Database Management System) is a DBMS built on the relational model: data is held in tables (relations) of rows (tuples) and columns (attributes), and tables are linked to each other by keys.

Its functions include:

  • creating, altering and dropping tables and other database objects (DDL);
  • inserting, updating, deleting and retrieving rows (DML);
  • supporting a full query language — SQL — for ad-hoc questioning of the data;
  • enforcing integrity: primary keys, foreign keys, domains and NOT NULL;
  • controlling concurrent access so simultaneous transactions do not interfere;
  • providing security: accounts, privileges and views;
  • backup, logging and recovery after failure;
  • maintaining indexes so retrieval stays fast as the tables grow;
  • joining related tables together so the answer to a question can be assembled from several tables.

short.q: Define the terms “DDL” and “DML”.
short.a:
DDL — Data Definition Language. The part of SQL that defines and changes the structure of the database rather than its contents. Its statements are CREATE, ALTER, DROP and TRUNCATE, e.g. CREATE TABLE Student (...);

DML — Data Manipulation Language. The part of SQL that works on the data inside the tables. Its statements are SELECT, INSERT, UPDATE and DELETE, e.g. SELECT sname FROM Student WHERE major = 'CS';

The practical difference: DDL changes the container, DML changes what is in it. DDL statements normally take effect immediately and cannot be rolled back, whereas DML changes can be committed or rolled back as a transaction.

short.q: Define the terms “SQL” and “Data security”.
short.a:
SQL — Structured Query Language. The standard language used to communicate with a relational database. It is non-procedural: you describe the data you want and the DBMS works out how to fetch it. SQL covers data definition (CREATE, ALTER, DROP), data manipulation (SELECT, INSERT, UPDATE, DELETE), transaction control (COMMIT, ROLLBACK) and data control (GRANT, REVOKE).

Data security — the protection of database contents from loss, corruption and unauthorised access or disclosure, achieved through user accounts and passwords, privileges and views, encryption, auditing, and regular backup with recovery procedures.

long.q: Define database and DBMS. Explain the advantages of a database system over a flat-file system.
long.a:
Database. An organised collection of interrelated data stored once and shared by many users and applications, arranged so that it can be accessed, managed and updated easily.

DBMS. The collection of programs that lets users create and maintain that database: it defines the structure, stores and retrieves the data, enforces the rules, controls who may see what, and recovers the data after a failure. MySQL, Oracle, PostgreSQL and SQL Server are all DBMSs.

Advantages of a database system over a flat-file system

Problem with flat filesWhat the database does instead
Duplication. The same fact is copied into several departments' files, wasting space.Data is stored once and shared, so redundancy is minimised.
Inconsistency. Because there are several copies, an update made in one file and missed in another leaves contradictory values.One copy means one value; updates are applied once and every reader sees the change.
No data sharing. Each application owns its own private file and other applications cannot easily use it.All authorised applications share the same integrated data.
Data dependence. The file's layout is built into the program, so changing the layout means rewriting every program that reads it.Data independence — the description of the data is separate from the programs, so the structure can change without touching them.
Poor security. Files are protected only by the operating system's file permissions, which is all-or-nothing.The DBA grants precise privileges on precise tables, and views can hide columns entirely.
No concurrency control. Two users updating the same file at once overwrite each other.Transactions are serialised and locked, so simultaneous updates cannot corrupt the data.
Lengthy development. Every new program has to re-implement storage, searching and sorting.The DBMS provides indexing, querying and integrity once, for all programs.
No recovery or integrity. A crash loses the data, and nothing checks that the values make sense.Backup, logs and rollback restore the data; constraints enforce the rules on every write.

The one honest disadvantage is cost and complexity: a DBMS needs bought software, capable hardware and a trained administrator, so it is overkill for a single small, unchanging file.

long.q: Explain different models used in the database.
long.a:
A database model is the logical structure that decides how data is organised, stored and related. The models used in database systems are:

1. Hierarchical model. Data is arranged as a tree of parent and child records; every child has exactly one parent. Fast for one-to-many data such as an organisation chart, but rigid: a many-to-many link cannot be represented directly, and reaching a child means walking down from the root.

2. Network model. An extension of the hierarchical model in which a child may have several parents, so records form a graph of sets rather than a tree. It handles many-to-many relationships, but the structure is complex to design and a change to it usually breaks the programs that navigate it.

3. Relational model. Data is held in simple two-dimensional tables of rows and columns, and tables are linked by primary and foreign keys. It is the dominant model: easy to understand, backed by SQL, and it gives true data independence. MySQL, Oracle and PostgreSQL are relational systems.

4. Object-oriented model. Data is stored as objects exactly as it appears in an object-oriented program, with attributes, methods, classes and inheritance. It suits multimedia, CAD and engineering data, but it never displaced the relational model in general business use.

5. Object-relational model. A relational database extended with object features — user-defined types, arrays and methods — giving some of the object model's power while keeping SQL.

6. Entity-Relationship model. Strictly a design tool rather than a storage model: entities, attributes and relationships are drawn as an E-R diagram, which is then converted into relational tables.

long.q: Explain the database model with suitable examples.
long.a:
A database model is the logical framework that determines how data is stored, organised and manipulated — the shape the data takes before anything is written to disk.

Hierarchical model — example. A university stores University → Faculty → Department → Student. Each student hangs off exactly one department, and each department off one faculty. The tree is quick to traverse downwards but cannot express a student enrolled in two faculties without duplicating the student record.

Network model — example. The same university, but now a Student record may be linked to several Course records and each Course to many Student records. The many-to-many enrolment is represented directly by set links, at the cost of a much harder structure to design and maintain.

Relational model — example. The data is broken into flat tables: Student(snum, sname, major), Course(cid, cname) and Enrol(snum, cid). The many-to-many enrolment is now just rows in Enrol, and any question is answered by joining the tables in SQL — no navigation is required.

Object-oriented model — example. A Student object carries its own attributes and its own methods (enrol(), gpa()) and inherits from Person. Objects are stored whole, which suits engineering and multimedia data that does not fit neatly into rows and columns.

The relational model won because it is simple enough for non-specialists to understand, flexible enough to answer questions nobody anticipated, and independent of the application programs that use it.

long.q: What is a hierarchical database model? List out the advantages and disadvantages of the hierarchical database model.
long.a:
The hierarchical database model organises data as an inverted tree. The single record type at the top is the root; every other record type is a child with exactly one parent, so relationships are strictly one-to-many and the structure looks like an organisation chart or a family tree. Records are reached by navigating down from the root, parent by parent.

Advantages

  • Simplicity. The tree is easy to picture and to explain to users.
  • Speed. Because the links are pre-defined pointers, traversing a known path is very fast — no searching or joining is needed.
  • Data integrity of the structure. A child cannot exist without its parent, so orphans are impossible by construction.
  • Suits one-to-many data. Organisation charts, bills of materials and file-directory trees map onto it naturally.

Disadvantages

  • Cannot express many-to-many. A student in several courses has to be duplicated, which reintroduces the redundancy the database was meant to remove.
  • Rigid. Adding a new relationship usually means restructuring the whole tree and rewriting every program that navigates it.
  • No data independence. Programs contain the navigation path, so a change of structure breaks them.
  • Difficult access to children. A record can only be reached through its ancestors, so querying across branches is awkward.
  • Anomalies. Inserting, updating and deleting a child is constrained by the parent, producing the classic insert/update/delete anomalies.

long.q: What is the purpose of the E-R diagram? List out the different symbols used in the E-R diagram with their meanings and examples.
long.a:
An E-R diagram is drawn during database design to show, in one picture, what the system must remember: the entities, their attributes and the relationships between them. Its purpose is to produce an agreed, technology-free model of the data before any table is created, and to expose missing entities, wrong relationships and redundancy while they are still cheap to fix. Once approved, the diagram converts mechanically into relational tables.
SymbolMeaningExample

Double ovalA multi-valued attribute (one that can hold several values)phone_number for a student with two numbers
Dashed ovalA derived attribute, calculated from othersage derived from date_of_birth
