long.q: Why is normalization needed? Explain the normalization process with examples.
long.a:
Why normalization is needed. A badly designed table stores the same fact many times over, and that redundancy produces three anomalies. An insert anomaly — you cannot add a new department until a student joins it, because the department only exists as a column of the student row. An update anomaly — changing the head of a department means changing it in every student row of that department, and missing one leaves contradictory values. A delete anomaly — deleting the last student of a department also deletes the only record that the department existed at all. Normalization removes these by splitting the data into well-formed tables joined by keys.

The process, with an example

Start with the un-normalized Student_Info table, where snum + cid is the key:

Student_Info(snum, sname, dept, head, cid, cname, grade)

First Normal Form (1NF) — remove repeating groups so every cell holds one atomic value. A row such as snum=1, courses='{CS101, CS102}' is not 1NF; it must be split into two rows, one per course. After 1NF the table has a key and no repeating group.

Second Normal Form (2NF) — remove partial dependency: every non-key column must depend on the whole key, not part of it. In Student_Info, sname and dept depend only on snum, and cname only on cid — both are partial. Split them out:

Student(snum, sname, dept, head)
Course(cid, cname)
Enrol(snum, cid, grade)

Third Normal Form (3NF) — remove transitive dependency: no non-key column may depend on another non-key column. In Student, head depends on dept, not on snum, so it is transitive. Move it out:

Student(snum, sname, dept)
Department(dept, head)

Now each fact is stored exactly once. Adding a department, changing its head, or removing its last student are all independent operations, and the three anomalies are gone. The cost of normalization is that answering a question now needs joins, which is why heavily normalised designs are sometimes deliberately de-normalised for reporting speed.

long.q: Define the term RDBMS. Explain the centralized and decentralized database models.
long.a:
An RDBMS (Relational Database Management System) is a database management system based on the relational model. Data is held in two-dimensional tables: each table (relation) has named columns (attributes) and holds rows (tuples); each column draws its values from a domain; rows are identified by a primary key; and tables are linked to one another by foreign keys. Because the tables are independent of any access path, any question can be answered by joining tables in SQL rather than by navigating a fixed structure. MySQL, Oracle, PostgreSQL and SQL Server are RDBMSs.

Centralized database model

All the data lives at one site, on one machine, and every user reaches it from there. The single copy gives strong consistency, simple security and backup, low cost and easy administration. The drawbacks are that the site is a single point of failure, remote users suffer network delay, and the whole system stops if the link or the machine does.

Decentralized (distributed) database model

The data is split across several independent sites, each with its own local database and its own DBMS, linked by a network. Each site runs autonomously and can keep working when the others are unavailable; users get fast local access to the data they use most, and the system grows by adding sites. The price is complexity: keeping the copies consistent, managing distributed transactions and recovery, and reconciling updates made at different sites are all hard problems, and the software and network cost more.

In practice the choice is a trade-off — centralized for control and simplicity, distributed for availability, local speed and growth.

long.q: What are the advantages of distributed database system over a centralized database system?
long.a:
A distributed database spreads data over several networked sites that cooperate so that users see one logical database. Compared with a centralized database it offers:
  • Availability and reliability. If one site or link fails the others keep running, so there is no single point of failure — the whole system does not stop with one machine.
  • Faster local access. Data can be stored near the users who use it most, so most queries are answered locally instead of crossing a slow wide-area link.
  • Modular growth. Capacity is increased by adding another site, which is cheaper and less disruptive than replacing one ever-larger central machine.
  • Lower communication cost for local work. Only genuinely shared data has to travel across the network.
  • Better match to the organisation. A company with branches in several cities naturally keeps each branch's data at that branch, while still reporting across all of them.
  • Sharing with autonomy. Each site controls its own local data yet can still take part in global queries.

The trade-offs are honesty worth stating: keeping replicas consistent and managing distributed transactions and recovery are much harder, security has to be enforced at every site, and the software, network and administration all cost more.

long.q: Who is a database administrator? What are the major responsibilities of a Database Administrator?
long.a:
A database administrator (DBA) is the person responsible for the database as a whole — not for one application, but for the data asset itself. The DBA decides how the data is structured, who may use it, and how it is kept safe and recoverable.

Major responsibilities:

  • Defining the schema. Deciding the logical and physical design — tables, columns, data types, keys, indexes and constraints — in consultation with users.
  • Defining security and integrity. Creating accounts, granting and revoking privileges, defining views, and setting the constraints the data must obey.
  • Backup and recovery. Scheduling regular backups, keeping them off-site, and rehearsing recovery so the database can be restored after hardware failure, corruption or human error.
  • Tuning performance. Monitoring response times, adding or dropping indexes, reorganising storage and rewriting expensive queries.
  • Controlling concurrency. Making sure simultaneous transactions do not corrupt each other.
  • Capacity planning. Watching growth in data and users and adding storage before it runs out.
  • Maintaining documentation. Keeping the data dictionary and the design current so others can work on the system.
  • Liaising with users. Training them, answering their questions, and handling changes to requirements.

long.q: What do you understand by the term data integrity? Why is it an important thing to be considered while designing a database?
long.a:
Data integrity is the guarantee that the data in the database is correct, complete and consistent — that the values are the right values and that they do not contradict one another. A DBMS enforces it through rules applied automatically to every write: entity integrity (a unique, non-NULL primary key for every row), domain integrity (values must come from the permitted type, length and range), referential integrity (a foreign key must match an existing primary key or be NULL) and user-defined integrity (the organisation's own business rules).

Why it matters when designing a database:

  • Bad data is worse than no data. Decisions are made from the database — salaries, marks, stock levels, medical doses. A wrong value is acted upon.
  • It must be designed in, not cleaned up later. Once inconsistent data has accumulated, finding and correcting it is far more expensive than rejecting it at entry.
  • It prevents redundancy-driven inconsistency. Constraints and keys are what make it safe to store each fact once; without them the copies drift apart.
  • It protects relationships. Referential integrity stops a marks row being written for a student who does not exist, or a department being deleted while students still belong to it.
  • It enforces the rules uniformly. A constraint in the database applies to every user and every program, including new ones written years later, whereas a check in one application only applies to that application.
  • It supports audit and trust. Users only trust a system whose numbers they know are right.

long.q: What is the Relational database model? List the advantages and disadvantages of the Relational database model.
long.a:
The relational database model, proposed by E. F. Codd, stores data in two-dimensional tables called relations. Each relation has named columns (attributes), each column takes values from a domain, and each row (tuple) is one record identified by a primary key. Tables are linked by foreign keys, and any data needed is produced by joining tables with SQL.

Advantages

  • Simplicity. A table is familiar to everyone; no pointers or navigation paths to learn.
  • Data independence. The physical storage can change without affecting the logical view or the applications.
  • Flexibility. New questions can be answered by new queries and new joins, without redesigning the database.
  • Reduced redundancy with consistency. Normalization, keys and constraints keep each fact stored once.
  • Powerful querying. SQL is non-procedural — the user states what is wanted, not how to get it.
  • Integrity and security. Constraints, views and privileges are enforced by the DBMS itself.
  • Maturity. Decades of tooling, standards, trained people and proven recovery mechanisms.

Disadvantages

  • Performance cost. Answering a question often means joining several tables, which is slower than following a pre-built pointer.
  • Hardware and software cost. An RDBMS needs substantial memory, disk and licensing.
  • Poor fit for complex data. Graphs, multimedia, CAD models and nested structures do not sit comfortably in flat rows and columns.
  • Impedance mismatch. Object-oriented programs must map objects to rows, which is why object-relational mappers exist.
  • Design effort. Getting a properly normalised design takes real analysis; a rushed one gives slow queries.

practical.q: Consider the schema Student (snum, sname, major, standing, age). (a) Specify your own required data type and length for the attributes. (b) Specify the primary key. (c) Insert details in the student table. (d) Find the names of the students whose major is Computer Science.
practical.a:
The relation is Student(snum, sname, major, standing, age). A reasonable design, with the data types and lengths chosen to suit each attribute, is:

CREATE TABLE Student (
    snum      INT           NOT NULL,   -- roll number, whole number
    sname     VARCHAR(40)   NOT NULL,   -- name, up to 40 characters
    major     VARCHAR(30)   NOT NULL,   -- subject, up to 30 characters
    standing  VARCHAR(10)   NOT NULL,   -- First / Second / Third / Fourth
    age       INT           NOT NULL,   -- whole number of years
    PRIMARY KEY (snum)
);

(a) Data types and lengths. snum and age are whole numbers, so INT is used. sname, major and standing are text of varying length, so VARCHAR is used with a sensible maximum — 40 for a name, 30 for a subject and 10 for the year of study. All five are declared NOT NULL because a student record is meaningless without any of them.

(b) Primary key. snum is the primary key. It is unique for every student and never NULL, so it identifies exactly one row. age and major obviously cannot be keys, and a name cannot be either, because two students may share one.

(c) Inserting rows.

INSERT INTO Student (snum, sname, major, standing, age) VALUES
    (1, 'Ram Sharma',    'Computer Science', 'First',  18),
    (2, 'Sita Adhikari', 'Physics',          'Second', 19),
    (3, 'Hari Thapa',    'Computer Science', 'Third',  20),
    (4, 'Gita Rai',      'Mathematics',      'First',  18);

(d) Names of the students whose major is Computer Science.

SELECT sname
FROM   Student
WHERE  major = 'Computer Science';

This returns Ram Sharma and Hari Thapa. The WHERE clause keeps only the rows whose major column matches the value, and the SELECT list asks for the sname column only, so the other four columns are not printed.

practical.q: Consider the schema pilots (sid, sname, rating, age). (a) Specify your own required data type and length for the attributes. (b) Specify the primary key. (c) Insert details in the pilots table. (d) Find all pilots who are teens.
practical.a:
The relation is pilots(sid, sname, rating, age). The design, with data types and lengths chosen for each attribute, is:

CREATE TABLE pilots (
    sid     INT          NOT NULL,   -- pilot id, whole number
    sname   VARCHAR(40)  NOT NULL,   -- pilot name, up to 40 characters
    rating  INT          NOT NULL,   -- flying rating, whole number
    age     INT          NOT NULL,   -- whole number of years
    PRIMARY KEY (sid)
);

(a) Data types and lengths. sid, rating and age are all whole numbers, so INT is used for each. sname is text of varying length, so VARCHAR(40) is used. Every column is NOT NULL because a pilot record is incomplete without any of them.

(b) Primary key. sid is the primary key: it is unique per pilot and always present, so it identifies exactly one row. Neither rating nor age can serve, because several pilots share the same value, and sname cannot either, because two pilots may share a name.

(c) Inserting rows.

INSERT INTO pilots (sid, sname, rating, age) VALUES
    (1, 'Bikash Gurung', 7, 34),
    (2, 'Anita Shrestha', 5, 17),
    (3, 'Dinesh Karki',  8, 42),
    (4, 'Nisha Tamang',  4, 16),
    (5, 'Ramesh Bista',  6, 29);

(d) All pilots who are teens. A teenager is anyone aged 13 to 19 inclusive, so the age is tested with BETWEEN:

SELECT sid, sname, rating, age
FROM   pilots
WHERE  age BETWEEN 13 AND 19;

This returns Anita Shrestha (17) and Nisha Tamang (16). BETWEEN 13 AND 19 is inclusive at both ends, so it is equivalent to writing WHERE age >= 13 AND age <= 19 — either form is accepted.

mcq.q: Which of the following principles apply to 2NF?

key_terms.meaning: Raw, un-interpreted, unorganized facts and figures that can be processed into information.
Processed data, arranged in an order that is useful to the person receiving it.
A collection of interrelated data organized so that it can be easily accessed, managed and updated.
Database Management System — a collection of programs that enables users to create and maintain a database.
A collection of interrelated data plus a set of application programs to access, update and manage that data.
The same data duplicated in many places; a DBMS reduces it using primary keys.
The description of data is kept separate from the applications, so changes to the definition do not require changes to every program.
The smallest unit of memory — either 0 or 1.
A collection of 8 bits representing an alphabet, number, sign or symbol (e.g. ASCII 01000001 = 'A').
A single fact or attribute of an entity; a column of a table. Also called a data item or attribute.
A collection of related fields representing one complete unit of information; a row or tuple.
A collection of related records of an entity set.
A structured collection of data organized into rows and columns.
One row of a relation; each tuple holds exactly one value per attribute.
The name of a column in a relation; a property that characterizes an entity.
The set of all permitted values that an attribute may take; can be viewed as a data type.
Indicates that a value is either not available or not applicable. A primary key must not be NULL.
Any field or combination of fields that can uniquely identify a record.
A candidate key that was not chosen as the primary key.
The candidate key chosen to identify each record; unique and never NULL.
An attribute whose value is derived from the primary key of another table; it links the two tables.
A set of one or more attributes that together uniquely identify an entity.
A real-world thing, person or object that is distinguishable from all others (student, book, loan…).
A set of entities of the same type that share the same attributes.
The association between entities — one-to-one, one-to-many, many-to-one or many-to-many.
A graphical representation of entities and their relationships: rectangle = entity, oval = attribute, diamond = relationship, line = link.
The logical structure of the database.
The way a particular application views the data it uses.
A file containing metadata — 'data about data' — consulted before data are read or modified.
Data Definition Language — declarative commands that define database structure: CREATE, ALTER, DROP, RENAME, TRUNCATE.
Data Manipulation Language — imperative commands that work on the data: SELECT, INSERT, UPDATE, DELETE.
Transaction Control Language — manages transactions: COMMIT and ROLLBACK.
The user must specify what data are needed AND how to get them.
The user specifies what data are needed, without specifying how to get them.
A database using a single file for a table; fine for one user, hard to maintain when large.
Relational Database Management System — the database is a set of tables related through common fields.
The process of presenting a database in a normal form to remove repetition, inability to represent information and loss of information.

Ensuring data is kept safe from corruption and that access to it is suitably controlled.

quick_revision.title: Foundations
points: Data = raw facts; Information = processed data.
DBMS = programs to create and maintain a database; it hides the database's internal complexity from applications.
Why a database? File systems duplicate data, cannot share it, secure it poorly and are hard to search.
3 file-processing problems: data duplication, data dependence, lack of data integration.
8 objectives of a DBMS: storage, easy access, prompt response, immediate updates, no redundancy, multi-user, growth, protection.

quick_revision.title: Data hierarchy and keys
points: Bit → character (8 bits) → field → record → file → database.
Table = relation; row = tuple/record; column = field/attribute.
Objects: tables, views, indexes, sequences, stored procedures, triggers, constraints.
Keys: candidate (can identify), alternate (not chosen), primary (chosen, unique, not null), foreign (from another table's PK), super (set that identifies).

quick_revision.title: Pros and cons
points: 10 advantages: sharing, less redundancy, integrity, independence, availability, standards, security, consistency, multiple interfaces, backup & recovery.
8 disadvantages: high initial cost, training, one fault affects all, complex, overhead of security/recovery/integrity, hardware upgrades, bad design problems, migration cost.

quick_revision.title: Languages
points: DDL (declarative): CREATE, DROP, ALTER, TRUNCATE, RENAME — defines structure.
DML (imperative): SELECT, INSERT, UPDATE, DELETE — works on data.
TCL: COMMIT, ROLLBACK — manages transactions.
Data dictionary = metadata, 'data about data'.

quick_revision.title: Database models
points: Good model: simple, accurate, secure, scalable, consistent/flexible/extensible.
Hierarchical: inverted tree, one parent per child, fast if parent known, cannot do many-to-many, deleting a parent deletes the children.
Network: a node may have several parents, many-to-many allowed, fast via pointers, complex and less secure.
Relational: two-dimensional tables, one entity per row and one attribute per column, low redundancy, normalizable, but complex and rule-heavy.

quick_revision.title: E-R modelling
points: Entity = thing/person/object; Attribute = its property; Relationship = association.
4 relationship types: 1–1, 1–many, many–1, many–many.
Symbols: rectangle = entity, oval = attribute, diamond = relationship, line = link.
7 advantages of an E-R diagram: visual, simple, communicative, flexible, supports physical creation, high-level description, can be generalized/specialized.

quick_revision.title: Normalization
points: Purpose: remove repetition, inability to represent information and loss of information.
1NF — atomic attributes, no repeating groups.
2NF — in 1NF and no partial dependency on part of the key.
3NF — in 2NF and no transitive dependency.
For most designs 3NF is far enough; BCNF and 4NF exist for specialized cases.

quick_revision.title: Centralized vs distributed
points: Centralized: one site, cheap, simple, secure — but a server failure stops everything and it does not scale.
Distributed: several sites, reliable, better performance, scales — but complex, costly and a higher theft/hacking risk.
DBA: 6 functions — internal schema, external schema, liaise with users, security & integrity rules, backup & recovery, monitor performance.

quick_revision.title: Integrity and security
points: 3 integrity types: entity (PK not null), referential (FK matches or is null), domain (permitted values).
Loss of data: accidental (crashes, logic errors, distribution) or intentional (unauthorized read, modify, destroy).
5 security levels: physical, human, operating system, network, database system.
Tools: rollback, backup, recovery, cryptography, authentication, firewalls, anti-virus, intrusion detection.

quick_revision.title: SQL at a glance
points: CREATE TABLE with constraints: NOT NULL, UNIQUE, PRIMARY KEY, FOREIGN KEY, CHECK, DEFAULT.
ALTER … ADD / ALTER COLUMN / DROP COLUMN / CHANGE; DROP TABLE; RENAME; TRUNCATE.
DML: INSERT INTO … VALUES; SELECT … FROM … WHERE; DELETE FROM … WHERE; UPDATE … SET … WHERE.
Ordering: ORDER BY … ASC / DESC. Logic: AND, OR, NOT.
Aggregates: avg, min, max, sum, count. Plus DISTINCT, LIKE (% and _), GROUP BY, HAVING, IN, BETWEEN, CASE, LIMIT, ROUND, INNER JOIN, LEFT JOIN.
Lab stack: XAMPP (Apache + MySQL + PHP) → phpMyAdmin at http://localhost/phpmyadmin.

teaching_plan.activity: Open with the question 'what is the difference between 1, Ram, Kathmandu and a student address table?' to introduce data vs information. Draw the DBMS block diagram and drill the 8 objectives.
Build the storage hierarchy from bit up to database on the board. Then two tables side by side to show primary key vs foreign key.
Advantages (10) and disadvantages (8) as a class brainstorm, then a written drill. This is the most repeated exam question.
DDL vs DML with the 5-point comparison table. Give each student three commands and ask which category they belong to.
Draw the hierarchical inverted tree and the network graph side by side. Then the relational tables and the JOIN/PROJECT example.
Entity/attribute/relationship using the school itself as an example. The four relationship diagrams: 1–1, 1–many, many–1, many–many.
E-R diagram symbols on flash cards. Students draw an E-R diagram for their own school library in pairs.
Work the student table through 1NF → 2NF → 3NF on the board, step by step, then repeat with the employee-project table as an exercise.
Centralized vs distributed with the 7-point difference table. Discuss which one the school's own system is and why. Cover the 6 DBA functions and the 3 integrity types.
Data security: the 5 security levels as a layered diagram, plus accidental vs intentional loss. Discuss real breaches the students have heard of.
Computer lab: install XAMPP, start Apache + MySQL, open phpMyAdmin, create a 'school' database and a 'student' table through the GUI.
In the phpMyAdmin SQL tab, type every DDL and DML command from the chapter live: CREATE/ALTER/DROP the student table, INSERT rows, SELECT with WHERE, then the aggregate functions.
DISTINCT, LIKE wildcards, GROUP BY + HAVING, IN, BETWEEN, CASE, LIMIT, ROUND, and INNER vs LEFT JOIN on two real tables. Finish with COMMIT and ROLLBACK.
Work through the 14 short and 11 long questions orally, run the 38 MCQs as a timed quiz, then review with the answer key.

blocks.text: The term communication refers to the sending, receiving and processing of information by electronic media. It started with wire telegraphy in the eighteen forties (1840s), developing with telephony some decades later and radio at the beginning of the last century. Radio communication was made possible by the invention of the triode tube (one kind of vacuum tube) and was greatly stimulated by the work done during World War II. It became even more widely used and refined through the invention of the transistor, integrated circuits and other semiconductor devices. More recently, the use of satellites and fibre optics has made communications even more widespread, with an increasing emphasis on computer and other data communications.

A modern communication system is first concerned with the processing and storing of information before its transmission. The forms of communication include radio telephony and telegraphy, broadcasting, point-to-point and mobile communications, computer communications, and radio aids to navigation.

blocks.title: The big shift — teaching point
blocks.text: The old model was ONE big computer serving the whole organisation. That model has been replaced by a large number of separate but INTERCONNECTED computers doing the job together. This system is called a computer network.

Two or more computing devices linked together to communicate, sharing information (files and software programs) and other hardware resources (printers, hard disks, plotters). The concept of connected computers sharing resources is called networking.

Most networks are constructed around a cable connection that links the computers. This connection permits the computers to share (talk and listen) through a wire. More recently, several wireless solutions have become available: infrared ports, Bluetooth, radio links, Wi-Fi, satellite and other protocols allow a variety of new devices to link with PCs.
Advantages of using a computer network

items: Resource sharing: sharing a resource is an important area in which a network exceeds the stand-alone computer. Most institutions cannot afford enough laser printers, fax machines, MODEMs, scanners and CD-ROM players for each computer; if these peripherals are added to a network they can be shared by all users in a node (a computer in a network is known as a node).

Centralized control and management: the entire computers in the network are normally connected to a server, which defines the policy and security measures for the resources used by the network members.
Speedy and cost-effective communication: since the computers are connected, a message can be sent from one computer to another within a few seconds.

Backup and recovery: data are securely handled by the server, which provides the mechanism for backup on other devices. The network is also used to recover data and system in case of a system crash, using the backup or through the server.
Flexible access: the network allows people to easily access their files from any computer throughout the network.

Workgroup computing: workgroup software (such as Microsoft Office) allows many users to work on a document or project concurrently — for example, experts located at various schools could simultaneously contribute their ideas about new curriculum standards to the same document.

blocks.text: Disadvantages of using a computer network

items: Expensive: connecting computers needs extra devices and resources like NIC, hub and cables, which increases the cost of operation.

Security problem: data are shared in a public medium so extra precaution is needed for secure transmission and storage. Because computers are connected, computer crimes increase — sending viruses, software piracy, hacking, plagiarism, pornography, spoofing.
Needs special technical knowledge: skilled manpower is required to establish, maintain and operate a networking system.
Network failure: failure of the network may hamper the day-to-day operation of the organization (for example, network failure in a bank affects transactions).
Complex: the network itself is difficult to establish, manage and operate.

blocks.text: Exam hook: 'Advantages and disadvantages of networking' is Long Answer Question 1 of Exercise 2. Teach it as 6 + 5 points with one-line explanations each.
A communication system is a system which describes the information exchange between two points. The process of transmission and reception of information is called communication.
The three basic elements

items: Transmitter of information: the transmitter's function is to process the message signal into a form suitable for transmission over the communication channel. It is the sender which sends data to the receiver.
Channel or medium of communication: its function is to provide a pathway between the transmitter's output and the receiver's input. It transmits data from the sender to the receiver.
Receiver of information: the job of the receiver is to process the received signal to recover the appropriate message signal. It receives data sent by the sender.

sections.title: Block Diagram of Communication System / Model

blocks.caption: Block diagram of a communication system — information source → transmitter → channel → receiver → user of information, with noise entering the channel.

blocks.text: The chain runs: Information Source → Input Signal → Transmitter → Transmitted Signal → Channel → Received Signal → Receiver → Message Signal → User of Information. Noise is added to the signal while it travels along the channel.

Draw this on the board left-to-right and point out that every block has an input name and an output name (e.g. transmitter: input signal in, transmitted signal out). Students lose marks by labelling the arrows instead of the blocks.

items: Information or input signal: communication systems have been developed for communicating useful information from one place to another. The information can be in the form of sound signals like speech or music, or it can be in the form of pictures.

Input transducer: information in the form of sound, picture or data signals cannot be transmitted as it is — first it has to be converted into a suitable electrical signal. Commonly used input transducers are microphones, TV cameras, etc.

Transmitter: the function of the transmitter block is to convert the electrical equivalent of the information into a suitable form. It increases the power level of the signal so that a large range is covered. It consists of electronic circuits such as amplifier, mixer, oscillator and power amplifier.
Communication channel or medium: the medium used for the transmission of electronic signals from one place to another. It can be conducting wires, cables, optical fibres or free space.

Noise: an unwanted electrical signal which gets added to the transmitted signal when it is travelling towards the receiver. Due to noise the quality of the transmitted information degrades. Once added, the noise cannot be separated from the information — hence noise is a big problem in communication systems.

Receiver: reception is exactly the opposite process of transmission. The received signal is amplified and demodulated and converted into a suitable form. The receiver consists of electronic circuits like a mixer, oscillator, detector and amplifier.
Output transducer: it converts the electrical signal at the output of the receiver back to the original form, i.e. sound or TV pictures. Typical examples are loudspeakers and picture tubes.

blocks.title: Remember
blocks.text: Input transducer = real-world signal → electrical signal (microphone). Output transducer = electrical signal → real-world signal (loudspeaker). They are mirror images of each other.
Communication mode defines the direction of data flow in the communication.
There are three types of communication mode: simplex, half-duplex and duplex (full-duplex).

blocks.caption: Simplex, half-duplex and full-duplex communication.

items: Simplex: transmission is possible in only one direction, similar to a one-way street. A simplex line can either only receive or only send data. The full capacity of the channel is used for one-way communication. Examples: communication between keyboard and CPU, remote and television, loudspeaker, fire alarm system.

Half-duplex: transmission is possible in both directions but not simultaneously (one direction at a time). A half-duplex line can both send and receive data, but one at a time — like a narrow street where traffic is allowed in both directions but only one lane at a time. It also uses the full capacity of the channel for one-way communication. Examples: walkie-talkie, wireless microphone, CC camera.

Duplex (full-duplex): transmission is possible in both directions simultaneously, similar to a two-way street. A duplex line allows the sending and receiving of data at the same time. The capacity of the channel is divided into two halves for two-way communication. Example: mobile / telephone communication.

blocks.caption: Comparing the three communication modes
head: Mode
Direction
Channel capacity
Example
rows: Full capacity, one way at a time

Based on geographical-area coverage (geographical spread), a computer network is classified into three basic types: Local Area Network (LAN), Metropolitan Area Network (MAN) and Wide Area Network (WAN).
Local Area Network (LAN)
The interconnection of computers in a limited geographical area — a single room, rooms within a building, or buildings on one site. It is smaller, simpler and cheaper than other networks.

In a typical LAN there is a server which consists of additional software and hardware. A LAN is useful for sharing resources like files, software programs, printers, plotters, disk drives, games or other application services. A LAN can operate at a speed of about 100 Mbps. Most LANs are built with relatively cheap hardware such as Ethernet cables, network adapters and hubs; wireless LAN and other advanced LAN hardware are also used at present. A network operating system is required — for example, Microsoft Windows provides a software package called Internet Connection Sharing (ICS) that supports controlled access to LAN resources.

blocks.caption: A typical Local Area Network — computers, printer and server sharing a connecting bus.

blocks.text: Metropolitan Area Network (MAN)

A network extended up to a city or a larger geographical area than the LAN. A MAN can connect several LANs. It is used to connect multiple systems or networks within a single city and can use either wired or wireless transmission media.
A MAN mostly uses bridges, repeaters, routers and switches. A cable TV network is an example of a MAN.

Disadvantages

Public libraries and government agencies typically use a MAN
More expensive to run than LAN

blocks.text: Wide Area Network (WAN)

A network used to interconnect computers spread over a larger geographical area such as separate cities or countries. It is also known as a Long Haul Network (LHN). It often connects multiple smaller networks such as LANs or MANs.

Communication is usually done through satellite, microwave systems or optical fibres. It uses devices like routers, gateways and switches, which are much more expensive than those used in a LAN. WAN provides most of the facilities found in LAN and MAN, but transmission speed is usually slower and maintaining security is comparatively complex. Key technologies often found in WANs include SONET, Frame Relay and ATM.

The wires, cables and other means through which data travels from its source to its destination. Transmission media are often called communication media.

The basic requirements for the working of a communication system are: a sender (source), which creates the message to be transmitted; a medium, which carries the message from sender to receiver; and a receiver (sink), which receives the message.
Types of transmission media
Transmission media are categorized as guided media (bounded or wired media) and unguided media (unbounded or wireless media).

items: Guided (bounded / wired) media contains wires or cables: (i) twisted pair cable, (ii) coaxial cable, (iii) fibre optic cable.
Unguided (unbounded / wireless) media includes: (i) microwave system, (ii) satellite communication, (iii) infrared technology.

blocks.text: Twisted pair cable

Twisted pair is the oldest and still the most common transmission medium. It contains a pair of cables twisted with each other. The tighter the twisting, the greater the transmission rate and the fewer the chances of error. Its most common applications are the telephone system and LAN. Nearly all telephones are connected to the telephone office by twisted pair cable. Twisted pair can only run a few metres without amplification; for longer distances repeaters are needed. It is cheaper, lighter, thinner, more flexible and easier to install than coax or fibre-optic cable, so it is ideal for offices and small networks.

There are categories of twisted pair specified by EIA/TIA: Category 1 — voice only, data rate less than 100 Kbps; Category 2 — data up to 2 Mbps; Category 3 — data up to 10 Mbps; Category 4 — data up to 20 Mbps; Category 5 — data up to 100 Mbps; Category 6 — data up to 200 Mbps.

The twisted pair cable is connected with the help of an RJ-45 connector (for LAN) or RJ-11 (for telephone). RJ stands for Registered Jack. Twisted pair cable is of two types: UTP (Unshielded Twisted Pair) and STP (Shielded Twisted Pair).

blocks.text: Coaxial cable (COAX)

Coaxial cable carries data signals of higher frequency and at a faster speed than twisted pair cable. Its common use is for transmission of signals in cable television systems and broadband transmission. Broadband and cable TV take advantage of coax's ability to transmit many signals at the same time; each signal is called a channel and each channel travels at a different frequency, so it does not interfere with the other channels. Coax has a large bandwidth, so it can handle plenty of traffic at high speeds, and it can carry signals over a significant distance. However, it is difficult to install and bend compared to twisted pair.

A coaxial cable has a single copper conductor at its centre. A plastic layer provides insulation between the centre conductor and a braided metal shield, and the whole thing is surrounded by an external insulation layer. The metal shield blocks outside interference from fluorescent lights and other computers. The BNC (Bayonet-Neill-Concelman) connector is required for connecting this cable. Coaxial cable is of two types: thin coax (thinnet) — 10base2, i.e. 10 Mbps up to 200 metres; and thick coax (thicknet) — 10base5, i.e. 10 Mbps up to 500 metres.

blocks.caption: Coaxial cable — copper conductor, plastic layer, braided metal shield and external plastic layer.
Coaxial cable — advantages and disadvantages
head: Advantages
Disadvantages
rows: Provides faster data transmission than twisted pair cable
Can transmit data over medium-range distances
Not appropriate for long distance transmission
Easier to install, modify and manage the network
Rarely used at present for a computer network

blocks.text: Fibre optic cable (optical fibre cable)

A fibre-optic cable is made of glass or plastic and transmits signals in the form of light. It contains single or multiple hair-like thin filaments of glass fibres wrapped by a protective jacket. These glass filaments can transmit data in the form of light at a transmission speed of around 2 billion bits per second — about 10 times faster than coaxial cable and 200 times faster than twisted pair cable. Fibre-optic can carry voice, video and data. It has enormous bandwidth and can carry signals for extremely long distances. Because it uses light pulses, it is immune to electromagnetic interference and is extremely fast and more secure than other cables. Despite its many advantages, fibre optics implementation in a LAN is difficult to install and costlier.

Optical fibre cabling consists of a glass core at the centre surrounded by several layers of protective material; the fibre itself is a core fibre surrounded by cladding, with a protective covering around both. LEDs (light emitting diodes) send the signals down the cable, and a detector receives the signals and converts them back into electrical impulses that computers can understand and use. It is used for services like telecommunication, video conferencing and interactive services, and is connected with the help of an S-T connector.

blocks.caption: Optical fibre cable
Fibre optic cable — advantages and disadvantages
head: Advantages
Disadvantages
rows: Fastest data transmission of all transmission media
Highly expensive and difficult to install
Can be used for both short and long distance transmission
Not appropriate for short distances because of its thickness and difficulty in bending
Skilled technical manpower is required and is rare
Can transmit multiple data at the same time using multiple fibres in a cable
Not preferred in hillside areas with up-and-down field connections between stations

blocks.text: Microwave system

A microwave system uses very high-frequency radio signals to transmit data through the air. The transmitter and receiver of a microwave system should be in the line of sight because the radio signal cannot bend. For this reason, transmitting and receiving antennas must be placed on tall buildings or towers, hills and mountain peaks. Long-distance transmission is not possible with a microwave. To overcome the problem of line of sight and shorter distance, repeaters are used at intervals of 25 to 30 kilometres; when one repeating tower receives the signal it amplifies it and sends it to the next tower. The frequency at which microwave radio signals are transmitted is commonly called radio frequency (RF). Radio frequencies used for commercial microwave transmission are 2, 4, 6, 11, 18 and 23 GHz.

blocks.caption: Microwave system — transmitting and receiving antennas in line of sight.

blocks.text: Satellite communication

Satellite communication is the most common worldwide communication system at present. It uses a satellite as a repeater — the satellite is a repeater that orbits in space. Satellite communication systems have receivers and transmitters located in ground stations. In this communication, the microwave signal is transmitted from a transmitter on earth to the satellite in space; the satellite amplifies the weak signal and transmits it back to the receiver. To make communication possible over even longer distances, multiple satellites are used.

blocks.caption: Satellite communication — uplink, geostationary orbit and downlink between ground stations.

blocks.text: IR (Infrared)

Infrared signals can be used for short-range communication in a closed area using line-of-sight communication. Because infrared signals have a high frequency they cannot penetrate walls, which prevents interference from one system to another. It is mainly used in wireless remote control, wireless LAN (WLAN), wireless mouse and keyboard. It cannot be used outside the building because sun rays contain infrared waves that can interfere with the communication.

blocks.title: Exam-ready summary
blocks.text: Guided = twisted pair, coaxial, fibre optic. Unguided = microwave, satellite, infrared. Speed order (textbook): fibre (≈2 Gbps) > coaxial > twisted pair.
Long Answer Question 5 asks for short notes on UTP, STP and fibre optical cable. Short Answer Questions 6 and 7 cover transmission media types and any two media with diagrams.

In a data communication system, analog and digital signals go through the transmission media. Transmission media are not ideal — there are imperfections, so the signals transmitted at the beginning of the medium are not the same as the signals received at the end of the medium: what is sent is not what is received. This imperfection causes signal impairment and tends to deteriorate the quality of the signals.

items: Jitter: small irregular delays during data transfers, i.e. the delay between when a signal is transmitted and when it is received. It can be produced by several factors including network congestion, collisions and signal interference.

Attenuation: the loss or reduction in the strength of a transmission signal in networking cables or connections. An amplifier is used to increase the signal strength, which gives the original signal back and compensates for this loss. It is measured in decibels (dB).
Distortion: the change in the form or shape of the original signal or waveform. This is generally seen in frequencies.

Noise: the random or unwanted signal that mixes up with the original signal. Several types of noise — industrial noise, induced noise, crosstalk noise, thermal noise and impulse noise — may corrupt the signal.
Echo: a reflection of sound that arrives at the listener with a delay after the direct sound. It is also one type of noise signal, which reflects back the transmitted signal.

Singing: singing may be regarded as echo that is completely out of control. It occurs at the frequency at which the circuit is resonant; under such conditions the circuit losses at the singing frequency are so low that oscillation continues even after the ending of its original pulse.

Crosstalk: unwanted signals in a communication channel caused by the transference of energy from another circuit. It is caused by undesired capacitive, inductive or conductive coupling from channel to channel or transmission media.

Bandwidth: the maximum amount of data transfer rate of a network or Internet connection in a given amount of time. For example, a gigabit Ethernet connection has a bandwidth of 1 Gbps. Due to transmission impairments the bandwidth also decreases.
Number of receivers: every connected node in the network introduces some attenuation and distortion, so when the number of receivers increases, the transmission distance and/or data rate are limited.

blocks.text: Nine terms, one mark each — this is a favourite 'define any five' slot. Mnemonic: JAD NECSB — Jitter, Attenuation, Distortion, Noise, Echo, Crosstalk, Singing, Bandwidth, receivers.

Network architecture explains how the computers in a network interact with each other and with the network devices. It is defined as the physical and logical design of the software, hardware, protocols and media of transmission of data. Simply put, it is how computers are organized and how tasks are allocated to the computers.
Based on network architecture, a computer network can be classified into: peer-to-peer architecture and client/server architecture.
Peer-to-peer architecture

In a peer-to-peer architecture all computers have equal authority to access data and are therefore known as peers. Each computer functions as both a client and a server, and there is no dedicated server. A peer-to-peer network is also called a workgroup — the term workgroup refers to a small group of individual computers that work together. This architecture is a good choice where there are few computers and users, security is not an issue and centralized control is not needed.

blocks.caption: Peer-to-peer — advantages and disadvantages
head: Advantages
Disadvantages
rows: Simple and easier to set up
Administration of the network is difficult without a dedicated server
Overall cost of implementing and managing the network is cheaper
Data security is poor in this architecture
If a computer fails to operate, it will not affect others
Data recovery and backup processes are difficult
Users can manage their own system, so a dedicated system administrator is not required
Not appropriate for a large organization with a large number of computers

blocks.text: Client-server architecture

The client-server architecture contains at least one dedicated server and client computers. The server always provides services to clients and a client always receives services from the server. The server provides services like data, web page, email, SMS, file and print services.

For example, a file server houses hard drives containing files that all network users can access from their individual workstations. Another example is a server set up as a dedicated 'post office' for an entire organization, collecting everyone's email from outside sources for internal distribution and serving as the transporter for all outgoing emails — in this case each user's computer is a client of the mail server. Client-server networking has become the standard networking model. As the network increases in size and traffic, more than one server is needed; spreading the task among several servers ensures that each task is performed in the most efficient possible manner.

head: Advantages
Disadvantages
rows: Centralized administration is possible through the network
Expensive due to the use of dedicated servers
High security can be provided by using the appropriate server
Appropriate for a large organization with a large number of computers
Experienced administrators are required to implement and manage the network
Data recovery and backup processes are easier
If the server fails, it affects the network

sections.title: Some Basic Terms and Tools Used in Computer Networks

blocks.text: IP address

An Internet Protocol (IP) address is a unique identifying number assigned to each computing device connected to a network that uses the Internet protocol for communication. A typical IP address looks like this: 216.27.61.137

To make it easier for humans to remember, IP addresses are normally expressed in decimal format as above, but computers communicate in binary form. The same IP address in binary is: 11011000.00011011.00111101.10001001. The four numbers in an IP address are called octets. An IP address has two main functions: identification of the network and identification of a particular host (computer) in that network.

Two Internet Protocol versions are in use: IPv4 and IPv6. Because of its prevalence, the generic term 'IP address' typically still refers to addresses defined by IPv4. (The gap in the version sequence between IPv4 and IPv6 resulted from the assignment of number 5 to the experimental Internet Stream Protocol in 1979; it was never referred to as IPv5.) An IP address that can be accessed over the Internet is called a public IP address.
IPv4 classes

blocks.caption: The five classes of IPv4 addresses
head: Class
First octet range
Network bits / host bits
Example (network . host)
Used for

blocks.title: 127 is special
blocks.text: The number 127 is reserved for loopback and is used for internal testing on the local machine.
IPv6

A new Internet addressing system, Internet Protocol version 6 (IPv6), is being deployed to fulfil the need for more Internet addresses. IPv6 addresses are 128-bit IP addresses written in hexadecimal and separated by colons. An example IPv6 address could be written like this: 3ffe:1900:4545:3:200:f8ff:fe21:67cf. With IPv6 we can have up to 128-bit (approximately 3.403 × 10³⁸) addresses, which is deemed sufficient for the foreseeable future.
Subnet mask and gateway

The subnet mask number helps to define the relationship between the host (computers, routers, switches, etc.) and the rest of the network. As the name indicates, the subnet mask is used to subdivide a network into smaller, more manageable chunks.

Source IP = 192.168.40.15, destination IP = 192.168.40.39, subnet mask = 255.255.255.0 (also written as a /24 mask). The 255 octets in the mask tell us that the corresponding numbers in the IP address are static and never change, so the first three octets — 192.168.40 — designate the network portion. The fourth octet is 0, so that is the host octet and individual devices can be assigned any number from 1–254. Therefore 192.168.40.15 and 192.168.40.39 belong to the same subnet.

A gateway IP refers to a device on a network which sends local network traffic to other networks. A gateway is a network node that serves as an access point to another network, often involving not only a change of addressing but also a different networking technology. The default gateway always resides in the same subnet as the end device IP. The gateway can really be any unique address within the subnet, but most network administrators designate the first number of the subnet as the gateway — so 192.168.99.1 would be the default gateway given a 255.255.255.0 subnet mask.
MAC address

A Media Access Control (MAC) address is a unique number associated with a network adapter (NIC). It is also known as the physical or hardware address and is used to uniquely identify each node (computer) of a network. It is usually assigned by the manufacturer of the network interface card (NIC) and stored in its ROM — every NIC developed contains a unique MAC address.

A MAC address is a 12-digit hexadecimal number (48 bits in length). By convention MAC addresses are usually written in one of two formats: MM:MM:MM:SS:SS:SS or MM-MM-MM-SS-SS-SS. The first half of a MAC address contains the ID number of the adapter manufacturer (these IDs are regulated by an Internet standards body); the second half represents the serial number assigned to the adapter by the manufacturer.
In the example 0:A0:C9:14:C8:29 the prefix 00A0C9 indicates that the manufacturer is Intel Corporation and 14C829 indicates a particular host.
Internet

The Internet is an interconnected network of thousands of networks and millions of computers linking businesses, educational institutions, government agencies and individuals together. At present no central authority owns the Internet — it is managed by the people who use it, and several organizations influence the system and monitor its operations. Among the governing bodies of the Internet are the Internet Society (ISOC), the Internet Architecture Board (IAB) and the Internet Engineering Task Force (IETF).

In 1969 the Department of Defense (DOD) of the United States of America started a network called ARPANET (Advanced Research Project Administration Network). It began modestly with one computer in California and three in Utah. Later, to share software and hardware resources, the military allowed universities to join the network, from where students started using it and giving birth to the very popular Internet.

blocks.caption: The Internet — a global network of networks.

blocks.text: The Internet is mainly used for applications like: search information; e-mail service; communication; file transfer; remote login; publishing of articles, reports and newsletters; online education; online shopping; entertainment.
Intranet

An intranet is a private network that uses Internet protocols, network connectivity and possibly the public telecommunication system to securely share part of an organization's information or operations with its employees. An intranet is a LAN or WAN that uses the TCP/IP protocol but belongs exclusively to a corporation, school or organization, and is accessible only to the organization's workers. If the intranet is connected to the Internet it is secured by a firewall to prevent unauthorized users from gaining access.

blocks.title: Advantages of an intranet
items: Workforce productivity: intranets help employees quickly find and view information and applications relevant to their roles and responsibilities. Via a simple-to-use web browser interface, users can access data held in any database the organization wants to make available, anytime and — subject to security provisions — from anywhere.

Time: organizations can make more information available to employees on a 'pull' basis (employees link to relevant information at a time which suits them) rather than deluging them indiscriminately with emails.
Communication: intranets serve as powerful tools for communication within an organization, vertically and horizontally.

blocks.text: Difference between intranet and Internet

blocks.caption: Intranet vs Internet
head: Basis
Intranet
Internet
rows: Your own employees, who know a lot about the company, its structure and terminology
Customers, who know much less about the company and care less about it
Everyday work inside the company, including complex applications
Mainly finding out information about products
Draft reports, project progress reports, HR information and other detailed information
Marketing information and customer support information
Typically ten to a hundred times as many pages as the public website
Smaller, because much work-in-progress is never published
Often a hundred to a thousand times faster, so rich graphics and multimedia are feasible

blocks.text: Extranet

An extranet is a private intranet that can be accessed by outside users over the Internet using a dedicated and secure channel. To gain entrance to the extranet's resources, an external user typically must log on to the network by providing a valid user ID and password. The extranet is a blend of the public Internet and the closed intranet — fundamentally it is a part of the Internet, since it is accessed by people in many different companies who will be using your public website but will not have access to the truly internal parts of your intranet.

Network tools are used for supporting easier and effective network connections. Some of the network tools are:

items: Packet tracer: Packet Tracer is an innovative and powerful network simulator that can be used to practise building your own network with routers, switches, wireless and much more. It allows you to experiment with network behaviour, build models and ask 'what if' questions. It is used to trace the movement of data packets in data communication. Packet Tracer provides simulation, visualization, authoring, assessment and collaboration capabilities to facilitate the teaching and learning of complex technology concepts.

Remote login: remote login allows a user terminal to connect to a host computer via a network or direct telecommunications link and to interact with that host computer as if the user terminal were directly connected to it. It is a process in which a user can log in to a remote site computer and use the services available on the remote computer, and can understand the result of transferring the result of processing from the remote computer to the local computer. For example, Telnet enables a user to manage an account or device remotely.

blocks.text: Network connecting devices are used for connecting computers to the network and sharing resources between the computers in the network. The common networking devices are described below.
Network Interface Card (NIC)

A Network Interface Card is a device that connects the computer and the network cable. The cards are installed in an expansion slot in each computer or built into the system. The NIC coordinates the transfer of information between the computer and the network, and each NIC is assigned a unique MAC (physical) address which is stored in ROM.

blocks.title: Functions of the NIC
items: Prepare data from the computer for the network cable.
Send/receive the data to another computer.
Control the flow of data between the computer and the cabling system.

blocks.caption: A Network Interface Card (NIC).

blocks.text: MODEM

The word MODEM stands for MOdulator and DEModulator. It is a device which translates data from binary codes to analog data that can be transmitted over the telephone network, and translates analog data into binary codes. Modulation is the process of converting data from binary (digital) to analog and demodulation is the reverse process. A MODEM is required when digital data stored in the computer has to be transmitted over an analog medium like the traditional telephone system. When all telephone lines become digital, the MODEM will no longer be necessary.

blocks.caption: Modem — (a) internal  (b) external

blocks.text: Router

A router is used to connect two or more different networks. Its main job is to find out the best route (path) that can be used for transmission. The router manages a routing table, which is used to determine the most efficient routes to the various network nodes. In general, routers are responsible for getting traffic from here to there along the most efficient possible path. It operates at the network layer of the OSI model.

blocks.caption: A wireless router.

blocks.text: Switch

A switch, or more properly a switching hub, attempts to select the most direct path needed to send a data packet to its destination. It is also known as an intelligent hub. When the switch receives a data packet it creates a direct connection between sender and receiver and forwards the data packet to the destination computer only.

Recently the cost of intelligent switching hubs has come down to the point that many companies are using them instead of a conventional hub. The bandwidth speed of each port is automatically sensed and set appropriately.

blocks.caption: A port switch.

blocks.text: Hub

A hub is a connectivity device with multiple ports for connecting computers in a star topology. It accepts data, amplifies them and then broadcasts. Because of broadcasting, data traffic is increased. It is also used to split network segments and propagate signals through them. Its major disadvantage is that it cannot filter network traffic and it imposes a limitation on the number of computers that can be connected.

blocks.caption: An 8-port hub.

blocks.text: Difference between switch and hub

blocks.caption: Switch vs hub
head: Basis
Switch
Hub
rows: Connects many devices together on a computer network, manages ports and VLAN security settings. Operates at Layer 2 (Data Link Layer) of the OSI model
Connects many network devices together so that devices can exchange data. Operates at Layer 1 (Physical layer) of the OSI model
Half/full duplex, multi-port bridge with 24/48 ports
Intelligent device and an active device (with software)
Non-intelligent device and a passive device (without software)
Many spanning-trees possible; no collisions occur in a full-duplex switch
No spanning-tree; collisions occur commonly in setups using hubs

blocks.text: Bridge

A bridge is used to connect two different network segments. It is the connecting device between hubs and passes data packets between multiple network segments that use the same communication protocol. A bridge is more intelligent than a hub, as it examines the destination address of each packet and only passes through those that need to get from one segment to the other. Bridges are often used to reduce data traffic on a busy network. It operates at the data-link layer of the OSI model.
Repeater

A repeater is a device that amplifies a signal being transmitted on the network. It is used to increase the length of the transmission media over which data can be transmitted. It receives signals, amplifies them and retransmits them towards the receiver.

Using a UTP cable we can send data up to a maximum of 100 metres without amplification. If the data travel beyond that distance without amplification they become weaker and after some time the signal is destroyed. A repeater provides a solution for this problem too. It operates at the physical layer of the OSI model.
Bluetooth and Wi-Fi

Bluetooth is a wireless technology standard for exchanging data over short distances (using short wavelength radio transmissions) from fixed and mobile devices, creating personal area networks (PANs) with high levels of security. It was created by telecoms vendor Ericsson in 1994. It can connect several devices, overcoming problems of synchronization.

blocks.caption: The Bluetooth symbol.

blocks.text: Wi-Fi refers to wireless fidelity. A Wi-Fi enabled device such as a laptop, mobile phone, smart phone or digital audio player can connect to the network or Internet when within range of a wireless network connected to the Internet. The coverage of a Wi-Fi network depends on one or more (interconnected) access points; it generally comprises an area equal to the size of a few rooms but may be expanded to cover many square miles, depending on the number of access points with overlapping coverage. Wi-Fi also allows communications directly from one computer to another without the involvement of an access point — this is called the ad hoc mode of Wi-Fi transmission.

blocks.caption: The Wi-Fi symbol.

blocks.text: Short Answer Question 9: 'Explain router and Wi-Fi.' Short Answer Question 10: 'Differentiate between switch and HUB' — use the 5-point table.

The physical or logical layout with the geometrical pattern/arrangement of interconnection of computers in a network is called topology. In the context of a network, the term topology refers to the way the computers are connected to the network.

Types of network topologies: bus topology (linear topology), star topology, ring topology, tree topology, mesh topology and hybrid topology. Note: as per our curriculum only the bus, ring and star topologies are explained below.
Bus topology

A bus topology connects each computer to a segment called the trunk (bus). Coaxial cables are mostly used. It consists of the main cable with terminators at both ends; the terminator absorbs the signals so they do not reflect across the bus. It uses a broadcasting mechanism for data transmission, which increases the data traffic, thereby resulting in a data error rate.

blocks.caption: Bus topology — trunk cable with 50 ohm terminators at both ends.
Bus topology — advantages and disadvantages
head: Advantages
Disadvantages
rows: Well suited for a temporary network
Limited cable length and number of nodes
Typically the cheapest topology to implement
A cable break can disable the entire network
Failure of one computer (node) does not affect others
Data traffic is high, which increases the data collision rate and data error rate

blocks.text: Star topology

The star topology is the most common network topology found in most offices and home networks. In a star topology each computer or node is connected to a central device such as a hub. Data on the star network passes through the hub before reaching its destination. It uses a broadcasting mechanism: when data is transmitted from one computer to another it reaches the hub, the hub amplifies the data signal and broadcasts it — due to broadcasting, data traffic will be high, which may increase the data collision rate and data error rate. Adding and removing computers is easier. Twisted pair cable is commonly used.

blocks.caption: Star topology — every node has its own link to the central hub.
Star topology — advantages and disadvantages
head: Advantages
Disadvantages
rows: Easier to add or remove computers
Failure of the hub affects all nodes
Each computer requires a dedicated cable, so more cable is needed and proper cable naming is required
Failure of one computer does not affect the entire network
More expensive than bus topology because of the cost of the hub
A centralized control system can be established
Data traffic, data collision rate and data error rate are high

blocks.text: Ring topology

In the ring topology each station is attached to nearby computers on a point-to-point basis so that the entire system is in the form of a ring — that is, all the computers are connected in a closed loop. Data are transmitted in only one direction (either clockwise or anti-clockwise at a time). The method by which the data are transmitted around the ring is called token passing. MAU (Multi-station Access Unit) is used as a control device. A twisted pair or optical fibre is used as the transmission media.

blocks.caption: Ring topology — a closed loop with token passing.
Ring topology — advantages and disadvantages
head: Advantages
Disadvantages
rows: Growth of the system has minimal impact on performance
More expensive than bus topology because of the cost of the MAU
Terminators are not necessary as in bus topology
Difficult to set up compared to bus and star topology
Data traffic is reduced as data flows in only one direction
Failure of a computer affects the entire network
Each computer has equal priority to communicate on the network
Less flexible — difficulty in adding and removing computers from the ring

blocks.text: Selection criteria for a network topology

items: i. Cost
ii. Data error rate
iii. Simplicity
iv. Data security
v. Transmission speed
vi. Flexibility
vii. Maintainability
viii. The volume of data traffic

blocks.text: Why do people prefer star topology for a LAN in an organization?

items: Reliability: if a cable or device fails, only the affected node is impacted and other devices continue to function normally. This reliability is crucial for critical systems used in the organization.

High performance: star topology ensures that data collisions do not occur. Each device has its own dedicated link to the central hub or switch, allowing efficient data transmission without interference.

Cost-effective: unlike other topologies where each device needs multiple connections, star topology requires only one input/output port per device. This simplicity reduces costs, especially in large networks.

Easy installation, fault detection and maintenance: setting up a star network is straightforward because each device connects directly to the central hub. Identifying faults is easier because the failed link can be quickly pinpointed, so maintenance is easier.

blocks.text: Thus star topology provides reliability, better performance, cost-effectiveness and ease of maintenance — qualities that make it suitable for LANs in any organization.

sections.title: Basic Concept of the OSI Reference Model

blocks.text: The Open System Interconnection (OSI) model includes a set of protocols that attempt to define and standardize the data communications process. The OSI protocols were defined by the International Organization for Standardization (ISO) and have received the support of most major computer and network vendors, many large customers and most governments, including the United States.

The OSI model is a concept that describes how data communications should take place. It divides the process into seven groups, called layers, and defines a 'layered' architecture in the form of a protocol stack. There are specific, discrete functions that take place at each layer of the protocol stack, with lower-level layers providing services to upper layers and vice versa. When two systems communicate on the network, information is sent down through the protocol stack of one system, over the cable, and then up through the protocol stack to the appropriate layer on the other system.
Need for the OSI model

The OSI model was established to standardize the design and construction of computer networks for developers and hardware manufacturers. Standards allow hardware and software components from a variety of different vendors to operate together. Without standards, everything would be vendor-specific and interoperability would suffer.

blocks.caption: The seven layers of the OSI model with the function of each layer.

blocks.text: The seven layers (top to bottom, as listed in the book)

items: Application layer: provides direct access to network services. It serves as the interface between the user and the network by providing services that directly support user applications. (Function: to allow access to network resources.)

Presentation layer: responsible for data translation (formatting), compression and encryption (converting readable contents into an unreadable format for data security). It is primarily concerned with translation, interpreting and converting data from various formats — for example EBCDIC characters might be converted into ASCII. Data is compressed for transmission and uncompressed when received, and encryption is also implemented at this layer.

Session layer: responsible for establishing, maintaining and terminating a connection called a 'session'. A session is a period in which data can be exchanged between computers. Managing the session involves synchronization of user tasks and dialogue control (who transmits and for how long). Synchronization uses checkpoints in the data stream — in the event of a failure only the data from the last checkpoint have to be resent. Login name recognition and security functions take place at this layer.

Transport layer: responsible for flow control and ensuring messages are delivered error-free. On the sending side messages are packaged to form data packets for efficient transmission and assigned a tracking number (packet number) so they can be reassembled in proper order. On the receiving side the packets are reassembled, checked for errors and acknowledged. The transport layer performs error handling: it ensures all data is received in the proper sequence and without errors, and data is retransmitted if there are errors.

Network layer: primarily concerned with addressing and routing. Logical addresses (e.g. an IP address) are translated into physical addresses (i.e. the MAC address) for transmission; on the receiving side the translation process is reversed. It is at the network layer that the route from the source to the destination computer is determined, based on packet addresses and network conditions. Traffic control measures are also implemented here.

Data link layer: defines how the signal will be placed on or taken off from the NIC. At this layer the data frame is broken down into individual bits that can be translated into electronic signals and sent over the network; on the receiving side the bits are reassembled into frames for processing by upper layers. Error detection and correction are also performed here — if an acknowledgment is expected and not received, the frame will be resent, and corrupted data is also identified at the data link layer.

Physical layer: establishes the physical characteristics of the network (type of cable, connectors, length of cable, etc.) and defines the electrical characteristics of the signals used to transmit the data. It transmits binary data (bits) as electrical or optical signals depending on the medium.

blocks.caption: OSI layers at a glance (bottom to top)
head: Layer
Name
Key job
