Long Answer Question 6: 'Explain the 7 layers of the OSI/ISO model of networking.' Write one definition + one function line per layer and draw the stack. MCQ 9 and 10 also test this.

When devices communicate with each other over a local area network or across the Internet, the message transmitted is ultimately directed to the target device's network hardware address that is programmed into the device by the manufacturer. This hardware address is the MAC address.

Unfortunately, MAC addresses do not help route communication messages outside of a small number of locally interconnected devices, because they are randomly scattered around the world — a device with MAC address 10:20:30:40:50:60 could be in New York and another with 10:20:30:40:50:61 could be in Kathmandu.

To enable devices to find each other easily no matter where they are in the world, the creators of the Internet came up with a logical addressing scheme that made it much easier for devices to find each other. These logical Internet Protocol addresses are commonly referred to as 'IP addresses'.

items: Each IP address string is made up of two components: a network identifying component, which is the leftmost part of the address; and a device-identifying component, which is the rightmost part of the address.

The network identifying component is used by network routing devices (routers) to determine the best way to send a communication message to take it closer to its final destination, the target device itself.
The device identifying component of the IP address is only of significance to the target device and any other devices sharing the same local area network (LAN).
The length of the network and device identifying components may vary based upon the number of devices that an organization needs to address.

blocks.title: The key idea
blocks.text: An IP address is used for connecting the computers for communication. Once they are connected they share their MAC address, and further communication takes place using the MAC address.

sections.title: Lab Work — ipconfig, ping, cabling and assigning an IP address

blocks.text: ipconfig (Internet Protocol Configuration)

A command-line tool used to display and control the current TCP/IP configuration settings of the network on the screen. It also refreshes the DNS and IP address in case of dynamic IP configurations. Used without additional parameters, ipconfig simply displays the IP address, default gateway and subnet mask for all available adapters.

blocks.title: Steps to use ipconfig
items: Open the Run window by pressing Windows + R keys, type cmd, and click the OK button.

Type ipconfig and press Enter. It will display the IP address, subnet mask, default gateway and other current network settings. ipconfig /all will display all the network connections and their settings for each adapter in the computer.

blocks.caption: Opening the command prompt from the Run dialog.
Output of the ipconfig command showing the IPv4 address, subnet mask and default gateway.

blocks.text: Ping

Ping is a command-line tool used to test the connection between two devices. It sends data packets to a host (or another device in a network) and listens to its response. It serves two primary purposes: to check if the host is available, and to measure how long the response takes.
Syntax: ping ipaddress / name_of_the_host_computer / domain_name — for example: ping 192.168.1.5

blocks.title: Steps to use ping
items: Open the Run window by pressing Windows + R keys, type cmd, and click the OK button.
Type ping ipaddress_of_host and press Enter. It will display whether there is a connection or not. If the devices are connected, reply information is displayed.

blocks.caption: ping google.com — replies received, so the connection works.
ping when there is no connection — no reply is received.

blocks.text: Twisted pair cabling

Twisted pair cable is the popular communication media used to connect computers in a local area network. This cable contains an RJ-45 connector at its tip, used to connect the cable with the networking devices and the computer. The process of connecting RJ-45 with the cable is called cabling. A clamper is used to connect the RJ-45 after the wires are adjusted to the appropriate pins.
Twisted pair cables are constructed using two methods: straight-through cabling and crossover cabling.

blocks.caption: Wiring standards — T568A and T568B
head: Pin No.
T568A
T568B

blocks.text: Straight-through cabling: on a straight-through cable the wired pins match on both sides. It uses one wiring standard — both ends use T568A, or both ends use T568B. It is primarily used for connecting unlike devices, such as switch to router, switch to PC or server, hub to PC or server.

blocks.caption: Straight-through cable — both ends wired to the T568B standard.

blocks.text: Crossover cabling: unlike the straight-through cable, the RJ45 crossover cable uses two different wiring standards — one end uses T568A and the other end uses T568B. The internal wiring of Ethernet crossover cables reverses the transmit and receive signals. It is most often used to connect two devices of the same type, such as switch to switch, switch to hub, hub to hub, router to router, router Ethernet port to PC NIC, and PC to PC.

blocks.caption: Crossover cable — T568A at one end and T568B at the other.

blocks.text: Assigning a private IP address in a LAN network

Every computer connected to a network contains a unique IP address. This address is assigned to a computer automatically by the DHCP (Dynamic Host Control Protocol) server (if the network contains a DHCP server), or manually by the administrator. Here we are assigning it manually.

blocks.title: Steps
items: Step 1: Open Network Connections. Open the Run window by pressing Windows + R keys, type ncpa.cpl and click the OK button.
Step 2: Select the network in which you want to assign an IP address. Right-click on the selected network and select Properties. A network properties window will open.
Step 3: Double-click Internet Protocol Version 4 (TCP/IPv4); an Internet Protocol Version 4 (TCP/IPv4) Properties window will open.

Step 4: Select the radio button 'Use the following IP address' and set an IP address, subnet mask, default gateway, preferred DNS server and alternate DNS server, and click OK. If the IP address matches/conflicts with any computer in the network, an error message stating 'IP Conflict' will be displayed; otherwise the assigned IP will be set.

blocks.caption: Network Connections window opened with ncpa.cpl.
Internet Protocol Version 4 (TCP/IPv4) Properties — setting a static IP address.

blocks.text: To check whether the IP address is properly set, use the ipconfig command. To check whether the computer is connected to the network, use the ping command.
Run this as a live demo in the lab: ipconfig → ping the gateway → ping google.com → then a cabling demo with an RJ-45, clamper and a straight-through cable.

short.q: What is Network? List out the benefits of Networks.
short.a:
A network is two or more computing devices connected by a communication link so that they can exchange data and share resources. Any device that is part of the network — computer, printer, server, phone — is called a node.

Benefits of networking:

  • Resource sharing — one printer, one scanner or one internet connection serves everyone instead of being bought repeatedly.
  • File and data sharing — a document lives on a server and every authorised user works on the same current copy.
  • Centralised software and data — applications and databases are installed and updated once.
  • Communication — e-mail, messaging, voice and video calls, and collaborative work.
  • Cost saving — shared peripherals, licences and storage cost far less per user.
  • Reliability through redundancy — if one machine or path fails, another can take over.
  • Central backup and security — data is backed up and protected in one controlled place.

short.q: Define computer networks and explain their uses.
short.a:
A computer network is a set of two or more computers and other devices linked by communication channels so that they can exchange information and share hardware, software and data. The link may be cable, fibre or radio.

Its uses:

  • Sharing hardware — printers, scanners, plotters and storage.
  • Sharing software and data — one licensed application or one database serves every workstation.
  • Communication — e-mail, chat, voice and video conferencing.
  • Internet access — the whole network reaches the internet through one connection.
  • Remote work — accessing files and applications from another building or city.
  • Centralised administration — accounts, backups, updates and security policy are managed from one place.
  • Entertainment and information — streaming media, online learning and research.

short.q: Explain different communication flow modes.
short.a:
The communication flow mode (or transmission mode) describes which direction data may travel in over a link.

Simplex. One way only — one end always transmits and the other always receives. There is no way to send anything back. Example: a keyboard to the CPU, or a television broadcast.

Half-duplex. Both directions, but only one at a time — the two ends take turns, and while one is sending the other must listen. Example: a walkie-talkie.

Full-duplex. Both directions at the same time — each end can send and receive simultaneously. Example: a telephone conversation, or a modern switched Ethernet link.

short.q: Differentiate between LAN and WAN with the help of a diagram.
short.a:
LAN (Local Area Network)WAN (Wide Area Network)
Covers a small area — one room, building or campus. Covers a large area — a city, a country or the world.
Owned and administered by one organisation. Usually built from leased lines and links owned by several carriers.
High speed, about 100 Mbps or more; low delay. Lower speed and higher delay because of the long distances.
Low error rate, because the links are short and controlled. Higher error rate, because signals travel further through more equipment.
Cheap to install — the organisation owns the cable. Expensive — lines must be rented from telecommunication providers.
Uses its own media: twisted pair, coaxial cable, fibre. Uses telephone lines, microwave, satellite and fibre backbones.
Design and maintenance are simple. Design and maintenance are complex.

Diagram (description): on the left, one building contains several computers joined to a single switch — that is the LAN. On the right, two or more such LANs in different cities are joined by long-distance links (leased line, satellite or fibre) through routers — that collection of links is the WAN. A MAN sits between the two: it spans a single city and joins several LANs together.

short.q: What are the selection criteria for a network topology?
short.a:
The criteria used when choosing a network topology:
  • Cost — how much cable, how many ports and how much installation labour the layout needs.
  • Scalability — how easily stations, or whole segments, can be added later without redesigning the network.
  • Reliability and fault tolerance — what happens when one cable, node or device fails; whether the rest of the network keeps working.
  • Ease of installation and reconfiguration — how disruptive it is to move a workstation or add a floor.
  • Ease of maintenance and troubleshooting — how quickly a fault can be isolated and repaired.
  • Performance — expected throughput and delay under the real traffic load, including behaviour at peak times.
  • Cable length and distance limits — the maximum run the chosen medium allows between nodes.
  • Future growth — whether the topology can carry the traffic the organisation expects in a few years.

short.q: What is the purpose of transmission media? Explain its types.
short.a:
Transmission media are the physical paths that carry a signal from the transmitter to the receiver. Without a medium there is no channel, so no data can move — the medium determines the bandwidth, the maximum distance, the error rate and the immunity to noise and interference.

Media are divided into two families:

Guided (bounded / wired) media — the signal is confined to a physical path:

  • Twisted pair — two insulated copper wires twisted around each other to cancel interference. UTP (unshielded) is cheap and is the standard LAN cable; STP (shielded) adds a metallic shield for noisier environments.
  • Coaxial cable — a central copper conductor inside insulation, a braided metal shield and an outer jacket. Better shielding and longer runs than twisted pair; used for cable television and older Ethernet.
  • Fibre optic cable — pulses of light through a glass or plastic core. Enormous bandwidth, very low loss over long distances, and complete immunity to electromagnetic interference; more expensive and harder to terminate.

Unguided (unbounded / wireless) media — the signal travels through free space:

  • Radio wave — broadcast in all directions; used for Wi-Fi, Bluetooth and mobile phones.
  • Microwave — line-of-sight, point-to-point beams between dish antennas; used for long-distance trunks and mobile backhaul.
  • Infrared — very short range, line of sight, blocked by walls; used for remote controls.
  • Satellite — a microwave signal bounced off an orbiting satellite, giving coverage of the whole earth and reaching places no cable can.

short.q: Explain any two transmission media with appropriate diagrams.
short.a:
1. Twisted pair cable. Two insulated copper conductors are twisted around each other; the twisting makes each wire pick up the same interference, which cancels out. UTP is unshielded, cheap, light and easy to install, and is the ordinary LAN cable (Cat 5e / Cat 6 with RJ-45 connectors). STP adds a foil or braided shield for noisy environments. Its limits are a short segment length (about 100 m) and susceptibility to crosstalk and external noise.

Diagram (description): two copper wires, drawn as two parallel lines that spiral around one another, enclosed in a plastic sheath; in UTP the sheath is the only covering, while in STP a metal foil or braid sits between the wires and the sheath.

2. Fibre optic cable. Data is carried as pulses of light along a very thin glass or plastic core. Light enters at one end and is confined by the cladding around it through total internal reflection, so it can travel for kilometres with little loss.

Diagram (description): from the centre outwards — the core (glass, carrying the light), the cladding (glass of lower refractive index, reflecting the light back in), a buffer coating, strengthening aramid yarn, and the outer jacket.

Its advantages over copper are enormous bandwidth, very low attenuation over long distances, total immunity to electromagnetic interference, no crosstalk, and no electrical hazard or eavesdropping. Its disadvantages are higher cost, fragile fibres, and the skill and equipment needed to terminate and splice them.

short.q: Describe the 'Coaxial cable' and 'Satellite' with examples.
short.a:
Coaxial cable. A single copper conductor runs down the centre of the cable, surrounded by a layer of insulation, then a cylindrical braided metal shield that acts as the second conductor and blocks external noise, and finally a protective plastic jacket. Because the shield surrounds the inner conductor, coaxial cable resists interference and carries a signal much further than twisted pair. Examples: cable television distribution, the older thick and thin Ethernet (10Base2 / 10Base5) networks, and the connection from a satellite dish or antenna to its receiver.

Satellite communication. A satellite is a microwave repeater placed in orbit. A ground station transmits an uplink signal to the satellite; the satellite amplifies it, shifts it to a different frequency to avoid interference with the uplink, and retransmits it as a downlink that covers a large area of the earth's surface. A geostationary satellite orbits above the equator at about 36,000 km and appears stationary, so the ground dishes never have to move. Examples: satellite television (Dish, Sky), GPS navigation, long-distance telephone and internet trunks, weather imaging, and connecting remote villages where no cable exists.

The trade-off is the propagation delay — the signal travels up and back down, so a geostationary hop adds a noticeable delay of roughly a quarter of a second, which is why satellite links are poor for real-time conversation.

short.q: Explain router and Wi-Fi.
short.a:
Router. A network-layer device that connects two or more different networks and forwards packets between them. It reads the destination IP address in each packet and chooses the best next hop from its routing table, so it can join a home LAN to the internet and keep each network's traffic separate. Routers work at layer 3 of the OSI model, do not forward broadcasts, and are what make the internet possible.

Wi-Fi. Short for Wireless Fidelity — the common name for wireless networking based on the IEEE 802.11 family of standards. A wireless access point or router turns data into radio signals in the 2.4 GHz or 5 GHz band so that laptops, phones and printers can join the network and reach the internet without a cable. Wi-Fi is convenient and supports mobility, but its range is short, its speed and reliability vary with distance, obstacles and interference from other devices, and because the signal travels through the air it must be secured with WPA2 or WPA3 encryption.

short.q: Differentiate between switch and HUB.
short.a:
SwitchHub
Works at the data link layer (layer 2) and forwards frames using MAC addresses. Works at the physical layer (layer 1) and has no addressing at all.
Sends a frame only to the port of the destination device. Copies every bit to every other port.
Intelligent — it learns which MAC address is on which port and builds a table. Unintelligent — it is simply a multi-port repeater.
Each port is its own collision domain, so several conversations happen at once. All ports share one collision domain, so only one device may transmit at a time.
Gives each device the full bandwidth of its port. Bandwidth is shared by every device on the hub.
Supports full-duplex communication. Half-duplex only.
More expensive. Cheaper, and now largely obsolete.
Used in every modern LAN. Used only in very small or legacy networks, or for monitoring traffic.

long.q: What is networking? Explain the advantages and disadvantages of networking.
long.a:
Networking is the practice of linking two or more computing devices by a communication channel so that they can exchange data and share resources. The connected devices are called nodes, and the pattern in which they are linked is the network topology.

Advantages

  • Resource sharing. One printer, one scanner, one internet connection and one file server serve every user, instead of being duplicated on every desk.
  • Cost saving. Shared peripherals, shared software licences and shared storage cost far less per user than buying them individually.
  • Data sharing and consistency. Everyone works on the same current copy of a file, so there are no conflicting versions.
  • Communication. E-mail, instant messaging, voice and video calls, and collaborative editing.
  • Centralised administration. Accounts, security policy, backup and software updates are managed in one place.
  • Reliability. Data can be replicated across machines and there can be alternative paths, so one failure need not stop the work.
  • Scalability. Users and devices are added without rebuilding the system.

Disadvantages

  • Security risk. Every connected machine is a potential entry point, and data on the wire can be intercepted unless it is encrypted.
  • Malware spreads fast. A virus or worm can move from one machine to every machine on the network.
  • Dependence on the server. If the central server fails, every user stops working — there is a single point of failure.
  • Cost of infrastructure. Cabling, switches, routers, firewalls and the staff to run them are expensive.
  • Maintenance burden. Networks need configuring, monitoring, patching and troubleshooting.
  • Performance degrades with load. Bandwidth is shared, so heavy use slows everyone down.
  • Privacy concerns. Centralising data makes misuse, accidental disclosure and unauthorised access easier to carry out on a large scale.

long.q: Describe 'simplex', 'half duplex', and 'full duplex' with diagram.
long.a:
The transmission mode states which direction data may flow across a communication channel.

Simplex — one direction only. One end is permanently the transmitter and the other is permanently the receiver; nothing can ever be sent back. The full capacity of the channel is used in that single direction.

Diagram: A ————————> B (one arrow, one way)

Examples: keyboard to CPU, computer to printer, radio and television broadcasting.

Half-duplex — both directions, one at a time. Both ends can send and receive, but not simultaneously; they take turns, and while one transmits the other listens. The channel's capacity is used alternately in each direction.

Diagram: A ————————> B then A <———————— B (the arrow reverses; only one at a time)

Examples: walkie-talkie, old hub-based Ethernet, a citizen-band radio.

Full-duplex — both directions at once. Both ends transmit and receive simultaneously, which either needs two physical channels or one channel divided between the two directions.

Diagram: A <————————> B (arrows both ways at the same time)

Examples: telephone conversation, modern switched Ethernet, a broadband internet connection.

long.q: What is networking? Distinguish between star topology and ring topology of networking principles with the help of a clean diagram.
long.a:
Networking is linking two or more computers and devices by a communication channel so they can exchange data and share hardware, software and information. A network topology is the geometric arrangement of those devices and the cables or links between them — the shape of the network.

Star topology

Every device has its own cable running to a central device — a hub or, nowadays, a switch. No device connects directly to another; all traffic goes through the centre.

Diagram (description): a central box (the switch) with lines radiating outwards like the points of a star, one to each computer. No line joins two computers directly.

Advantages: a fault in one cable affects only that one computer, so the rest of the network keeps working; a workstation is added or removed without disturbing anyone else; faults are easy to locate at the centre.

Disadvantages: the central device is a single point of failure — if the switch dies the whole network stops; more cable is used than in a bus; the switch's capacity limits the network.

Ring topology

Devices are joined one after another in a closed loop. Data travels in one direction from node to node, and each node receives the frame, checks whether it is the destination, and if not passes it on.

Diagram (description): computers drawn around a circle, each joined to its two neighbours by a short length of cable, with the last joined back to the first to close the loop.

Advantages: no central device is needed, so there is no single point of failure of that kind; every node gets an equal chance to transmit, so performance does not collapse under load as it can on a bus; cable runs are short and orderly.

Disadvantages: a break in any one cable, or one switched-off node, breaks the whole ring; adding a node requires the ring to be interrupted; a fault is hard to isolate because every node looks the same.

The comparison

PointStarRing
Central deviceRequired — hub or switchNot required
One cable breaksOnly that node is cut offThe whole ring stops
Cable neededMoreLess
Adding a nodeEasy, no interruptionInterrupts the ring
CostHigher — the switch costs moneyLower
Use todayStandard — virtually every LANRare; FDDI and some backbones

long.q: What is network topology? What are the different types of LAN topology? Explain.
long.a:
A network topology is the geometric layout of a network — the pattern in which the nodes are connected and the way the cables or links run between them. It describes the physical and logical shape of the network independently of the devices attached to it.

The main LAN topologies are:

1. Bus topology. Every device is attached to one single central cable, the bus or backbone. A signal sent by any station travels in both directions along the cable and is heard by every station, but only the addressed one accepts it; the two ends are closed with terminators to stop reflections.

Advantages: the least cable of any layout, so the cheapest and simplest to install; easy to extend by tapping into the backbone.

Disadvantages: a break anywhere in the backbone brings down the whole network; faults are hard to isolate; as more stations are added collisions increase and performance falls sharply; there is a limit on cable length and on the number of stations.

2. Star topology. Every device has its own cable to a central hub or switch, which passes traffic to the destination.

Advantages: one faulty cable affects only one station; stations are added or moved without interrupting the network; faults are easy to find at the centre.

Disadvantages: the central device is a single point of failure; more cable is needed than for a bus; the central device's capacity limits the network.

3. Ring topology. Devices are joined in a closed loop and data is passed from one node to the next in a fixed direction until it reaches its destination.

Advantages: no central device; orderly access, so performance stays steady under load; short, tidy cable runs.

Disadvantages: one broken link or one failed node stops the whole ring; adding a node interrupts the network; faults are hard to locate.

4. Mesh topology. Every device is connected directly to every other device. A full mesh connects all of them; a partial mesh connects only the ones that carry most traffic.

Advantages: the most reliable — if any link fails, traffic is routed another way; no collision or sharing problem, and traffic is private between the two ends.

Disadvantages: the most expensive, because a full mesh needs one link per pair of devices; the cabling is bulky and installation is difficult.

5. Tree (hierarchical) topology. Star networks are connected to a central backbone bus, giving groups of stars arranged in levels like a family tree.

Advantages: it scales to large networks and is easy to extend; each branch is managed separately, so a fault isolates to a branch.

Disadvantages: the backbone is a single point of failure; configuration is more complex; the whole network depends on the quality of the backbone.

6. Hybrid topology. Any combination of the above — for example a star of star networks joined by a bus — chosen to suit a building that does not fit one clean shape. It is flexible and scalable, but it is the most complex to design and to troubleshoot.

long.q: What do you mean by transmission media? Write short notes on UTP cable, STP, and fiber optical cable.
long.a:
Transmission media are the physical pathways that carry information from the transmitter to the receiver. The medium decides the bandwidth, the maximum distance, the error rate and how much the signal suffers from noise. Media are grouped into guided (wired) and unguided (wireless) types.

UTP — Unshielded Twisted Pair

UTP is the ordinary LAN cable. It contains four pairs of insulated copper wires, each pair twisted around the other. The twisting is the trick: because the two wires of a pair are always side by side, interference induced in one is induced in the other and cancels out. There is no metallic shielding, which makes the cable cheap, thin, light and easy to install, and it is terminated with RJ-45 plugs.

Categories rate the cable — Cat 5e for gigabit Ethernet, Cat 6 and Cat 6a for higher speeds. Its weaknesses are a segment limit of about 100 m, vulnerability to crosstalk between the pairs, and no protection against strong external electromagnetic interference.

STP — Shielded Twisted Pair

STP is twisted pair with a metallic foil or braided shield around each pair, and sometimes around the whole bundle, plus a drain wire to earth it. The shield blocks external electromagnetic interference and cuts crosstalk and radiation, so STP carries data faster and over longer runs in electrically noisy places such as factories or near heavy machinery.

The price is that it is thicker, heavier, more expensive, harder to install, and it must be properly grounded at one end — a badly earthed shield can make interference worse than no shield at all.

Fibre optic cable

Fibre carries data as pulses of light rather than electricity. At the centre is a very thin core of glass or plastic, surrounded by cladding of a lower refractive index; light entering the core is reflected back into it and travels the length of the cable by total internal reflection. Around that come a buffer coating, strengthening yarn and the outer jacket. Single-mode fibre uses a very narrow core and a laser for long telecommunication routes; multimode fibre uses a wider core and a cheaper LED for shorter runs inside a building.

Its advantages are decisive: bandwidth in the gigabits and terabits, attenuation so low that signals travel tens of kilometres without a repeater, complete immunity to electromagnetic interference and crosstalk, no electrical hazard, no lightning risk, and very difficult eavesdropping. Its disadvantages are higher cable and equipment cost, fragile glass that must be handled carefully, and the specialised tools and skill needed to terminate and splice it.

long.q: Explain about 7 layers of the OSI/ISO model of networking.
long.a:
The OSI (Open Systems Interconnection) reference model — also called the ISO-OSI model — describes network communication as seven layers. Each layer provides a service to the layer above it and uses the service of the layer below it, and each communicates with its peer layer on the other machine through its own protocol. Splitting the job into layers means one layer can be changed without rewriting the others.
LayerNameWhat it doesExample
7ApplicationServices that the user's program talks to directly — network applications and their protocols.HTTP, FTP, SMTP, DNS
6PresentationTranslates, encrypts and compresses data so both sides agree on the format — the syntax layer.SSL/TLS, JPEG, ASCII
5SessionOpens, manages and closes the conversation between two applications, and keeps them in step.NetBIOS, RPC
4TransportDelivers the whole message reliably and in the right order, end to end, with flow and error control. Data is called a segment.TCP, UDP
3NetworkMoves packets from the source to the destination across several networks by choosing a route and addressing the packets. Data is called a packet.IP, ICMP, routers
2Data linkTransfers frames reliably between two directly connected nodes, using physical addresses, and detects and corrects errors on the link. Data is called a frame.Ethernet, switches, MAC addresses
1PhysicalPuts the actual bits on the wire as electrical, light or radio signals; defines the cables, connectors, voltages and pin layouts.UTP cable, fibre, hubs, RJ-45

A useful way to remember it: the top three layers (5–7) are about the application and the conversation, layer 4 carries the message, and the bottom three (1–3) are about getting the bits across each hop and then across the whole network.

long.q: Differentiate between the Internet and Intranet.
long.a:
InternetIntranet
A global, public network of networks that anyone may join. A private network belonging to one organisation.
No single owner and no central control. Owned, controlled and administered by the organisation.
Access is open to the general public. Access is restricted to employees and authorised users.
Uses public IP addresses and the full TCP/IP suite; traffic crosses the public internet. Uses the same TCP/IP technology, but usually with private IP addresses and its traffic stays inside the organisation.
Security is weak by nature — everything is exposed, so firewalls and encryption are essential. Security is stronger — it sits behind a firewall and is reached only through the organisation's own controls.
Virtually unlimited number of users. Limited to the number of users in the organisation.
Content is uncontrolled and unregulated. Content is controlled by the organisation's policy.
Used to reach the world — web, e-mail, commerce. Used internally — staff directory, policies, forms, internal applications.
No centralised backup — each site is responsible for its own. Centralised backup and administration.

Both use the same web technologies, which is why an intranet looks exactly like a website — the difference is who is allowed in. A third term, extranet, is an intranet with parts of it opened to trusted outsiders such as suppliers.

long.q: Define the term peer-to-peer network and client-server network.
long.a:
Peer-to-peer (P2P) network. A network in which all computers are equal — there is no dedicated server. Every machine can act as both a client, asking for resources, and a server, providing them, so each user decides what to share from their own computer. It is also called a workgroup.

Characteristics: no central server, so no expensive hardware is needed; easy and cheap to set up; each user administers their own machine; no central security, backup or control; performance degrades as machines are added; and shared files are unavailable when the owner's computer is switched off. It suits small groups of up to about ten computers — a home, a small office or a classroom.

Client-server network. A network built around one or more dedicated servers that provide services, and clients that request them. The server runs server software, holds the shared files, the database and the applications, and controls access; the client is the ordinary workstation a user works at and it never serves others.

Characteristics: centralised control and administration from one place; strong, uniform security through accounts and permissions; central backup; reliable because the server is always on and is built for the job; scales to hundreds or thousands of users; handles heavy load better. The cost is an expensive server, server software and a trained administrator, and the server is a single point of failure — if it goes down, everyone stops.

The comparison in one line: peer-to-peer shares the work and the risk equally among cheap machines, while client-server concentrates the work and the control in one powerful machine that everybody depends on.

long.q: Define the term Communication Protocol, IP Address, and MAC address.
long.a:
Communication protocol. A formal set of rules that two devices must follow to exchange data. It fixes what is communicated, how it is communicated and when, covering the format and order of messages, the meaning of each field, addressing, error detection and recovery, and the speed and synchronisation of the exchange. Without a shared protocol two devices simply cannot talk, however good the cable between them is. TCP/IP, HTTP, FTP and SMTP are protocols; TCP/IP is the suite the internet runs on.

IP address. A unique logical number that identifies a device on a network, assigned by software and used to route packets to the right destination. IPv4 is a 32-bit address written as four decimal numbers separated by dots, each octet ranging from 0 to 255 — for example 216.27.61.137. Part of the address names the network and part names the host; the subnet mask (such as 255.255.255.0) draws the line between them, and a default gateway passes traffic on to other networks. Because IPv4 addresses are running out, IPv6 uses 128-bit addresses written in hexadecimal and separated by colons.

MAC address. A unique physical address burned into the network interface card by the manufacturer, used to deliver frames between two devices on the same local link. It is 48 bits long, written as six pairs of hexadecimal digits separated by colons or hyphens — for example 00:1A:2B:3C:4D:5E. The first half identifies the manufacturer and the second half is that card's serial number.

How they work together. The IP address is the postal address that gets a packet to the right network anywhere in the world, and it can change when the device moves. The MAC address is the nameplate on the individual network card, it does not normally change, and it is used only for the final hop within one local network. Switches forward frames using MAC addresses; routers forward packets between networks using IP addresses.

quick_revision.title: The chapter in one line
points: Communication = sending + receiving + processing information by electronic media.
A computer network links two or more devices so they can share information and hardware.

6 advantages (resource sharing, centralized control, speedy comms, backup/recovery, flexible access, workgroup computing) and 5 disadvantages (expensive, security, skilled staff, network failure, complex).

quick_revision.title: Communication system
points: Basic elements: transmitter, channel, receiver.
Full chain: information source → input transducer → transmitter → channel (+noise) → receiver → output transducer → user of information.
Modes: simplex (one way), half-duplex (both, one at a time), full-duplex (both, at once).

quick_revision.title: Networks by area
points: LAN: room/building, ~100 Mbps, cheap and fast, hub/switch/NIC.
MAN: a city, connects several LANs, cable TV is an example.
WAN: cities/countries, also called Long Haul Network, uses routers/gateways, SONET/Frame Relay/ATM.

quick_revision.title: Transmission media
points: Guided: twisted pair (UTP/STP, RJ-45), coaxial (BNC, thinnet 200 m / thicknet 500 m), fibre optic (light, ~2 Gbps, S-T connector).
Unguided: microwave (line of sight, repeaters every 25–30 km, 2/4/6/11/18/23 GHz), satellite (uplink + downlink), infrared (short range, cannot pass walls).

quick_revision.title: Impairments (9)
points: Jitter, attenuation (dB), distortion, noise, echo, singing, crosstalk, bandwidth, number of receivers.

quick_revision.title: Architecture
points: Peer-to-peer = workgroup, no dedicated server, cheap, poor security.
Client-server = dedicated server, centralized administration, expensive, server failure affects all.

quick_revision.title: Addressing
points: IP = logical, 4 octets; classes A 1–126, B 128–191, C 192–223, D 224–239 (multicast), E 240–255 (reserved); 127 = loopback.
IPv6 = 128-bit hexadecimal, colons, ~3.403 × 10³⁸ addresses.
MAC = 48-bit hardware address (MM:MM:MM:SS:SS:SS), first half = manufacturer.
Subnet mask 255.255.255.0 = /24; gateway usually the first address in the subnet.

quick_revision.title: Devices
points: NIC (MAC address in ROM), MODEM (modulate/demodulate), router (network layer, best path), switch (data link layer, intelligent hub), hub (physical layer, broadcasts), bridge (data link layer, filters), repeater (physical layer, amplifies).
Bluetooth = short-range PAN (Ericsson, 1994); Wi-Fi = wireless fidelity, ad hoc mode needs no access point.

quick_revision.title: Topologies
points: Bus: trunk + 50 Ω terminators, cheapest, cable break kills the network.
Star: hub at the centre, twisted pair, most popular for LANs (reliable, no collisions, easy fault finding).
Ring: closed loop, token passing, MAU, one direction, one failure breaks the ring.
Selection criteria: cost, data error rate, simplicity, data security, transmission speed, flexibility, maintainability, volume of data traffic.

quick_revision.title: OSI model
points: 7 layers: Application, Presentation, Session, Transport, Network, Data Link, Physical (All People Seem To Need Data Processing).
Purpose: standards so that hardware and software from different vendors interoperate.

quick_revision.title: Lab commands
points: ipconfig → shows IP address, subnet mask, default gateway (ipconfig /all for everything).
ping <address or name> → tests connectivity and response time.
T568A vs T568B: pins 1,2,3,6 are the pairs that swap between the two standards.

teaching_plan.activity: Introduce communication with the history timeline (telegraphy → telephony → radio → transistor → satellite/fibre). Draw the block diagram and the three communication modes on the board. Drill the 6 advantages and 5 disadvantages as a chant.
LAN / MAN / WAN with the three figures, then the 8-point LAN vs WAN table as a fill-in-the-blanks worksheet.
Pass around real RJ-45, coaxial and (if possible) fibre cable ends. Compare guided vs unguided and build the speed ladder: twisted pair < coaxial < fibre.
Nine impairment terms as flash cards. Then peer-to-peer vs client-server using the school computer lab as the example.
IP addressing on the board: convert 192.168.1.10 to binary, classify addresses into A–E, and work the 192.168.40.x subnet example step by step.
Device gallery: NIC, modem, router, switch, hub, bridge, repeater. Show the real devices if the lab has them; otherwise use the figures. End with the switch vs hub table.
Draw bus, star and ring on the board and ask students which one their school lab uses and why. Cover the 8 selection criteria.
Build the OSI stack with seven student volunteers holding layer cards and passing a 'data' envelope down and back up.
In the computer lab: ipconfig, ipconfig /all, ping the gateway, ping google.com, then locate the IPv4 Properties dialog. Demonstrate cabling with an RJ-45 and clamper.
Work through the 10 short and 9 long questions orally, then run the 33 MCQs as a timed quiz and review the answers with the class.

blocks.text: Web technology is the mechanism that enables two or more computing devices to communicate over a network — mainly the Internet. Web technologies are the various tools and techniques that are utilised in the process of communication between different types of devices over the Internet.

In the term web technology, the web refers to the World Wide Web, more commonly known as WWW. All the web pages, documents and other resources are identified and located with the help of their URLs on the Internet; collectively they form the World Wide Web. Technology refers to the tools and techniques that make these resources available on the Web.

blocks.caption: Chapter opener illustration — Web Technology II.

blocks.text: Key Components of Web Technology

blocks.title: Web technologies include:
items: Web browsers and the fundamentals of web-app development.
Different programming / scripting languages and frameworks used in the development of websites.
Databases that are used at the back end to store data required or collected by websites.
Some protocols — that is, the rules for communicating on the web (HTTP, HTTPS, TCP/IP, FTP…).
Graphic, audio-visual and other multimedia elements.
Data formats that are usually used to transmit data over the Internet (HTML, XML, JSON, CSS…).

blocks.caption: Web technology in practice: devices and networks sharing resources over the Internet.

blocks.title: Exam note
blocks.text: Start this chapter by opening a browser's View Source and then the Network tab on any website. Students see HTML (structure), CSS (presentation) and JavaScript (behaviour) arriving as three separate downloads — which is exactly the split this chapter teaches: HTML + CSS + client script on the browser, PHP + MySQL on the server.

This chapter is therefore built around two technologies that sit on opposite sides of that split: JavaScript (client-side scripting, runs in the browser) and PHP (server-side scripting, runs on the web server and talks to a MySQL database).
Scripting Language

A language similar to a programming language that is used to create dynamic web documents. It provides the programming logic in web development. Scripting languages are mostly used to automate processes at the application level; at the command line, or through a web server, they execute programs running on a web server and display the appropriate results to the users.

blocks.title: The one-line distinction
blocks.text: A scripting language is different from a programming language because after translation it generates markup code (HTML code), whereas a programming language generates machine code.
Type of Scripting Language

items: Client-side scripting language.
Server-side scripting language.

blocks.text: Client-Side Scripting

Client-side scripting generates code that can run on the client end (the browser) without needing server-side processing. These scripts are placed inside an HTML document. Client-side scripting can be used to examine the user's form for errors before it is submitted, and to change content according to the user's input. The web requires three elements for its functioning: the client, the database and the server.

Effective client-side scripting can significantly reduce the server load. It is designed to run as a scripting language using a web browser as the host program. When a user requests a web page through the browser, the server simply sends the HTML and CSS as plain text, and the browser interprets and renders the content on the client end.
Server-Side Scripting

Server-side scripting is a method of designing websites so that the process or user request is run on the originating server. Server-side scripts provide an interface to the user, limit access to proprietary data and help keep control of the script source code. Many languages may be used to create these scripts — ASP, JavaScript using SSJS (for example node.js), Perl, PHP, R and Ruby.

blocks.title: How the two work together
blocks.text: Client-side and server-side scripting work in a coordinated manner. Client-side scripting emphasises making the interface of the web application more appealing and functional. Server-side scripting emphasises data-access methods, error handling and fast processing.
Difference between Server-side Scripting and Client-side Scripting

blocks.caption: Server-side vs client-side scripting
head: S.N.
Client-Side Scripting
Server-Side Scripting
rows: Used at the front end, which users can see from the browser.
Used at the back end, where the source code is not viewable and is hidden from the browser.
Its main function is to provide the requested output to the end user.
Its primary function is to manipulate and provide access to the respective database as per the request.
It runs on the user's computer.
It runs on the web server.
Does not need any server interaction.
When a server-side script is processed, it communicates with the server.
Usually depends on the browser and its version.
Any server-side technology can be used; it does not depend on the client.
Useful in minimising the load on the server.
Useful in customising web pages and implementing dynamic changes in websites.
Not as secure — the client-side script is visible to users.
More secure than client-side scripting, because the scripts are hidden from the client end.
Languages involved: HTML, CSS and JavaScript.
Languages involved: PHP, ASP.NET, Python, C#, JSP, etc.

blocks.text: Difference between Programming Language and Scripting Language

blocks.caption: Programming language vs scripting language
head: S.N.
Programming Language
Scripting Language
rows: A set of instructions that can be provided to a computer to achieve a specific output.
A programming language supporting scripts written exclusively for a special run-time environment, to automate the execution of a specific action / function.
Compressed into a smaller package that does not need to be interpreted by another language or application.
Written in one language and interpreted within another program — for example, JavaScript is incorporated within HTML and interpreted by the browser.
Used to create dynamic web applications.
Does not create an .exe file; it requires a host to execute.
All programming languages are not scripting languages.
All scripting languages are programming languages.
Normally uses a compiler to convert source code into machine code.
Normally uses an interpreter to convert source code into machine code.

blocks.text: Exam trap: the book's own example list puts PHP under programming languages in row 7 while the rest of the chapter calls PHP a server-side scripting language. Teach it as: PHP is a scripting language (interpreted, no .exe) that is also a full programming language. If asked 'is PHP compiled or interpreted?' the answer is interpreted.

Computer Internet technology refers to the devices, software, hardware and transmission protocols used to connect computers together in order to receive or send data from one computer to another — within a small network, or as part of a small network inside a larger network such as the Internet. Included are local-area networks (LANs), wide-area networks (WANs), bridging, switching, routing, voice and data integration, wireless integration, dial-up technology, cable access technology, network security and network management.

The Internet is a vast network of networks that spans the entire globe. Data are transferred from computer to computer and from network to network using packet-switching technology and a suite of Internet protocols called TCP/IP, after its two most important protocols.
A Short History (very frequently asked)

blocks.caption: Milestones in the development of the Internet
head: Year
Event
rows: The Soviet Union launched Sputnik, the first earth-orbiting satellite. The United States awoke to the fact that it was being overtaken in the space race.
One result of that realisation was the establishment of the Advanced Research Projects Agency (ARPA).
ARPA set up a research project called ARPANET to create a secure, de-centralised network able to function when parts of the infrastructure were destroyed or disabled (for example in a nuclear war).
Tim Berners-Lee, a computer scientist at the CERN laboratories in Switzerland, developed the hypertext-based information system that became the World Wide Web.
The military closed down ARPANET; several commercial organisations offered Internet access to the general public for the first time.

The National Centre for Supercomputing Applications (NCSA), at the University of Illinois, released the Mosaic browser — the first browser to offer a user-friendly graphical interface that could display images as well as text.
Growing public interest in the Internet.
Use of the term 'Internet' had become commonplace.

blocks.text: How the Internet Has Changed Communication

items: Electronic mail — although it predates the Internet, e-mail now lets businesses and private individuals send text and file attachments to anyone, anywhere in the world.
Social interaction — Internet Relay Chat (IRC), social networking sites such as Facebook and Myspace, and multi-player online gaming.
Business — video conferencing with colleagues, customers and suppliers anywhere in the world.

Telephony — even private long-distance and international calls can be made using Voice Over IP (VOIP) technologies such as Skype, at a fraction of the cost of conventional landlines, or free of charge if both parties have an Internet connection, a computer and a suitable headset or Internet phone.

blocks.title: Memory hook for the timeline
blocks.text: 57 Sputnik → 58 ARPA → 69 ARPANET → 89 WWW (Berners-Lee / CERN) → 92 commercial access → 93 Mosaic → 96 the word 'Internet' goes mainstream.
There are typically three ways to add JavaScript to a web page:

items: Embedding the JavaScript code between a pair of <SCRIPT> and </SCRIPT> tags.
Creating an external JavaScript file with the .js extension and then loading it within the page through the src attribute of the <SCRIPT> tag.
Placing the JavaScript code directly inside an HTML tag using special tag attributes such as onclick, onmouseover, onkeypress, onload, etc.

blocks.text: i. Embedding the JavaScript code

We can embed JavaScript directly within web pages by placing it between <SCRIPT> and </SCRIPT>. The <SCRIPT> tag indicates to the browser that the contained statements are to be interpreted as executable script and not HTML.

<!DOCTYPE HTML>
<HTML>
<HEAD>
<TITLE>Embedding JavaScript </TITLE>
</HEAD>
<BODY>
<SCRIPT>
var greet='Hello World!';
document.write(greet);   //Prints: Hello World!
</SCRIPT>
</BODY>
</HTML>
Output: Hello World!
ii. Calling an external JavaScript file

You can also place your JavaScript code into a separate file with a .js extension, then call that file in your document through the src attribute of the <script> tag. This is useful when you want the same scripts available to multiple documents — it saves repeating the same task and makes the website much easier to maintain.
<script src="js/hello.js"></script>
Create a JavaScript file named hello.js and place the following code in it:
Now call that external JavaScript file within a web page using the <SCRIPT> tag:

<!DOCTYPE html>
<html>
<head>
   <title>External JS Demo</title>
   <script src="js/hello.js"></script>
</head>
<body>
   <input type="button" onclick="sayHello()" value="Click Me">
</body>
</html>

blocks.caption: Output: the Click Me button and the alert box produced by the external file.

blocks.text: iii. Placing the JavaScript code inline

You can also place JavaScript inline by inserting it directly inside the HTML tag using the special tag events like onclick, onmouseover, onkeypress, onload, etc. Avoid placing a large amount of JavaScript inline — it clutters up your HTML and makes the JavaScript difficult to maintain.

<!DOCTYPE HTML>
<HTML lang="en">
<HEAD>
   <META charset="UTF-8">
   <TITLE>Inline JavaScript </TITLE>
</HEAD>
<BODY>
   <BUTTON onclick="alert('Hello World!')">Click Me</BUTTON>
</BODY>
</HTML>

Board-work: write all three versions of the same 'Hello World' on the board and ask which one you would use for a 40-page school website. The answer is (ii) — one external .js file, cached by the browser, edited in one place.

JavaScript (abbreviated JS) is an interpreted scripting language that enables the creation of dynamically updating content, controlling multimedia and animating images using a few lines of code. In general, scripting languages are easier to learn and faster to code. It is considered an object-based scripting language because every identifier in JS is an object and we do not need a class to create an object.

blocks.caption: JavaScript — the object-based scripting language of the web.

blocks.text: JavaScript is a client-side scripting language that is one of the core technologies of the World Wide Web, along with HTML and CSS. Around 96% of websites use JavaScript on the client side for web page behaviour, and almost all web browsers have a dedicated JavaScript engine to execute the code on the user's device.

It is a light-weight, object-based scripting language used by many websites for scripting web pages. It is an interpreted, full-fledged programming language that enables dynamic interactivity on websites when applied to an HTML document. Using JavaScript, users can build modern web applications that interact directly without reloading the page every time.
Features of JavaScript

items: All popular web browsers support JavaScript, as they provide built-in execution environments.
It is a structured programming language and follows the syntax and structure of the C programming language.
It is an object-based programming language that uses prototypes rather than classes for inheritance.
It is light-weight and interpreted.
It is a case-sensitive language.
It is supported on several operating systems, including Windows and Mac OS.
It gives the user good control over the web browser.

blocks.text: Uses of JavaScript
JavaScript is used to create interactive websites. It is mainly used for:

items: Client-side validation.
Dynamic drop-down menus.
Displaying date and time.
Displaying pop-up windows and dialog boxes (alert, confirm and prompt dialog boxes).
Displaying clocks.

blocks.title: JS is not Java
blocks.text: JavaScript has nothing to do with Java apart from the name and a C-like syntax. Java is compiled to byte-code and runs on a JVM; JavaScript is interpreted by the browser. Never write 'JavaScript is a version of Java' in an exam answer.

JavaScript is the language of the web: if we want to code for the web, we need to know JavaScript. It has grown into a powerful and complex language with features such as classes, promises, arrow functions, generators, string templates and many others.
Language Fundamentals

blocks.title: The fundamentals covered in this chapter are:
items: Variables.
Data types.
Arithmetic, assignment and comparison operators.
Unary, logical, comma and spread operators.
Operator precedence.
Strict mode.
Functions.

Data types basically specify what kind of data can be stored and manipulated within a program. JavaScript provides different data types to hold different types of values. There are two types of data types in JavaScript: primitive and non-primitive (reference).
i. Primitive Data Types
Primitive data types can hold only one value at a time. There are five primitive data types in JavaScript:

blocks.caption: Primitive data types in JavaScript
head: Data type
Description
rows: Represents a sequence of characters, e.g. "hello".
Represents a Boolean value, either false or true.
Represents null, i.e. no value at all.

blocks.text: ii. Non-primitive Data Types
Non-primitive data types can hold collections of values and more complex entities:

blocks.caption: Non-primitive (reference) data types in JavaScript
head: Data type
Description
rows: Represents an instance through which we can access members.
Represents a group of similar values.

blocks.text: Exam answer (Q12, Q28): 'Data types in JavaScript are primitive and non-primitive.' Primitive = String, Number, Boolean, Undefined, Null. Non-primitive = Object, Array, RegExp. Notice JavaScript has no separate int / float / char — there is only Number.
JavaScript Variables

An identifier whose value may change during the execution of the program. A JavaScript variable is simply the name of a storage location. There are two types of variables in JavaScript: local variable and global variable.
Rules while declaring a JavaScript variable

items: The name must start with a letter (a–z or A–Z), an underscore ( _ ), or a dollar ( $ ) sign.
After the first letter we can use a single digit or a combination of digits (0–9) — for example, value12.
JavaScript variables are case sensitive — for example, a and A are different variables.

blocks.text: <script> var x = 10; var y = 20; var z = x + y; document.write(z); </script> → Output: 30
JavaScript Variable Scope

The scope of a variable is the region of your program in which it is defined. Scope in JavaScript defines the accessibility of variables, objects and functions. A variable declared without the var keyword becomes global irrespective of where it is declared. There are two types of variable scope in JavaScript:
i. JavaScript Local Variable
A JavaScript local variable is declared inside a block or function. It is accessible within the function or block only.

<script>
function abc(){
   var x = 10;      //local variable
}
</script>

//Or:

<script>
if(10 < 13){
   var y = 20;      //JavaScript local variable
}
</script>
ii. JavaScript Global Variable
A JavaScript global variable is accessible from any function. A variable declared outside a function, or declared with the window object, is known as a global variable.

<script>
var data = 200;          //global variable
function a(){
   document.writeln(data);
}
function b(){
   document.writeln(data);
}
a();                     //calling JavaScript function
b();
</script>
Three Ways to Declare a Variable: var, let and const
In JavaScript we can declare a variable in three different ways, using the var, let and const keywords. Each keyword is used under specific conditions.
1. var
Used to declare the variable globally; the variable is accessible globally and is changeable. Good for short code — if the code gets huge you will get confused.

<!DOCTYPE html>
<html>
<body>
<script>
var a = 30;
var b = 26;
var dif = a - b;
document.write("The value of difference is: " + dif);
</script>
</body>
</html>

// Output
The value of difference is: 4

blocks.title: Note
blocks.text: In this example, a, b and dif are variables.
2. let
Used to declare the variable locally; the variable is accessible only within its block and is changeable. It is the better choice when the code gets huge.

<!DOCTYPE html>
<html>
<body>
<script>
let x = 20;
let y = 6;
let z = x * y;
document.write("The value of z is: " + z);
</script>
</body>
</html>

// Output
The value of product, z is: 120
3. const

Also declares the variable locally, with block scope like let. The difference between let and const is that a variable declared with const cannot be reassigned — so you must assign the value while declaring it.

blocks.title: History you must know for the exam
blocks.text: The let and const keywords were included in 2015 AD. Older browsers support only var. The var keyword was used in all JavaScript code from 1995 to 2015. A const keyword is used to declare values that are constant and cannot be changed. Variables are containers for storing values.

blocks.text: Function

Functions are blocks of code with names. When a block of code is frequently required in a program, we define a function. A function is a group of reusable code that can be called anywhere in your program. This eliminates the need to write the same code again and again and helps programmers write modular code. Functions allow a programmer to divide an extensive program into a number of small and manageable functions.

Like any other advanced programming language, JavaScript supports all the features necessary to write modular code using functions. You have already seen functions such as alert() and write() — they were written in core JavaScript only once, and we simply keep calling them. JavaScript allows us to write our own functions as well.
Advantages of JavaScript functions

items: Reusability of the code: we can call a function several times, so it saves coding in the program.
Less coding: it makes our program compact; there is no need to write many lines of code each time to perform a common task.

blocks.text: Function Definition

Before we use a function we need to define it. The most common way to define a function in JavaScript is by using the function keyword, followed by a unique function name, a list of parameters (which may be empty) and a statement block surrounded by curly braces.
Calling a Function

<html>
<head>
<script type = "text/javascript">
function sayHello() {
   document.write ("Hello there!");
}
</script>
</head>
<body>
<script>
sayHello();
</script>
</body>
</html>

// Output
Hello there!
Function Parameters

A function without parameters is only half the story. There is a facility to pass different parameters while calling a function; these passed parameters can be captured inside the function and manipulated. A function can take multiple parameters separated by a comma.
The Return Statement

A JavaScript function can have an optional return statement. It is required if you want to return a value from a function, and it should be the last statement in the function. For example, you can pass two numbers to a function and expect the function to return their multiplication to the calling program.

blocks.text: Control Structures

Control structures define the flow of execution of data within a program. They are essential for directing the flow of a JavaScript program, enabling developers to create complex and dynamic behaviour in their applications. There are different forms of control structures, including conditional statements (if, if-else, if-else-if, nested if and switch-case), loops (for, while and do-while) and the switch statement.
1. Conditional Statements
Conditional statements allow the program to execute different blocks of code based on specified conditions. They include:

items: a. if statement
b. if-else statements
c. if-else-if statements (nested if)
d. switch-case statement

blocks.text: a. if statement
It evaluates the content only if the expression is true.
b. if-else statement
c. if-else-if statement
The if…else if… statement is an advanced form of if…else that allows JavaScript to make a correct decision out of several conditions.

There is nothing special about this code — it is just a series of if statements, where each if is part of the else clause of the previous statement. The statement(s) are executed based on the true condition; if none of the conditions is true, the else block is executed.
d. switch-case statement

The basic syntax of the switch statement is to give an expression to evaluate and several different statements to execute based on the value of the expression. The interpreter checks each case against the value of the expression until a match is found. If nothing matches, a default condition is used.
Why break matters: without it, execution 'falls through' to the next case and prints several lines at once. This is the single most common JavaScript exam error — always pair every case with a break.
Loops in JavaScript
JavaScript loops are used to iterate, or repeat, the execution of code using for, while, do-while or for-in loops.
a. for loop
The for loop iterates the elements for a fixed number of times. It should be used when the number of iterations is known.
b. while loop

The while loop is mainly used when the number of iterations is unknown. Its purpose is to execute a statement or code block repeatedly as long as the expression is true; once the expression becomes false the loop is exited.
c. do-while loop

The do…while loop is similar to the while loop except that the condition check happens at the end of the loop. This means the loop will always be executed at least once, even if the condition is false.

blocks.title: Why the do-while example prints once
blocks.text: The condition is count < 0 and count starts at 0, so the test is false — but because the test happens after the body, the body still ran once and printed Current Count : 0. This is the clearest demonstration of the difference between while and do-while.

blocks.text: Object based Programming

JavaScript is an object-based language — everything is an object in JavaScript. A JavaScript object is an entity having state and behaviour (properties and methods). Examples: car, pen, bike, chair, glass, keyboard, monitor.

JavaScript is template based, not class based. We do not create a class to get an object — we create objects directly. (This is exactly why the chapter calls it object based rather than object oriented.)
Creating Objects in JavaScript (3 ways)
1. By object literal
Syntax: object = {property1:value1, property2:value2 … propertyN:valueN}; — the property and value are separated by a colon.

<html>
<body>
<script>
emp = {id:1, name:"Anil Sharma", salary:15000}
document.write(emp.id+" "+emp.name+" "+emp.salary);
</script>
</body>
</html>

// Output
1 Anil Sharma 15000
2. By creating an instance of Object directly (using new keyword)
3. By using an object constructor (using new keyword)
Here we create a function with arguments and assign each argument value to the current object using the this keyword. The this keyword refers to the current object.

<html>
<body>
<script>
function emp(id, name, salary){
   this.id = id;
   this.name = name;
   this.salary = salary;
}
e = new emp(1, "Anil Sharma", 15000);
document.write(e.id+" "+e.name+" "+e.salary);
</script>
</body>
</html>

// Output
1 Anil Sharma 15000

blocks.text: Event Handling

JavaScript's interaction with HTML is handled through events that occur when the user or the browser manipulates a page. When the page loads, that is an event. When the user clicks a button, that click is an event. Other examples include pressing a key, closing a window and resizing a window.

Developers can use these events to execute JavaScript-coded responses, which cause buttons to close windows, messages to be displayed to users, data to be validated and virtually any other type of response imaginable.
Image Object

The image object embeds an image or video clip into the current document. The <img> tag allows the insertion of .jpg, .png, .bmp and .gif image files into an HTML document. If we want to create one or more clickable regions within an image, we use the <map> element.
Methods that return the image object

items: document.createElement("img")
new Image(width, height)
images.item(nameOrIndex [, subIndex])
images.namedItem(name)

Event Object

When an event occurs in HTML, the event belongs to a certain event object — a mouse click event belongs to the Mouse Event object. All events are based on the Event object and inherit all of its properties and methods. The event object represents an object that contains information about an event that has occurred.
Types of Event Object
Some of the seven event objects are listed below.
1. onclick
The most frequently used event type; it occurs when a user clicks the left button of the mouse. We can put validation or a warning against this event type.

The onmouseover event triggers when we bring the mouse over any element, and onmouseout triggers when we move the mouse out of that element.

The onfocus event occurs when an element gets focus; it is most often used with <input>, <select> and <a>. The onblur event occurs when an object loses focus; it is most often used with form validation code (for example when the user leaves a form field). It is the opposite of the onfocus event.

a.addEventListener("focus", myFocus, true);
a.addEventListener("blur", myBlur, true);
function myFocus() {
   document.getElementById("myInput").style.backgroundColor = "red";
}
function myBlur() {
   document.getElementById("myInput").style.backgroundColor = "";
}

blocks.text: Form Object

The form object is used to access an HTML form. If a user wants to access all forms within a document, the forms array can be used. The form object is actually a property of the document object that is uniquely created by the browser for each form present in a document. We can access a <form> element by using getElementById(), for example var x = document.getElementById("myForm");
A form is used to collect user input through elements such as text fields, check boxes, radio buttons, select options, text areas and submit buttons.
List of Fruits:

blocks.title: Note
blocks.text: The form object can also be accessed using an indexing method similar to the image object — for example document.form[0].fruit.value;
3.11.1 Form Validation

Form validation used to occur at the server: the client entered all the necessary data, pressed Submit, and only then did the server check it. If the data were incorrect or simply missing, the server had to send all the data back to the client and request that the form be resubmitted with correct information. This was a really lengthy process that put a lot of burden on the server.
JavaScript provides a way to validate the form's data on the client's computer before sending it to the web server. Form validation generally performs two functions.

items: Basic form validation: first of all the form must be checked to make sure all the mandatory fields are filled in. It requires just a loop through each field in the form, checking for data.
Data format validation: secondly, the data that have been entered must be checked for correct form and value. Your code must include appropriate logic to test the correctness of the data.

blocks.text: The sample form

Name
EMail
Zip Code
Country
Output (the rendered form): Name — EMail — Zip code — Country [choose yours] — Submit.
1. Basic Form Validation
In the form above we are calling validate() to validate the data when the onsubmit event occurs. Here is the implementation of that validate() function.

<script type = "text/javascript">
function validate() {
   if( document.myForm.Name.value == "" ) {
      alert( "Please provide your name!" );
      document.myForm.Name.focus() ;
      return false;
   }
   if( document.myForm.EMail.value == "" ) {
      alert( "Please provide your Email!" );
      document.myForm.EMail.focus() ;
      return false;
   }
   if( document.myForm.Zip.value == "" || isNaN( document.myForm.Zip.value ) ||
       document.myForm.Zip.value.length != 5 ) {
      alert( "Please provide a zip in the format #####." );
      document.myForm.Zip.focus() ;
      return false;
   }
   if( document.myForm.Country.value == "-1" ) {
      alert( "Please provide your country!" );
      return false;
   }
   return( true );
}
</script>
2. Data Format Validation

Now we see how to validate entered form data before submitting it to the web server. The following example validates an email address. An email address must contain at least an '@' sign and a dot (.). Also the '@' must not be the first character of the email address, and the last dot must be at least one character after the '@' sign.

<script type = "text/javascript">
function validateEmail() {
   var emailID = document.myForm.EMail.value;
   atpos = emailID.indexOf("@");
   dotpos = emailID.lastIndexOf(".");
   if (atpos < 1 || ( dotpos - atpos < 2 )) {
      alert("Please enter correct email ID")
      document.myForm.EMail.focus() ;
      return false;
   }
   return( true );
}
</script>

Read the email test carefully: atpos < 1 rejects an address where '@' is missing (indexOf returns -1) or is the very first character (index 0). dotpos - atpos < 2 rejects 'a@b' with no room for a dot after the '@'. Point out that returning false from onsubmit cancels the submission — that is the whole mechanism of client-side validation.
3.11.2 jQuery

A lightweight ('write less, do more'), fast, small and feature-rich JavaScript library. It makes it much easier to code JavaScript on a website: it reduces development time, makes it easy to add animation and event-handling programs, simplifies HTML document navigating and Ajax interactions, and provides an easy-to-use API for rapid web development.

JavaScript is a client-side (in-the-browser) scripting language, whereas jQuery is a library (framework) built with JavaScript. Using jQuery we can replace multiple lines of JavaScript code with a single line.
Features of jQuery

items: HTML/DOM manipulation. (DOM stands for Document Object Model — an application programming interface (API) for HTML.)
CSS manipulation.
HTML event methods.
Effects and animations.
AJAX.
Utilities.

blocks.text: In addition, jQuery has plugins for most tasks.
Why jQuery?

blocks.title: Reasons to use jQuery:

Easily integrated with other IDEs.
Faster.
Animation becomes easy.
SEO friendly.
Runs in all major browsers.

blocks.text: jQuery is the most popular and most widely used framework. It requires much less code, has a wide range of plugins all over the Internet, and is easy to implement. It works for all browsers and makes web pages more interactive, simple and user-friendly; it can also be optimised in terms of SEO. There are lots of other JavaScript libraries, but jQuery is probably the most popular and the most extendable — many of the biggest companies on the web use it, such as Google, Microsoft, IBM and Netflix.

jQuery Selectors

jQuery selectors are used to select and manipulate HTML elements; they are a very important part of the jQuery library. With them you can find or select HTML elements based on their id, classes, attributes, types and much more, from a DOM. In simple words: selectors select one or more HTML elements, and once an element is selected you can perform various operations on it. All jQuery selectors start with a dollar sign and parentheses, e.g. $() — known as the factory function.

blocks.text: Some common Functions used in jQuery

items: html() — used to change the entire content of the selected elements; it replaces the selected element content with new content.

text() — used to set or return the text content of the selected elements. To return content, it returns the combined text content of all matched elements without the HTML markup. To set content, it overwrites the content of all matched elements.
val() — two uses: to get the current value of the first element in the set of matched elements, and to set the value of every matched element.

css() — used to get (return) or set style properties or values for selected elements. (a) Return a CSS property: get the value of a specified CSS property. (b) Set a CSS property: set a specific value for all matched elements.
hide() — used to hide the selected elements.
show() — used to show the selected elements.
toggle() — a special method used to toggle between hide() and show(): it shows the hidden elements and hides the shown element.

if (number > 0) {
   document.write("The number is positive");

// check if number is 0

3. Find the factorial of a given positive number

<html>
<head>
   <title> JS program to find the factorial </title>
</head>
<body>
<script>
// program to find the factorial of a number
// take input from the user
const number = parseInt(prompt('Enter a positive integer: '));
// checking if number is negative
if (number < 0) {
   alert('Error! Factorial for negative number does not exist.');
}
// if number is 0
else if (number === 0) {
   alert("The factorial of "+number+" is 1");
}
// if number is positive
else {
   let fact = 1;
   for (i = 1; i <= number; i++) {
      fact *= i;
   }
   alert('The factorial of '+number+' is '+ fact);
}
</script>
</body>
</html>
