short.q: Write short notes on Internet technology.
short.a:
Internet technology is the collection of tools, protocols and services that let computers anywhere in the world exchange information. It grew out of ARPANET, the 1969 research network built to survive the loss of part of its infrastructure, and it runs on the TCP/IP protocol suite, which breaks data into packets, addresses them and routes them independently to the destination, where they are reassembled.

Its main components are:

  • The World Wide Web (WWW) — the collection of pages and resources identified by a URL and linked by hyperlinks.
  • HTTP/HTTPS — the protocol a browser uses to request a page and a server uses to return it.
  • HTML, CSS and JavaScript — the three core languages: structure, presentation and behaviour.
  • DNS — the naming system that turns a name like www.example.com into an IP address.
  • E-mail (SMTP, POP3, IMAP) and file transfer (FTP) — the classic services.
  • Server-side scripting such as PHP, used with a database to build dynamic sites.

An ISP provides the connection, and a browser is the client that makes the whole thing usable.

short.q: Differentiate between server-side and client-side scripting.
short.a:
Client-side scriptingServer-side scripting
The script is downloaded with the page and executed by the user's browser. The script is executed on the web server before the page is sent.
JavaScript is the main language. PHP, ASP, JSP, Python and similar languages are used.
The source code is visible to the user (View Source). Only the output — plain HTML — reaches the browser; the source stays hidden.
Does not need the server or a round trip, so it is instant. Every request must travel to the server and back.
Cannot access databases or files on the server. Can read and write databases and files on the server.
Used for validation, menus, animation, and interaction with the DOM. Used for login, database work, personalised pages, and generating content.
Depends on the browser — it can be disabled, and different browsers behave differently. Independent of the browser, because the browser only receives HTML.
Less secure — never trust it for validation, because the user can change it. More secure — the checks happen where the user cannot reach them.

A real application uses both: JavaScript for immediate feedback, and server-side code for anything that matters.

short.q: How can you add JavaScript to an HTML page? Illustrate with the example.
short.a:
JavaScript is added to an HTML page in three ways.

1. Inline — written directly in an HTML event attribute. Quickest for one small action, but it mixes behaviour into the markup and is now discouraged.

<button onclick="alert('Namaste!');">Click me</button>

2. Embedded (internal) — placed in a <script> element inside the page, usually just before </body> so the HTML exists before the script runs. This is the usual way for code that belongs to a single page.

<!DOCTYPE html>
<html>
<head>
    <title>My Page</title>
</head>
<body>
    <h1>Hello</h1>
    <p id="demo"></p>

    <script>
        document.getElementById("demo").innerHTML = "Namaste from JavaScript!";
    </script>
</body>
</html>

3. External — written in a separate .js file and linked with the src attribute. This is the best practice for anything substantial: the same file is reused by every page, the browser caches it, and the markup stays clean. Note that a script with a src attribute must be empty — inline code alongside src is ignored.

<!-- in the page -->
<script src="script.js"></script>
// script.js
function greet() {
    document.getElementById("demo").innerHTML = "Namaste from an external file!";
}
window.onload = greet;

Historically the tag was written <script type="text/javascript">; in HTML5 the type attribute is optional because JavaScript is the default.

short.q: Explain different data types used in JavaScript.
short.a:
JavaScript has two groups of data types.

Primitive (value) types — the simplest values, which are copied when assigned:

  • Number — all numeric values, integers and floating point alike. var n = 25; var price = 99.90; It also holds the special values Infinity, -Infinity and NaN (not a number).
  • String — text, in single or double quotes. var name = "Ram"; Strings are immutable; they have a length property and methods such as toUpperCase() and split().
  • Boolean — only true or false, produced by comparisons and used in conditions. var pass = true;
  • Undefined — a variable that has been declared but never given a value. var x; // x is undefined
  • Null — an intentional, explicit "no value". var y = null;
  • Symbol (ES6) — a unique, immutable identifier, mainly used as an object key.
  • BigInt (ES2020) — integers larger than the safe Number limit, written with an n suffix.

Reference (object) types — the variable holds a reference, not the value itself:

  • Object — an unordered collection of key/value pairs: var student = {name: "Ram", age: 18};
  • Array — an ordered, indexed list: var marks = [80, 75, 90];
  • Function — a callable object: function add(a, b) { return a + b; }
  • Date, RegExp and the wrapper objects String, Number and Boolean.

JavaScript is dynamically typed: you declare with var, let or const and the type is decided at run time from the value, so the same variable can hold a number and later a string. That is checked with the typeof operator, and the one to be careful of is typeof null, which reports "object" — a long-standing quirk of the language.

short.q: What is jQuery? Write down its uses.
short.a:
jQuery is a fast, small, open-source JavaScript library, released by John Resig in 2006. Its motto is "write less, do more": it wraps the awkward parts of plain JavaScript in short, chainable methods and hides the differences between browsers, so the same code works everywhere. It is added by linking the library file and then writing code inside $(document).ready(...).

Its main uses are:

  • Selecting and traversing the DOM with CSS-style selectors — $("#id"), $(".class"), $("p") — far shorter than document.getElementById.
  • Event handling with .click(), .on(), .hover(), .submit().
  • Manipulating content and style — .html(), .text(), .val(), .css(), .addClass(), .append().
  • Effects and animation — .hide(), .show(), .fadeIn(), .slideUp(), .animate().
  • AJAX — $.get(), $.post(), $.ajax() exchange data with the server and update part of a page without reloading it.
  • Cross-browser compatibility and a huge ecosystem of plugins for sliders, date pickers, form validation and menus.

Example: $("#btn").click(function(){ $("#box").fadeOut(); }); — one line that hides an element smoothly when a button is clicked.

short.q: What is event handling in JavaScript?
short.a:
There are three ways to attach a handler, of which the third is the modern recommendation.

1. Inline, as an HTML attribute — quick, but it mixes JavaScript into the markup and only one handler can be attached.

<button onclick="sayHello()">Click</button>
<script>
    function sayHello() { alert("Namaste!"); }
</script>

2. As a DOM property — keeps the JavaScript out of the markup, but still allows only one handler per event.

<button id="btn">Click</button>
<script>
    document.getElementById("btn").onclick = function () {
        alert("Namaste!");
    };
</script>

3. With addEventListener() — the recommended way. It keeps markup and behaviour separate, lets several handlers be attached to the same event, and lets a handler be removed later with removeEventListener().

<button id="btn">Click</button>
<script>
    var btn = document.getElementById("btn");

    function greet(event) {
        alert("Namaste! You clicked " + event.target.tagName);
    }

    btn.addEventListener("click", greet);
</script>

The handler automatically receives an event object describing what happened — which key, which mouse button, the co-ordinates, and event.target, the element the event came from. Calling event.preventDefault() cancels the browser's default action, which is exactly how form validation stops a form with empty fields from being submitted. Events also bubble up from the element that was clicked to its parents, which is why a single listener on a container can serve every button inside it.

short.q: What is PHP? Explain its uses and advantages.
short.a:
PHP (PHP: Hypertext Preprocessor) is an open-source, server-side scripting language designed for web development. PHP code is embedded in an HTML page inside <?php ... ?> tags, runs on the web server, and produces plain HTML that is sent to the browser — the user never sees the PHP source. It was created by Rasmus Lerdorf and works with Apache or Nginx and, classically, a MySQL database.

Uses:

  • building dynamic pages whose content changes with the user, the time or the database;
  • processing HTML forms — login, registration, search, contact and feedback;
  • working with databases: creating, reading, updating and deleting records;
  • session and cookie handling, so a site can remember a logged-in user;
  • file upload and download, and reading and writing files on the server;
  • sending e-mail, generating PDFs and images;
  • powering content management systems and shops — WordPress, Drupal and Magento are all written in PHP.

Advantages:

  • Free and open source, with no licence cost.
  • Easy to learn — the syntax resembles C and the embedding model is simple.
  • Cross-platform — runs on Windows, Linux and macOS, with Apache or Nginx.
  • Excellent database support, especially MySQL.
  • Fast — it is interpreted but well optimised, and it runs on the server, so nothing is required of the client.
  • Secure in the sense that the source never reaches the browser; only the generated HTML does.
  • Huge community — abundant documentation, frameworks (Laravel, CodeIgniter) and hosting that supports it everywhere.

Its main weaknesses are an inconsistent standard library and a long history of insecure example code, so it must be written carefully.

short.q: Write down the basic PHP syntax and an example of a PHP program.
short.a:
Basic PHP syntax. A PHP script is an ordinary HTML file; everything between <?php and ?> is executed on the server and replaced by its output. Every statement ends with a semicolon, variables begin with $, comments use // or # for one line and /* ... */ for a block, and text is printed with echo or print. Strings are joined with a dot, not a plus sign.

<?php
    // a one-line comment
    $name   = "Ram";        // variables start with $
    $age    = 18;
    $height = 5.6;

    echo "Namaste " . $name;          // . joins strings
    echo "Age: $age";                 // variables expand inside " "
    print "<br>Height: $height";
?>

A complete example — a page that greets the user and prints today's date.

<!DOCTYPE html>
<html>
<head>
    <title>My First PHP Page</title>
</head>
<body>
    <h1>Welcome</h1>

    <?php
        $visitor = "Sita";
        echo "<p>Namaste, $visitor!</p>";
        echo "<p>Today is " . date("l, d F Y") . ".</p>";

        for ($i = 1; $i <= 5; $i++) {
            echo "Number: $i <br>";
        }
    ?>
</body>
</html>

When this file is requested, the server runs the PHP block and sends the resulting HTML to the browser. The browser receives only <p>Namaste, Sita!</p> and so on — viewing the source shows HTML, never the PHP. That is the essential difference between PHP and JavaScript.

short.q: Explain the different operators used in PHP.
short.a:
PHP operators are grouped by what they act on.

Arithmetic operators — + add, - subtract, * multiply, / divide (always gives a float, even for 6/3), % modulus (remainder), ** exponentiation.

Assignment operators — =, and the combined forms +=, -=, *=, /=, %= and .= for appending to a string.

Comparison operators — == equal after type juggling, === identical in value and type, != / <> not equal, !== not identical, <, >, <=, >=, and <=> the spaceship operator, which returns -1, 0 or 1.

Logical operators — and / &&, or / ||, xor, and ! for not.

Increment/decrement operators — ++$x pre-increment, $x++ post-increment, --$x and $x--.

String operators — . concatenates and .= appends.

Array operators — + union, == same key/value pairs, === same pairs, same order and same types.

Conditional (ternary) operator — $result = ($age >= 18) ? "adult" : "minor"; and the short form ??, which returns its left operand if it exists and is not null.

short.q: Write a PHP program to display the largest among three numbers.
short.a:
Read three numbers, compare them with each other and print the largest. Comparing the first two, then comparing the winner with the third, is the simplest correct approach.

<?php
    $a = 25;
    $b = 80;
    $c = 47;

    if ($a >= $b && $a >= $c) {
        $largest = $a;
    } elseif ($b >= $a && $b >= $c) {
        $largest = $b;
    } else {
        $largest = $c;
    }

    echo "Numbers: $a, $b, $c <br>";
    echo "The largest number is $largest";
?>

Output: Numbers: 25, 80, 47 / The largest number is 80. The same result is obtained with $largest = max($a, $b, $c);, but the comparison version is the one to write in an exam because it shows the logic.

short.q: Write a JavaScript to print the largest & smallest numbers among 10 elements of an array.
short.a:
Store ten numbers in an array, then walk through it once keeping the largest and smallest values seen so far. Both are initialised to the first element, so the loop starts at index 1.

<!DOCTYPE html>
<html>
<body>
<?php
    $num = array(45, 12, 78, 3, 56, 89, 23, 67, 9, 34);

    $largest  = $num[0];
    $smallest = $num[0];

    for ($i = 1; $i < count($num); $i++) {
        if ($num[$i] > $largest)  { $largest  = $num[$i]; }
        if ($num[$i] < $smallest) { $smallest = $num[$i]; }
    }

    echo "Array: " . implode(", ", $num) . "<br>";
    echo "Largest number  = " . $largest  . "<br>";
    echo "Smallest number = " . $smallest;
?>
</body>
</html>

An array is created with array() or the shorter [...] form, and count() gives the number of elements, so the loop works for an array of any length. implode() joins the elements into one string for printing. The JavaScript version is the same idea written as a for loop over var num = [45, 12, 78, 3, 56, 89, 23, 67, 9, 34];.

short.q: How can we use array in PHP? Demonstrate with a suitable example.
short.a:
An array in PHP is an ordered map: one variable that holds many values, each reached by an index or a key. It is created with array() or the shorter [...] form, and its elements may be of mixed types. There are three kinds.

<?php
    // 1. Indexed array - automatic numeric keys starting at 0
    $marks = array(80, 75, 90, 65, 88);
    echo $marks[0];                 // 80
    echo count($marks);             // 5

    // 2. Associative array - named keys
    $student = array(
        "name"   => "Ram Sharma",
        "class"  => 12,
        "stream" => "Science"
    );
    echo $student["name"];          // Ram Sharma

    // 3. Multidimensional array - an array of arrays
    $class12 = array(
        array("Ram",  80, 75),
        array("Sita", 90, 88),
        array("Hari", 65, 70)
    );
    echo $class12[1][0];            // Sita
?>

A worked example — adding an element, walking through the array, and sorting it.

<?php
    $fruits = array("Mango", "Banana", "Apple");

    $fruits[] = "Orange";           // append to the end

    echo "The fruits are:<br>";
    foreach ($fruits as $fruit) {
        echo "- $fruit <br>";
    }

    sort($fruits);                  // sort into ascending order

    echo "Sorted: " . implode(", ", $fruits) . "<br>";
    echo "Total fruits: " . count($fruits);
?>

Useful array functions are count() for the number of elements, sort() and rsort() for sorting values, asort() and ksort() for sorting associative arrays by value or by key, array_push() to append, in_array() to test membership, array_sum() and array_merge(), and implode() and explode() to convert between arrays and strings. To see the whole structure while learning, use print_r($fruits); or var_dump($fruits);.

long.q: What is Object-based programming? Explain different JavaScript objects.
long.a:
Object-based programming is programming with objects — self-contained units that bundle data (properties) with the functions that work on it (methods) — but without the full inheritance and polymorphism machinery that a class-based object-oriented language provides. JavaScript is object-based: almost everything it manipulates is an object, and an object is really just a collection of named properties, created with an object literal and reached with the dot operator.

JavaScript objects fall into three groups.

1. Built-in (core) objects, provided by the language:

  • String — length, toUpperCase(), charAt(), indexOf(), split(), substring().
  • Number — toFixed(), toPrecision(), parseInt(), parseFloat().
  • Array — length, push(), pop(), sort(), join(), forEach().
  • Math — Math.random(), Math.max(), Math.round(), Math.sqrt().
  • Date — getFullYear(), getDay(), getHours(), toLocaleString().
  • Boolean and RegExp.

2. User-defined objects, which the programmer creates:

// object literal - the simplest way
var student = {
    name:    "Ram Sharma",
    age:     18,
    stream:  "Science",
    display: function () {
        return this.name + " is " + this.age + " years old.";
    }
};

document.write(student.name);        // Ram Sharma
document.write(student.display());   // Ram Sharma is 18 years old.

// or with a constructor function and new
function Student(name, age) {
    this.name = name;
    this.age  = age;
}
var s1 = new Student("Sita", 17);

3. Browser (host) objects, supplied by the browser so that JavaScript can reach the page and the window. Together they form the DOM (Document Object Model), which represents the page as a tree of objects that a script can read and change.

// window - the browser window itself
window.alert("Namaste");
window.open("https://example.com");

// document - the page
document.title = "New title";
document.getElementById("demo").innerHTML = "Changed by JavaScript";
document.write("Hello");

// form - an HTML form and its controls
document.forms[0].elements["username"].value;

// image - an <img> in the page
document.images[0].src = "photo.jpg";

// history and location - navigation
history.back();
location.href = "next.html";

The point of all of it is that JavaScript has no classical classes in its original form: objects are built from literals or constructor functions, and the browser supplies a whole family of ready-made objects — window, document, form, image, history and location — that make the page programmable.

long.q: Explain form validation using JavaScript with the example.
long.a:
Form validation is checking what the user typed before the form is sent to the server, so mistakes are caught instantly instead of after a round trip. In JavaScript this is done by handling the form's onsubmit event: if the handler returns false, or calls event.preventDefault(), the submission is cancelled.

<!DOCTYPE html>
<html>
<head>
    <title>Form Validation</title>
    <script>
    function validate() {
        var name  = document.forms["reg"]["name"].value;
        var email = document.forms["reg"]["email"].value;
        var pass  = document.forms["reg"]["pass"].value;
        var msg   = "";

        if (name == "") {
            msg += "Name must be filled in.\n";
        }
        if (email == "" || email.indexOf("@") == -1) {
            msg += "A valid e-mail is required.\n";
        }
        if (pass.length < 6) {
            msg += "Password must be at least 6 characters.\n";
        }

        if (msg != "") {
            alert(msg);
            return false;          // cancel submission
        }
        return true;               // allow submission
    }
    </script>
</head>
<body>
    <h2>Registration Form</h2>

    <form name="reg" action="save.php" method="post" onsubmit="return validate()">
        Name:     <input type="text"  name="name"><br>
        E-mail:   <input type="text"  name="email"><br>
        Password: <input type="password" name="pass"><br>
        <input type="submit" value="Register">
    </form>
</body>
</html>

How it works. onsubmit="return validate()" is the key: the function's return value decides whether the browser sends the form. document.forms["reg"]["name"].value reads the contents of the field called name. Each test appends a line to msg, and if msg is not empty the messages are shown and false is returned, so nothing is submitted. The email.indexOf("@") == -1 test is a deliberately simple check that the address contains an at sign.

Two things are worth stating in an exam answer. First, this is client-side validation: it is a convenience for the user, nothing more, because the user can switch JavaScript off or edit the page. Anything that matters — a login, a payment — must be validated again on the server. Second, the modern approach uses the HTML5 attributes required, type="email" and minlength, which the browser enforces by itself, with JavaScript kept for the rules HTML cannot express.

long.q: Define SQL. Write down the SQL queries to create a database, create a table in the database, insert data in the table, and query the data to display it.
long.a:
SQL (Structured Query Language) is the standard language for communicating with a relational database. It is non-procedural — you state the data you want and the DBMS decides how to fetch it. The statements are grouped into DDL, which defines structure, and DML, which works on the data itself.

-- 1. create the database
CREATE DATABASE school;

USE school;

-- 2. create a table in the database
CREATE TABLE student (
    roll     INT          NOT NULL,
    name     VARCHAR(40)  NOT NULL,
    class    INT,
    marks    INT,
    PRIMARY KEY (roll)
);

-- 3. insert data into the table
INSERT INTO student (roll, name, class, marks) VALUES
    (1, 'Ram Sharma',    12, 85),
    (2, 'Sita Adhikari', 12, 92),
    (3, 'Hari Thapa',    12, 78);

4. Querying the data — SELECT is the statement that retrieves it.

-- show everything
SELECT * FROM student;

-- only some columns, only some rows
SELECT name, marks FROM student WHERE marks >= 80;

-- in order, highest first
SELECT name, marks FROM student ORDER BY marks DESC;

-- a summary
SELECT COUNT(*) AS total, AVG(marks) AS average FROM student;

The four statements therefore map directly onto the four jobs in the question: CREATE DATABASE makes the database, CREATE TABLE defines the table's columns and its primary key, INSERT INTO adds rows, and SELECT reads them back, optionally filtered with WHERE, sorted with ORDER BY and summarised with an aggregate function.

long.q: Write down the server-side script to create a database, connect with it, create a table and insert data in it.
long.a:
On the server side the same four steps are carried out by a PHP script instead of by typing SQL by hand. The script connects to the MySQL server with mysqli_connect(), creates the database, selects it, creates a table and inserts records — checking for an error after each step. The version below uses the mysqli extension, which is what should be written in an exam: the older mysql_* functions were removed from PHP.

<?php
// 1. connect to the MySQL server
try {
   $conn = mysqli_connect("localhost", "root", "");
} catch (mysqli_sql_exception $e) {
   die("Connection failed: " . $e->getMessage());
}


echo "Connected successfully.<br>";

// 2. create the database
$sql = "CREATE DATABASE IF NOT EXISTS school";
if (mysqli_query($conn, $sql)) {
    echo "Database 'school' created.<br>";
} else {
    echo "Error creating database: " . mysqli_error($conn);
}

// 3. select the database
mysqli_select_db($conn, "school");

// 4. create a table
$sql = "CREATE TABLE IF NOT EXISTS student (
            roll  INT         NOT NULL,
            name  VARCHAR(40) NOT NULL,
            class INT,
            marks INT,
            PRIMARY KEY (roll)
        )";
if (mysqli_query($conn, $sql)) {
    echo "Table 'student' created.<br>";
} else {
    echo "Error creating table: " . mysqli_error($conn);
}

// 5. insert data
$sql = "INSERT INTO student (roll, name, class, marks) VALUES
            (1, 'Ram Sharma',    12, 85),
            (2, 'Sita Adhikari', 12, 92)";

if (mysqli_query($conn, $sql)) {
    echo "Records inserted. ID of last insert: " . mysqli_insert_id($conn) . "<br>";
} else {
    echo "Error inserting: " . mysqli_error($conn);
}

// 6. read them back to prove it worked
$result = mysqli_query($conn, "SELECT roll, name, marks FROM student");

echo "<table border='1'><tr><th>Roll</th><th>Name</th><th>Marks</th></tr>";
while ($row = mysqli_fetch_assoc($result)) {
    echo "<tr><td>" . $row["roll"]  . "</td>"
       . "<td>"     . $row["name"]  . "</td>"
       . "<td>"     . $row["marks"] . "</td></tr>";
}
echo "</table>";

// 7. close the connection
mysqli_close($conn);
?>

Notes on the script. mysqli_connect() takes the host, the MySQL user name and the password; on XAMPP that is "localhost", "root" and an empty password, and MySQL runs once Apache and MySQL are started in the control panel. IF NOT EXISTS makes the script safe to run twice. mysqli_query() runs any SQL statement and returns true on success, while mysqli_error() reports what went wrong. mysqli_fetch_assoc() returns each row as an associative array, which is looped over with while to build an HTML table. Finally mysqli_close() releases the connection.

The same job with the object-oriented style is $conn = new mysqli("localhost", "root", ""); followed by $conn->query($sql) — either style is accepted, but the procedural one above is easier to read at this level.

practical.q: [JS] Write a JavaScript program to calculate the simple interest using principal, rate, and time.
practical.a:
<!DOCTYPE html>
<html>
<body>
<h2>Simple Interest</h2>
<script>
    var p = parseFloat(prompt("Enter the principal:"));
    var r = parseFloat(prompt("Enter the rate of interest:"));
    var t = parseFloat(prompt("Enter the time in years:"));

    var si   = (p * r * t) / 100;
    var amt  = p + si;

    document.write("Principal      = Rs. " + p.toFixed(2) + "<br>");
    document.write("Rate           = " + r + "% <br>");
    document.write("Time           = " + t + " years <br>");
    document.write("Simple Interest= Rs. " + si.toFixed(2) + "<br>");
    document.write("Amount         = Rs. " + amt.toFixed(2));
</script>
</body>
</html>

parseFloat() turns the text returned by prompt() into a number, which is essential — without it + would join the strings instead of adding them. The formula is SI = (P × R × T) / 100 and the amount is P + SI. toFixed(2) rounds the money to two decimal places.

practical.q: [JS] Write a JavaScript program to convert temperatures from Fahrenheit (f) to Celsius (c). [Formula: c/5 = (f-32)/9, where c = temperature in Celsius and f = temperature in Fahrenheit].
practical.a:
<!DOCTYPE html>
<html>
<body>
<h2>Fahrenheit to Celsius</h2>
<script>
    var f = parseFloat(prompt("Enter temperature in Fahrenheit:"));

    // c/5 = (f - 32) / 9   =>   c = (f - 32) * 5 / 9
    var c = (f - 32) * 5 / 9;

    document.write(f + " °F = " + c.toFixed(2) + " °C");
</script>
</body>
</html>

The question gives the relation as c/5 = (f-32)/9. Rearranging for c gives c = (f - 32) * 5 / 9, which is what the program uses. Check it: 98.6 °F gives 37 °C, and 32 °F gives 0 °C.

practical.q: [JS] Write a JavaScript program to check whether the given number is positive or negative.
practical.a:
<!DOCTYPE html>
<html>
<body>
<h2>Positive or Negative</h2>
<script>
    var n = parseFloat(prompt("Enter a number:"));

    if (n > 0) {
        document.write(n + " is positive.");
    } else if (n < 0) {
        document.write(n + " is negative.");
    } else {
        document.write("The number is zero.");
    }
</script>
</body>
</html>

A number is positive if it is greater than zero, negative if it is less than zero, and zero otherwise. The third branch matters — without it, zero would be reported as negative.

practical.q: [JS] Write a JavaScript program to check if a given number is even or odd.
practical.a:
<!DOCTYPE html>
<html>
<body>
<h2>Even or Odd</h2>
<script>
    var n = parseInt(prompt("Enter an integer:"));

    if (n % 2 == 0) {
        document.write(n + " is even.");
    } else {
        document.write(n + " is odd.");
    }
</script>
</body>
</html>

The % operator gives the remainder after division. Dividing by 2 leaves a remainder of 0 for an even number and 1 for an odd one, so n % 2 == 0 is the whole test.

practical.q: [JS] Write a JavaScript program to display the largest among three given numbers.
practical.a:
<!DOCTYPE html>
<html>
<body>
<h2>Largest of Three Numbers</h2>
<script>
    var a = parseFloat(prompt("Enter first number:"));
    var b = parseFloat(prompt("Enter second number:"));
    var c = parseFloat(prompt("Enter third number:"));

    var largest;

    if (a >= b && a >= c) {
        largest = a;
    } else if (b >= a && b >= c) {
        largest = b;
    } else {
        largest = c;
    }

    document.write("Numbers: " + a + ", " + b + ", " + c + "<br>");
    document.write("The largest is " + largest);
</script>
</body>
</html>

Each number is compared against the other two; the one that is greater than or equal to both is the largest. The same result can be had with Math.max(a, b, c).

practical.q: [JS] Write a JavaScript program to display the reverse of a given number.
practical.a:
<!DOCTYPE html>
<html>
<body>
<h2>Reverse a Number</h2>
<script>
    var n    = parseInt(prompt("Enter a number:"));
    var temp = n;
    var rev  = 0;

    while (temp > 0) {
        var digit = temp % 10;        // take the last digit
        rev       = rev * 10 + digit; // append it to the reverse
        temp      = Math.floor(temp / 10); // drop the last digit
    }

    document.write("Number  = " + n + "<br>");
    document.write("Reverse = " + rev);
</script>
</body>
</html>

Peel the digits off one at a time from the right. temp % 10 gives the last digit; rev * 10 + digit shifts the digits already collected one place left and adds the new one; Math.floor(temp / 10) removes the digit just used. The loop ends when nothing is left. For 1234 it produces 4321.

practical.q: [JS] Write a JavaScript program to check if a given number is a palindrome or not.
practical.a:
<!DOCTYPE html>
<html>
<body>
<h2>Palindrome Number</h2>
<script>
    var n    = parseInt(prompt("Enter a number:"));
    var temp = n;
    var rev  = 0;

    while (temp > 0) {
        rev  = rev * 10 + (temp % 10);
        temp = Math.floor(temp / 10);
    }

    if (rev == n) {
        document.write(n + " is a palindrome.");
    } else {
        document.write(n + " is not a palindrome.");
    }
</script>
</body>
</html>

A palindrome reads the same forwards and backwards, so reverse the number with the same loop as the previous program and compare the result with the original. 121 and 1331 are palindromes; 123 is not. The original must be kept in a separate variable, because temp is destroyed by the loop.

practical.q: [JS] Write a JavaScript program to calculate the factorial of a given number.
practical.a:
<!DOCTYPE html>
<html>
<body>
<h2>Factorial</h2>
<script>
    var n   = parseInt(prompt("Enter a number:"));
    var fact = 1;

    for (var i = 1; i <= n; i++) {
        fact = fact * i;
    }

    document.write(n + "! = " + fact);
</script>
</body>
</html>

n! = 1 × 2 × 3 × ... × n. The accumulator fact starts at 1, not 0, because multiplying by 0 would leave it at 0. By definition 0! = 1, which this loop gives correctly. For n = 5 it prints 120.

practical.q: [JS] Write a JavaScript program to print the largest and smallest numbers among 10 elements of an array.
practical.a:
<!DOCTYPE html>
<html>
<body>
<h2>Largest and Smallest of 10 Array Elements</h2>
<script>
    var num = [45, 12, 78, 3, 56, 89, 23, 67, 9, 34];

    var largest  = num[0];
    var smallest = num[0];

    for (var i = 1; i < num.length; i++) {
        if (num[i] > largest)  { largest  = num[i]; }
        if (num[i] < smallest) { smallest = num[i]; }
    }

    document.write("Array    : " + num.join(", ") + "<br>");
    document.write("Largest  : " + largest  + "<br>");
    document.write("Smallest : " + smallest);
</script>
</body>
</html>

Both answers start as the first element, so the loop can begin at index 1 and every remaining element is compared with the best so far. Using num.length rather than the literal 10 means the program still works if the array grows.

practical.q: [JS] Write a JavaScript program to sort the data of an array.
practical.a:
<!DOCTYPE html>
<html>
<body>
<h2>Sort an Array</h2>
<script>
    var num = [45, 12, 78, 3, 56, 89, 23];

    document.write("Before sorting: " + num.join(", ") + "<br><br>");

    num.sort(function (a, b) { return a - b; });   // numeric, ascending

    document.write("After sorting : " + num.join(", "));
</script>
</body>
</html>

This is the trap in this question: sort() on its own compares elements as strings, so it would order [3, 12, 45] as [12, 3, 45]. Passing a comparator, function (a, b) { return a - b; }, sorts numerically. Swap a - b for b - a to sort descending.

practical.q: [JS] Write a JavaScript program to reverse a given string.
practical.a:
<!DOCTYPE html>
<html>
<body>
<h2>Reverse a String</h2>
<script>
    var str = prompt("Enter a string:");
    var rev = "";

    for (var i = str.length - 1; i >= 0; i--) {
        rev = rev + str.charAt(i);
    }

    document.write("Original : " + str + "<br>");
    document.write("Reversed : " + rev);
</script>
</body>
</html>

Walk backwards from the last character (str.length - 1) down to index 0, adding each character to rev. The one-line alternative is str.split("").reverse().join("") — split into an array of characters, reverse the array, join it back into a string.

practical.q: [JS] Write a JavaScript program to count the number of vowels present in the given string.
practical.a:
<!DOCTYPE html>
<html>
<body>
<h2>Count Vowels in a String</h2>
<script>
    var str   = prompt("Enter a string:").toLowerCase();
    var count = 0;

    for (var i = 0; i < str.length; i++) {
        var ch = str.charAt(i);
        if (ch == 'a' || ch == 'e' || ch == 'i' || ch == 'o' || ch == 'u') {
            count++;
        }
    }

    document.write("String      : " + str + "<br>");
    document.write("Vowel count : " + count);
</script>
</body>
</html>

toLowerCase() first, so A and a count the same. Then each character is tested against the five vowels. A neater version puts the vowels in a string and uses indexOf: if ("aeiou".indexOf(ch) != -1) { count++; }.

practical.q: [JS] Write a JavaScript program to calculate the factorial of a number using the concept of recursion.
practical.a:
<!DOCTYPE html>
<html>
<body>
<h2>Factorial using Recursion</h2>
<script>
    function factorial(n) {
        if (n == 0 || n == 1) {
            return 1;               // base case - stops the recursion
        }
        return n * factorial(n - 1); // recursive call
    }

    var num = parseInt(prompt("Enter a number:"));
    document.write(num + "! = " + factorial(num));
</script>
</body>
</html>

A recursive function calls itself with a smaller problem until it reaches the base case, which returns a value without recursing — here 0! and 1! are both 1. Without the base case the function would call itself for ever and the browser would stop with a stack overflow. For n = 5 the calls unwind as 5 × 4 × 3 × 2 × 1 = 120.

practical.q: [PHP] Write a PHP program to swap the values of two variables.
practical.a:
<?php
    $a = 10;
    $b = 20;

    echo "Before swap: a = $a, b = $b <br>";

    // swap using a temporary variable
    $temp = $a;
    $a    = $b;
    $b    = $temp;

    echo "After swap : a = $a, b = $b";
?>

A third variable is needed because assigning $a = $b; first would overwrite the old value of $a and both variables would end up holding 20. Two alternatives are worth knowing: the arithmetic method, $a = $a + $b; $b = $a - $b; $a = $a - $b;, and PHP's own list($a, $b) = array($b, $a);.

practical.q: [PHP] Write a PHP program to calculate the sum of 1 to 10.
practical.a:
<?php
    $sum = 0;

    for ($i = 1; $i <= 10; $i++) {
        $sum = $sum + $i;
    }

    echo "The sum of 1 to 10 is $sum";
?>

The accumulator $sum starts at 0 and each value of $i is added to it, giving 1 + 2 + ... + 10 = 55. The closed form sum = n(n+1)/2 gives the same answer directly, and array_sum(range(1, 10)) does it in one line.

practical.q: [PHP] Write a PHP program to calculate the sum of all even numbers up to 100.
practical.a:
<?php
    $sum = 0;

    for ($i = 2; $i <= 100; $i = $i + 2) {
        $sum = $sum + $i;
    }

    echo "The sum of even numbers up to 100 is $sum";
?>

Starting at 2 and stepping by 2 visits only the even numbers, so no if test is needed. The answer is 2 + 4 + ... + 100 = 2550. The same result using a test inside the loop would be if ($i % 2 == 0) { $sum += $i; } with the loop running over every integer.

practical.q: [PHP] Write a PHP program to display the prime numbers less than 100.
practical.a:
<?php
    echo "Prime numbers less than 100:<br>";

    for ($n = 2; $n < 100; $n++) {
        $prime = true;

        for ($i = 2; $i <= sqrt($n); $i++) {
            if ($n % $i == 0) {
                $prime = false;   // a factor was found, so not prime
                break;
            }
        }

        if ($prime) {
            echo $n . " ";
        }
    }
?>

A prime has exactly two factors, 1 and itself. Rather than testing every number below $n, the inner loop only goes as far as sqrt($n) — if $n has a factor larger than its square root, it must also have one smaller, which has already been tested. The flag $prime starts true and is set false the moment a factor appears, and break leaves the inner loop early. The output begins 2 3 5 7 11 13 ... 97; note that 2 is prime and 1 is not, which is why the loop starts at 2.

practical.q: [PHP] How can we use array in PHP? Demonstrate with a suitable example.
practical.a:
<?php
    // creating arrays
    $marks   = array(80, 75, 90, 65, 88);          // indexed
    $student = array("name" => "Ram", "age" => 18); // associative

    echo "First mark: " . $marks[0] . "<br>";
    echo "Name: " . $student["name"] . "<br>";

    // adding an element
    $marks[] = 95;

    // walking through the array
    echo "All marks: ";
    foreach ($marks as $m) {
        echo $m . " ";
    }
    echo "<br>";

    // useful functions
    echo "Count  : " . count($marks)   . "<br>";
    echo "Total  : " . array_sum($marks) . "<br>";
    echo "Average: " . (array_sum($marks) / count($marks)) . "<br>";
    echo "Highest: " . max($marks)     . "<br>";

    sort($marks);
    echo "Sorted : " . implode(", ", $marks);
?>

An array holds many values in one variable. It is created with array() (or [...]), elements are reached by their index or their key, and foreach steps through them without needing to know how many there are. The functions worth remembering are count(), array_sum(), max(), min(), sort(), rsort(), in_array(), array_push() and implode(). Use print_r($marks); to see the whole structure while you are learning.

practical.q: [PHP] Write a PHP program to print the largest and smallest numbers among 10 elements of an array.
practical.a:
<?php
    $num = array(45, 12, 78, 3, 56, 89, 23, 67, 9, 34);

    $largest  = $num[0];
    $smallest = $num[0];

    for ($i = 1; $i < count($num); $i++) {
        if ($num[$i] > $largest)  { $largest  = $num[$i]; }
        if ($num[$i] < $smallest) { $smallest = $num[$i]; }
    }

    echo "Array    : " . implode(", ", $num) . "<br>";
    echo "Largest  : $largest <br>";
    echo "Smallest : $smallest";
?>

Both variables start at the first element, so the loop begins at index 1 and each element is compared against the best found so far. PHP also gives the answer directly with max($num) and min($num), and count($num) keeps the loop correct whatever the length of the array.

practical.q: [PHP] Write a PHP program to sort the data of an array.
practical.a:
<?php
    $num = array(45, 12, 78, 3, 56, 89, 23);

    echo "Before: " . implode(", ", $num) . "<br>";

    sort($num);           // ascending
    echo "Ascending : " . implode(", ", $num) . "<br>";

    rsort($num);          // descending
    echo "Descending: " . implode(", ", $num) . "<br>";

    // sorting an associative array
    $age = array("Ram" => 18, "Sita" => 17, "Hari" => 19);
    asort($age);          // by value, keeping the keys
    print_r($age);
?>

sort() arranges the values in ascending order and renumbers the keys; rsort() does the same descending. For an associative array use asort() (by value) or ksort() (by key), both of which keep each key with its value. All of them act on the array in place and return true on success, which is why the array is printed again afterwards rather than assigning the result.

practical.q: [PHP] Write a PHP program to check if a string is a palindrome or not.
practical.a:
<?php
    $str = "liril";

    $rev = strrev($str);

    if ($str == $rev) {
        echo "$str is a palindrome.";
    } else {
        echo "$str is not a palindrome.";
    }
?>

strrev() reverses the string, so the test is a single comparison. For "liril" the reverse is identical, so it is a palindrome. Without the built-in function the same result is obtained with a loop that walks backwards through the string, or with implode("", array_reverse(str_split($str))). If the input may contain capitals, compare strtolower($str) == strtolower($rev) instead.

practical.q: [Practical] Design the following form in HTML and display the value in the result box after calculating basic arithmetic operations based on user input with the use of JavaScript.
practical.a:
<!DOCTYPE html>
<html>
<head>
    <title>Arithmetic Calculator</title>
    <script>
    function calculate(op) {
        var a = parseFloat(document.getElementById("n1").value);
        var b = parseFloat(document.getElementById("n2").value);
        var result;

        if (isNaN(a) || isNaN(b)) {
            result = "Please enter both numbers";
        } else if (op == '+') {
            result = a + b;
        } else if (op == '-') {
            result = a - b;
        } else if (op == '*') {
            result = a * b;
        } else if (op == '/') {
            result = (b == 0) ? "Cannot divide by zero" : a / b;
        }

        document.getElementById("result").value = result;
    }
    </script>
</head>
<body>
    <h2>Simple Calculator</h2>

    <form onsubmit="return false">
        First number:  <input type="text" id="n1"><br><br>
        Second number: <input type="text" id="n2"><br><br>

        <input type="button" value="+" onclick="calculate('+')">
        <input type="button" value="-" onclick="calculate('-')">
        <input type="button" value="*" onclick="calculate('*')">
        <input type="button" value="/" onclick="calculate('/')">
        <br><br>

        Result: <input type="text" id="result" readonly>
    </form>
</body>
</html>

The design. Two text boxes take the operands, four buttons call the same function with a different operator, and a read-only box shows the answer. parseFloat() converts the input text to numbers; isNaN() rejects input that is not a number; and the division branch guards against a zero divisor instead of printing Infinity. onsubmit="return false" keeps the page from reloading when Enter is pressed, and readonly on the result box stops the user typing over the answer.

practical.q: [Practical] Write a JavaScript program to display the current day and time in the following format. Today is: Tuesday. The current time is: 10 PM: 30: 38
practical.a:
<!DOCTYPE html>
<html>
<body>
<h2>Current Day and Time</h2>
<p id="out"></p>

<script>
    var now   = new Date();
    var days  = ["Sunday", "Monday", "Tuesday", "Wednesday",
                 "Thursday", "Friday", "Saturday"];

    var day  = days[now.getDay()];      // 0 = Sunday ... 6 = Saturday

    var hours = now.getHours();         // 0 - 23
    var ampm  = (hours >= 12) ? "PM" : "AM";
    hours     = hours % 12;
    if (hours == 0) { hours = 12; }     // midnight and noon show as 12

    var minutes = now.getMinutes();
    var seconds = now.getSeconds();

    // pad to two digits
    if (minutes < 10) { minutes = "0" + minutes; }
    if (seconds < 10) { seconds = "0" + seconds; }

    document.getElementById("out").innerHTML =
        "Today is: " + day + ".<br>" +
        "The current time is: " + hours + " " + ampm + ": " + minutes + ": " + seconds;
</script>
</body>
</html>

new Date() captures the moment the page runs. getDay() returns a number from 0 to 6, which is used to look the weekday name up in an array. getHours() returns 24-hour time, so hours % 12 converts it to 12-hour time, the remainder being 0 at both midnight and noon — hence the special case that turns 0 into 12. Finally minutes and seconds are padded with a leading zero so the output keeps the asked-for shape: Today is: Tuesday. The current time is: 10 PM: 30: 38.

practical.q: [Practical] Write a PHP script to connect the MySQL database and demonstrate data insertion in table product (id, product_name, price, expire_date, company name).
practical.a:
<!DOCTYPE html>
<html>
<body>
<h2>Insert a Product</h2>

<form method="post" action="">
    Product name: <input type="text" name="product_name"><br>
    Price:        <input type="text" name="price"><br>
    Expiry date:  <input type="date" name="expire_date"><br>
    Company:      <input type="text" name="company"><br>
    <input type="submit" name="save" value="Save Product">
</form>

<?php
if (isset($_POST['save'])) {
    // 1. connect to MySQL
    try {
       $conn = mysqli_connect("localhost", "root", "", "shop");
    } catch (mysqli_sql_exception $e) {
       die("Connection failed: " . $e->getMessage());
    }

    

    // 2. create the table if it does not exist
    mysqli_query($conn, "CREATE TABLE IF NOT EXISTS product (
                            id           INT AUTO_INCREMENT PRIMARY KEY,
                            product_name VARCHAR(50) NOT NULL,
                            price        DECIMAL(10,2) NOT NULL,
                            expire_date  DATE,
                            company      VARCHAR(50)
                         )");

    // 3. read the form and insert the record
    $name    = $_POST['product_name'];
    $price   = $_POST['price'];
    $expire  = $_POST['expire_date'];
    $company = $_POST['company'];

    $sql = "INSERT INTO product (product_name, price, expire_date, company)
            VALUES ('$name', '$price', '$expire', '$company')";

    if (mysqli_query($conn, $sql)) {
        echo "Product saved. Record id: " . mysqli_insert_id($conn);
    } else {
        echo "Error: " . mysqli_error($conn);
    }

    mysqli_close($conn);
}
?>
</body>
</html>

The fourth argument of mysqli_connect() selects the database directly — here it is shop. The form posts to the same page, so the script checks isset($_POST['save']) before doing anything: on the first visit nothing has been submitted and only the form is shown. AUTO_INCREMENT on id means the id is generated by MySQL rather than supplied by the user.

A security note worth writing in the exam: putting $_POST values straight into SQL is unsafe — a value containing a quote breaks the query, and a crafted value can change its meaning. Real code uses a prepared statement: $stmt = $conn->prepare("INSERT INTO product (product_name, price, expire_date, company) VALUES (?, ?, ?, ?)"); followed by $stmt->bind_param("sdss", $name, $price, $expire, $company); and $stmt->execute();.

practical.q: [Practical] Write a PHP program to connect a database name 'employee'.
practical.a:
<?php
    // connect to the MySQL server and select the 'employee' database
    try {
       $conn = mysqli_connect("localhost", "root", "", "employee");
    } catch (mysqli_sql_exception $e) {
       die("Connection failed: " . $e->getMessage());
    }

    

    echo "Connected to the 'employee' database successfully.";

    mysqli_close($conn);
?>

mysqli_connect() takes four arguments: the host (localhost when MySQL runs on the same machine, as it does under XAMPP), the MySQL user name (root by default in XAMPP), the password (empty by default) and the name of the database to select. Always test the result — if it is false, mysqli_connect_error() says why, which is far more useful than a blank page. The object-oriented equivalent is $conn = new mysqli("localhost", "root", "", "employee"); with the error in $conn->connect_error.

practical.q: [Practical] Write a PHP program to insert a record in a database name 'employee' with fields id, name and salary.
practical.a:
<!DOCTYPE html>
<html>
<body>
<h2>Add an Employee</h2>

<form method="post" action="">
    ID:     <input type="text" name="id"><br>
    Name:   <input type="text" name="name"><br>
    Salary: <input type="text" name="salary"><br>
    <input type="submit" name="submit" value="Insert Record">
</form>

<?php
if (isset($_POST['submit'])) {
    try {
       $conn = mysqli_connect("localhost", "root", "", "employee");
    } catch (mysqli_sql_exception $e) {
       die("Connection failed: " . $e->getMessage());
    }

    

    // the table this record goes into
    mysqli_query($conn, "CREATE TABLE IF NOT EXISTS emp (
                            id     INT PRIMARY KEY,
                            name   VARCHAR(50) NOT NULL,
                            salary INT
                         )");

    $id     = $_POST['id'];
    $name   = $_POST['name'];
    $salary = $_POST['salary'];

    $sql = "INSERT INTO emp (id, name, salary) VALUES ('$id', '$name', '$salary')";

    if (mysqli_query($conn, $sql)) {
        echo "Record inserted successfully.";
    } else {
        echo "Error: " . mysqli_error($conn);
    }

    mysqli_close($conn);
}
?>
</body>
</html>

The script connects to the employee database, makes sure the emp table exists, reads the three fields from the form and runs an INSERT. Because the form's action is empty, the page submits to itself and the isset($_POST['submit']) guard keeps the insert from running on the first visit.

practical.q: [Practical] Write a PHP program to display all records (according to previous questions 4 and 5) of employee's record who are securing salary greater than Rs. 45,000.
practical.a:
<?php
    try {
       $conn = mysqli_connect("localhost", "root", "", "employee");
    } catch (mysqli_sql_exception $e) {
       die("Connection failed: " . $e->getMessage());
    }

    

    // employees earning more than Rs. 45,000
    $sql    = "SELECT id, name, salary FROM emp WHERE salary > 45000 ORDER BY salary DESC";
    $result = mysqli_query($conn, $sql);

    if (mysqli_num_rows($result) > 0) {
        echo "<h3>Employees earning more than Rs. 45,000</h3>";
        echo "<table border='1' cellpadding='6'>";
        echo "<tr><th>ID</th><th>Name</th><th>Salary</th></tr>";

        while ($row = mysqli_fetch_assoc($result)) {
            echo "<tr>";
            echo "<td>" . $row['id']     . "</td>";
            echo "<td>" . $row['name']   . "</td>";
            echo "<td>" . $row['salary'] . "</td>";
            echo "</tr>";
        }

        echo "</table>";
    } else {
        echo "No employee earns more than Rs. 45,000.";
    }

    mysqli_close($conn);
?>

The WHERE salary > 45000 clause does the filtering in the database, which is always better than fetching every row and filtering in PHP. mysqli_num_rows() reports how many rows came back, so the "no records" case can be handled politely, and mysqli_fetch_assoc() returns one row at a time as an associative array whose keys are the column names. The loop ends on its own when the rows run out.

practical.q: [Practical] Write a PHP program to delete a record of an employee whose salary is less than Rs. 30,000.
practical.a:
<?php
    try {
       $conn = mysqli_connect("localhost", "root", "", "employee");
    } catch (mysqli_sql_exception $e) {
       die("Connection failed: " . $e->getMessage());
    }

    

    // delete every employee earning less than Rs. 30,000
    $sql = "DELETE FROM emp WHERE salary < 30000";

    if (mysqli_query($conn, $sql)) {
        echo "Records deleted: " . mysqli_affected_rows($conn);
    } else {
        echo "Error deleting: " . mysqli_error($conn);
    }

    mysqli_close($conn);
?>

DELETE FROM emp WHERE salary < 30000 removes the matching rows, and mysqli_affected_rows() reports how many were taken out.

The warning that must be written in the answer: a DELETE without a WHERE clause empties the whole table. Always run the matching SELECT first to see which rows the condition catches, and take a backup before running a delete against real data. Note also that mysqli_query() returns true even when nothing was deleted — it is mysqli_affected_rows() that tells you the count.

mcq.q: Which of the following is generally used for either extraction or removal or changes or addition of records in the database table?
mcq.teacher_note: DML (INSERT, UPDATE, DELETE, SELECT) works on the records. DDL (CREATE, ALTER, DROP) works on the structure.

mcq.q: Which of the following keywords are used to declare a variable in JavaScript?
mcq.teacher_note: JavaScript has no int / float / char. Modern JavaScript adds const as well, but of the pairs given only var or let are both valid.

mcq.q: What will be the output of the following JavaScript code? var p = 100; let q = 100; document.write(p === q);
mcq.teacher_note: === compares value AND type. Both are the number 100, so the result is true.

mcq.q: What will be the output of the following JavaScript code? var p = "100"; let q = 100; document.write(p === q);
mcq.teacher_note: p is the string "100" and q is the number 100. === requires the same type, so the result is false. (== would give true.)

mcq.q: Critically analyze the expected output of the provided JavaScript snippet. What would be the value of 'q' in the following JavaScript code? var a = 40; var b = 80; q = a % b;
mcq.teacher_note: % is the remainder operator. 40 ÷ 80 = 0 remainder 40, so q = 40.

mcq.q: Which of the following is a server-side scripting language?
mcq.teacher_note: PHP runs on the server. JavaScript and jQuery run in the browser; MySQL is a database, not a scripting language.

mcq.q: Which of the following commands is executed in PHP to concatenate the variables $x with $y?
mcq.teacher_note: The dot (.) is the PHP concatenation operator. + would add the two numbers instead.

mcq.q: What will be the output of the following PHP code? $x = 60; $y = 120; if ($x != $y) echo "Nepal in Europe."; else echo "Nepal in Asia.";
mcq.teacher_note: 60 != 120 is TRUE, so the if-branch runs and prints 'Nepal in Europe.'

mcq.q: Which of the following is a valid statement in PHP?
mcq.teacher_note: Every PHP variable name must begin with a dollar sign ($). var and let are JavaScript keywords.

mcq.q: What will be the value of s calculated in the following JavaScript code if the value of a is input as 5 and that of b is input as 10? var a = prompt("enter a positive integer"); var b = prompt("enter another positive integer"); var s = a + b; alert("The value of s is: " + s);
mcq.teacher_note: prompt() always returns a STRING, so + concatenates: "5" + "10" = "510". Use parseInt() to add them numerically.

mcq.q: How do you declare a datatype in JavaScript as a constant type?
mcq.teacher_note: const declares a block-scoped variable whose value cannot be reassigned.

mcq.q: Data types in JavaScript are …
mcq.teacher_note: Primitive = String, Number, Boolean, Undefined, Null. Non-primitive = Object, Array, RegExp.

mcq.q: Which of the following methods is used to access HTML elements using JavaScript?
mcq.teacher_note: All three are valid DOM access methods, so 'all of the above' is the answer.

mcq.q: What is the correct syntax for referring to an external JavaScript script?
mcq.teacher_note: An external script is loaded with the src attribute of the <script> tag.

mcq.q: Predict the output of the following JavaScript code: var a = 20; a === "20" ? document.write("true") : document.write("false"); a == "20" ? document.write("true") : document.write("false");
mcq.teacher_note: === compares type as well, so 20 === "20" is false. == converts types, so 20 == "20" is true.

mcq.q: Which of the following is the correct syntax to write PHP code?
mcq.teacher_note: The canonical PHP tag is <?php … ?> (case-insensitive). A space after <? is not allowed.

mcq.q: Which syntax is used for opening and closing a PHP script?
mcq.teacher_note: <?php opens the script and ?> closes it.

mcq.q: What output will be obtained from the following JavaScript? var a = 10; var b = 0; console.log(a / b);
mcq.teacher_note: JavaScript does not throw a divide-by-zero error; it returns the special value Infinity.

mcq.q: What will be the result of combining a string with another data type in PHP?
mcq.teacher_note: PHP converts (juggles) the other type to text, so the result is always a string.

mcq.q: What happens in the following JavaScript code snippet? var count = 0; while(count < 10) console.log(count); count++;
options: The value of the count from 0 to 9 is displayed in the console.
The value of the count is logged or stored in a particular location or storage.
mcq.teacher_note: The printed key is (a), and that is clearly the intended answer. Strictly, as printed there are no braces, so only console.log(count) is inside the loop and count++ never runs — the snippet is an INFINITE loop printing 0 forever. With braces around both statements the answer (a) is correct.

mcq.q: Which of the following is the right way to define a constant in PHP?
mcq.teacher_note: The const keyword is used, and a constant name does NOT carry a dollar sign.

mcq.q: What will be the output for the given PHP code? <?php const $PI = '3.1415'; echo $PI; ?>
mcq.teacher_note: A constant name cannot begin with $, so PHP raises a parse error and nothing is printed.

mcq.q: What function do you need to call to ask the user of the program to enter text in JavaScript?
mcq.teacher_note: The printed key is (a) readLine, and that is what you should write in the exam. Be aware that the JavaScript function actually used for this is prompt() — see the next question.

mcq.q: Which JavaScript function is used for text input?
mcq.teacher_note: prompt() displays a dialog box with a text field and returns what the user typed.

mcq.q: Which one of the following is a standard way to show a pop-up alert box in JavaScript?
mcq.teacher_note: alert() is a method of the window object, so window.alert() (or simply alert()) is correct.

mcq.q: Which one of the following methods is used in jQuery to hide the selected elements?
mcq.teacher_note: The printed key is (b) hide(). Note that show() is also a genuine jQuery method — the question as printed is incomplete, and the answer key is what you should follow.

mcq.q: JavaScript is …
mcq.teacher_note: The printed key is (b). Note the tension: this chapter repeatedly calls JavaScript an OBJECT-BASED language (no classes needed to make an object). Write (b) in the exam, but be ready to justify 'object based' from section 3.4.1.

mcq.q: Data types in JavaScript are …
mcq.teacher_note: Same as question 12: primitive (String, Number, Boolean, Undefined, Null) and non-primitive (Object, Array, RegExp).

mcq.q: PHP stands for …
mcq.teacher_note: PHP is a recursive acronym for 'PHP: Hypertext Pre-processor'.

mcq.q: concat() is …
mcq.teacher_note: concat() combines the text of two strings and returns a new string.

mcq.q: … is an identifier whose value may change during the execution of the program.
mcq.teacher_note: That is the textbook definition of a variable (section 3.7).

mcq.q: … is a method of designing websites so that the process or user request is run on the originating server.
mcq.teacher_note: Server-side scripting runs on the originating server (section 3.2).

mcq.q: … is performed to generate a code that can run on the client end (browser) without needing server-side processing.
mcq.teacher_note: Client-side scripting runs in the browser with no server round-trip.

mcq.q: … defines the flow of control within the program.
mcq.teacher_note: Control structures (if, switch, for, while, do-while) direct the flow of execution.

mcq.q: … returns today's date and time.
mcq.teacher_note: The Date() method of the JavaScript Date object returns today's date and time.

mcq.q: … extracts a section of a string and returns a new string.
mcq.teacher_note: slice() extracts a section; split() breaks a string into an array of substrings.

mcq.q: What is the correct syntax for a 'for-loop' in JavaScript?
mcq.teacher_note: All three parts — initialisation, test condition and iteration — must be present and separated by semicolons.

mcq.q: Which PHP function is commonly used to execute SQL queries on a database connection established using the mysqli extension?
mcq.teacher_note: mysqli_query() (or $conn->query() in the object-oriented style) runs the query. mysql_query() is deprecated since PHP 5.5.

key_terms.meaning: The tools and techniques that let two or more computing devices communicate over a network, mainly the Internet.
The collection of web pages, documents and resources identified and located by their URLs on the Internet.
Uniform Resource Locator — the address used to identify and locate a resource on the Internet.
A language used to create dynamic web documents; it is interpreted inside a host program (the browser or the web server) and generates markup code rather than machine code.
Scripting that runs in the user's browser without server-side processing, e.g. JavaScript embedded in HTML.
Scripting whose code is executed on the originating web server, e.g. PHP, ASP, JSP; the source is hidden from the client.
The suite of Internet protocols named after its two most important members, used with packet switching to move data between networks.
The 1969 ARPA research project that created a secure, de-centralised network able to survive the loss of parts of its infrastructure.
A light-weight, interpreted, object-based client-side scripting language, one of the three core technologies of the web alongside HTML and CSS.
An identifier whose value may change during the execution of a program; the name of a storage location.
The three JavaScript declaration keywords: var is function- or global-scoped and re-assignable; let is block-scoped and re-assignable; const is block-scoped and cannot be reassigned.
The region of a program in which a variable is defined and therefore accessible — local (inside a block or function) or global.
A symbol that signifies an operation; the values it acts on are called operands.
A JavaScript data type that holds only one value at a time: String, Number, Boolean, Undefined, Null.
A JavaScript data type that holds collections or complex entities: Object, Array, RegExp.
A named, reusable block of code that can be called from anywhere in the program, optionally taking parameters and returning a value.
A value passed into a function when it is called and captured inside the function for manipulation.
A construct that defines the flow of execution in a program: conditional statements (if, if-else, if-else-if, switch) and loops (for, while, do-while).
Programming around objects that are created directly from a template rather than from a class. JavaScript is template based, not class based.
In JavaScript, a keyword that refers to the current object inside an object constructor.
Document Object Model — an application programming interface (API) for HTML that represents the page as a tree of objects.
Something that happens to the page or the user — a load, a click, a key press, a resize — that JavaScript can respond to.
Writing JavaScript-coded responses that execute when an event occurs.
The JavaScript object that embeds an image or video clip into the current document; accessible by index or by name.
A property of the document object, created by the browser for each HTML form, used to read and validate user input.
Checking a form's data on the client's computer before sending it to the web server: basic validation (mandatory fields filled) and data-format validation (correct form and value).
A lightweight, fast, feature-rich JavaScript library — 'write less, do more' — that simplifies DOM/CSS manipulation, events, effects, animations and AJAX.
The jQuery selector entry point; every jQuery selector starts with a dollar sign and parentheses. Its building blocks are tag name, tag ID (#) and tag class (.).
Asynchronous JavaScript And XML — a technique for exchanging data with a server without reloading the whole page.
Content Delivery Network — a network of servers from which a library such as jQuery can be loaded directly, e.g. code.jquery.com.
A recursive acronym for 'PHP: Hypertext Pre-processor'; a server-side scripting language embedded in HTML, used for dynamic content, databases and session tracking.
The mechanism of separating normal HTML from PHP code, normally with the canonical <?php … ?> tags.
A PHP data type that holds a single value: boolean, integer, float, string.
A PHP data type that can hold multiple values: array and object.
The two PHP special types: a resource holds a reference to an external resource such as a database call; NULL means a variable with no value.
A PHP array whose index is a string key rather than a number, e.g. $salary["Sony"] = "350000".
The PHP dot (.) used to join two strings; .= appends the right-hand string to the left-hand variable.
A predefined PHP variable that is always accessible regardless of scope, e.g. $GLOBALS, $_SERVER, $_REQUEST, $_POST, $_GET, $_FILES, $_ENV, $_COOKIE, $_SESSION.
A form submission method that appends encoded data to the URL after '?'; limited to 1024 characters and never to be used for passwords.
A form submission method that sends data inside the HTTP header with no size restriction; it can carry ASCII and binary data.
The PHP function used to open a connection to a MySQL database; mysqli_close() closes it.
PHP Data Objects — a database-access abstraction layer that works with many database brands, not only MySQL.
A mysqli result method that returns one row of the result set as an associative array keyed by column name.
A property of a mysqli result object that reports how many rows the query returned.
All-in-one packages that install Apache, MySQL and PHP together on Windows/Linux/Mac, Linux, or Mac respectively.

quick_revision.title: Where the code runs
points: Client-side scripting (JavaScript) runs in the browser; the source is visible and no server round-trip is needed.
Server-side scripting (PHP) runs on the web server; the source is hidden and it can reach the database.
A scripting language is interpreted and produces markup code; a programming language is compiled and produces machine code.
The web needs three elements: the client, the server and the database.

quick_revision.title: Internet in five dates
points: 1957 Sputnik → 1958 ARPA → 1969 ARPANET → 1989 Tim Berners-Lee at CERN invents the WWW → 1993 Mosaic, the first graphical browser.
Data move by packet switching using the TCP/IP protocol suite.
1992: the military closed ARPANET and commercial organisations offered public Internet access.

quick_revision.title: Adding JavaScript to a page
points: Three ways: between <SCRIPT> and </SCRIPT>; as an external .js file loaded with src=; or inline inside an HTML tag using onclick, onmouseover, onload…
Prefer the external .js file for a real website — one copy, cached by the browser, edited in one place.
Around 96% of websites use JavaScript; it is light-weight, interpreted, case-sensitive and C-like in syntax.
JavaScript is object-BASED: every identifier is an object and no class is needed to create one.

quick_revision.title: Data types and variables
points: Primitive: String, Number, Boolean, Undefined, Null. Non-primitive: Object, Array, RegExp.
Declare with var (function/global scope, 1995–2015), let (block scope, changeable) or const (block scope, cannot be reassigned).
Names start with a letter, _ or $; they are case sensitive.
Operators: arithmetic, comparison (== vs ===), logical (&& || !), bitwise, assignment and special (?: , delete in instanceof new typeof void yield).

quick_revision.title: Functions and control structures
points: Four kinds: no parameter / no return, with parameter / no return, with parameter / with return, no parameter / with return.
Conditionals: if, if-else, if-else-if (nested if) and switch-case — always pair every case with break.
Loops: for (known count), while (unknown count, tested first), do-while (tested last, so it always runs at least once).

quick_revision.title: Objects, events and forms
points: Three ways to make an object: object literal, new Object(), or an object constructor function using the this keyword.
Predefined objects: Date, Number, String, Array and Math — each with its own method set.
Seven event objects to know: onclick, onsubmit, onmouseover/onmouseout, onfocus/onblur, onselect, onchange, ondblclick.
Form validation has two jobs: basic (all mandatory fields filled) and data-format (the values are well formed).
jQuery: $('#id'), $('.class'), $('p'); methods html(), text(), val(), css(), hide(), show(), toggle().

quick_revision.title: PHP essentials
points: Always use the canonical tag <?php … ?>; every command ends with a semicolon.
Every variable starts with $; keywords and function names are NOT case sensitive, variable names ARE.
8 data types: boolean, integer, float, string (scalar); array, object (compound); resource, NULL (special).
Double quotes expand variables; single quotes print them literally.
String concatenation uses the dot (.); combining a string with any other type yields a string.

quick_revision.title: PHP and MySQL
points: Since PHP 5.5 mysql_connect() is deprecated — use mysqli_connect() or PDO.
Every database script follows the same six steps: connect → check connect_error → build the SQL string → query → report success or error → close.
Read a result with $result = $conn->query($sql); test $result->num_rows; loop with while($row = $result->fetch_assoc()).
The three SELECT clauses: SELECT … FROM (which columns), WHERE (which rows), ORDER BY (which order).
Superglobals $_GET (URL, 1024-char limit, never for passwords) and $_POST (header, no size limit) collect form data.

teaching_plan.activity: Open a browser's View Source and Network tab on any site to show HTML, CSS and JS arriving separately. Then teach web technology, its components, and the client-side vs server-side split using the 8-point comparison table.

Internet history as a timeline on the board: 1957 Sputnik → 1958 ARPA → 1969 ARPANET → 1989 WWW → 1992 commercial access → 1993 Mosaic → 1996 'Internet' goes mainstream. Discuss how e-mail, IRC, social networks, video conferencing and VOIP changed communication.
Write 'Hello World' three times on the board — embedded, external and inline — and ask which belongs on a real 40-page site. Then cover the features and uses of JavaScript.
Walk through the language-fundamentals checklist, then drill the five primitive and three non-primitive data types. Contrast with C's int/float/char to make the point that JavaScript has only Number.
Naming rules and case sensitivity, then var vs let vs const with the scope demonstration. LAB: run the three declarations in a browser and try to reassign a const.
Arithmetic, comparison, logical, bitwise, assignment and special operators. Spend extra time on == vs === using MCQ 3, 4 and 15. LAB: run the arithmetic operator page and explain '43Test'.
Function definition, calling, parameters and return. Build the four-kinds table and run the worked example that demonstrates all four in one page.
if, if-else, if-else-if and switch-case (stress break). Then for, while and do-while; use the book's do-while example with count < 0 to prove the body runs once.
Three ways to create an object; then the predefined Date, Number, String, Array and Math objects with their method tables. Finish with the idea of event handling and the DOM.
Image, event and form objects. Demonstrate onclick, onsubmit, onmouseover/onmouseout, onfocus/onblur, onselect, onchange and ondblclick, then the fruit-selection form example.
Form validation: build the sample form, then add validate() for basic validation and validateEmail() for format validation. Show that returning false from onsubmit cancels the submission.

jQuery: what it is, why it is used, how to load it (local file or CDN), the $() factory function with tag / #id / .class, and the seven common methods. Then run the solved JavaScript programs section.

LAB SESSION: students type and run solved programs 1–11 (simple interest, positive/negative/zero, factorial, largest of three, odd numbers to 50, prime, multiplication table, array min/max, area of circle, sum, addition form).

Move to the server side: what PHP is, its five features, its strengths and weaknesses, its history (Rasmus Lerdorf, 1994), common uses and five characteristics. Then the software and hardware requirements and the XAMPP/WAMP/LAMP/MAMP install process.

OOP bridge (encapsulation, inheritance, polymorphism in PHP). Then the four PHP tags, comments, whitespace insensitivity, variable case sensitivity and blocks. LAB: install XAMPP and run a first .php page from htdocs.
The eight PHP data types with the three array kinds (numeric, associative, multidimensional) and foreach. Then work through PHP examples 1–15 in the lab.
PHP operators — arithmetic, comparison, logical, assignment, ternary, increment/decrement and string — then the precedence table. Finish with variable variables, superglobals and GET vs POST.
Database connectivity: mysqli vs PDO, connect → check → query → report → close. Work through creating a database, a table, an insert, and the three SELECT examples (plain, WHERE, ORDER BY).
LAB: the Exercise-3 practical programs — form-based arithmetic calculator, current day and time, and the PHP employee / product database scripts (connect, insert, select with WHERE, delete).
Quick-revision round, then Exercise-3: 12 short, 4 long, 28 practical. Finish with the 38 multiple-choice questions as a timed self-test using the show/hide answer key.
