sections.title: Introduction and features of C Language

blocks.text: C is a programming language developed at AT & T's Bell Laboratories of the USA in the 1970s. It was designed and developed by Dennis M. Ritchie. C stands in between a high-level language and a low-level language — that is why it is often called a Middle-level language. It is designed to have both: relatively good programming efficiency (as compared to machine-oriented languages) and relatively good machine efficiency.
Features of the C language

items: Portability: one of the reasons for C's popularity. We can easily transform a program written in C from one computer to another with few or no changes and compile it with an appropriate compiler.

Faster and efficient: C is desirable because it is faster and more efficient than the comparable program in most other high-level languages. For example, a program to increment a variable from 0 to 15000 takes about 50 seconds in BASIC while it takes 1 second in C.

Supports structured programming: it is well suited for structured programming, which means the problem might be solved in terms of function modules or blocks. The modular structure makes program debugging, testing and maintenance easier.
Extendibility: C is basically a collection of functions that are supported by the C library. We can continuously add (or extend) our own functions to the C library.

Flexible: C permits us to write any complex program with the help of its rich set of built-in functions and operators. In addition, it permits the use of low-level language. Hence it is also called a middle-level language, and it is well suited for both system and application software development.

blocks.title: Exam phrasing
blocks.text: 'C is a middle-level language' means it combines the programming efficiency of a high-level language with the machine efficiency of a low-level language. Always name Dennis M. Ritchie and AT & T Bell Laboratories, 1970s in the introduction.

items: A program is a sequence of instructions. An instruction of a C program is written as a statement, and a statement is terminated by a semicolon (;).
One or more statements form a block (compound statement) enclosed within a pair of braces, i.e. { }.
All executable statements must be inside a function. A function is a collection of statements that performs some specific task.
Every C program consists of one or more functions, and every C program must contain a special function named main(). The statements within this function are the first ones to be executed.
A comment is written within the delimiters /* and */.

blocks.text: Output:

Hello, Grade XII
Welcome to C Programming

Draw the skeleton on the board and drill it until every student can write it from memory: #include <stdio.h> → void main() → { → statements → }. Every program in this chapter is this skeleton with a different body.
A character set in C contains any alphabet, digit or special symbol used to represent information. The following table shows the valid alphabets, numbers and special symbols allowed in C.

blocks.caption: Table: The C character set
head: Group
Characters allowed
rows: A, B, C, …… Y, Z    and    a, b, c, ….. y, z, and _ (underscore).

blocks.title: Counting the alphabets
blocks.text: There are 53 alphabetic characters in C: 52 letters (A–Z and a–z) plus the underscore ( _ ). This is why the underscore may be used anywhere a letter may be used — including as the first character of an identifier.

In any programming language a program is made up of the smallest individual syntactic elements. The basic and smallest element used to develop the program and recognised by the C compiler is called a C token. It is the individual unit in a program — a piece of source-program text that the compiler does not break down into component elements.

blocks.title: C tokens include:
items: Identifier.
Keyword.
Constant and variable.
Operator.

blocks.text: a. Identifier

The identifier is the name given to various program elements such as a variable, function, label and other user-defined items. It can be a combination of numbers, alphabets and the special symbol underscore ( _ ). The first character of an identifier must be an alphabet or an underscore. In an identifier, uppercase and lowercase alphabets are treated differently (because of case sensitivity). Identifiers are strings of alphanumeric characters that do not begin with numbers.
For example, sum, Sum, a_b, _temp, field4, Year2011 and roll_no are valid identifiers.
Case Sensitive
Uppercase letters and lowercase letters are treated as different — this is known as case sensitive. For example, apple is different from Apple, aPPle, ApPlE, APPLE, ApPle, aPple and APPLe.
b. Keyword

A keyword is a reserved word that has a standard and predefined meaning in C. We cannot use a keyword for any other purpose other than as a predefined task in a C program; its meaning has already been defined by the C compiler. ANSI C defines 32 keywords. Keywords cannot be used as variable names, because doing so would be trying to assign a new meaning to the keyword, which the compiler does not allow.

blocks.title: Note
blocks.text: "All data types are keywords but all keywords are not data types."

blocks.caption: Table: List of all 32 keywords available in C
head: Group
Keywords

blocks.text: c. Constant

A quantity that does not change during program execution. This quantity can be stored at a location in the memory of the computer. Constants refer to fixed values that may not be altered by the program. For example, radius = 3.14 is a constant.
C has four basic types of constants:

items: Integer constant: an integer-valued number; it can be positive or negative, and it can be a decimal, octal or hexadecimal integer constant.
Floating-point constant: a fractional number; it can be written either in decimal form or in an exponent form, or both. It can also be a decimal, octal or hexadecimal floating-point constant.
Character constant: a single character, enclosed in apostrophes (single quotation marks), e.g. 'A'.
String constant: any number of consecutive characters enclosed in double quotation marks, e.g. "Kathmandu".

blocks.text: d. Variable

Variables are the most fundamental part of any programming language. A variable is a symbolic name which is used to store different types of data in the computer's memory and may change during program execution. When the user gives a value to the variable, that value is stored at the same location occupied by the variable. A variable may be of integer, character, string or floating type.
Variable Declaration and Initialization

All variables need to be declared before they are used. For a variable declaration we state its type followed by the variable name. For example, int i; declares an integer variable i. We can also declare any number of variables of the same type in a single statement.
Syntax to declare a variable in C: <Data type> <list of variables>;
e. Operators

C is very rich in built-in operators. An operator is a symbol that instructs C to perform some operation or action on one or more operands. An operand is something that an operator acts on. Operators that require two operands are binary (dyadic) operators; an operator that requires one operand is unary (monadic); and an operator that requires three operands is a ternary operator. For example, in the mathematical expression A + B, A and B are the operands, + is the operator, and A + B is an expression.

blocks.title: The C language offers the following types of operators:
items: Arithmetic operator.
Relational operator.
Equality operator.
Logical operator.
Assignment operator.
Increment / Decrement operator.
Conditional operator (ternary operator).
Bitwise operator.
Special operator.

blocks.text: A data type is an instruction used to declare the category or type of the variable being used in the program. Any variable used in the program must be declared before using it. The data type determines the way a computer organises data in memory — how much space it occupies in storage and how the bit pattern stored is interpreted. A data type can be either basic (fundamental) or derived. The basic data types are int, float, char, void and double, whereas the derived data types are array, string, structure and union.

blocks.caption: Figure: Data Types in C — basic, derived, user-defined and valueless types.

items: int: represents integer numbers (numbers without a fraction, e.g. 546). It requires 2 bytes of memory space. It can be either signed or unsigned. Derived data types from int are short int and long int.
float: represents real numbers (numbers with a fraction, e.g. 3.14). It requires 4 bytes of memory space. It can also be signed or unsigned. Derived data types from float are double and long double.
char: represents a single alphabet or symbol (e.g. 'A', 'f', '@') or, for a string, multiple alphabets or symbols. It requires 1 byte of memory space and can be either signed or unsigned.
double: used to hold real numbers; it can represent fractional as well as whole numbers. It occupies 8 bytes of memory and its format specifier is %lf.
void: has no values. It is used as the return type for functions that do not return a value.

blocks.caption: C data types at a glance
head: Data type
Stores
Bytes (typical)
Format specifier

blocks.text: The byte sizes given here (int = 2, float = 4, double = 8) are the values printed in this textbook and are the ones to write in an exam. Modern 64-bit compilers usually give int 4 bytes, so a sizeof demonstration in the lab may print a different number — explain the difference rather than marking the book wrong.

An operation using a function that deals with the interaction of the console (screen/keyboard) — getting input from the user through the keyboard and displaying the output on the screen. In simple words, console input and output means to read from, or write to, a screen.
printf()

printf() can be used to output data of different types in different formats — performing rounding, aligning columns, right/left justification, inserting literal characters, exponential format, hexadecimal format, and fixed width and precision. Every printf() call returns a value: the number of characters output; if it returns a negative number then an error has occurred.
The general form of an output function is: printf(format-string, arg1, arg2, ...., argn)
scanf()

scanf() is the general-purpose console input function. It can read all the built-in data types and automatically convert numbers into the proper internal format. The general form is: scanf(format-string, arg1, arg2, ..., argn);

#include <stdio.h>
scanf("%d\n", &n);      // note the ampersand — scanf needs the ADDRESS

blocks.title: The ampersand rule
blocks.text: printf() needs values: printf("%d", n);. scanf() needs addresses: scanf("%d", &n);. The single most common beginner error in C is a missing & in scanf(). The only exception is reading into a character array (string), where the array name is already an address: scanf("%s", name);
Some other I/O Functions

items: getchar() and putchar() — read / write a single character.
getc() and putc() — read / write a single character from / to a stream.
getch() and putch() — read / write a character without echoing it to the screen (declared in conio.h).
getche() — read a character and echo it to the screen.

Output: Computer

As the name suggests, control structures enable us to specify the order in which the various instructions in a program are to be executed by the computer. The control instructions determine the "flow of control" in a program. They are:

blocks.caption: The five categories of control instruction
head: Category
Created using
Meaning
rows: Also known as a linear statement; control flows from top to bottom.
switch, if, if-else, nested if-else, ladders of if-else, if else-if else
Also known as iteration or repetition.
Transfers control to another part of the program.
Marks a position that a jump can target.

blocks.text: i. Sequence

In a sequential statement, program control flows from top to bottom. Program statements are executed one after another in a sequence (statement 3 will be executed only after statement 2). It is the simplest type of control structure; it does not contain any condition or looping statement.
ii. Decision (Selection)
Decision allows us to control the flow of a program's execution based upon a condition. The conditional expression is mainly used for decision making.
a. if statement

The if statement is used to express conditional expressions. If the given condition is true then it will execute the statements; otherwise it will execute the optional statements. The braces { and } are used to group declarations and statements into a compound statement or a block.
b. if..else statement
Either of the two statements is executed depending upon the value of the expression. statement1 is executed if the expression is true, else statement2 is executed.
c. nested if-else statement
An if..else statement that is again inside an if..else statement is called a nested if..else statement.
d. if–else–if statement (ladders of if-else)

A common programming construct is the if–else–if ladder, so called because of its appearance. The conditions are evaluated from the top to bottom: as soon as a true condition is found, the statement associated with it is executed and the rest of the ladder is bypassed. If none of the conditions is true, the final else is executed. If the final else is not present, no action takes place if all the conditions are false.
e. switch-case statement

The switch statement is a special decision maker that tests whether an expression matches one of a number of signed integer constants or character constant values. A switch statement can only be used to test for equality — we cannot use a relational or logical expression as we can in if..else. The switch expression must evaluate to an integer or a character constant value. No two case constants can be the same.

blocks.title: switch vs if-else
blocks.text: Use switch only when you are comparing one integer or character value against a list of constants (a menu, a day number, a grade letter). The moment you need >, <, && or ||, you must use if–else. And always end each case with break; or execution falls through into the next case.

An operation that repeats the execution of a statement until a certain condition is satisfied. The computer has the ability to perform a set of instructions repeatedly — either for a specified number of times or until a given condition is satisfied. This repetitive operation is done by a loop control statement.
There are three methods for generating repetition of a certain part of the program: the for statement, the while statement and the do…while statement.
a. for loop

The for loop is the most commonly used statement in C. It consists of three expressions: the first is used to initialise the index value, the second to check whether the loop is to be continued again, and the third to change the index value for further repetition.

for (initialization; condition; increment/decrement)
   statement(s);

First the initialization is executed. Then the condition is evaluated: if the condition is nonzero (true) the statement(s) are executed, and after the statement(s) the increment/decrement is executed.
b. while loop
The while loop first checks whether the initial condition is true or false and, finding it true, enters the loop and executes the statement.
c. do..while loop

In the case of the do-while loop, control enters the loop at least once and only then checks whether the given condition is true or false. As long as the test condition is true the statements are repeated again and again; otherwise the loop terminates.

blocks.caption: for vs while vs do-while
head: Loop
Condition tested
Use when
Body runs at least once?
rows: The number of repetitions is known in advance.
The number of repetitions is not known.
You must run the body once before testing.

1. Simple interest and amount
2. Fibonacci series up to the nth term
3. Factorial of a given positive number
4. Prime or not

blocks.text: The prime test used here counts divisors: a number is prime when it has exactly two divisors (1 and itself). Point out that looping only up to n/2 would be enough, and ask students to rewrite it as an exercise. Note also that printing the factorial without braces around the else body works but is poor style — the book's layout omits the braces, and you should add them.

A collection of variables of the same type represented by a common name — that is, a collection of homogeneous data types (it contains all similar elements). If it contains the int data type, all the data of the array must be int; if float, then all the data must be float.

A specific element of an array is accessed by an index. Each array element is accessed by specifying the array name followed by a subscript/index enclosed in square brackets — so an array is also called a subscripted / indexed variable. The subscript is used to denote the size of the array. For example, in int a[6], int is the data type of the array, a is the name of the array and 6 is the size (6 elements); each subscript must be a non-negative number.
For example, int c[12]; — the index of the first element is 0, the second element has an index of 1 and so on. The last element has an index of (array size − 1).
Array Declaration

In C all variables must be declared before they are used, so an array must be declared so that the compiler understands the type of the variable and the array size in the first line after main(). Declaring the name and type of an array and setting the number of elements in the array is known as dimensioning the array.

blocks.title: Syntax
items: data_type array_name[size];
data_type array_name[size] = {list of elements};
data_type array_name[] = {list of elements};

blocks.text:
int   number[40];                            /* 40 integers */
char  letter[52];                            /* 52 characters */
float a[4] = {6.3, 12.56, 18.78, 60.88};     /* size taken from the list */
int   b[]  = {6, 612, -5, 10};               /* size taken from the list */
Type of Array (dimension)

blocks.caption: Array dimensions
head: Dimension
Declaration
Example

blocks.text: As the number of subscripts increases, the dimension of the array also increases proportionately.
1. Ask ten numbers from the user and display them using an array
2. Count the employees getting a salary from 5000 to 10000
3. Sort 10 numbers in ascending order

The inner loop of this bubble sort runs j from 0 to 9 and compares num[j] with num[j+1] — on the last pass that reads num[10], which is outside the array. The safe bound is j < 9 (or j < n-1-i). Show the bug on the board; it is a genuine off-by-one error in the printed program and an excellent debugging exercise.
4. Find the largest among 'n' numbers

We can represent a character easily with the char data type, whereas a string is a group of characters that can ONLY be represented by a character array. Consider the declaration char x; — we can store only one character at a time, always enclosed in a single quote, e.g. char x = 'a';
To represent a string we declare and initialize as follows:
We can use quoted strings to initialize character arrays:
char s[10] = "C program ";

blocks.title: The null character
blocks.text: Here the null character (a special character used in a string to mark the end of the string) is appended by the compiler, i.e. the character '\0'. Note that a space is also a character, so it also takes 1 byte. This is why a string of 9 visible characters needs an array of at least 10 bytes.
Array of Strings

A two-dimensional array can be thought of as an array of one-dimensional arrays. Since a string can be assigned to a one-dimensional array of char type, we can use a two-dimensional char array as an array of strings.
char months[12][10];
The left dimension determines the number of strings, and the right dimension specifies the maximum length of each string.
String Functions (header file string.h)

Purpose
Syntax

Combines two strings together to form a whole string.
Compares two strings: returns 0 if the two strings are equal, otherwise −1 or 1.
Changes an uppercase string to a lowercase string (skipping characters already lowercase).
Changes a lowercase string to an uppercase string (skipping characters already uppercase).

blocks.text: There are other string-related library functions defined under the string.h header file. In addition, there are further string / character functions under other header files such as ctype.h and stdlib.h.

blocks.title: Exam answer (MCQ 1)
blocks.text: strcat(str1, str2); appends str2 to the end of str1. With str1 = "Hello" and str2 = "world", puts(str1); prints Helloworld — there is no space inserted between them.
1. Count the number of vowels in a string
2. Palindrome word
Order matters: strcpy(word1, word); must be done before strrev(), because strrev() reverses the string in place — it destroys the original. This is the classic palindrome trap.
3. Sort the names of 'n' students in alphabetical order

blocks.caption: Output of the program that sorts student names alphabetically.

blocks.title: Strings cannot be assigned with =
blocks.text: You cannot write name[i] = name[j]; for character arrays. You must always use strcpy() (or a loop). This single rule explains most student errors in this section.

A self-contained program segment, or block of statements, that performs some specific, well-defined task. Every C program comprises one or more such functions. The execution of any program always begins by executing the instructions in the main() function.

In a program there may be any number of functions and their definitions can appear in any order, but they should be independent of one another. We need to access the function (which is known as calling a function) in order to carry out the intended task. A single function can be accessed or called from different places within a program. After execution of the intended task, control returns to the point from which the function was accessed or called.

blocks.caption: Figure: Proper use of the function in a program.

blocks.text: Advantages of Functions

items: Functions increase code reusability by avoiding rewriting of the same code over and over.
If a program is divided into multiple functions, then each function can be independently developed, so program development will be easier.
Program development will be faster.
Program debugging will be easier.
Functions reduce program complexity.
They facilitate top-down modular programming: the high-level logic of the overall problem is solved first while the details of each lower-level function are addressed later.
The length of the program can be reduced by using a function at appropriate places.
A function may be used by many other programs — a C programmer can build on what others have already done instead of starting over from scratch.
With functions it is easier to understand the logic involved in the program.
The recursive call is possible through a function.
Irrelevant details, from the user's point of view, can be hidden through a function.
Functions increase program readability.

blocks.text: In C programming, functions can be classified into two types: library (built-in) functions and user-defined functions.
i. Library Function

A library function is a predefined function in a header file or pre-processor directive. The programmer can use this function by simply adding the header file to the program. The programmer cannot change or alter the meaning of this function, and does not have to declare and define it.

blocks.caption: Common header files and their functions
head: Header file
Functions it provides
Purpose
rows: Pause the program and clear the console screen.

blocks.text: Advantages of library functions

items: Time-saving: developers avoid rewriting common functionalities, thus speeding up the development process.
Reliability: library functions are thoroughly tested and optimised, reducing the possibility of errors in the program.
Portability: programs using standard library functions are more portable across different systems and compilers.
Readability: using well-known library functions makes the code more readable and understandable to others familiar with C.

blocks.text: ii. User-Defined Function

A user-defined function is declared, defined and used by the programmer according to their need. Examples: a function to calculate the area of your room; a function to sort 10 entered numbers using an array.
Advantages of user-defined functions

items: Modularity: they help break down complex programs into smaller pieces, promoting modularity.
Reusability: once defined, they can be reused in different parts of the program or even in different programs.
Readability and maintainability: functions encapsulate specific tasks, making the code more organised and easier to read, debug and maintain.
Abstraction: they let programmers abstract complex operations, simplifying the main program logic.

Library function
User-defined function

Not predefined; it is defined by the programmer according to the need.
The programmer simply uses it by including the respective header file.

blocks.text: Functions are the essential building blocks that encapsulate specific tasks or operations. Each function in C has several components that define its behaviour and its interaction with other parts of the program. A function contains the following components:

items: Function declaration (prototype).
Function call.
Function definition (body).
Return statement of the function.

blocks.text: i. Function Prototype (Function declaration)
The function prototype is also termed a function declaration. It provides the following information:

items: It provides the name of the function.
It specifies the type of value returned by the function (this is optional; the default is an integer).
It provides the number and type of arguments that must be supplied in the call to the function.
It facilitates error checking between calls to a function and the corresponding function definition.

blocks.text: When we write the user-defined function ahead of the main() function it is not necessary to use a function prototype, because the user-defined function will already have been defined before the first access. However, many programmers prefer a "top-down" approach, in which main() appears ahead of the user-defined function. In that case the function call within main() precedes the function definition, which would confuse the compiler unless it is first alerted that the function will be defined later — that is exactly what the prototype does.

/* Syntax for a function prototype */
return_type function_name(parameter-list);
ii. Function call

A function call is a statement that activates the execution of the function. When a function call is encountered in a program, control of the program jumps to the called function and execution of that function starts.

/* Syntax for a function call */
function_name(argument-list);
During a function call, arguments may or may not be passed to the called function.
iii. Function Definition

A function definition provides the actual body of the function. It contains the statements that will be executed when the function is called, together with the function name, the list of parameters and the return type.

blocks.caption: Figure: Example of a function definition.

blocks.title: Details of the syntax
items: function-name: any valid identifier.
return-value-type: the data type of the result. It can be omitted, in which case it defaults to int; void indicates that the function returns nothing.

parameter-list: a comma-separated list that declares the parameter variables. The function body contains the statements that define the action to be taken; those statements can be expression statements, compound statements, control statements and so on. Variables can be declared inside blocks. All variables declared inside functions are local variables (known only inside the function).

blocks.title: Note
blocks.text: Functions cannot be defined inside other functions. Every function definition must stand on its own at file level.
iv. return and void statements of a function
return statement

One of the main features of a function is that it can return a value to the calling function. For a function to return a value it should have a return statement, comprising the keyword return followed by the value to be returned. That value may be an expression, a variable, a constant, or even another function call. The returned expression may be enclosed in parentheses; this is often done although it is not necessary. In general terms the return statement is written as:
return expression;

When a return statement is executed it immediately transfers control back to the calling program. A function call can return only a single value each time it is called. As soon as a return statement is executed the function terminates.

blocks.caption: Uses of the return keyword in a function
head: Returning nothing (void)
Returning a value
rows:
void func(int n)
{
  if (n < 1)
  {
    puts("Number is not positive");
    return;
  }
  if (n % 2 == 0)
    puts("Number is even");
  else
    puts("Number is odd");
}

int maximum(int a, int b)
{
  if (a > b)
    return a;
  else
    return b;
}

blocks.title: Note
blocks.text: A function definition can contain multiple return statements — however, only one of them gets executed.
void

If a function does not return a value we say its return type is void: it does not give any output to the caller. Even a function of return type void may contain a return keyword — when it does, that keyword is used simply to transfer control to the end of the function.

In the example above, the objective of func() is to print the given number as even or odd, but we only want it to do the job if the number is positive. If and only if the number is positive does it print even or odd; otherwise control is transferred to the end of the function.

The void statement is an advanced concept in C that needs an explanation of the pointer. An example is void *p; — here *p can hold the address of any type of variable, such that the variable needs to be type-cast with (void *).
Actual argument and Formal Argument

Any variable declared in the body of a function is said to be local to that function. Variables that are declared neither as arguments nor inside the function body are considered global to the function and must be defined externally. Arguments defined inside the function are called formal arguments, whereas the arguments from which values have been passed to a function are known as actual arguments.
When a function is called, the value of the arguments is copied to the corresponding parameters in the function definition.

blocks.caption: Figure: Arguments passing example — actual and formal arguments.

sections.title: Accessing a function by passing values

blocks.text: In C, "accessing a function by passing values" typically refers to calling a function with arguments. This can be done in two primary ways: call by value and call by reference. Understanding these concepts is crucial for controlling how functions interact with the data they process.
1. Call by Value

When a function is called, the values of the arguments are copied into the function parameters. The function operates on these copies, and changes to the parameters do not affect the original variables in the calling function.

Explanation of the output: before the call, b is 60 and this is printed. Inside changeValue, the function receives a copy of b (called a); it changes a to 20 and prints it. That change does not affect b in main(). After the call, b remains 60, because the function only modified a copy.
2. Call by Reference

When a function is called, the addresses of the arguments are passed to the function parameters. The function operates on the actual variables via these addresses, so changes to the parameters directly affect the original variables in the calling function.
Categories of User-Defined Function
Depending on the presence or absence of arguments, and whether a value is returned or not, a function can be categorised as:

blocks.text: Use the return type void and omit the return statement. Here we simply call a function without passing arguments, and the called function does not have to return any value to the calling function.

sections.title: Concept of Storage: Automatic and External

blocks.text: The storage class of a variable determines its scope (visibility), its storage duration and its linkage. Scope defines where the variable can be referenced in the program. Storage duration defines how long a variable exists in memory. Linkage specifies the files in which the variable is known.

blocks.title: A storage class of a variable defines:
items: Where the variable would be stored.
What the initial value of the variable will be if an initial value is not specifically assigned (the default initial value).
What the scope of the variable is — that is, in which functions the value of the variable would be available.
What the life of the variable is — that is, how long the variable would exist.

blocks.text: The storage class is determined by the position of the declaration in the source file and by the storage class specifiers auto, extern, static or register. There are four storage classes in C:

blocks.caption: List of storage classes and their keywords
head: Storage class
Keyword

blocks.text: Among these classes, this section discusses only the automatic storage class and the external storage class.
1. Automatic Storage Class
This is the default classification for all variables declared within a function body. Its features are:

items: Automatic variables are truly local.
They are unknown to other functions.
When the function is exited, the values of automatic variables are not retained.
They are normally implemented using a stack.
They are recreated each time the function is called.
The automatic variable may begin with the class specifier auto, but this is optional.

blocks.title: What this prints
blocks.text: a and b were never initialised, so they hold garbage values — whatever happened to be on the stack. An automatic variable has no default value; this is the single most important fact about auto.
2. External Storage Class (Global variable)
A variable of the external storage class is declared outside any function. These are also called global variables. Its features are:

items: External variables are declared outside the function.
All functions in the program can access and modify global variables.
The scope of the variable is global, i.e. within the whole program.
The life-time of the variable is as long as the program's execution does not come to an end.
The default initial value for this variable is zero.
An external variable may begin with the class specifier extern.

blocks.text: The three-word summary students remember best: auto = local, garbage, temporary; extern = global, zero, permanent.

A function that calls itself. A function will be recursive if it contains the following two features: (1) the function should call itself, and (2) the function should have a stopping condition (base criteria) — and every time the function calls itself it must be closer to that base criteria.
The concept of using a recursive function to repeat the execution of statements many times is known as recursion.

2. Sum of all natural numbers up to n, using recursion

Ask students to trace factorial(4) on paper: 4 × factorial(3) → 4 × 3 × factorial(2) → 4 × 3 × 2 × factorial(1) → 4 × 3 × 2 × 1 = 24. The if (n == 0 || n == 1) return 1; line is the base criteria — remove it and the program crashes with a stack overflow. That is the one sentence to write in any recursion exam answer.

A collection of one or more variables, possibly of different data types (e.g. int, float, char), grouped together under a single name for convenient handling. Structures help to organise data, particularly in large programs, because they allow a group of related variables to be treated as a single unit.

Once the structure has been declared we can create a variable of its type. In some languages structures are known as records, and the elements of a structure are known as fields, members or components.
Declaration of Structure
The four parts of a declaration are the keyword (struct), the structure name or tag, the structure members and the structure variables.
Let us create a structure to illustrate the above declaration:

The keyword struct introduces a structure declaration, which is a list of declarations enclosed in braces. The variables declared within the structure declaration are called its structure members. The struct declaration defines a data type, and the variables emp1 and emp2 that follow it are defined as variables of this type, with storage space set aside for them.

blocks.title: Declaration vs definition
blocks.text: A structure declaration that is not followed by a list of variables reserves no storage space — it merely describes the template. In other words, the structure is only defined, not declared. We can declare a variable later, for example struct employee emp3;.

The word following the keyword struct (employee in this case) is called the structure tag and is optional: it only names the type defined by the declaration, so that it can be used as a substitute later. For example, a new variable emp3 of type struct employee could be declared as employee emp3; without the struct keyword.
Initialization of Structure

Like other variables and arrays, structure variables can also be initialized where they are declared. The format is quite similar to that used to initialize arrays: we list the values for the individual members, separated by commas and enclosed in braces. The initial values must appear in the order in which they will be assigned to their corresponding structure members.
Size of Structure
The elements of a structure are always stored in contiguous memory locations. Taking the example above:

Every structure member takes its own memory. In this example name takes 35 bytes (char takes 1 byte and it is a character array of size 35, so 35 characters take 35 bytes). age takes 2 bytes because it is unsigned int. address takes 50 bytes as it is also a character array. salary takes 4 bytes. Altogether the size of the structure is 91 bytes, so every structure variable of type employee takes 91 bytes.

blocks.caption: Figure: Allocation of the memory of the structure.

blocks.text: After declaring the structure name and the structure variables, a structure member is always referred to and accessed using the structure variable:
structure_variable.structure_member
This structure member access operator "." connects the structure name and the structure member name. For example, to print the name of the employee:

#include <stdio.h>
printf("The employee's name is %s", emp1.name);
4.3.2.1 Nested Structures

Nested structures are nothing but a structure within a structure. Taking the employee example, the address member could itself be a structure storing the house number, the street name, the area name and the pin code.
If a variable emp3 has been declared, then to access street_name we write:
emp3.address.street_name
This form is valid for any kind of nested structure declaration seen above.
A collection of similar types of structure placed in a common variable name is called an array of structure.

Pointers are basically the same as any other variable. What is different about them is that instead of containing actual data, they contain a pointer to the memory location where the information can be found. This is a very important concept and many programs and ideas rely on pointers as the basis of their design.

Variable names are not sufficient to provide all the requirements of C during manipulation: local variables are meaningful only within their declaring functions. However, memory addresses are global to all functions. One function can pass the address of a local variable to another function, and the second function can use that address to access the contents of the first function's local variable. Hence we use a pointer variable, which can store an address (memory location) and points to whatever that memory location contains.
Pointer Notation
Consider the declaration int i = 3;. This tells the C compiler to:

items: Reserve space in memory to hold the integer value.
Associate the name i with this memory location.
Store the value 3 at this location.

blocks.text: We may represent i's location in memory by the following memory map.

blocks.caption: Memory map of a variable: location name (i), value at location (3) and location number (65490).

blocks.text: Why should we use a pointer?

items: Pointers enable us to access a variable that is defined outside the function.
Pointers reduce the length and complexity of a program and increase execution speed.
Pointers are more efficient in handling data tables.
Using a pointer array to character strings saves data storage space in memory.
Pointers are more efficient in handling data arrays.
Pointers manipulate arrays more easily by moving pointers to them instead of moving the arrays themselves.
Pointers are used to create complex data structures such as linked lists and trees.
Pointers are used to communicate information about memory — for example, returning the location of free memory.

blocks.text: Advantages of Pointer

items: Pointers increase the execution speed and thus reduce program execution time.
With the help of a pointer we can handle any type of data structure.
By using pointers you can access data that is available outside a function.
By using a pointer variable we can implement dynamic memory allocation.
Pointers provide an efficient tool for manipulating dynamic data structures such as structures, linked lists, queues, stacks and trees.
Pointers reduce the length and complexity of programs.
Pointers allow us to pass variables, arrays, functions, strings and structures as function arguments.

blocks.text: Disadvantages of Pointer

items: Pointers add a level of complexity to the code — for example, the null pointer.
They can cause memory leaks and security vulnerabilities (buffer overflows).
They can cause portability issues.
They require manual memory management.

blocks.text: Pointer Declaration

In the above program two different operators have been used: & (ampersand) and * (asterisk). The & operator gives the address of the variable associated with it and is called the "address of" operator. The * operator gives the value stored at a particular address; it is called the "value at address" operator, also known as the indirection operator.

blocks.caption: Variable i, pointer j and the addresses they hold.

blocks.title: Reading a declaration
blocks.text: float *s means 's is going to contain the address of a floating-point value'. Similarly char *ch means 'ch is going to contain the address of a char value', and int *i means 'i is going to contain the address of an integer value'.
Given a variable, C allows its address to be extracted; conversely, given an address, it is possible to obtain the contents at that address. Consider the declaration:
int *x, *y, z = 10;

The C "address of" operator is the ampersand, &. It is a unary operator that, applied to a variable (strictly, to a value), yields its memory address. &z is the address at which the computer stores the int variable z, and this remains fixed throughout program execution — attempting to change it in any way is an error. This address may be assigned to x because x has been declared to be a pointer to variables of type int:
x = &z;
x now holds the address of z, which you may print:

#include <stdio.h>
printf("The address of z is: \t%u\n", x);

Like all unary operators, & has a priority just below the parenthesis operator and groups from right to left. The address-of operator is not unfamiliar: the scanf() function has an argument list of pointers to memory locations.

Reciprocally, C has the "contents at address" (or dereferencing, or indirection) operator: the asterisk, *. This unary operator yields the value residing at a memory address. Applied to a pointer variable that has been initialised to an address, it finds the contents at that address. After x = &z;, *x gives the contents at the address held in x — the output of the printf() below is therefore the value of z, 10:

#include <stdio.h>
printf("The contents of the address held in x are:%d", *x);
To clarify these concepts further, assume that the address of the int variable z is 38790 and that the content at this address is 10.

blocks.caption: Pointer x holding the address of z (38790), and the address of x itself (56780).

blocks.text: After x = &z;, x gets the value "address of z", i.e. 38790. Suppose the address of x is 56780 — then the contents at 56780 will be 38790. The content of x is the address of z (38790); the content of z is the value 10. The subsequent assignment *x = 20 changes the value of z to 20 using the indirection operator.

For example, let ptr be an integer pointer currently holding the address 6222; after ptr++, ptr contains 6224. (The expression ptr-- points to the memory location of the previous element.) All pointers increase or decrease by the length of the data type they point to.

In the same way we may add or subtract integers to or from pointers. The expression ptr = ptr + 2 makes ptr point to the second element of ptr's type beyond the one it currently points to, and ptr = ptr - 2 makes ptr point to the second element before the one it currently points to.

sections.title: Call by Values and Call by Reference (Parameter Passing Technique)

blocks.text: Call by value

In a call by value, the values of variables are passed to the function from the calling section. This method copies the value of the actual parameters into the formal parameters: when the function is called, a separate copy of the variables is created in memory and the value of the original variables is given to these copies. So any change made in the value inside the called function is not reflected in the original variable of the calling function. It can return only one value.
Call by reference

In a call by reference we pass the address (location number) of a variable to the function during the function call. Pointers are used to call a function by reference. When a function is called by reference, the formal argument becomes a reference to the actual argument: the called function does not create its own copy of the values, it refers to the original values only by the reference name. This function works with the original data and the changes are made in the original data itself. It can return more than one value at a time.
Differentiate between 'call by value' and 'call by reference'

blocks.caption: Call by value vs call by reference
head: Call by value
Call by reference
rows:
void fun(int x, int y);
void main()
{
  int a = 5, b = 10;
  fun(a, b);
  printf("a=%d,b=%d", a, b);
  getch();
}
void fun(int x, int y)
{
  x = x + 100;
  y = y + 100;
}

Result: a=5, b=10

void fun(int*, int*);
void main()
{
  int a = 5, b = 10;
  fun(&a, &b);
  printf("a=%d,b=%d", a, b);
  getch();
}
void fun(int *x, int *y)
{
  *x = *x + 100;
  *y = *y + 100;
}

Result: a=105, b=110

The arguments 'a' and 'b' are passed by value: their values are copied into 'x' and 'y' in fun(). The statements x = x + 100 and y = y + 100 change only the copies and do not affect the original values. The modifications made to x and y inside fun() do not affect a and b in main().

We passed the address (memory location) of the variables 'a' and 'b' with fun(&a, &b). The address operator (&) denotes the address of a variable, and those addresses are pointed at by the pointers *x, *y. The statements *x = *x + 100 and *y = *y + 100 change the original values, because the pointers point directly at the memory locations of a and b. The pointer declaration and initialisation during the call look like int *x = &a; and int *y = &b;.
The value of the actual argument is copied into the formal parameter of the function.
The memory address of the actual argument is assigned to the formal argument parameter.

blocks.text: Many applications require that information be written to, or read from, an auxiliary storage device. Such information stored in the disk (secondary storage device) is in the form of the data file. Data files therefore allow information to be stored permanently, and to be accessed and retrieved (extracted) whenever necessary — that method is file handling in C.

As we know, while the program is processing, the contents of the variables are stored in RAM. The problem is that if such values are needed in the future, they are lost — the values exist only while the program is being processed, and after the program is over the content of RAM gets erased. To overcome this problem we use a data file to save the content into it, so that we can retrieve the content from the data file whenever we want it.

blocks.caption: Figure: Block diagram of file accessing — content written to a file and read from a file using various functions.

blocks.text: File Operation Modes
There are different ways in which a file is to be opened.

blocks.caption: File opening modes
head: File opening mode
Description
rows: Used to open the file for reading, provided the file must exist to read it.
Used for opening the file for writing. If the file exists, its contents will be erased; if the file doesn't exist, then it will be created.

Used for opening the file to append (to add the content from the last offset) if the file exists; but if the file doesn't exist, a new file will be created and the pointer will be at the first offset, at location 0, ready to put the content from the beginning of the file.
Used for opening the file for both reading and writing. The file must already exist before performing the operation.
Used for opening the file for both writing and reading; if the file exists its contents are erased.

Used for opening the file for both reading and appending (to add the content from the last offset) if the file exists; but if the file doesn't exist, a new file will be created and the pointer will be at the first offset, at location 0, ready to put the content from the beginning of the file.

blocks.text: EOF (End Of File)

This character is written to a file while writing the content into a file and especially when the fclose() statement is called — this character is written then. It is used in the program while reading the content back from the file. After the detection of the EOF character is reached, the reading of the file stops. So it is used to signify the end of the file while reading back the content.

blocks.title: Note
blocks.text: EOF is only applicable to a text-mode file. In binary mode the offset pointer keeps track of the end of the file from the number of data to be read as per the data type given.
Data File Operation

Before we can write a file to disk or read it, we must open it. Opening a file establishes an understanding between our program and the operating system about which file we are going to access and how we are going to do it. We provide the operating system with the name of the file and other information, such as whether we plan to read or write to it.

items: Opening a file starts with the declaration of a variable of type pointer to a file, in the statement FILE *fptr;

Then we open the file with the statement below, where fptr is a file pointer which points to our data file. Syntax: fopen("path:\\filename.ext", "file operation mode"); For example fptr = fopen("c:\\name.txt", "w"); — where name.txt is a file which is going to be created at the C: drive in write mode. After the file has been opened for a read/write mode we use the various functions shown in the block diagram above: fputc, fputs, fprintf, fwrite to write to a file, or fgetc, fgets, fscanf, fread to read the content from a file.
Now, after we have finished reading/writing to a file we need to close it. This is carried out with the statement fclose(file pointer or filename); — for example fclose(fptr);

blocks.text: The single most common exam slip: forgetting fclose(). Without it the buffer may not be flushed, so content written with fprintf() never actually reaches the disk. Also remind students that in C a literal Windows path needs double backslashes — "c:\\name.txt" — because a single \ starts an escape sequence.
The approach to read or to write the content from/to the file is known as file processing. There are basically two types of file processing technique.
a. Sequential file processing
In this technique the content is stored sequentially and read back sequentially in a normal way, using a loop and some functions such as rewind(), ftell(), etc.
b. Random file processing
In this technique the content is stored sequentially and read back from any position of the file. It can be performed using functions such as rewind(), fseek() and ftell().

blocks.title: Note
blocks.text: The offset pointer movement is of utmost importance for fetching the content from the file.
rewind()
The rewind() function places the offset pointer at the beginning of the file, irrespective of the current offset position.
fseek()

The fseek() function lets us move the pointer from one record to another. In a program, to move the pointer to the required position we use this function. It takes three arguments, as given in the following syntax:

SEEK_SET, SEEK_CUR or SEEK_END are macros defined in stdio.h. All of these act as a reference from which the pointer should be offset: SEEK_END means move the pointer from the end of the file, SEEK_CUR means move the pointer with reference to its current position, and SEEK_SET means move the pointer with reference to the beginning of the file. fp is the file pointer and the number is the offset by which to move. If the number is positive the pointer moves from left to right; if the number is negative the pointer is moved from right to left.
ftell()

If we wish to know where the pointer is positioned right now, we can use the function ftell(). It returns the current position as a long int, which is an offset from the beginning of the file. The value returned by ftell() can be used in subsequent calls to fseek(). A sample call looks like this:
position = ftell(fp);      /* where position is long int */

sections.title: Opening, Reading, Writing and Appending on/from Data File

blocks.text: a. Integer I/O

Integer data can be written to, or read from, the file using the functions putw() and getw() respectively. putw() is used to write integer data into the file and getw() is used to read integer data from the file.
b. Character I/O
First, data can be read or written one character at a time. Library functions such as fgetc() and fputc() read the data from the keyboard and write it to the file on the disk.
c. String I/O
Secondly, data can be read or written as a string, with functions such as fgets() to read data and fputs() to store data in a file.
Here some text is entered into the character array line; thereafter the content stored in the array is stored in the file named info.txt until the null character '\0' is encountered in the array.

Here the fgets() statement reads a maximum of 251 characters at a stretch into line, but as we have passed 6 as an argument only 6 characters, including the null, will be read at a time. While reading, if the end of the file is reached, fgets() returns a NULL.
d. Formatted I/O

Thirdly, data can be read or written in a format generated by the printf() and scanf() functions — as a collection of values that may be mixed characters, strings, floating-point and integer numbers, and so on. These formatted data can be stored and read using the fprintf() and fscanf() functions.

blocks.caption: Output of the fprintf() program — the formatted records being entered.
Output of the fscanf() program — the records read back from myname.dat.

blocks.title: Note
blocks.text: With formatted I/O the data are always stored to a disk or a file in text mode.
e. Record Block I/O

Fourthly, data may be read or written in a new format called a record or block. A record is a fixed-length group of data and is commonly used to store a succession of similar data items, such as array elements or structures. This operation can be performed by the fread() and fwrite() functions.

Draw the parallel on the board: getw/putw for integers, fgetc/fputc for characters, fgets/fputs for strings, fscanf/fprintf for formatted (mixed) data, and fread/fwrite for whole records. The first four are text mode; only the last pair is binary mode.

sections.title: Some other operations on Data File

items: Closing the file: every file needs to be closed after it is opened. The function fclose() is used to close the file. Syntax: fclose(file_pointer);  Example: fclose(fp);
Renaming the file: the function rename() is used to rename a file. Syntax: rename("old_file_name", "new_file_name");  Example: rename("student.dat", "new.dat");
Removing/Deleting the file: the function remove() is used to remove or delete the file. Syntax: remove("file_name");  Example: remove("new.dat");

blocks.text: In text mode every digit or text is stored as a character, and while reading the content back, conversion is required from character to the appropriate format — which takes a lot of space. In binary mode there is no conversion: every digit or text is stored in binary format (stored without performing translation, i.e. whatever format has been used to store the value in memory, in the same format the content is stored in a file without conversion — therefore, while reading the content, no conversion is necessary).
The character I/O, string I/O and formatted I/O use text mode, whereas fread() and fwrite() use binary mode.

blocks.title: Worked example — how big is the file?
blocks.text: Suppose we want to store the value of PI, 3.14159, in a float. What would the file size be? If this value is stored in character format the file size would be 8 bytes (count each character, including the decimal point and EOF). If the same content is stored in binary format, only 4 bytes are occupied, because a float type has been used.

Binary mode

In binary mode the offset pointer keeps track of the end of the file from the number of data to be read, as per the data type given.

blocks.text: Appending on a data file means to add more content at the end of the existing file — that is, wherever the EOF flag is placed, from that point the content is added.

The file opening mode must be "a", which stands for append. However, "a+" mode can also be used, for appending as well as for reading the file. Moreover, if the file hasn't been created yet, the file will be created and the offset pointer is placed at the zeroth offset; if the file has already been created, the offset pointer is moved to the EOF flag.
