short.q: What is C programming? Write down its features.
short.a:
C is a general-purpose, structured, middle-level programming language developed by Dennis Ritchie at Bell Laboratories around 1972, originally to write the UNIX operating system. It is called middle-level because it combines the control of a low-level language — pointers, direct memory access, bit operations — with the readability and structure of a high-level one.

Its main features:

  • Simple and efficient — a small set of keywords (32 in ANSI C) and a compiler that produces fast, compact machine code.
  • Structured — the program is built from functions and blocks with sequence, selection and repetition, instead of goto.
  • Portable — a C program written to the standard compiles on any machine with a C compiler, which is why UNIX itself could be moved.
  • Rich set of operators — arithmetic, relational, logical, bitwise, assignment, conditional and pointer operators.
  • Rich library — a large standard library of ready-made functions for input/output, strings and mathematics, included with #include.
  • Extensible — the programmer adds their own functions to the library.
  • Low-level access — pointers and address arithmetic reach memory and hardware directly.
  • Modular — a large program is split into separate files and functions.
  • Foundation of other languages — C++, Java, C# and PHP all borrow its syntax.

Its weaknesses are worth stating too: there is no automatic bounds checking on arrays, no garbage collection, and no object orientation.

short.q: Define identifier, keyword, constant, and variable.
short.a:
Identifier. The name a programmer gives to a variable, function, array or any other program element — marks, total, main. An identifier may contain letters, digits and the underscore, must not begin with a digit, must not be a keyword, and is case-sensitive, so total and Total are different names.

Keyword. A word whose meaning is fixed by the language and which cannot be used as an identifier. C has 32 of them, including int, float, char, if, else, while, for, return, break, continue, switch, struct, union, typedef, static and sizeof. They are always written in lower case.

Constant. A fixed value that never changes while the program runs. C has integer constants (100), floating constants (3.14), character constants ('A') and string constants ("Kathmandu"). A constant may also be given a name with #define PI 3.14159 or const int MAX = 100;.

Variable. A named location in memory whose value can change during the program. It must be declared with a type before use, which tells the compiler how much memory to reserve and how to interpret it — int age = 18; reserves an integer cell called age and stores 18 in it.

short.q: Describe the different data types which are used in C-programming.
short.a:
C provides three families of data types.

1. Primary (basic) types — the building blocks:

  • int — a whole number, typically 2 or 4 bytes. int roll = 25;
  • float — a single-precision real number, 4 bytes, about 6 decimal digits. float price = 99.50;
  • double — a double-precision real number, 8 bytes, about 15 digits. double pi = 3.14159265;
  • char — a single character, 1 byte, written in single quotes. char grade = 'A';
  • void — an empty type, used for functions that return nothing and pointers with no fixed base type.

2. Derived types — built from the primary types:

  • Array — several values of one type under one name: int marks[5];
  • Function — a named block that returns a value: int add(int, int);
  • Pointer — a variable holding an address: int *p;

3. User-defined types — defined by the programmer:

  • struct — a group of related items of possibly different types: struct student { int roll; char name[30]; };
  • union — like a struct, but all members share the same memory:

    union data { int i; float f; };
  • enum — a set of named integer constants: enum day {sun, mon, tue};
  • typedef — a new name for an existing type: typedef int marks;

The size and the sign of the basic types are adjusted with the qualifiers short, long, signed and unsigned.

short.q: Describe 'Sequence', 'Selection', and 'Loop' with a flowchart and example.
short.a:
The three control structures of structured programming say in what order the statements of a program run.

1. Sequence. Statements are executed one after another, top to bottom, with no branching. This is the default.

Flowchart: [Start] → [Read a, b] → [sum = a + b] → [Print sum] → [Stop] — four rectangles in a straight line.

#include <stdio.h>

int main() {
    int a, b, sum;

    printf("Enter two numbers: ");
    scanf("%d %d", &a, &b);

    sum = a + b;                 /* sequence: each step follows the last */

    printf("Sum = %d\n", sum);
    return 0;
}

2. Selection. A condition decides which of several statements runs, so the program chooses a path. C offers if, if-else, an else-if ladder, switch and the conditional operator ?:.

Flowchart: [Start] → [Read n] → <n > 0?> — a diamond. Its yes branch runs [Print "positive"] and its no branch runs [Print "not positive"]; both then reach [Stop].

#include <stdio.h>

int main() {
    int n;

    printf("Enter a number: ");
    scanf("%d", &n);

    if (n > 0)                   /* selection: one branch is taken */
        printf("Positive\n");
    else
        printf("Not positive\n");

    return 0;
}

3. Loop (repetition). A block is repeated while a condition holds, or a set number of times. C offers while, do-while and for.

Flowchart: [Start] → [i = 1] → <i <= 10?>. The yes branch runs [Print i] then [i = i + 1] and loops back to the diamond; the no branch goes to [Stop].

#include <stdio.h>

int main() {
    int i;

    for (i = 1; i <= 10; i++) {  /* loop: the body repeats */
        printf("%d ", i);
    }

    return 0;
}

Every C program is built from these three: statements in sequence, decisions that pick a branch, and loops that repeat work.

short.q: Differentiate between while and do-while loops.
short.a:
while loopdo-while loop
An entry-controlled loop: the condition is tested before the body runs. An exit-controlled loop: the body runs first and the condition is tested afterwards.
The body may execute zero times, if the condition is false at the start. The body executes at least once, whatever the condition.
while (condition) { body; } do { body; } while (condition);
No semicolon after the condition. A semicolon is required after while (condition).
Used when the number of repetitions is not known in advance — read until end-of-file, or until the user types 0. Used when the body must happen at least once — a menu that has to be shown before the user can choose to quit.

Examples:

/* while: may run zero times */
#include <stdio.h>

int main() {
    int i = 1;

    while (i <= 5) {
        printf("%d ", i);
        i++;
    }

    return 0;
}
/* do-while: always runs at least once */
#include <stdio.h>

int main() {
    int n;

    do {
        printf("Enter a number (0 to stop): ");
        if (scanf("%d", &n) != 1) break;
        printf("You typed %d\n", n);
    } while (n != 0);

    return 0;
}

In the second program the prompt is always shown before the test, which is exactly why do-while is the right loop for a menu or an input prompt.

short.q: What is an array? Why is it required? Explain with its types.
short.a:
An array is a collection of elements of the same data type stored in consecutive memory locations and reached by one name plus an index. For example int marks[5]; sets aside five integer cells, referenced as marks[0] through marks[4] — the index always starts at 0.

Why it is required. Without an array, storing the marks of 50 students needs 50 separate variables, 50 lines of input, 50 comparisons to find the highest and 50 lines of printing. With an array it is one name and one loop, and the same code works for 50 students or 5,000. Arrays also make sorting and searching possible, because any element can be reached directly by its index in constant time.

Types of array:

  • One-dimensional (single-subscripted) — a simple list. int marks[5] = {80, 75, 90, 65, 88};
  • Two-dimensional — a table of rows and columns. int matrix[3][4]; gives 12 elements, reached as matrix[row][col].
  • Multi-dimensional — three or more subscripts, for example int cube[3][4][5];, used rarely.
  • Character array (string) — an array of char ending in the null character '\0'. char name[20] = "Ram";

short.q: What is a string? Explain the library functions for a string with their syntax and example.
short.a:
A string in C is a one-dimensional array of characters terminated by the null character '\0'. The terminator is what tells every string function where the text ends, which is why char name[20] holds at most 19 usable characters — one cell is spent on the null. C has no string type of its own; strings are handled through char arrays and the library declared in <string.h>.

The common library functions:

FunctionSyntaxWhat it does
strlen()strlen(s)Returns the number of characters before the null.
strcpy()strcpy(dest, src)Copies src into dest.
strcat()strcat(dest, src)Appends src to the end of dest.
strcmp()strcmp(s1, s2)Compares two strings; returns 0 if equal, negative if s1 sorts first, positive otherwise.
strrev()strrev(s)Reverses s in place (non-standard, but present in Turbo C).
strlwr() / strupr() strlwr(s)Converts to lower / upper case.

Example:

#include <stdio.h>
#include <string.h>

int main() {
    char first[20] = "Ram";
    char last[20]  = "Sharma";
    char full[40];

    printf("Length of first : %d\n", strlen(first));

    strcpy(full, first);          /* full = "Ram"          */
    strcat(full, " ");            /* full = "Ram "         */
    strcat(full, last);           /* full = "Ram Sharma"   */

    printf("Full name       : %s\n", full);

    if (strcmp(first, last) == 0)
        printf("The names are equal\n");
    else
        printf("The names are different\n");

    return 0;
}

Two things to remember: strings cannot be assigned with =, only copied with strcpy(), and they cannot be compared with ==, only with strcmp() — because both names are really addresses of arrays, so == would compare addresses rather than text.

short.q: What is a function? List out the advantages of functions.
short.a:
A function is a named, self-contained block of statements that performs one specific task and can be called by name from anywhere in the program. Every C program has at least one, main(), and execution begins there. A function receives data through its parameters, works on it, and sends a result back with return.

Advantages of using functions:

  • Modularity. A large problem is broken into small, understandable pieces, each of which can be written and tested on its own.
  • Reusability. The function is written once and called as many times as needed, from as many places as needed.
  • No repetition. The same code is not written out again and again, so the program is shorter and one change fixes every use.
  • Easier debugging and testing. A fault is traced to one function instead of to a whole program.
  • Easier maintenance. The inside of a function can be rewritten without touching the code that calls it, provided its interface stays the same.
  • Division of work. Different programmers can write different functions.
  • Abstraction. The caller needs to know what the function does, not how it does it.

short.q: What do you mean by library function? How is it different from a user-defined function?
short.a:
A library function is one that already exists in the C standard library: it is written, compiled and supplied with the compiler, and the programmer only calls it after including the right header. printf() and scanf() come from <stdio.h>, strlen() and strcpy() from <string.h>, sqrt() and pow() from <math.h>, and malloc() from <stdlib.h>.

A user-defined function is written by the programmer to do something the library does not provide, such as factorial() or sortMarks().

Library functionUser-defined function
Already available; no need to write it. Written by the programmer for a specific need.
The body is not visible or changeable. The body is fully visible and changeable.
Used by including a header, e.g. #include <stdio.h>. Must be declared (prototyped) and defined before or above the call.
Cannot be modified or extended. Can be modified freely.
General purpose, used by many programs. Specific to this program's problem.
Examples: printf, scanf, sqrt, strcpy. Examples: area(), largest(), factorial().

short.q: What are the different components of functions? Explain.
short.a:
A user-defined function has three parts, and a fourth that belongs to its use.

1. Function declaration (prototype). Placed before main(), it tells the compiler the function's name, the type it returns and the number and types of its parameters, so calls can be checked before the body is seen. The parameter names are optional. int add(int, int);

2. Function definition. The actual body — the header repeated without the semicolon, followed by the statements that do the work. int add(int a, int b) { return a + b; }

3. Function call. The point where control jumps to the function, with the arguments supplied. sum = add(10, 20);

The two remaining pieces are the parameters — the variables a and b in the definition, which receive the values — and the return statement, which sends a value back to the caller and ends the function. A function declared void returns nothing and needs no return, though return; can still be used to leave early.

short.q: Explain different types of user-defined functions with an example.
short.a:
User-defined functions are classified by whether they take arguments and whether they return a value, giving four categories.
CategoryTakes argumentsReturns a value
1. No arguments, no return valueNoNo
2. No arguments, returns a valueNoYes
3. Takes arguments, no return valueYesNo
4. Takes arguments and returns a valueYesYes

An example of each:

#include <stdio.h>

/* 1. no arguments, no return value */
void line(void) {
    printf("--------------------\n");
}

/* 2. no arguments, returns a value */
int getNumber(void) {
    int n;
    printf("Enter a number: ");
    scanf("%d", &n);
    return n;
}

/* 3. arguments, no return value */
void printSum(int a, int b) {
    printf("Sum = %d\n", a + b);
}

/* 4. arguments and returns a value */
int add(int a, int b) {
    return a + b;
}

int main() {
    int x, y;

    line();                       /* type 1 */

    x = getNumber();              /* type 2 */
    y = getNumber();

    printSum(x, y);               /* type 3 */

    printf("Total = %d\n", add(x, y));  /* type 4 */

    line();
    return 0;
}

void in the return position means "returns nothing", and void between the parentheses means "takes nothing" — writing empty parentheses instead is legal in C but means the arguments are unchecked, so it is better to write void.

short.q: Explain recursive function with an example.
short.a:
A recursive function is one that calls itself, directly or indirectly, to solve a smaller instance of the same problem. Each call pushes a fresh set of local variables onto the stack, and the calls must converge on a base case whose answer is known and which returns without recursing — without it the function would call itself for ever and the program would crash when the stack ran out.

Example — factorial:

#include <stdio.h>

long factorial(int n) {
    if (n == 0 || n == 1)        /* base case - stops the recursion */
        return 1;
    else
        return n * factorial(n - 1);   /* recursive call */
}

int main() {
    int n = 5;

    printf("%d! = %ld\n", n, factorial(n));
    return 0;
}

How it unwinds. factorial(5) needs 5 × factorial(4), which needs 4 × factorial(3), and so on down to factorial(1), which returns 1. The answers then multiply back up: 1, 2, 6, 24, 120. Recursion gives an elegant solution to factorial, the Fibonacci series, binary search and tree traversal, but each call costs stack space and time, so an iterative loop is faster where one is easy to write.

short.q: What do you mean by storage class? Explain different storage classes with examples.
short.a:
A storage class in C decides four things about a variable: where it is stored (memory or a CPU register), its default initial value, its scope (the part of the program in which it can be used) and its lifetime (how long it keeps its value). C has four storage classes.

1. auto — the default for local variables. Stored in memory, scope limited to the block in which it is declared, destroyed on leaving that block and recreated on re-entering it, with an unpredictable initial value (garbage) if not initialised.

2. register — a request to keep the variable in a CPU register for speed. It behaves like auto in scope and lifetime, but its address cannot be taken with &, and the compiler may ignore the request if no register is free. It suits a loop counter used very heavily.

3. static — keeps its value between calls. Stored in memory for the whole run of the program. A static local variable is visible only inside its function but remembers its value from one call to the next, and is automatically initialised to zero once. A static global variable or function is private to the file it is declared in, which is how C hides things.

4. extern — declares a global variable defined in another file, so one variable can be shared across several source files. It allocates no storage of its own; it only says "this name is defined elsewhere", and it is automatically initialised to zero.

short.q: Define a structure with an example.
short.a:
A structure is a user-defined data type that groups variables of different types under one name, so that everything belonging to one record — a student's roll number, name and marks — is held in a single unit. It is declared with the struct keyword, its members are reached with the dot operator, and each member gets its own memory.

#include <stdio.h>
#include <string.h>

struct student {
    int  roll;
    char name[30];
    float marks;
};

int main() {
    struct student s1;

    s1.roll = 1;
    strcpy(s1.name, "Ram Sharma");
    s1.marks = 85.5;

    printf("Roll  : %d\n",   s1.roll);
    printf("Name  : %s\n",   s1.name);
    printf("Marks : %.2f\n", s1.marks);

    return 0;
}

struct student is the new type, s1 is a variable of it, and s1.roll reaches the member. Note that the name is copied with strcpy(), not assigned with =. A typedef is often used to shorten the declaration: typedef struct { int roll; char name[30]; } Student; after which Student s1; is enough.

short.q: Define union with an example.
short.a:
A union is a user-defined type like a structure, except that all its members share the same block of memory. The compiler reserves as many bytes as the largest member needs, and only one member holds a meaningful value at any moment — writing to one member overwrites the others.

#include <stdio.h>
#include <string.h>

union data {
    int   i;
    float f;
    char  str[20];
};

int main() {
    union data d;

    d.i = 10;
    printf("d.i   = %d\n", d.i);

    d.f = 3.14;
    printf("d.f   = %.2f\n", d.f);

    strcpy(d.str, "Ram");
    printf("d.str = %s\n", d.str);

    printf("Size of the union = %lu bytes\n", sizeof(d));

    return 0;
}

After d.f = 3.14; the integer member is meaningless, because the float now occupies the same bytes — which is exactly the point. The size printed is 20 bytes, the size of the largest member, not the sum of all three. That is what makes a union useful: it saves memory when a field can hold one of several things but never more than one at a time.

short.q: Differentiate between structure and union.
short.a:
StructureUnion
Declared with the struct keyword. Declared with the union keyword.
Each member gets its own memory. All members share the same memory.
Size is at least the sum of the members (plus padding). Size is that of the largest member.
All members can hold values at the same time. Only one member holds a meaningful value at a time.
Changing one member does not affect the others. Changing one member overwrites the others.
Uses more memory. Uses less memory — that is its purpose.
A member can be initialised at declaration. Only the first member can be initialised.
Used to model a record: a student, an employee. Used when a field holds one of several types, or to look at the same bytes differently.

short.q: Differentiate between array and structure with examples.
short.a:
ArrayStructure
Holds elements of the same data type. Holds members of different data types.
Reached by an index in square brackets. Reached by a member name with the dot operator.
Declared with int marks[5]; Declared with struct student { ... };
Elements are stored in consecutive locations. Members are stored in the order declared (with padding for alignment).
Size = number of elements × size of one element. Size = sum of the members, plus any padding.
Represents many values of one kind — the marks of one student. Represents one record made of many kinds — roll, name and marks together.
Cannot be assigned to another array with =. Can be assigned to another structure of the same type with =.

Examples. An array — int marks[5] = {80, 75, 90, 65, 88}; holds five integers, reached as marks[0] … marks[4]. A structure — struct student { int roll; char name[30]; float marks; }; holds one student's complete record, reached as s1.roll, s1.name, s1.marks. The two combine naturally: struct student class12[50]; is an array of 50 structures, one per student.

short.q: What is nested structure? Explain with the example.
short.a:
A nested structure is a structure used as a member of another structure. It is how C models a record that contains a record — a student who has an address, where the address itself has a street, a city and a postcode. Members of the inner structure are reached by applying the dot operator twice.

#include <stdio.h>
#include <string.h>

struct address {
    char street[40];
    char city[20];
    int  postcode;
};

struct student {
    int  roll;
    char name[30];
    struct address addr;        /* nested structure */
};

int main() {
    struct student s;

    s.roll = 1;
    strcpy(s.name, "Ram Sharma");
    strcpy(s.addr.street, "New Road");
    strcpy(s.addr.city, "Kathmandu");
    s.addr.postcode = 44600;

    printf("Name    : %s\n", s.name);
    printf("Street  : %s\n", s.addr.street);
    printf("City    : %s\n", s.addr.city);
    printf("Postcode: %d\n", s.addr.postcode);

    return 0;
}

s.addr reaches the inner structure and s.addr.city reaches the member inside it, so the dots chain from the outside in. Nesting may go several levels deep, and when the outer variable is reached through a pointer the arrow operator is used instead: p->addr.city.

short.q: Define the term pointer with its key features.
short.a:
A pointer is a variable whose value is the address of another variable — it points to the memory location where the data lives rather than holding the data itself. It is declared by putting * before the name: int *p; declares a pointer to an integer.

Key features:

  • It stores an address, never a value. p = &a; puts the address of a into p.
  • & (address-of) gives the address of a variable and * (indirection / dereference) gives the value stored at an address, so *p and a are the same thing once p = &a.
  • It is typed: an int * points to an int, and the type tells the compiler how many bytes to read and how far to move during arithmetic.
  • It supports pointer arithmetic — p++ advances to the next element of the base type, not the next byte.
  • It can hold the null pointer (NULL or 0), meaning "points at nothing"; dereferencing it is an error.
  • Dynamic memory comes from it: malloc(), calloc() and free() work with pointers, so arrays can be sized while the program runs.
  • It enables call by reference, letting a function change the caller's variable.
  • It makes arrays, strings and structures efficient to pass around, since only an address is copied rather than the whole object.
  • Its size does not depend on what it points to — every pointer on a given machine is the same number of bytes (typically 4 on a 32-bit system, 8 on a 64-bit one).

short.q: Write down the advantages and disadvantages of using a pointer.
short.a:
Advantages of pointers:

  • Efficiency with large data. Passing a pointer to a structure or an array copies only an address instead of the whole object, so function calls stay fast and memory is saved.
  • Call by reference. A function can change the caller's variables, so swap() actually works and a function can return more than one result.
  • Dynamic memory. malloc() and calloc() allocate memory at run time, so arrays, linked lists, stacks, queues and trees can grow and shrink as needed.
  • Direct hardware and memory access. Pointers reach specific addresses, which is why C is used to write operating systems and device drivers.
  • Faster array and string handling. Walking an array by incrementing a pointer is often quicker than indexing it.
  • Complex data structures. Linked lists, trees and graphs are impossible without them.

Disadvantages:

  • Hard to learn and error-prone. Confusing * and & is a classic beginner mistake.
  • Dangling pointers. A pointer to memory that has been freed, or to a local variable of a function that has returned, points at garbage.
  • Memory leaks. Forgetting free() on memory obtained from malloc() slowly consumes all available memory.
  • Uninitialised pointers. A pointer that was never given an address holds an unpredictable value; dereferencing it can crash the program or corrupt other data.
  • No bounds checking. C never checks that a pointer is still inside the array it came from, so walking off the end silently corrupts memory.
  • Security and safety risk. Most serious software vulnerabilities — buffer overflows, use-after-free — are pointer bugs.
  • Difficult to debug. The symptom usually appears far from the mistake that caused it.

short.q: What do you mean by the term address of (&) and indirection (*) operator?
short.a:
The & (address-of) operator is a unary operator that returns the memory address of its operand. If a is an integer variable stored at address 1000, then &a is 1000. It is used to put an address into a pointer — p = &a; — and to pass a variable to scanf(), which needs the address so it can store what it reads.

The * (indirection or dereference) operator is the opposite: applied to a pointer it returns the value stored at the address the pointer holds. If p holds 1000 and 25 is stored there, *p is 25. The same * is used in a declaration, where it means something different — "pointer to" — as in int *p;.

#include <stdio.h>

int main() {
    int a = 25;
    int *p;

    p = &a;                  /* & gives the address of a */

    printf("Value of a          = %d\n", a);
    printf("Address of a        = %p\n", (void *)&a);
    printf("Value of p (address)= %p\n", (void *)p);
    printf("Value at *p         = %d\n", *p);

    *p = 100;                /* *p on the left changes a itself */
    printf("Now a = %d\n", a);

    return 0;
}

The last pair of lines is the point: because *p and a are the same memory cell, assigning through *p changes a. The two operators are exact inverses — *(&a) is a again.

short.q: Explain the importance of the pointer in C programming. Illustrate pointer operations with an example. Show the relation between array and pointers with the example.
short.a:
Importance of pointers in C. Pointers are what make C a middle-level language. They allow call by reference, so a function can alter the caller's data; they make dynamic memory allocation possible through malloc() and free(); they let large arrays and structures be passed to functions by address rather than copied; they are the only way to build linked lists, trees and graphs; and they give the direct memory and hardware access that operating systems need.

Pointer operations.

#include <stdio.h>

int main() {
    int a = 10, b = 20;
    int *p, *q;

    /* assignment */
    p = &a;
    q = p;                       /* q now points to a as well */

    /* dereferencing */
    printf("*p = %d\n", *p);     /* 10   */

    /* assignment through a pointer */
    *p = 99;
    printf("a  = %d\n", a);      /* 99   */

    /* pointer arithmetic */
    int arr[5] = {10, 20, 30, 40, 50};
    int *r = arr;                /* r points at arr[0] */

    printf("%d\n", *r);          /* 10        */
    r++;                         /* move to the next int, not the next byte */
    printf("%d\n", *r);          /* 20        */
    r += 2;
    printf("%d\n", *r);          /* 40        */

    /* comparison and subtraction */
    printf("Elements apart = %ld\n", r - arr);   /* 3 */

    /* swapping two variables through pointers */
    p = &a; q = &b;
    int temp = *p; *p = *q; *q = temp;
    printf("a = %d, b = %d\n", a, b);

    return 0;
}

The relation between arrays and pointers. The name of an array is a constant pointer to its first element, so arr and &arr[0] are the same address. That gives the four equivalent forms below, which are the whole relationship in one line: arr[i] == *(arr + i) == *(i + arr) == i[arr]. The essential difference is that arr is a constant — it cannot be made to point somewhere else, so arr++ is illegal, whereas a pointer variable r can be moved freely through the array. Note also that sizeof(arr) gives the size of the whole array, while sizeof(r) gives only the size of a pointer.

short.q: Differentiate between structures and pointers with examples.
short.a:
StructurePointer
A collection of variables of possibly different types under one name. A single variable that holds the address of another variable.
Declared with the struct keyword. Declared with the * operator.
Members are reached with the dot operator: s.roll. The pointed-to value is reached with the indirection operator: *p.
Holds actual data. Holds an address; the data lives elsewhere.
Its size is the sum of its members. Its size is fixed by the machine, typically 4 or 8 bytes, whatever it points to.
Not used for dynamic memory by itself. The basis of malloc(), calloc() and dynamic data structures.
struct student s1; allocates a whole record. int *p; allocates space for one address only.

Examples. A structure — struct student { int roll; char name[30]; } s1; holds a complete record, and s1.roll reaches a field. A pointer — int a = 10, *p = &a; holds only the address of a, and *p reaches the value.

The two combine, which is where they are most useful: a pointer to a structure, struct student *sp = &s1;, is how structures are passed to functions without copying them. The members are then reached with the arrow operator, sp->roll, which is simply a shorthand for (*sp).roll.

short.q: What are the differences between array and pointer?
short.a:
ArrayPointer
Declares and reserves memory for a fixed number of elements. Declares space for one address only; it points at memory that already exists or is allocated later.
The name is a constant pointer — it cannot be reassigned. A pointer variable — it can be made to point at anything of the right type.
arr++ is illegal. p++ is legal and moves to the next element.
sizeof(arr) gives the size of the whole array. sizeof(p) gives the size of the pointer (4 or 8 bytes).
Memory is allocated at compile time (or on the stack) and cannot change size. Can be given memory at run time with malloc(), and that memory can be resized or freed.
Elements are reached by index: arr[2]. The value is reached by dereferencing: *(p + 2).
Cannot be assigned to another array: arr = brr; is illegal. Can be assigned: p = q; copies the address.
Storing beyond the declared size corrupts memory — there is no check. Same danger, plus the risk of a dangling or uninitialised pointer.

The link between them. The name of an array behaves as a pointer to its first element, so arr equals &arr[0] and arr[i] is exactly *(arr + i). That is why a function can be written to take either int arr[] or int *arr — inside the function they are the same thing — and why pointer arithmetic walks through an array cleanly.

short.q: Differentiate between call by value and call by reference.
short.a:
In call by value the function receives a copy of the argument's value. It may change the copy freely, but the caller's original variable is untouched, because two separate memory cells are involved. In call by reference the function receives the address of the argument, so through that address it changes the caller's own variable.

#include <stdio.h>

/* call by value - the copy is swapped, the originals are not */
void swapByValue(int x, int y) {
    int t = x;
    x = y;
    y = t;
}

/* call by reference - the originals are swapped */
void swapByReference(int *x, int *y) {
    int t = *x;
    *x = *y;
    *y = t;
}

int main() {
    int a = 10, b = 20;

    swapByValue(a, b);
    printf("After call by value    : a = %d, b = %d\n", a, b);

    swapByReference(&a, &b);
    printf("After call by reference: a = %d, b = %d\n", a, b);

    return 0;
}

Output: the first line prints a = 10, b = 20 — unchanged — and the second prints a = 20, b = 10. C always passes arguments by value; "call by reference" is achieved by passing a pointer by value and then dereferencing it inside the function. That is also why scanf("%d", &a) needs the &: without the address the function could not put the value it read back into a.

short.q: What is a data file? Write down the syntax to create a new file.
short.a:
A data file is a named collection of records stored on a secondary storage device such as a disk, so that the data survives after the program finishes. It is how a program keeps information permanently, shares it with other programs, and handles quantities too large to hold in memory at once.

A file is opened with fopen(), which returns a FILE pointer, and every later operation goes through that pointer:

#include <stdio.h>
FILE *fp;

fp = fopen("student.dat", "w");   /* create a new file for writing */

The two arguments are the file's name and its mode. The modes for creating and opening files are "r" (read, the file must already exist), "w" (write — creates the file, or empties it if it exists), "a" (append — creates the file, or adds to the end of it), and the same three with b or t appended for binary or text mode ("wb", "rt"), plus the read/write forms "r+", "w+" and "a+".

The call must always be checked, because it returns NULL when it fails — the disk is full, the path does not exist, or the file is not readable:

#include <stdio.h>
fp = fopen("student.dat", "w");
if (fp == NULL) {
    printf("Cannot create the file\n");
    return 1;
}

Note that opening an existing file with "w" destroys its contents, which is the classic way to lose data — use "a" when the intention is to add to it.

short.q: List out all the file manipulation functions with examples of each.
short.a:
Every file operation needs #include <stdio.h> and goes through a FILE * obtained from fopen(). The complete set:
FunctionSyntaxPurpose
fopen()fopen("a.dat", "w") Opens or creates a file and returns a FILE *, or NULL.
fclose()fclose(fp) Closes the file and flushes the buffer.
fprintf()fprintf(fp, "%d", x) Writes formatted output to the file.
fscanf()fscanf(fp, "%d", &x) Reads formatted input from the file.
fputc()fputc('A', fp) Writes one character.
fgetc()ch = fgetc(fp) Reads one character, or EOF.
fputs()fputs("Ram", fp) Writes a string.
fgets()fgets(s, 40, fp) Reads a line into s, or NULL at end of file.
fwrite()fwrite(&s, sizeof(s), 1, fp) Writes a block of bytes (records).
fread()fread(&s, sizeof(s), 1, fp) Reads a block of bytes (records).
fseek()fseek(fp, 0L, SEEK_SET) Moves the file position.
ftell()ftell(fp) Reports the current position in bytes.
rewind()rewind(fp) Moves the position back to the start.
feof()feof(fp) Returns non-zero once the end of the file has been reached.
remove()remove("a.dat") Deletes the file.
rename()rename("a.dat", "b.dat") Renames the file.

A short example that uses several of them:

#include <stdio.h>

int main() {
    FILE *fp;
    char line[80];

    /* write */
    fp = fopen("note.txt", "w");
    if (fp == NULL) { printf("Cannot open file\n"); return 1; }

    fprintf(fp, "Roll: %d\n", 1);
    fputs("Name: Ram Sharma\n", fp);
    fclose(fp);

    /* read back */
    fp = fopen("note.txt", "r");
    if (fp == NULL) { printf("Cannot open file\n"); return 1; }

    while (fgets(line, sizeof(line), fp) != NULL) {
        printf("%s", line);
    }

    fclose(fp);
    return 0;
}

Two habits are worth stating: always test the pointer returned by fopen() before using it, and always call fclose(), because output is buffered — without closing, what was written may never reach the disk.

short.q: Write the functions of rename() and remove() with example.
short.a:
rename() changes a file's name, and can move it to another directory at the same time. It returns 0 on success and non-zero on failure, which happens if the old file does not exist, the new name is already taken, or the program lacks permission.

#include <stdio.h>

int main() {
    if (rename("student.dat", "student_old.dat") == 0)
        printf("File renamed successfully.\n");
    else
        printf("Unable to rename the file.\n");

    return 0;
}

remove() deletes a file from the disk permanently. It also returns 0 on success.

#include <stdio.h>

int main() {
    if (remove("student_old.dat") == 0)
        printf("File deleted successfully.\n");
    else
        printf("Unable to delete the file.\n");

    return 0;
}

Both are declared in <stdio.h>, and neither works on a file that is still open — call fclose() first. Because remove() cannot be undone, it is worth confirming with the user before deleting anything real.

short.q: Explain the functions of fprintf() and fscanf() with example.
short.a:
fprintf() and fscanf() are the file versions of printf() and scanf(): they do exactly the same formatting, but to and from a file instead of the screen. The only difference in the call is the extra FILE * as the first argument.

#include <stdio.h>

int main() {
    FILE *fp;
    int roll;
    char name[30];
    float marks;

    /* write formatted data to the file */
    fp = fopen("student.dat", "w");
    if (fp == NULL) { printf("Cannot open file\n"); return 1; }

    fprintf(fp, "%d %s %.2f\n", 1, "Ram", 85.50);
    fprintf(fp, "%d %s %.2f\n", 2, "Sita", 92.00);

    fclose(fp);

    /* read it back */
    fp = fopen("student.dat", "r");
    if (fp == NULL) { printf("Cannot open file\n"); return 1; }

    printf("Roll  Name   Marks\n");
    while (fscanf(fp, "%d %s %f", &roll, name, &marks) == 3) {
        printf("%-5d %-6s %.2f\n", roll, name, marks);
    }

    fclose(fp);
    return 0;
}

fscanf() returns the number of items successfully read, or EOF when there is nothing left, which makes while (fscanf(...) != EOF) the standard way to walk through a file of records. Note that fscanf stops at whitespace, so %s reads a single word — a name containing a space needs fgets() instead.

short.q: Define the terms FILE and EOF in file handling.
short.a:
FILE is a structure declared in <stdio.h> that represents an open file. It holds everything the library needs to keep track of that file — the position indicator, a pointer to its buffer, and error and end-of-file flags. The programmer never touches its members; they work with a pointer to it, obtained from fopen() and passed to every other file function: FILE *fp; fp = fopen("a.dat", "r");

EOF is an integer constant, defined in <stdio.h> as -1, that means "end of file". The character-input functions return it when there is nothing left to read: fgetc() returns EOF, fscanf() returns EOF, and fgets() returns NULL.

Two details matter. Because EOF is -1 and not a character, the variable that receives fgetc() must be an int, not a char — a char may be unable to represent -1. And feof() is different: it only becomes true after a read has already failed, so testing while (!feof(fp)) before reading processes the last record twice. The correct pattern is to read first and then test the result.

short.q: Describe any five 'file handling functions' with examples.
short.a:
Five of the most-used file handling functions, each with an example. All need #include <stdio.h> and a FILE * from fopen().

1. fopen() — opens or creates a file. fp = fopen("a.dat", "w"); Returns NULL on failure.

2. fclose() — closes a file and flushes its buffer. fclose(fp); Returns 0 on success.

3. fprintf() — writes formatted data. fprintf(fp, "%d %s\n", roll, name);

4. fscanf() — reads formatted data. fscanf(fp, "%d %s", &roll, name); Returns the number of items read, or EOF.

5. fgets() / fputs() — read and write a whole line or string. fgets(line, 80, fp); and fputs("Ram", fp);

A complete program using them:

#include <stdio.h>

int main() {
    FILE *fp;
    int roll;
    char name[30];

    fp = fopen("student.dat", "w");            /* fopen  */
    if (fp == NULL) { printf("Error\n"); return 1; }

    fprintf(fp, "%d %s\n", 1, "Ram");          /* fprintf */
    fputs("2 Sita\n", fp);                     /* fputs   */
    fclose(fp);                                /* fclose  */

    fp = fopen("student.dat", "r");
    if (fp == NULL) { printf("Error\n"); return 1; }

    while (fscanf(fp, "%d %s", &roll, name) == 2) {   /* fscanf */
        printf("Roll: %d  Name: %s\n", roll, name);
    }

    fclose(fp);
    return 0;
}

short.q: Write a program which reads name, roll-number and age from a file named "student.dat" and displays them.
short.a:
#include <stdio.h>

int main() {
    FILE *fp;
    int roll, age;
    char name[30];

    /* open the file for reading */
    fp = fopen("student.dat", "r");
    if (fp == NULL) {
        printf("Cannot open student.dat\n");
        return 1;
    }

    printf("Name\t\tRoll\tAge\n");
    printf("-----------------------------\n");

    while (fscanf(fp, "%s %d %d", name, &roll, &age) == 3) {
        printf("%s\t\t%d\t%d\n", name, roll, age);
    }

    fclose(fp);
    return 0;
}

The file is opened in read mode "r", which means it must already exist — fopen returns NULL if it does not, and that is tested before anything is read. fscanf() reads one record per call and returns EOF when the file is exhausted, so the loop finishes on its own. Because %s stops at whitespace, this reads a single-word name; for a full name with spaces, write the record with fprintf(fp, "%d %d %s\n", roll, age, name) putting the name last and read the line with fgets().

short.q: Describe fscanf and fprintf function.
short.a:
fscanf() and fprintf() are the file-handling counterparts of scanf() and printf(). They use the same format strings and the same conversion specifiers; the only difference is the extra FILE * as the first argument, which says which file to use instead of the keyboard and screen.

fprintf() — formatted output to a file.

#include <stdio.h>
int fprintf(FILE *fp, const char *format, ...);

fprintf(fp, "Roll: %d, Name: %s, Marks: %.2f\n", roll, name, marks);

It returns the number of characters written, or a negative value on error. It is the usual way to build a text file of records.

fscanf() — formatted input from a file.

#include <stdio.h>
int fscanf(FILE *fp, const char *format, ...);

fscanf(fp, "%d %s %f", &roll, name, &marks);

It returns the number of items successfully converted and assigned, or EOF if the end of the file is reached before anything is read — which is why while (fscanf(...) != EOF) is the standard reading loop. Two rules apply to both: the arguments after the format string must be addresses for fscanf (hence &roll) and values for fprintf; and %s stops at the first whitespace, so a name containing a space needs fgets() rather than fscanf.

long.q: Describe 'Sequence', 'Selection' and 'Loop' control structures with their flowcharts and a C example of each, and differentiate between the while and do-while loops.
long.a:
C, like every structured language, is built from three control structures: sequence, selection and repetition.

1. Sequence. Statements run one after another, top to bottom, with no branching. It is the default order of execution.

Flowchart. [Start] → [Read a, b] → [sum = a + b] → [Print sum] → [Stop] — a straight chain of rectangles.

#include <stdio.h>

int main() {
    int a, b, sum;

    printf("Enter two numbers: ");
    scanf("%d %d", &a, &b);

    sum = a + b;
    printf("Sum = %d\n", sum);

    return 0;
}

2. Selection. A condition decides which branch runs. C provides if, if-else, the else-if ladder, switch and ?:.

Flowchart. [Start] → [Read marks] → <marks >= 40?>. The yes branch runs [Print "Passed"] and the no branch runs [Print "Failed"]; both then reach [Stop].

#include <stdio.h>

int main() {
    int marks;

    printf("Enter marks: ");
    scanf("%d", &marks);

    if (marks >= 40)
        printf("Passed\n");
    else
        printf("Failed\n");

    return 0;
}

3. Loop (repetition). A block repeats while a condition holds. C provides while, do-while and for.

Flowchart. [Start] → [i = 1] → <i <= 10?>. The yes branch runs [Print i] and then [i = i + 1], which arrows back to the diamond; the no branch goes to [Stop].

#include <stdio.h>

int main() {
    int i;

    for (i = 1; i <= 10; i++) {
        printf("%d ", i);
    }

    return 0;
}

while versus do-while.

#include <stdio.h>
/* while - entry controlled, may run zero times */
int i = 1;
while (i <= 5) {
    printf("%d ", i);
    i++;
}

/* do-while - exit controlled, always runs at least once */
int n;
do {
    printf("Enter a number (0 to stop): ");
    if (scanf("%d", &n) != 1) break;
} while (n != 0);

The difference is the position of the test. while tests before the body, so if the condition is false at the start the body never runs. do-while tests after the body, so the body always runs at least once — which is why it is the right loop for a menu or an input prompt. Its other distinguishing mark is the semicolon that must follow while (condition);.

long.q: What is a function? Explain its components (prototype, call, definition and return statement) and the four categories of user-defined function with a program of each.
long.a:
A function is a named, self-contained block of statements that performs one task, receives data through its parameters and returns a result to its caller.

1. Function prototype (declaration). Placed before main(), it tells the compiler the return type, the name and the parameter types so that calls can be checked before the body appears. Parameter names are optional.

int add(int, int);        /* prototype */
int add(int a, int b);   /* the same, with names - clearer to read */

2. Function definition. The header without the semicolon followed by the body that does the work.

int add(int a, int b) {   /* definition */
    int result = a + b;
    return result;
}

3. Function call. Control jumps to the function, the arguments are copied into the parameters, and the call expression is replaced by the returned value.

int sum;
sum = add(10, 20);       /* call; sum becomes 30 */

4. The return statement. It sends a value back to the caller and ends the function immediately. A function whose return type is void returns nothing.

return result;      /* sends the value back   */
return;             /* legal in a void function - just leaves */

The four categories of user-defined function — by whether they take arguments and whether they return a value.

#include <stdio.h>

/* Category 1: no arguments, no return value */
void line(void) {
    printf("--------------------\n");
}

/* Category 2: no arguments, returns a value */
int getNumber(void) {
    int n;
    printf("Enter a number: ");
    scanf("%d", &n);
    return n;
}

/* Category 3: arguments, no return value */
void printTable(int n) {
    int i;
    for (i = 1; i <= 10; i++)
        printf("%d x %d = %d\n", n, i, n * i);
}

/* Category 4: arguments and returns a value */
int largest(int a, int b, int c) {
    if (a >= b && a >= c) return a;
    if (b >= a && b >= c) return b;
    return c;
}

int main() {
    int x, y;

    line();                                  /* 1 */

    x = getNumber();                         /* 2 */
    y = getNumber();

    printTable(x);                           /* 3 */

    printf("Largest = %d\n", largest(x, y, 100));  /* 4 */

    line();
    return 0;
}

Writing void between the parentheses matters: empty parentheses in C mean "arguments unspecified", so the compiler will not check the call, whereas (void) states positively that there are none.

long.q: Explain the concept of storage in C: describe the automatic and external storage classes with a program of each and a comparison table.
long.a:
A storage class determines where a variable is stored, its default initial value, its scope (where it can be used) and its lifetime (how long it keeps its value). C has four: auto, register, static and extern. Two of them are asked for here.

The automatic storage class (auto). This is the default for every variable declared inside a function. Stored in memory (on the stack), scope limited to the block where it is declared, and lifetime limited to that one execution of the block — the variable is created on entry and destroyed on exit, so it does not remember anything between calls. If it is not initialised, it holds garbage.

#include <stdio.h>

void demo(void) {
    auto int count = 0;      /* auto is the default and may be omitted */
    count++;
    printf("count = %d\n", count);
}

int main() {
    demo();                  /* prints count = 1 */
    demo();                  /* prints count = 1 again - it was recreated */
    demo();                  /* prints count = 1 */
    return 0;
}

The external storage class (extern). A global variable — one declared outside every function — has external storage by default: it is created once when the program starts, lives until the program ends, is initialised to zero if nothing is given, and can be seen by every function in the file. The extern keyword itself does not allocate storage; it declares that a global variable of that name is defined somewhere else, usually in another source file, which is how one variable is shared across several files.

#include <stdio.h>

int total = 100;             /* external (global) variable */

void addToTotal(int n) {
    total = total + n;       /* every function sees the same variable */
    printf("total = %d\n", total);
}

int main() {
    printf("total = %d\n", total);   /* 100 */
    addToTotal(50);                  /* 150 */
    addToTotal(25);                  /* 175 */
    return 0;
}

Comparison.

Automatic (auto) External (extern / global)
Keywordauto (optional) extern, or nothing at all for a global
Where declaredInside a function or block Outside every function
StorageMemory (stack) Memory (data segment)
ScopeLocal to the block Whole file, and other files via extern
LifetimeOnly while the block is running The whole run of the program
Default valueGarbage (unpredictable) Zero
Remembers between callsNoYes

A static local variable is the useful middle ground: it has a local scope but an external lifetime, so it keeps its value between calls while staying invisible to the rest of the file.

long.q: What is a structure? Explain how a structure is declared and initialised, how its members are accessed, nested structures, an array of structures, and how a structure is passed to a function.
long.a:
A structure is a user-defined type that groups variables of different types under one name, so that one record — a student, an employee — is held in a single unit.

Declaration. The keyword struct, a tag name, and the members inside braces, ending with a semicolon. This defines the type; no memory is reserved yet.

struct student {
    int  roll;
    char name[30];
    float marks;
};                       /* the semicolon is compulsory */

struct student s1, s2;   /* now two variables of that type exist */

/* or both at once, and optionally with a typedef for convenience */
typedef struct {
    int  roll;
    char name[30];
    float marks;
} Student;

Student s3;

Initialisation. Values are listed in the order the members were declared, inside braces.

struct student s1 = {1, "Ram Sharma", 85.5};

Accessing members. The dot operator, or the arrow operator when the structure is reached through a pointer. A structure of the same type can also be assigned as a whole.

#include <stdio.h>
s1.roll  = 1;
s1.marks = 85.5;
printf("%s", s1.name);

struct student *sp = &s1;
sp->roll = 2;            /* same as (*sp).roll = 2; */

s2 = s1;                 /* copies every member */

Nested structures — a structure as a member of another structure.

#include <stdio.h>
#include <string.h>
struct address {
    char street[40];
    char city[20];
};

struct student {
    int  roll;
    char name[30];
    struct address addr;      /* nested */
};

struct student s;
strcpy(s.addr.city, "Kathmandu");
printf("%s", s.addr.city);    /* dots chain from the outside in */

An array of structures — the way a whole class is held.

#include <stdio.h>
#include <string.h>
struct student class12[50];       /* 50 complete records */

class12[0].roll = 1;
strcpy(class12[0].name, "Ram");
class12[0].marks = 85.5;

for (int i = 0; i < 50; i++) {
    printf("%d  %s  %.2f\n", class12[i].roll,
                             class12[i].name,
                             class12[i].marks);
}

Passing a structure to a function. There are three ways, and the choice matters for large structures.

#include <stdio.h>
#include <string.h>

struct student {
    int  roll;
    char name[30];
    float marks;
};

/* by value - the function works on a copy, the original is unchanged */
void show(struct student s) {
    printf("%d  %s  %.2f\n", s.roll, s.name, s.marks);
}

/* by pointer - the function can change the caller's structure */
void giveGrace(struct student *s, float extra) {
    s->marks = s->marks + extra;
}

/* by pointer to const - no copy, and the original cannot be changed */
void showFast(const struct student *s) {
    printf("%d  %s  %.2f\n", s->roll, s->name, s->marks);
}

int main() {
    struct student s1 = {1, "Ram Sharma", 85.5};

    show(s1);                 /* prints 1  Ram Sharma  85.50 */
    giveGrace(&s1, 5.0);      /* s1.marks is now 90.50       */
    showFast(&s1);            /* prints 1  Ram Sharma  90.50 */

    return 0;
}

Passing by value copies the whole structure, which is wasteful for a large one; passing a pointer copies only an address and lets the function modify the original. Adding const to the pointer keeps the efficiency while promising not to change anything.

long.q: What is a pointer? Explain the address (&) and indirection (*) operators, pointer arithmetic, the relation between array and pointer, structure and pointer, and call by value versus call by reference.
long.a:
A pointer is a variable that holds the address of another variable rather than a value of its own.

The & and * operators. &a gives the address of a; *p gives the value stored at the address held by p. They are inverses, so *(&a) is a.

#include <stdio.h>
int a = 25;
int *p = &a;

printf("%p\n", (void *)p);   /* the address of a */
printf("%d\n", *p);          /* 25 - the value at that address */

*p = 100;                    /* changes a itself */
printf("%d\n", a);           /* 100 */

Pointer arithmetic. Only addition, subtraction, increment and decrement are meaningful, and they scale by the size of the base type: p + 1 moves to the next int, not the next byte. Subtracting two pointers into the same array gives the number of elements between them.

#include <stdio.h>
int arr[5] = {10, 20, 30, 40, 50};
int *p = arr;

printf("%d\n", *p);        /* 10 */
p++;                       /* now points at arr[1] */
printf("%d\n", *p);        /* 20 */
p += 2;                    /* now points at arr[3] */
printf("%d\n", *p);        /* 40 */
printf("%ld\n", p - arr);  /* 3 elements from the start */

Array and pointer. The name of an array is a constant pointer to its first element, so arr equals &arr[0] and arr[i] is exactly *(arr + i). The difference is that arr cannot be reassigned, while a pointer variable can walk through the array.

Structure and pointer. A pointer to a structure avoids copying the whole record into a function, and its members are reached with ->.

#include <stdio.h>
struct student s1 = {1, "Ram", 85.5};
struct student *sp = &s1;

printf("%d\n", sp->roll);     /* same as (*sp).roll */
sp->marks = 90.0;             /* changes s1.marks   */

Call by value versus call by reference. C always passes by value. "Call by reference" is produced by passing a pointer and dereferencing it.

#include <stdio.h>

void byValue(int x) {          /* works on a copy */
    x = x + 100;
}

void byReference(int *x) {     /* works on the original */
    *x = *x + 100;
}

int main() {
    int a = 10;

    byValue(a);
    printf("After byValue     : %d\n", a);    /* 10 - unchanged */

    byReference(&a);
    printf("After byReference : %d\n", a);    /* 110 - changed  */

    return 0;
}

long.q: What is a data file? Explain the file opening modes, the sequential and random file processing techniques, and the integer, character, string, formatted and record-block input/output functions with programs.
long.a:
A data file is a named collection of records kept on a secondary storage device, so that the data survives after the program ends. It is how a program stores information permanently, shares it with other programs, and works with amounts too large for memory.

File opening modes. The second argument of fopen() states what is to be done with the file.

ModeMeaning
"r"Open for reading; the file must already exist.
"w"Create for writing; if the file exists, its contents are destroyed.
"a"Open for appending; creates the file if needed and writes at the end.
"r+"Open an existing file for both reading and writing.
"w+"Create for reading and writing; destroys an existing file.
"a+"Open for reading and appending.
"rb", "wb", "ab" The same modes in binary rather than text.

Sequential file processing. Records are read or written one after another in order. To reach the hundredth record the first ninety-nine must be passed over. It is simple and is what tape-like access looks like, but it is slow for random enquiries.

#include <stdio.h>
/* sequential: read every record from the beginning */
FILE *fp = fopen("student.dat", "r");
struct student s;

while (fread(&s, sizeof(s), 1, fp) == 1) {
    printf("%d  %s\n", s.roll, s.name);
}
fclose(fp);

Random (direct) file processing. Any record is reached straight away by moving the file position with fseek(), because every record is the same size. It is fast for enquiries and updates, needs a fixed record length, and is only sensible on a disk.

#include <stdio.h>
/* random: jump straight to record n */
FILE *fp = fopen("student.dat", "rb");
struct student s;
int n = 9;                         /* the 10th record */

fseek(fp, n * sizeof(struct student), SEEK_SET);
fread(&s, sizeof(s), 1, fp);

/* change it and write it back at the same place */
s.marks += 5;
fseek(fp, n * sizeof(struct student), SEEK_SET);
fwrite(&s, sizeof(s), 1, fp);

fclose(fp);

The input/output functions, by what they move.

#include <stdio.h>

int main() {
    FILE *fp;
    int n = 123;
    char ch, str[40];

    /* ---------- character I/O ---------- */
    fp = fopen("a.txt", "w");
    fputc('A', fp);                     /* write one character */
    fclose(fp);

    fp = fopen("a.txt", "r");
    ch = fgetc(fp);                     /* read one character */
    printf("Character : %c\n", ch);
    fclose(fp);

    /* ---------- string I/O ---------- */
    fp = fopen("b.txt", "w");
    fputs("Namaste Nepal\n", fp);       /* write a string  */
    fclose(fp);

    fp = fopen("b.txt", "r");
    while (fgets(str, sizeof(str), fp) != NULL) {   /* read a line */
        printf("String    : %s", str);
    }
    fclose(fp);

    /* ---------- integer / formatted I/O ---------- */
    fp = fopen("c.txt", "w");
    fprintf(fp, "%d\n", n);             /* write formatted */
    fclose(fp);

    fp = fopen("c.txt", "r");
    fscanf(fp, "%d", &n);               /* read formatted  */
    printf("Integer   : %d\n", n);
    fclose(fp);

    return 0;
}

Record (block) I/O uses fread() and fwrite(), which move a whole structure at a time in binary — the fastest way to store records, though the file is not readable as text.

#include <stdio.h>
#include <string.h>

struct student {
    int  roll;
    char name[30];
    float marks;
};

int main() {
    FILE *fp;
    struct student s, out;

    s.roll = 1;
    strcpy(s.name, "Ram Sharma");
    s.marks = 85.5;

    /* write the whole record as one block */
    fp = fopen("student.dat", "wb");
    fwrite(&s, sizeof(s), 1, fp);
    fclose(fp);

    /* read it back */
    fp = fopen("student.dat", "rb");
    while (fread(&out, sizeof(out), 1, fp) == 1) {
        printf("%d  %s  %.2f\n", out.roll, out.name, out.marks);
    }
    fclose(fp);

    return 0;
}

fread() and fwrite() return the number of items actually transferred, not the number of bytes, so the loop above ends when the count is no longer 1.

long.q: Explain the difference between text mode and binary mode with reference to the file size of the same value, and describe appending on a data file with a program.
long.a:
The difference between text and binary mode is how the data is stored, and it shows most clearly in the size of the file.

Text mode. Data is stored as a sequence of characters, exactly as it would be printed. Numbers are converted to their decimal digit characters, so the integer 12345 is written as the five characters '1', '2', '3', '4', '5' and occupies 5 bytes (6 if a separator follows). Text mode is also where the newline translation happens: on Windows a '\n' written in text mode becomes the two bytes '\r' and '\n', which does not happen in binary mode.

Binary mode. Data is stored in the same internal representation the computer uses, with no conversion. The integer 12345 is written as the bytes of its binary value, which on a typical 32-bit machine is 4 bytes — and a float or a double keeps its exact value instead of being rounded to printed digits.

A program that shows the difference — it writes the same data twice and reports the size of each file.

#include <stdio.h>

int main() {
    FILE *fp;
    int n = 12345;
    long size;

    /* text mode: the digits are written as characters */
    fp = fopen("text.bin", "w");
    fprintf(fp, "%d", n);
    fclose(fp);

    fp = fopen("text.bin", "r");
    fseek(fp, 0L, SEEK_END);      /* go to the end */
    size = ftell(fp);             /* the offset is the file size */
    fclose(fp);
    printf("Text mode   : %ld bytes\n", size);

    /* binary mode: the internal representation is written */
    fp = fopen("binary.bin", "wb");
    fwrite(&n, sizeof(n), 1, fp);
    fclose(fp);

    fp = fopen("binary.bin", "rb");
    fseek(fp, 0L, SEEK_END);
    size = ftell(fp);
    fclose(fp);
    printf("Binary mode : %ld bytes\n", size);

    return 0;
}

Output: Text mode : 5 bytes and Binary mode : 4 bytes for that integer — the text file holds one byte per digit, the binary file holds the machine's own four-byte representation. The gap widens for floating-point values and for large collections of numbers. The trade-off is that the text file can be opened and read by a person, while the binary file cannot, but the binary file is smaller, is written faster, preserves values exactly, and supports random access because its records are a fixed size.

Appending to a data file. Opening with mode "a" (or "ab") leaves any existing contents alone and puts everything that is written at the end of the file — whereas "w" would wipe it.

#include <stdio.h>
#include <string.h>

struct student {
    int  roll;
    char name[30];
    float marks;
};

int main() {
    FILE *fp;
    struct student s;
    char more;

    /* open for appending - the old records are kept */
    fp = fopen("student.dat", "ab");
    if (fp == NULL) {
        printf("Cannot open the file\n");
        return 1;
    }

    do {
        printf("Enter roll, name and marks: ");
        if (scanf("%d %s %f", &s.roll, s.name, &s.marks) != 3) break;

        fwrite(&s, sizeof(s), 1, fp);      /* added at the end */

        printf("Add another record? (y/n): ");
        if (scanf(" %c", &more) != 1) break;
    } while (more == 'y' || more == 'Y');

    fclose(fp);

    /* show the whole file, old records included */
    fp = fopen("student.dat", "rb");
    printf("\nRoll  Name           Marks\n");
    while (fread(&s, sizeof(s), 1, fp) == 1) {
        printf("%-5d %-14s %.2f\n", s.roll, s.name, s.marks);
    }
    fclose(fp);

    return 0;
}

Two details in that program are worth pointing out. The space before %c in scanf(" %c", &more) swallows the newline left in the buffer by the previous scanf, without which the character read would be the newline itself. And the file is closed after appending and reopened for reading, because a single FILE * has only one position indicator.

practical.q: Write a C program that reads the principal, rate of interest and number of years and finds the simple interest and amount.
practical.a:
#include <stdio.h>

int main() {
    float p, r, t, si, amount;

    printf("Enter principal, rate and time: ");
    scanf("%f %f %f", &p, &r, &t);

    si     = (p * r * t) / 100.0;
    amount = p + si;

    printf("Simple Interest = %.2f\n", si);
    printf("Amount          = %.2f\n", amount);

    return 0;
}

SI = (P × R × T) / 100 and Amount = P + SI. The division is by 100.0, not 100, so the result stays floating point.

practical.q: Write a C program to read the radius of a circle and display its area.
practical.a:
#include <stdio.h>
#define PI 3.14159

int main() {
    float r, area;

    printf("Enter the radius: ");
    scanf("%f", &r);

    area = PI * r * r;

    printf("Area of the circle = %.2f\n", area);

    return 0;
}

Area = πr². Defining PI with #define is neater than typing the number twice.

practical.q: Write a C program to input an arbitrary number and find out whether it is positive or negative.
practical.a:
#include <stdio.h>

int main() {
    int n;

    printf("Enter a number: ");
    scanf("%d", &n);

    if (n > 0)
        printf("%d is positive.\n", n);
    else if (n < 0)
        printf("%d is negative.\n", n);
    else
        printf("The number is zero.\n");

    return 0;
}

practical.q: Write a C program that reads three numbers and displays the largest among them.
practical.a:
#include <stdio.h>

int main() {
    int a, b, c, largest;

    printf("Enter three numbers: ");
    scanf("%d %d %d", &a, &b, &c);

    if (a >= b && a >= c)
        largest = a;
    else if (b >= a && b >= c)
        largest = b;
    else
        largest = c;

    printf("The largest number is %d\n", largest);

    return 0;
}

practical.q: Write a program to display the name of the day in a week, depending on the number entered through the keyboard using the switch-case statement.
practical.a:
#include <stdio.h>

int main() {
    int day;

    printf("Enter a number (1-7): ");
    scanf("%d", &day);

    switch (day) {
        case 1: printf("Sunday\n");    break;
        case 2: printf("Monday\n");    break;
        case 3: printf("Tuesday\n");   break;
        case 4: printf("Wednesday\n"); break;
        case 5: printf("Thursday\n");  break;
        case 6: printf("Friday\n");    break;
        case 7: printf("Saturday\n");  break;
        default: printf("Invalid day number\n");
    }

    return 0;
}

switch is the natural choice when one variable is tested against several constant values. Each break is essential — without it execution falls through and every following case is printed too. The default clause catches anything outside 1 to 7.

practical.q: Write a C program to display all the natural numbers up to 100.
practical.a:
#include <stdio.h>

int main() {
    int i;

    printf("Natural numbers up to 100:\n");

    for (i = 1; i <= 100; i++) {
        printf("%d ", i);
    }

    printf("\n");
    return 0;
}

practical.q: Write a C program to display the sum of 'n' terms of 'even' numbers.
practical.a:
#include <stdio.h>

int main() {
    int n, i, sum = 0;

    printf("How many even numbers to add? ");
    scanf("%d", &n);

    for (i = 1; i <= n; i++) {
        sum = sum + (2 * i);      /* the i-th even number is 2*i */
    }

    printf("Sum of the first %d even numbers = %d\n", n, sum);

    return 0;
}

The nth even number is 2n, so the loop simply adds 2*i for i from 1 to n. For n = 5 that is 2 + 4 + 6 + 8 + 10 = 30. The closed form sum = n(n+1) gives the same answer.

practical.q: Write a program to check whether the given number is a palindrome or not. (Note: a palindrome is a string that reads the same from left to right and vice-versa. For e.g., LIRIL)
practical.a:
#include <stdio.h>

int main() {
    int n, temp, rev = 0, digit;

    printf("Enter a number: ");
    scanf("%d", &n);

    temp = n;

    while (temp > 0) {
        digit = temp % 10;         /* last digit        */
        rev   = rev * 10 + digit;  /* build the reverse */
        temp  = temp / 10;         /* drop that digit   */
    }

    if (rev == n)
        printf("%d is a palindrome.\n", n);
    else
        printf("%d is not a palindrome.\n", n);

    return 0;
}

A palindrome reads the same both ways, so reverse the digits and compare with the original — 121 and 1331 are palindromes. The original must be kept in n, because temp is destroyed by the loop.

practical.q: Write a program to find the factorial of a given positive number.
practical.a:
#include <stdio.h>

int main() {
    int n, i;
    long fact = 1;

    printf("Enter a number: ");
    scanf("%d", &n);

    for (i = 1; i <= n; i++) {
        fact = fact * i;
    }

    printf("%d! = %ld\n", n, fact);

    return 0;
}

The accumulator starts at 1, never 0. long is used because factorial grows quickly: 12! already exceeds the range of a 32-bit int.

practical.q: Write a C program to input 10 numbers and display the largest and the smallest among them.
practical.a:
#include <stdio.h>

int main() {
    int num[10], i, largest, smallest;

    printf("Enter 10 numbers:\n");
    for (i = 0; i < 10; i++) {
        if (scanf("%d", &num[i]) != 1) break;
    }

    largest = smallest = num[0];

    for (i = 1; i < 10; i++) {
        if (num[i] > largest)  largest  = num[i];
        if (num[i] < smallest) smallest = num[i];
    }

    printf("Largest  = %d\n", largest);
    printf("Smallest = %d\n", smallest);

    return 0;
}

Both start at the first element, so the loop can begin at index 1 and compare each remaining element with the best found so far.

practical.q: Write a C program to read the age of 40 students and count the number of students aged between 15 and 22.
practical.a:
#include <stdio.h>

int main() {
    int age[40], i, count = 0;

    printf("Enter the age of 40 students:\n");
    for (i = 0; i < 40; i++) {
        if (scanf("%d", &age[i]) != 1) break;
    }

    for (i = 0; i < 40; i++) {
        if (age[i] >= 15 && age[i] <= 22) {
            count++;
        }
    }

    printf("Students aged between 15 and 22 = %d\n", count);

    return 0;
}

The range test needs two comparisons joined by &&: "between 15 and 22" means age >= 15 AND age <= 22. Writing 15 <= age <= 22 is a classic error — C evaluates it left to right as (15 <= age) <= 22, which is always true.

practical.q: Write a C program to input several numbers and arrange them in ascending order.
practical.a:
#include <stdio.h>

int main() {
    int n, i, j, temp;
    int a[50];

    printf("How many numbers? ");
    scanf("%d", &n);

    printf("Enter %d numbers:\n", n);
    for (i = 0; i < n; i++) {
        if (scanf("%d", &a[i]) != 1) break;
    }

    /* bubble sort - ascending */
    for (i = 0; i < n - 1; i++) {
        for (j = 0; j < n - 1 - i; j++) {
            if (a[j] > a[j + 1]) {
                temp     = a[j];
                a[j]     = a[j + 1];
                a[j + 1] = temp;
            }
        }
    }

    printf("Numbers in ascending order:\n");
    for (i = 0; i < n; i++) {
        printf("%d ", a[i]);
    }
    printf("\n");

    return 0;
}

Bubble sort repeatedly swaps neighbouring elements that are in the wrong order, so the largest value "bubbles" to the end on each pass. The inner limit n - 1 - i skips the elements already settled. Change > to < for descending order.

practical.q: Write a C program to input a matrix of size r×c and transpose it.
practical.a:
#include <stdio.h>

int main() {
    int r, c, i, j;
    int a[10][10], t[10][10];

    printf("Enter rows and columns: ");
    scanf("%d %d", &r, &c);

    printf("Enter the matrix elements:\n");
    for (i = 0; i < r; i++)
        for (j = 0; j < c; j++)
            scanf("%d", &a[i][j]);

    /* transpose: rows become columns */
    for (i = 0; i < r; i++)
        for (j = 0; j < c; j++)
            t[j][i] = a[i][j];

    printf("Transpose of the matrix:\n");
    for (i = 0; i < c; i++) {
        for (j = 0; j < r; j++)
            printf("%d\t", t[i][j]);
        printf("\n");
    }

    return 0;
}

The whole idea is t[j][i] = a[i][j] — swap the two subscripts. Note that the transpose is printed with c rows and r columns, because the shape is turned around.

practical.q: Write a C program to input two matrices of size 2×3 and display their sum.
practical.a:
#include <stdio.h>

int main() {
    int a[2][3], b[2][3], sum[2][3];
    int i, j;

    printf("Enter 6 elements of the first matrix (2x3):\n");
    for (i = 0; i < 2; i++)
        for (j = 0; j < 3; j++)
            scanf("%d", &a[i][j]);

    printf("Enter 6 elements of the second matrix (2x3):\n");
    for (i = 0; i < 2; i++)
        for (j = 0; j < 3; j++)
            scanf("%d", &b[i][j]);

    for (i = 0; i < 2; i++)
        for (j = 0; j < 3; j++)
            sum[i][j] = a[i][j] + b[i][j];

    printf("Sum of the two matrices:\n");
    for (i = 0; i < 2; i++) {
        for (j = 0; j < 3; j++)
            printf("%d\t", sum[i][j]);
        printf("\n");
    }

    return 0;
}

Matrices can only be added when they have the same dimensions; the sum is formed element by element.

practical.q: Write a C program to input a matrix of size 3×2 and another of size 2×3 and perform the matrix multiplication.
practical.a:
#include <stdio.h>

int main() {
    int a[3][2], b[2][3], mul[3][3];
    int i, j, k;

    printf("Enter 6 elements of the first matrix (3x2):\n");
    for (i = 0; i < 3; i++)
        for (j = 0; j < 2; j++)
            scanf("%d", &a[i][j]);

    printf("Enter 6 elements of the second matrix (2x3):\n");
    for (i = 0; i < 2; i++)
        for (j = 0; j < 3; j++)
            scanf("%d", &b[i][j]);

    /* initialise the result to zero */
    for (i = 0; i < 3; i++)
        for (j = 0; j < 3; j++)
            mul[i][j] = 0;

    /* multiply */
    for (i = 0; i < 3; i++)
        for (j = 0; j < 3; j++)
            for (k = 0; k < 2; k++)
                mul[i][j] = mul[i][j] + a[i][k] * b[k][j];

    printf("Product of the two matrices:\n");
    for (i = 0; i < 3; i++) {
        for (j = 0; j < 3; j++)
            printf("%d\t", mul[i][j]);
        printf("\n");
    }

    return 0;
}

A 3×2 matrix multiplied by a 2×3 matrix gives a 3×3 result — the inner dimensions (2 and 2) must match. Each element is the sum of k products, which is what the innermost loop accumulates; the result array must start at zero, otherwise the accumulation adds to garbage.

practical.q: Write a C program to count the numbers of vowels and consonants in a given text.
practical.a:
#include <stdio.h>
#include <ctype.h>

int main() {
    char text[200];
    int i, vowels = 0, consonants = 0;
    char ch;

    printf("Enter a line of text: ");
    fgets(text, sizeof(text), stdin);

    for (i = 0; text[i] != '\0'; i++) {
        ch = tolower(text[i]);

        if (ch >= 'a' && ch <= 'z') {
            if (ch == 'a' || ch == 'e' || ch == 'i' ||
                ch == 'o' || ch == 'u')
                vowels++;
            else
                consonants++;
        }
    }

    printf("Vowels     = %d\n", vowels);
    printf("Consonants = %d\n", consonants);

    return 0;
}

tolower() makes the test case-insensitive, and ch >= 'a' && ch <= 'z' skips spaces, digits and punctuation so they are not counted as consonants.

practical.q: Write a C program to check if a string is a palindrome or not.
practical.a:
#include <stdio.h>
#include <string.h>

int main() {
    char str[50], rev[50];
    int i, len, flag = 1;

    printf("Enter a string: ");
    fgets(str, sizeof(str), stdin);
    str[strcspn(str, "\n")] = '\0';

    len = strlen(str);

    for (i = 0; i < len; i++) {
        rev[i] = str[len - 1 - i];
    }
    rev[len] = '\0';          /* terminate the reversed string */

    for (i = 0; i < len; i++) {
        if (str[i] != rev[i]) {
            flag = 0;
            break;
        }
    }

    if (flag)
        printf("%s is a palindrome.\n", str);
    else
        printf("%s is not a palindrome.\n", str);

    return 0;
}

The manual reverse shows the logic: copy the characters backwards and then compare. Turbo C also provides strrev(), which is not standard C, so the loop above is the portable answer. Remember the null terminator on rev.

practical.q: Write a C program to input the name of 20 students and arrange them in alphabetical order.
practical.a:
#include <stdio.h>
#include <string.h>

int main() {
    char name[20][30], temp[30];
    int i, j;

    printf("Enter the names of 20 students:\n");
    for (i = 0; i < 20; i++) {
        fgets(name[i], sizeof(name[i]), stdin);
    }

    /* sort alphabetically */
    for (i = 0; i < 19; i++) {
        for (j = i + 1; j < 20; j++) {
            if (strcmp(name[i], name[j]) > 0) {
                strcpy(temp,    name[i]);
                strcpy(name[i], name[j]);
                strcpy(name[j], temp);
            }
        }
    }

    printf("\nNames in alphabetical order:\n");
    for (i = 0; i < 20; i++) {
        puts(name[i]);
    }

    return 0;
}

A two-dimensional character array is an array of strings. strcmp() compares them alphabetically and returns a positive value when the first should come later, and strings are exchanged with strcpy() — never with =.

practical.q: Write a C program to input a number and calculate its reverse using function.
practical.a:
#include <stdio.h>

int reverse(int n) {
    int rev = 0;

    while (n > 0) {
        rev = rev * 10 + (n % 10);
        n   = n / 10;
    }

    return rev;
}

int main() {
    int num;

    printf("Enter a number: ");
    scanf("%d", &num);

    printf("Reverse of %d is %d\n", num, reverse(num));

    return 0;
}

int main() {

}

practical.q: Write a program in C to input principal, rate and time and calculate simple interest using the function.
practical.a:
#include <stdio.h>

float simpleInterest(float p, float r, float t) {
    return (p * r * t) / 100.0;
}

int main() {
    float p, r, t, si;

    printf("Enter principal, rate and time: ");
    scanf("%f %f %f", &p, &r, &t);

    si = simpleInterest(p, r, t);

    printf("Simple Interest = %.2f\n", si);
    printf("Amount          = %.2f\n", p + si);
