}

practical.q: Write a C program to store Kathmandu Valley's 7 days maximum and minimum temperature (in centigrade) and calculate the average, maximum, minimum temperature using function, and print 7 days temperature, minimum, maximum, and average temperature.
practical.a:
#include <stdio.h>

#define DAYS 7

void readTemp(float t[]) {
    int i;
    printf("Enter the maximum and minimum temperature for 7 days:\n");
    for (i = 0; i < DAYS; i++) {
        printf("Day %d (max min): ", i + 1);
        if (scanf("%f %f", &t[i * 2], &t[i * 2 + 1]) != 2) break;
    }
}

float average(float t[], int n) {
    int i;
    float sum = 0;
    for (i = 0; i < n; i++) sum = sum + t[i];
    return sum / n;
}

float maximum(float t[], int n) {
    int i;
    float max = t[0];
    for (i = 1; i < n; i++)
        if (t[i] > max) max = t[i];
    return max;
}

float minimum(float t[], int n) {
    int i;
    float min = t[0];
    for (i = 1; i < n; i++)
        if (t[i] < min) min = t[i];
    return min;
}

int main() {
    float temp[DAYS * 2];      /* pairs: max, min for each day */
    int i;

    readTemp(temp);

    printf("\nDay   Maximum   Minimum\n");
    printf("------------------------\n");
    for (i = 0; i < DAYS; i++) {
        printf("%-5d %-9.1f %.1f\n", i + 1, temp[i * 2], temp[i * 2 + 1]);
    }

    printf("\nMaximum temperature  : %.1f C\n", maximum(temp, DAYS * 2));
    printf("Minimum temperature  : %.1f C\n", minimum(temp, DAYS * 2));
    printf("Average temperature  : %.1f C\n", average(temp, DAYS * 2));

    return 0;
}

Each day's two readings are stored as a pair in one flat array, so temp[i*2] is the maximum and temp[i*2+1] the minimum of day i. The three statistics are then separate small functions working over the 14 values.

practical.q: Write a C program to calculate the factorial of a given number using functions.
practical.a:
#include <stdio.h>

long factorial(int n) {
    int i;
    long f = 1;

    for (i = 1; i <= n; i++) {
        f = f * i;
    }

    return f;
}

int main() {
    int n;

    printf("Enter a number: ");
    scanf("%d", &n);

    printf("%d! = %ld\n", n, factorial(n));

    return 0;
}

practical.q: Write a program using a user-defined function to calculate y raise to power x.
practical.a:
#include <stdio.h>

double power(double y, int x) {
    double result = 1;
    int i;

    for (i = 0; i < x; i++) {
        result = result * y;
    }

    return result;
}

int main() {
    double y;
    int x;

    printf("Enter the base and the exponent (y x): ");
    scanf("%lf %d", &y, &x);

    printf("%.2f raised to the power %d = %.2f\n", y, x, power(y, x));

    return 0;
}

Multiplying the base by itself x times gives y^x. The standard library's pow(y, x) from <math.h> does the same job, but writing the function is what the question asks for. Note that %lf is used in scanf for a double, while %f is correct in printf.

practical.q: Write a C program to calculate a term of Fibonacci series using a recursive function.
practical.a:
#include <stdio.h>

int fibonacci(int n) {
    if (n == 0)               /* base case 1 */
        return 0;
    else if (n == 1)          /* base case 2 */
        return 1;
    else
        return fibonacci(n - 1) + fibonacci(n - 2);  /* recursive */
}

int main() {
    int n, i;

    printf("Which term of the Fibonacci series? ");
    scanf("%d", &n);

    printf("The term at position %d is %d\n", n, fibonacci(n));

    printf("Series up to that term: ");
    for (i = 0; i <= n; i++) {
        printf("%d ", fibonacci(i));
    }
    printf("\n");

    return 0;
}

Each term is the sum of the two before it, which is precisely the recursive step; the two base cases (0 and 1) stop it. Be aware that this version recalculates the same terms over and over, so it is exponential in time — an iterative loop is far faster for a large term.

practical.q: Write a C program to calculate the factorial of a given number using recursive function.
practical.a:
#include <stdio.h>

long factorial(int n) {
    if (n == 0 || n == 1)        /* base case */
        return 1;
    else
        return n * factorial(n - 1);   /* recursive call */
}

int main() {
    int n;

    printf("Enter a number: ");
    scanf("%d", &n);

    printf("%d! = %ld\n", n, factorial(n));

    return 0;
}

factorial(5) needs 5 × factorial(4), which needs 4 × factorial(3), down to factorial(1), which returns 1. The answers then multiply back up: 1, 2, 6, 24, 120. Without the base case the function would never stop.

practical.q: Write a C program with functions, and input a menu from the keyboard and activate these functions: (a) print area of a circle() (b) reverse string().
practical.a:
#include <stdio.h>
#include <string.h>

#define PI 3.14159

float areaOfCircle(float r) {
    return PI * r * r;
}

void reverseString(char s[]) {
    int i, len;
    char temp;

    len = strlen(s);

    for (i = 0; i < len / 2; i++) {
        temp       = s[i];
        s[i]       = s[len - 1 - i];
        s[len - 1 - i] = temp;
    }
}

int main() {
    int choice;
    float radius;
    char str[50];

    do {
        printf("\n-------- MENU --------\n");
        printf("1. Area of a circle\n");
        printf("2. Reverse a string\n");
        printf("3. Exit\n");
        printf("Enter your choice: ");
        if (scanf("%d", &choice) != 1) break;

        switch (choice) {
            case 1:
                printf("Enter the radius: ");
                if (scanf("%f", &radius) != 1) break;
                printf("Area = %.2f\n", areaOfCircle(radius));
                break;

            case 2:
                printf("Enter a string: ");
                if (scanf("%s", str) != 1) break;
                reverseString(str);
                printf("Reversed string = %s\n", str);
                break;

            case 3:
                printf("Goodbye!\n");
                break;

            default:
                printf("Invalid choice. Try again.\n");
        }
    } while (choice != 3);

    return 0;
}

A do-while is the right loop for a menu, because the choices must be shown at least once before the user can decide to quit. Each case ends with break so the following case is not run as well, and the reversal swaps characters from the two ends inwards, stopping halfway (len / 2).

practical.q: Write a C program that reads roll_no, f_name, l_name and prints the records on the screen.
practical.a:
#include <stdio.h>

struct student {
    int  roll_no;
    char f_name[20];
    char l_name[20];
};

int main() {
    struct student s;
    FILE *fp;

    fp = fopen("student.dat", "wb");
    if (fp == NULL) { printf("Cannot open file\n"); return 1; }

    printf("Enter roll no, first name and last name: ");
    scanf("%d %s %s", &s.roll_no, s.f_name, s.l_name);

    fwrite(&s, sizeof(s), 1, fp);
    fclose(fp);

    fp = fopen("student.dat", "rb");
    if (fp == NULL) { printf("Cannot open file\n"); return 1; }

    printf("\nRoll No   First Name   Last Name\n");
    printf("-----------------------------------\n");
    while (fread(&s, sizeof(s), 1, fp) == 1) {
        printf("%-9d %-12s %s\n", s.roll_no, s.f_name, s.l_name);
    }

    fclose(fp);
    return 0;
}

Storing the whole record with fwrite() and reading it back with fread() is the binary way, and it needs mode "wb" / "rb". The loop tests the number of items returned, which is 1 while a record was read.

practical.q: Write a C program that takes name and marks of 10 students. Display data according to marks in descending order.
practical.a:
#include <stdio.h>
#include <string.h>

struct student {
    char name[30];
    int  marks;
};

int main() {
    struct student s[10], temp;
    int i, j;

    printf("Enter name and marks of 10 students:\n");
    for (i = 0; i < 10; i++) {
        if (scanf("%s %d", s[i].name, &s[i].marks) != 2) break;
    }

    /* sort in descending order of marks */
    for (i = 0; i < 9; i++) {
        for (j = i + 1; j < 10; j++) {
            if (s[i].marks < s[j].marks) {
                temp = s[i];
                s[i] = s[j];
                s[j] = temp;
            }
        }
    }

    printf("\nRank   Name           Marks\n");
    printf("---------------------------\n");
    for (i = 0; i < 10; i++) {
        printf("%-6d %-14s %d\n", i + 1, s[i].name, s[i].marks);
    }

    return 0;
}

Because a structure can be assigned as a whole, temp = s[i] swaps the entire record at once. Descending order just means the comparison is < rather than >.

practical.q: Write a C program that reads different names and addresses into the computer and rearranges the names into alphabetical order using the structure variables.
practical.a:
#include <stdio.h>
#include <string.h>

        if (scanf("%s", p[i].address) != 1) break;

    for (i = 0; i < n - 1; i++) {

    for (i = 0; i < n; i++) {
        printf("%-15s %s\n", p[i].name, p[i].address);
    }

    return 0;
}

practical.q: Write a C program to input emp_id, emp_name, emp_salary of 10 employees using structure and display the emp_id, emp_name and emp_salary of the employee receiving the highest salary.
practical.a:
#include <stdio.h>

struct employee {

Finding the largest value needs only one pass: remember the position of the best so far rather than the value, so the whole record can be printed at the end.

practical.q: Write any C program using union.
practical.a:
#include <stdio.h>
#include <string.h>

union data {
    int   i;
    float f;
    char  str[20];
};

int main() {
    union data d;

    d.i = 100;
    printf("After d.i = 100\n");
    printf("  d.i   = %d\n", d.i);

    d.f = 3.14;
    printf("After d.f = 3.14\n");
    printf("  d.f   = %.2f\n", d.f);
    printf("  d.i   = %d   (now meaningless - the bytes were reused)\n", d.i);

    strcpy(d.str, "Nepal");
    printf("After strcpy(d.str, \"Nepal\")\n");
    printf("  d.str = %s\n", d.str);

    printf("\nSize of the union = %lu bytes\n", sizeof(d));

    return 0;
}

The point of a union is that the members share memory: writing to one overwrites the others, so only one holds a meaningful value at a time. The size is that of the largest member — 20 bytes here, not the sum of all three. A union is used to save memory when a field holds one of several types, or to look at the same bytes in different ways.

practical.q: Write a C program using structure to input rollno, name and percentage of several students and arrange them in descending order by percentage.
practical.a:
#include <stdio.h>
#include <string.h>

struct student {
    int  rollno;
    char name[30];
    float percentage;
};

int main() {
    struct student s[50], temp;
    int n, i, j;

    printf("How many students? ");
    scanf("%d", &n);

    for (i = 0; i < n; i++) {
        printf("Enter roll no, name and percentage: ");
        if (scanf("%d %s %f", &s[i].rollno, s[i].name, &s[i].percentage) != 3) break;
    }

    /* descending order of percentage */
    for (i = 0; i < n - 1; i++) {
        for (j = i + 1; j < n; j++) {
            if (s[i].percentage < s[j].percentage) {
                temp = s[i];
                s[i] = s[j];
                s[j] = temp;
            }
        }
    }

    printf("\nRank  Roll No  Name            Percentage\n");
    printf("-----------------------------------------\n");
    for (i = 0; i < n; i++) {
        printf("%-5d %-8d %-15s %.2f\n", i + 1,
                                         s[i].rollno,
                                         s[i].name,
                                         s[i].percentage);
    }

    return 0;
}

practical.q: Write a C program to calculate two numbers using pointers.
practical.a:
#include <stdio.h>

int main() {
    int a, b;
    int *pa, *pb;

    printf("Enter two numbers: ");
    scanf("%d %d", &a, &b);

    pa = &a;
    pb = &b;

    printf("Sum        = %d\n",  *pa + *pb);
    printf("Difference = %d\n",  *pa - *pb);
    printf("Product    = %d\n",  *pa * *pb);

    if (*pb != 0)
        printf("Quotient   = %d\n", *pa / *pb);
    else
        printf("Quotient   = undefined (division by zero)\n");

    return 0;
}

Every value is reached through *pa and *pb rather than through a and b, which is what "using pointers" means. The division is guarded, because dividing by zero stops the program.

practical.q: Write a program in C to calculate the factorial of given numbers using pointers.
practical.a:
#include <stdio.h>

void factorial(int n, long *result) {
    int i;
    *result = 1;

    for (i = 1; i <= n; i++) {
        *result = *result * i;
    }
}

int main() {
    int num;
    long ans;

    printf("Enter a number: ");
    scanf("%d", &num);

    factorial(num, &ans);

    printf("%d! = %ld\n", num, ans);

    return 0;
}

Passing &ans lets the function write straight into the caller's variable, which is how a void function "returns" a result — the pointer version of call by reference. Note the guard *result = 1 inside the function, so the accumulator starts at one.

practical.q: Write a C program to swap two numbers using call by reference.
practical.a:
#include <stdio.h>

void swap(int *x, int *y) {
    int temp;

    temp = *x;
    *x   = *y;
    *y   = temp;
}

int main() {
    int a, b;

    printf("Enter two numbers: ");
    scanf("%d %d", &a, &b);

    printf("Before swap: a = %d, b = %d\n", a, b);

    swap(&a, &b);

    printf("After swap : a = %d, b = %d\n", a, b);

    return 0;
}

This is the classic demonstration of call by reference. Passing a and b by value would swap only the copies and leave the originals untouched; passing their addresses and dereferencing inside the function changes the originals.

practical.q: Write a C program to input principle, rate and time and calculate simple interest using pointers.
practical.a:
#include <stdio.h>

void simpleInterest(float p, float r, float t, float *si) {
    *si = (p * r * t) / 100.0;
}

int main() {
    float p, r, t, si;

    printf("Enter principal, rate and time: ");
    scanf("%f %f %f", &p, &r, &t);

    simpleInterest(p, r, t, &si);

    printf("Simple Interest = %.2f\n", si);
    printf("Amount          = %.2f\n", p + si);

    return 0;
}

practical.q: Write a program in C to check whether a number is even or odd using pointers.
practical.a:
#include <stdio.h>

void check(int *n) {
    if (*n % 2 == 0)
        printf("%d is even.\n", *n);
    else
        printf("%d is odd.\n", *n);
}

int main() {
    int num;

    printf("Enter a number: ");
    scanf("%d", &num);

    check(&num);

    return 0;
}

practical.q: Write a program in C to input a number, calculate its square and display the memory address of the inputted number and the square.
practical.a:
#include <stdio.h>

int main() {
    int num, square;
    int *p, *q;

    printf("Enter a number: ");
    scanf("%d", &num);

    p = #
    square = (*p) * (*p);
    q = □

    printf("Number        = %d\n",  *p);
    printf("Square        = %d\n",  *q);
    printf("Address of the number = %p\n", (void *)p);
    printf("Address of the square = %p\n", (void *)q);

    return 0;
}

%p is the correct format specifier for an address, and the pointer should be cast to void * when it is printed. The two addresses differ by the size of an int, because num and square are separate variables.

practical.q: Write a C program to input a number and display its multiplication table using pointers.
practical.a:
#include <stdio.h>

int main() {
    int num, i;
    int *p;

    printf("Enter a number: ");
    scanf("%d", &num);

    p = #

    printf("Multiplication table of %d:\n", *p);

    for (i = 1; i <= 10; i++) {
        printf("%d x %d = %d\n", *p, i, (*p) * i);
    }

    return 0;
}

practical.q: Write a C program for writing data in the file.
practical.a:
#include <stdio.h>

int main() {
    FILE *fp;
    char text[100];

    fp = fopen("data.txt", "w");
    if (fp == NULL) {
        printf("Cannot create the file\n");
        return 1;
    }

    printf("Enter a line of text to write in the file:\n");
    fgets(text, sizeof(text), stdin);

    fprintf(fp, "%s\n", text);

    fclose(fp);

    printf("Data written to data.txt\n");

    return 0;
}

Mode "w" creates the file, or empties it if it already exists. fclose() is not optional: output is buffered, so without closing the file the text may never actually reach the disk.

practical.q: Write a C program to show data writing and reading operation to/from a data file.
practical.a:
#include <stdio.h>

int main() {
    FILE *fp;
    char text[100];

    /* write */
    fp = fopen("data.txt", "w");
    if (fp == NULL) { printf("Cannot open file\n"); return 1; }

    printf("Enter text to write into the file: ");
    fgets(text, sizeof(text), stdin);

    fprintf(fp, "%s\n", text);
    fclose(fp);

    /* read */
    fp = fopen("data.txt", "r");
    if (fp == NULL) { printf("Cannot open file\n"); return 1; }

    printf("\nContents of the file:\n");

    while (fgets(text, sizeof(text), fp) != NULL) {
        printf("%s", text);
    }

    fclose(fp);
    return 0;
}

The file is closed after writing and reopened for reading, because a single FILE * keeps only one position indicator. fgets() returns NULL at the end of the file, which is what ends the loop.

practical.q: Write a C program to enter name, roll-number and marks of 10 students and store them in the file.
practical.a:
#include <stdio.h>

struct student {
    int  roll;
    char name[30];
    float marks;
};

int main() {
    FILE *fp;
    struct student s;
    int i;

    fp = fopen("student.dat", "wb");
    if (fp == NULL) { printf("Cannot open file\n"); return 1; }

    printf("Enter roll, name and marks of 10 students:\n");
    for (i = 0; i < 10; i++) {
        if (scanf("%d %s %f", &s.roll, s.name, &s.marks) != 3) break;
        fwrite(&s, sizeof(s), 1, fp);
    }

    fclose(fp);
    printf("Records saved.\n");

    return 0;
}

practical.q: Write a C program to store std_no, name and mark of 'n' students in a data file. Display the records in appropriate format reading from the file.
practical.a:
#include <stdio.h>

struct student {
    int  std_no;
    char name[30];
    float mark;
};

int main() {
    FILE *fp;
    struct student s;
    int n, i;

    printf("How many students? ");
    scanf("%d", &n);

    fp = fopen("student.dat", "wb");
    if (fp == NULL) { printf("Cannot open file\n"); return 1; }

    for (i = 0; i < n; i++) {
        printf("Enter std_no, name and mark: ");
        if (scanf("%d %s %f", &s.std_no, s.name, &s.mark) != 3) break;
        fwrite(&s, sizeof(s), 1, fp);
    }
    fclose(fp);

    /* read them back and display */
    fp = fopen("student.dat", "rb");
    if (fp == NULL) { printf("Cannot open file\n"); return 1; }

    printf("\nStd No   Name            Mark\n");
    printf("-----------------------------\n");
    while (fread(&s, sizeof(s), 1, fp) == 1) {
        printf("%-7d %-15s %.2f\n", s.std_no, s.name, s.mark);
    }

    fclose(fp);
    return 0;
}

practical.q: Write a C program that reads successive records from the new data file and displays each record on the screen in an appropriate format.
practical.a:
#include <stdio.h>

struct record {
    int  id;
    char name[30];
    float salary;
};

int main() {
    FILE *fp;
    struct record r;
    int n, i;

    printf("How many records? ");
    scanf("%d", &n);

    fp = fopen("records.dat", "wb");
    if (fp == NULL) { printf("Cannot open file\n"); return 1; }

    for (i = 0; i < n; i++) {
        printf("Enter id, name and salary: ");
        if (scanf("%d %s %f", &r.id, r.name, &r.salary) != 3) break;
        fwrite(&r, sizeof(r), 1, fp);
    }
    fclose(fp);

    /* read successive records from the file */
    fp = fopen("records.dat", "rb");
    if (fp == NULL) { printf("Cannot open file\n"); return 1; }

    printf("\nID     Name            Salary\n");
    printf("-----------------------------\n");

    while (fread(&r, sizeof(r), 1, fp) == 1) {
        printf("%-6d %-15s %.2f\n", r.id, r.name, r.salary);
    }

    fclose(fp);
    return 0;
}

Reading "successive records" is just repeating fread() until it no longer returns 1 — the file position advances by one record each time on its own, so no fseek() is needed.

practical.q: Write a C program to rename and delete a data file using rename and remove command.
practical.a:
#include <stdio.h>

int main() {
    FILE *fp;

    /* create a file so there is something to rename */
    fp = fopen("old.dat", "w");
    if (fp == NULL) { printf("Cannot create file\n"); return 1; }
    fprintf(fp, "Sample record\n");
    fclose(fp);

    /* rename it */
    if (rename("old.dat", "new.dat") == 0)
        printf("File renamed to new.dat\n");
    else
        printf("Unable to rename the file\n");

    /* delete it */
    if (remove("new.dat") == 0)
        printf("File deleted successfully\n");
    else
        printf("Unable to delete the file\n");

    return 0;
}

Both functions are declared in <stdio.h> and both return 0 on success. Neither will work on a file that is still open, so fclose() comes first — and remove() cannot be undone.

practical.q: Write a C program to open a new file and read roll-no, name, address and phone number of students until the user says "no"; after reading the data, write it to the file then display the content of the file.
practical.a:
#include <stdio.h>
#include <string.h>

struct student {
    int  roll;
    char name[30];
    char address[40];
    char phone[15];
};

int main() {
    FILE *fp;
    struct student s;
    char choice[5];

    fp = fopen("student.dat", "wb");
    if (fp == NULL) { printf("Cannot open file\n"); return 1; }

    do {
        printf("\nEnter roll, name, address and phone: ");
        if (scanf("%d %s %s %s", &s.roll, s.name, s.address, s.phone) != 4) break;

        fwrite(&s, sizeof(s), 1, fp);

        printf("Add another record? (yes/no): ");
        if (scanf("%s", choice) != 1) break;
    } while (strcmp(choice, "no") != 0);

    fclose(fp);

    /* display the contents */
    fp = fopen("student.dat", "rb");
    if (fp == NULL) { printf("Cannot open file\n"); return 1; }

    printf("\nRoll   Name            Address          Phone\n");
    printf("-------------------------------------------------\n");
    while (fread(&s, sizeof(s), 1, fp) == 1) {
        printf("%-6d %-15s %-16s %s\n", s.roll, s.name, s.address, s.phone);
    }

    fclose(fp);
    return 0;
}

The loop is do-while because at least one record has to be taken before the question "another?" makes sense, and it stops when the answer is "no" — compared with strcmp(), not with ==.

practical.q: Write a C program which asks name, age, roll_number of the student and writes it in a file student.dat.
practical.a:
#include <stdio.h>

struct student {
    char name[30];
    int  age;
    int  roll_number;
};

int main() {
    FILE *fp;
    struct student s;

    fp = fopen("student.dat", "wb");
    if (fp == NULL) {
        printf("Cannot open student.dat\n");
        return 1;
    }

    printf("Enter name, age and roll number: ");
    scanf("%s %d %d", s.name, &s.age, &s.roll_number);

    fwrite(&s, sizeof(s), 1, fp);
    fclose(fp);

    printf("Record written to student.dat\n");

    /* read it back to confirm */
    fp = fopen("student.dat", "rb");
    if (fp == NULL) { printf("Cannot open file\n"); return 1; }

    printf("\nName            Age   Roll Number\n");
    printf("-------------------------------\n");
    while (fread(&s, sizeof(s), 1, fp) == 1) {
        printf("%-15s %-5d %d\n", s.name, s.age, s.roll_number);
    }

    fclose(fp);
    return 0;
}

practical.q: Write a C program to enter ID, employee_name, and post of the employee and store them in a data file named "emp.txt". Display each record on the screen in an appropriate format.
practical.a:
#include <stdio.h>

struct employee {
    int  id;
    char employee_name[30];
    char post[25];
};

int main() {
    FILE *fp;
    struct employee e;
    int n, i;

    printf("How many employees? ");
    scanf("%d", &n);

    fp = fopen("emp.txt", "w");
    if (fp == NULL) { printf("Cannot open file\n"); return 1; }

    for (i = 0; i < n; i++) {
        printf("Enter id, employee name and post: ");
        if (scanf("%d %s %s", &e.id, e.employee_name, e.post) != 3) break;

        fprintf(fp, "%d\t%s\t%s\n", e.id, e.employee_name, e.post);
    }

    fclose(fp);

    /* display each record in an appropriate format */
    fp = fopen("emp.txt", "r");
    if (fp == NULL) { printf("Cannot open file\n"); return 1; }

    printf("\nID     Employee Name    Post\n");
    printf("------------------------------\n");
    while (fscanf(fp, "%d %s %s", &e.id, e.employee_name, e.post) == 3) {
        printf("%-6d %-16s %s\n", e.id, e.employee_name, e.post);
    }

    fclose(fp);
    return 0;
}

This version writes the records as text with fprintf() and reads them back with fscanf(), which suits a .txt file that a person may need to open. The fields are separated by tabs so they line up, and the reading loop ends when fscanf() returns EOF.

mcq.q:
What will be the output of the program code?
void main()
{
  char str1[20]="Hello", str2[20]="world";
  strcat(str1, str2);
  puts(str1);
}
mcq.teacher_note: strcat() appends str2 to the END of str1, so the result is Helloworld — the concatenation, not the reverse.

mcq.q: What type of data will a user-defined function return even though the return type of the function has not been defined, whenever called?
mcq.teacher_note: If the return type is omitted, C defaults to int. void must be written explicitly — a function returning void returns nothing at all.

mcq.q: The meaning of int a[5]; int *p; p=&a[0]; in C language is …
options: p is a pointer to 5 integers
p is a pointer to integer array
p is an array of 5 pointers to integer
p is a pointer to an array of 5 integers
mcq.teacher_note: &a[0] is the address of the first element, so p points into the array a[5] — a pointer to an array of 5 integers. Note that p is NOT an array of pointers, which would be declared int *p[5];

mcq.q: What is the correct way to open a file named "data.txt" in C for reading?
mcq.teacher_note: "r" = read (file must exist); "w" = write (erases/creates); "a" = append; "rb" = read binary.

mcq.q: … is a reserved word that has a standard and predefined meaning in C.
mcq.teacher_note: A keyword (there are 32 in ANSI C) is reserved — you cannot use one as a variable name. An identifier is the name you choose.

mcq.q: … is a quantity that doesn't change during program execution.
mcq.teacher_note: A constant (integer, floating-point, character or string) stays fixed; a variable may change.

mcq.q: … is a symbolic name, which is used to store different types of data in the computer's memory and may change during the program execution.
mcq.teacher_note: The definition mentions "may change during the program execution" — that makes it a variable, not merely an identifier.

mcq.q: … is a symbol that instructs C to perform some operation or action on one or more operands.
mcq.teacher_note: The operator acts, the operand is acted upon. Do not confuse the two — Q8 and Q9 are the mirror image of each other.

mcq.q: … is something that an operator acts on.
mcq.teacher_note: In a + b, the + is the operator and a and b are the operands.

mcq.q: … can be used to output data of different types in different formats.
mcq.teacher_note: printf() writes formatted output to the screen; scanf() reads formatted input from the keyboard.

mcq.q: … can read all the built-in data types and automatically convert numbers into the proper internal format.
mcq.teacher_note: scanf() is the input counterpart of printf(). Both live in stdio.h.

mcq.q: … is an operation that repeats the execution of a statement until a certain condition is satisfied.
mcq.teacher_note: for, while and do-while are the three looping statements in C.

mcq.q: … is a collection of variables of the same type represented by a common name.
mcq.teacher_note: Same type + common name = array. Different types = structure.

mcq.q: … is a self-contained program segment or the block of statements that performs some specific, well-defined task.
mcq.teacher_note: This is the textbook's own opening definition of a function in section 4.2.

mcq.q: What is the correct syntax to declare a structure in C?
mcq.teacher_note: A structure tag (the name) plus brace-enclosed members: struct employee { … };

mcq.q: In C, which operator is used to get the address of a variable?
mcq.teacher_note: & is the address-of operator; * is the value-at-address (indirection) operator; -> accesses a structure member through a pointer; . accesses it through a variable.

key_terms.meaning: The smallest individual unit of a C program — a keyword, identifier, constant, string or operator.
A reserved word with a standard, predefined meaning in C (there are 32 in ANSI C). It cannot be used as a variable name.
The programmer-chosen name of a variable, function or array. It must begin with a letter or underscore and C is case-sensitive, so sum and SUM differ.
A quantity that does not change during program execution: integer, floating-point, character or string.
A symbolic name that stores data in memory and whose value may change while the program runs.
A self-contained program segment, or block of statements, that performs one specific well-defined task.
The declaration of a function that tells the compiler its name, return type and the number and type of its arguments, so that calls made before the definition can be checked.
The value supplied at the point of the function call.
The parameter variable declared in the function definition that receives the actual argument's value.
Parameter passing in which a copy of the argument is passed, so changes inside the function do not affect the original variable.
Parameter passing in which the address of the argument is passed using a pointer, so the function works on the original variable.
The specifier (auto, extern, static, register) that determines a variable's scope, storage duration and default initial value.
A variable declared inside a function; it is truly local, has a garbage initial value and is destroyed when the function exits.
A variable declared outside any function; it is visible throughout the program, defaults to zero and lives until the program ends.
The technique in which a function calls itself, always moving closer to a base (stopping) condition.
A collection of one or more variables, possibly of different data types, grouped under a single name. Its members occupy their own memory, so its size is their sum.
A structure used as a member of another structure; members are reached with repeated dot operators, e.g. emp3.address.street_name.
A user-defined type whose members share memory; its size is the size of its largest member, and only one member is active at a time.
A variable that, instead of containing data, contains the address of the memory location where the data can be found.
The unary operator that yields the memory address of the variable it is applied to.
The unary operator that yields the value stored at the address held in a pointer. Also called the value-at-address or dereferencing operator.
Used to access a structure member through a pointer; ptr->name is shorthand for (*ptr).name.
Information stored in a secondary storage device (e.g. a hard disk) so that it is permanent and can be retrieved whenever needed.
The second argument of fopen() that states how the file will be used — r, w, a, r+, w+ or a+.
End Of File — the character written when fclose() is called, used to stop reading back a text-mode file.
Storing content sequentially and reading it back sequentially, usually with a loop plus rewind() and ftell().
Reading content back from any position of the file using rewind(), fseek() and ftell().
Moves the file's offset pointer by a given offset from SEEK_SET (beginning), SEEK_CUR (current position) or SEEK_END (end).
Returns the current offset pointer position as a long int, counted from the beginning of the file.
A file mode in which every digit or character is stored as a character and conversion is needed when reading back; used by character, string and formatted I/O.
A file mode in which data is stored byte-for-byte in the same format as in memory, with no conversion; used by fread() and fwrite().
Adding content at the end of an existing file, from wherever the EOF flag is placed; the opening mode must be "a" or "a+".

quick_revision.title: The shape of a C program
points: Every C program has one or more functions; execution always begins in main().
Documentation section → link section → definition section → global declaration → main() { declaration part; execution part; } → user-defined functions.
C has 32 keywords, is case-sensitive, and its tokens are keywords, identifiers, constants, strings and operators.
Data type sizes used in this book: int 2 bytes (%d), float 4 (%f), char 1 (%c), double 8 (%lf).

quick_revision.title: Decisions, loops and arrays
points: Five control categories: sequence, decision, looping, jump and label.
if / if-else / nested if / if-else-if ladder / switch for decisions; for, while and do-while for repetition.
while checks the condition first (may run zero times); do-while runs the body at least once.
An array is a fixed-size collection of same-type elements at contiguous addresses, indexed from 0.
A string is a character array ending in '\0'; the seven common functions are strlen, strcat, strcmp, strrev, strcpy, strlwr and strupr.

quick_revision.title: Functions
points: Two kinds: library (from a header, e.g. printf in stdio.h, strlen in string.h) and user-defined.
Four components: prototype (declaration), call, definition (body) and the return statement.
Return type omitted ⇒ int; return type void ⇒ returns nothing.
Four categories: with/without arguments × with/without return values.
auto = local, garbage initial value, destroyed on exit. extern = global, initial value zero, lives for the whole program.
A recursive function calls itself and must have a base (stopping) condition.

quick_revision.title: Structures and unions
points: struct groups different types under one name; members are accessed with the dot operator.
Members occupy their own memory, so the size of a structure is the sum of its members.
You can have arrays of structures, nested structures, and structure pointers (ptr->member).
union members SHARE memory; its size is that of its largest member and only one member is active.

quick_revision.title: Pointers
points: A pointer holds an address; declare it as data_type *name and initialise it with &variable.
& gives the address of a variable; * gives the value at an address.
Pointer arithmetic scales by the size of the base type: an int pointer + 1 advances by 2 bytes.
num[i] is exactly *(num + i), and &num[i] is num + i.
Call by value passes a copy (original unchanged); call by reference passes the address (original changed).

quick_revision.title: Files
points: Steps: FILE *fptr; → fptr = fopen("path","mode"); → read/write → fclose(fptr).
Modes: r (read, must exist), w (write, erases/creates), a (append), r+, w+, a+.
rewind() → beginning; fseek(fp, offset, SEEK_SET|SEEK_CUR|SEEK_END) → move; ftell() → current offset.
putw/getw (integer), fputc/fgetc (character), fputs/fgets (string), fprintf/fscanf (formatted), fwrite/fread (record block).
Text mode converts and needs EOF; binary mode does not convert and is smaller (3.14159 = 8 bytes in text, 4 bytes in binary).

teaching_plan.activity: Review the language: where C came from, its five features, the structure of a program and the character set. Then teach tokens — identifiers, case sensitivity, the 32 keywords grouped into 9 rows, the four constants, variable declaration and the nine operator families.

Walk through the data-types diagram (basic, derived, user-defined, void) and the byte-size/at-a-glance table. Then cover printf()/scanf(), the ampersand rule and the other I/O functions, and run the two solved programs.

Decisions and loops: the five control categories, then if / if-else / nested if / if-else-if ladder / switch, followed by for, while and do-while and the comparison table. Trace one loop by hand on the board.
Type and run the six solved programs: simple interest, Fibonacci series, factorial, prime check, primes 1–100 and the nested-loop number pattern. Discuss the pattern output screenshot.

Arrays: introduction, declaration and dimensions; then arrays in programs (largest/smallest, matrix sum, sorting). Move on to strings — the null character, an array of strings and the seven string functions — and run three string programs.
Work the 7 theoretical questions as oral revision, and allocate the 18 practical programs as lab/homework. Bring the teacher notes on the bubble-sort bound and on strcpy() before strrev().

Functions: definition, the advantages list, the proper-use figure, library vs user-defined functions with the comparison table, then the four components — prototype, call, definition and return/void. Close with actual vs formal arguments.

Call by value vs call by reference with both traced programs; then the four categories of user-defined function — write each of the four rectangle-area variants in class. Finish with the automatic and external storage classes and recursion (factorial, sum, Fibonacci).
Run the three function programs (power, positive/negative, even/odd), then drill Exercise 4B: 6 theoretical questions plus 10 practical programs, with the menu-driven program as the capstone.

Structures: definition, declaration, initialisation and the memory-allocation figure; accessing members with the dot operator; nested structures; arrays of structures; passing a structure to a function; and typedef.
Unions: the shared-memory idea, the union program and its output screenshot, then the seven-point union-vs-structure comparison. Run the two sorting programs that swap whole records.

Pointers: definition, why we use them, advantages and disadvantages, declaration, and the three memory maps (i, i and j, and z and x). Then the address-of and indirection operators, and pointer arithmetic with the increment/decrement programs.

Call by value vs call by reference side by side (a=5,b=10 → 5,10 versus 105,110); then array and pointer with the contiguous-address figure and num[i] == *(num+i); then structure pointers and the arrow operator.

Consolidation session: 12 theoretical questions across structures/unions and pointers, and 15 practical programs. Use the four-way comparison tables (array vs structure, structure vs pointer, array vs pointer) as the revision spine.

Files: the concept of a data file, the block diagram, the six opening modes, EOF and the three open/read-write/close steps. Then the two processing techniques with rewind(), fseek() and ftell(), and the five families of I/O function.

fclose(), rename() and remove(); text mode vs binary mode with the PI = 3.14159 file-size example and its screenshot; appending with mode "a". Then run the six solved file programs, including delete-a-record and the marks ≥ 75 filter.
Exercise 4E's 8 theoretical and 9 practical file questions, then the 16-question self-test on the site with the printed answer key, going through each teacher note.

learning_objectives: Introduce Object-Oriented Programming (OOP) with programming paradigms and features.
State advantages and applications of OOP.

blocks.text: An approach to solve problems using some programming language. It is an approach to solve a problem using some tools and techniques that are available to us. There are lots of programming languages and they need to follow some strategy when they are implemented — and this methodology/strategy is the paradigm.
Types of Programming Paradigm
Three main types of programming paradigms are:

items: Procedural paradigm
Structural paradigm
Object-Oriented paradigm

blocks.text: 1. Procedural Paradigm

It is a programming paradigm aimed at improving the clarity, quality, and development time of a computer program by making extensive use of the structured control flow constructs of selection (if/then/else) and repetition (while and for), block structures, and subroutines — in contrast to using simple tests and jumps such as the go-to statement. Early languages emphasizing structured programming: Algol 60, PL/I, Algol 68, Pascal, C. Examples: Fortran, C and COBOL.
2. Structural Paradigm

It is a programming paradigm aimed at improving the clarity, quality, and development time of a computer program by making extensive use of the structured control flow constructs of selection (if/then/else) and repetition (while and for), block structures, and subroutines — in contrast to using simple tests and jumps such as the go-to statement. Early languages emphasizing structured programming: Algol 60, PL/I, Algol 68, Pascal, C.
3. Object-Oriented Paradigm

In this paradigm, programs are written as a collection of classes and objects. A basic element is an object and all kinds of computation are performed on the objects only. It gives more emphasis on data rather than the procedure. Many languages designed from the 1980s to the present are object-oriented; some of them are C++, Ada 95, Java, C#, Ruby.

The book prints almost the same paragraph for the procedural and the structural paradigm. In the exam, the distinguishing line students should write is: procedural = the program is a sequence of procedure calls; structural = the same idea but organised into blocks and subroutines with no go-to; object-oriented = the program is a collection of objects that own their own data.

sections.title: Concept and Features of Object-Oriented Programming (OOP)

blocks.text: A programming paradigm (model) that uses “object” to design applications and computer programs. It utilises several techniques from previously established paradigms, including modularity, polymorphism, inheritance, and encapsulation. Due to the use of these strong features, these days it is commonly used in mainstream software development. Programming languages like C++, Java, JavaScript, PHP, C#, VB.Net and Objective-C are object-oriented programming languages.

Object-oriented programming may be seen as a collection of cooperative objects, as opposed to a traditional view in which a program may be seen as a collection of functions, or simply as a list of instructions to the computer. In OOP, each object is capable of receiving messages, processing data, and sending a message to the other objects.

The fundamental idea behind object-oriented programming is to combine data and function into a single unit; such a unit is called an object. An object's function is called a member function and the data are only accessible through a member function. If we want to read a data item in an object, we call a member function in the object. It will read the item and return the value to us. We can't access the data directly. The data is hidden, so it is safe from accidental alteration. Data and its functions are said to be encapsulated into a single entity. Data encapsulation and data hiding are the key terms in the description of object-oriented programming.

blocks.caption: Figure: Object-oriented Paradigm — three objects, each wrapping its own data and member functions.

blocks.text: An OOP program typically consists of several objects, which communicate with each other by calling one another's member functions.
The main concept of OOP

items: Problems are divided into objects.
It is not possible to access data freely.
Data hiding is possible.
It uses a bottom-up programming technique.
It is easy to add new data and functions.
Objects can exchange data through their function, whereas in structured programming a program consists of a list of instructions and the computer carries out.
As a program grows even larger and more complex, a structured programming approach begins to show signs of strain, but OOP is implemented more simply, fast, and secure.
Data and functions are encapsulated into a single entity.
In OOPs we create classes, which have the power of reusability — that is, these classes can be used by other programmers whenever needed.

blocks.text: The main features of OOP are:

items: Object
Class
Inheritance
Encapsulation
Polymorphism
Data abstraction

blocks.text: 1. Object
A concept or thing with defined boundaries that are relevant to the problem we are dealing with.
The object serves two purposes: (i) it helps to understand the real world, and (ii) it provides a practical basis for a computer application.

When we approach a programming problem in an object-oriented language, the problem is divided into different objects. An object consists of data and functions; the functions are used to perform the operations on data. The data contained in the object is called member data and the function is called a member function. The member functions can only access data through the object, so it provides data security.

The fundamental idea behind OOP is to combine both data and function in a single entity. This entity is also called an object. So, a particular instance of a class is known as an object. Every object has some properties, behaviours and relationships. An object is a particular entity with some characteristics and behaviour; it represents an entity that can store data and its associated functions.

An object is an instance of a class. It can be uniquely identified by its name, and it defines a state which is represented by the values of its attributes at a particular time — or it is an individual unit of run-time data storage that is used as the basic building block of programs. Each object is capable of receiving messages, processing data, and sending messages to other objects.
2. Class

A collection or group of similar objects that have the same properties, common behaviour, and relationships. Objects with similar properties and actions need to be grouped into a unit that can be used in a program.
Each class describes a set of individual objects. A class of persons, a class of animals, and a class of dogs are all examples of classes.

blocks.caption: Figure: Class — one class, many objects sharing the same member data and member functions.

blocks.text: The concept of class leads to the reusability of programming code. Code is written for an object of the class and can be reused by another object of the class; this concept helps to decrease the length of the programming code. It also incorporates the concept of data hiding.

During the definition of a class, a new abstract data type is created which is treated like any other built-in data type. Classes are used to group related variables and functions that share common properties and relationships. A class describes a collection of encapsulated instance variables and methods (functions), possibly with the implementation of those types together with a constructor function that can be used to create objects of the class. A class contains the rules by which objects behave; these objects are referred to as "instances" of that class. A class specifies the structure of data which each instance contains, as well as the methods (functions) which manipulate the data of the object and perform tasks — such methods are sometimes described as "behaviour". A method is a function with a special property that has access to data stored in an object.
3. Inheritance

The property that allows the reuse of an existing class to build a new class. The principle in this sort of division is that each subclass shares common properties with the class from which it is derived.

blocks.title: Everyday example
blocks.text: All vehicles in a class may share similar properties of having wheels and a motor. A class of animals can be divided into mammals, amphibians, insects, reptiles, etc. A class of vehicles is divided into cars, buses and motorcycles.

The idea of classes leads to the idea of inheritance. Inheritance is a way to form new classes (an instance of which is called an object). The new classes, known as derived classes, inherit attributes and behaviour of the pre-existing classes, which are referred to as base classes. It is intended to help the reuse of existing code with little or no modification. Inheritance allows different data types to share the same code, leading to a reduction in code size and an increase in functionality. Objects and classes extend the concept of abstract data types by adding the notation of inheritance. Such classes inherit their behaviour from the parent classes or base class.
Types of Inheritance
Four types of inheritance are: single inheritance, multiple inheritance, hierarchical inheritance and multilevel inheritance.
1. Single Inheritance

In this inheritance a derived class is created from a single base class. In the example, Class A is the parent class and Class B is the child class, since Class B inherits the features and behaviour of the parent class A.

blocks.caption: Single inheritance — one derived class created from a single base class.

blocks.text: 2. Multiple Inheritance

Under this type of inheritance the derived class has several base classes. If a child class is built from two or more than two parent classes, then this type of inheritance is called multiple inheritance. In the example, Class C inherits the properties and behaviour of Class B and Class A at the same level, so here Class A and Class B are both the parent classes for Class C.

blocks.caption: Multiple inheritance — Class C inherits from both Class A and Class B.

blocks.text: 3. Hierarchical Inheritance

In this inheritance more than one derived class is created from a single base class, and further child classes act as parent classes for more than one child class. In the example: Class B and Class C inherit the properties and behaviour of parent Class A. Similarly, Class D and E inherit the properties and behaviour of their parent Class C, as well as Class F and G inheriting the Class B.

blocks.caption: Hierarchical inheritance — several derived classes from one base class, which in turn become base classes themselves.

blocks.text: 4. Multilevel Inheritance

In this inheritance a derived class is created from another derived class. In the example, Class C inherits the properties and behaviour of Class B, and Class B inherits the properties and behaviour of Class A. So Class A is the parent class of B and Class B is the parent class of C — and Class C implicitly inherits the properties and behaviour of Class A along with Class B, i.e. there is a multilevel of inheritance.

blocks.caption: Multilevel inheritance — a derived class created from another derived class.
The four types of inheritance at a glance
head: Type
Shape
Description
rows: A derived class is created from a single base class.
A derived class is created from more than one base class.
More than one derived class is created from a single base class, and those children in turn become parents.
A derived class is created from another derived class.

blocks.text: 4. Encapsulation

The process that allows the selective hiding of data and functions in a class. All communication to an object is done via message. Messages define the interface to an object. Providing access to an object only through its message, while keeping the details private, is called information hiding.

Encapsulation is the wrapping up of data and associated functions in a single unit so that only essential details are exposed and the rest remain hidden. It groups all the pieces of an object into a neat package. It avoids undesired side effects of the member data when it is defined out of the class, and also protects against the intentional misuse of important data. Encapsulation ensures that only authorised functions access the relevant data, thereby guarding against unauthorised access to ensure data safety.
5. Polymorphism
Enables the same function to behave differently in different classes. Object-oriented languages try to make existing code easily modifiable without actually changing the code.

It is an important feature of OOPs. The word polymorphism is derived from the Greek/Latin roots 'poly', meaning 'many', and 'morph', meaning 'form'. Polymorphism is the concept that supports the capability of an object of a class to behave differently in response to a message or action. It is a property by which the same message can be sent to objects of several different classes, and each object can respond in a different way depending on its class. It is a major feature that allows the programmer to extend the language with new data types and operations. Polymorphism expresses how to carry out different processing steps using the same function name, and the ability of a single operator to perform more than one.

blocks.title: Classroom example
blocks.text: The + operator behaves differently with numbers (addition) and with strings (concatenation) — a single operator, many forms. Likewise a draw() method draws a circle in the Circle class and a square in the Square class.
6. Data abstraction

The process of identifying properties and methods related to a particular entity as relevant to the application. Thus it is the process of examining all the available information about an entity to identify the information that is relevant to the application.

By grouping objects into classes, we are in fact performing data abstraction of a problem. Common definitions are stored once per class rather than once per instance of the class. Methods can be written once for a class so that the objects in a class benefit from code reuse.

It is a collection of data and methods. It refers to the act of representing the essential features without including the background details or explanations. An abstract data type is a programmer-defined data type that can be manipulated like system-defined data types.

blocks.title: Switchboard
blocks.text: On a switchboard you only press certain switches according to your requirement. What is happening inside, and how it is happening, you needn't know. This is abstraction.

sections.title: Advantages and Disadvantages of using OOP

blocks.text: Advantages of OOP

items: The complexity of the software can be managed easily.
The data hiding concept helps the programmer to build secure programs.
Through the class concept, we can define the user-defined data types.
The inheritance concept can be used to eliminate the redundant code.
The message passing concept helps the programmer with communicating between different objects.
Through the inheritance concept, we can define different classes with combined features.
New data and functions can be easily coded whenever necessary.
OOP treats data as a critical element and does not allow it to flow freely around the program.
OOP ties data elements more closely to the functions that operate on them.

blocks.text: Disadvantages of OOP

items: Use of OOP is a wastage of time in the case of small projects or codes.
Object-oriented programs are much larger than other programs.
Object-oriented programs require a lot of work to create. Specifically, a great deal of planning goes into an object-oriented program well before a single piece of code is ever written.
Object-oriented programs are slower than other programs, partially because of their size. Other aspects of object-oriented programs also demand more system resources, thus slowing the program down.

blocks.text: The nine advantages and four disadvantages are a guaranteed short-answer question. The one-line pairing students remember: inheritance kills redundancy, encapsulation gives security, polymorphism gives flexibility, abstraction hides complexity.
Some of the application areas of OOP are:

items: Expert system
Artificial intelligence
Management information system
Decision support system
Computer-based training and education
Object-oriented database
Computer games
Mobile applications
Internet-based applications
Designing user interface for software
Security system
