short.q: Explain the concept of a class in Object-Oriented Programming.
short.a:
A class is the blueprint or template from which objects are made. It describes the data an object of that kind will hold — its attributes or member data — and the operations it can perform, its methods or member functions. The class itself is not an object and holds no values; it is the definition. Writing class Student { ... } creates the type; writing Student ram; creates an actual student from it.

Three ideas make the concept useful:

  • Abstraction. A class captures only the properties and behaviour that matter for the problem — a Student class keeps a roll number and marks, not a shoe size.
  • Encapsulation. The data and the functions that work on it live together in one unit, and the class decides what is visible from outside.
  • Reuse through inheritance. One class is declared once and many objects are created from it, and new classes can be built on top of it.

The relationship is the same as that between a biscuit cutter and the biscuits: the class is the cutter, the objects are what it produces, and every object made from one class has the same shape but its own filling.

short.q: What is a class, and how does it differ from an object in OOP?
short.a:
ClassObject
A template or blueprint — a logical definition. An instance of a class — a real thing that exists in memory.
Declared once: class Student { ... }; Created as many times as needed: Student ram, sita;
Occupies no memory for data when it is declared. Occupies memory for its own set of values.
Exists once in the program. Many objects can be made from one class.
Describes what the objects will have. Actually has those values.
Cannot be manipulated directly — it is only a description. Can be manipulated: its methods can be called and its state changed.
Example: the specification of a car model. Example: your particular car, with its own registration and mileage.

In short, the class is the type and the object is a variable of that type.

short.q: Describe the four main principles of Object-Oriented Programming.
short.a:
The four main principles of object-oriented programming are encapsulation, inheritance, polymorphism and abstraction — often remembered as the four pillars.

1. Encapsulation. Binding the data and the functions that operate on it into one unit (the class), and hiding the internal details from the outside world. The object is reached only through its methods, so its data cannot be put into an impossible state by accident.

2. Inheritance. A new class (the derived or child class) is created from an existing one (the base or parent class) and automatically gets its attributes and behaviour, adding or changing only what is different. It is the main mechanism for reusing code.

3. Polymorphism. "Many forms": one interface is used with different underlying types, so the same call behaves appropriately for the object it is made on. A single draw() call draws a circle as a circle and a square as a square.

4. Abstraction. Showing only what is essential and hiding the complexity behind it. The user of an object needs to know what it does, not how — you press the brake pedal without knowing how the braking system works.

Some authors add a fifth idea, modularity, and note that data hiding is the mechanism by which encapsulation is achieved.

short.q: Can you explain encapsulation and polymorphism in your own words?
short.a:
Encapsulation is the wrapping of data and the functions that work on that data into a single unit, with the internal state hidden from the outside. In my own words: an object keeps its belongings in a box and offers a small set of labelled buttons on the outside. You press the buttons; you do not reach into the box. Because the only way to change the state is through the object's own methods, those methods can check what they are given, so the object can never be put into a nonsense state — a bank account cannot be made to have a negative balance if withdraw() refuses the request.

Polymorphism means "many forms" — one name, many behaviours. The same operation is written once and each object carries out its own version of it. If Circle and Square both inherit from Shape and each defines its own area(), then a single loop can call area() on every shape in a list without ever asking what kind of shape it is holding. The call is the same; what happens depends on the object.

The two ideas support each other: encapsulation lets each class implement its own version behind a closed door, and polymorphism lets the rest of the program ignore which door it knocked on.

short.q: Illustrate how inheritance works in OOP.
short.a:
Inheritance is the mechanism by which a new class acquires the attributes and behaviour of an existing one. The existing class is the base (parent or super) class; the new one is the derived (child or sub) class. The derived class keeps everything the base class had, then adds its own members or redefines the ones it wants to behave differently. It models an is-a relationship — a Dog is an Animal.

How it works. The base class is written first with everything common to the whole family. The derived class is then declared as extending it, and it automatically contains the base class's data and methods. The derived class inherits the base class's behaviour by default, overrides a method when it needs a different version, and extends the base class by adding members that only it needs. A Student base class holding name and roll number can be extended by a GraduateStudent that adds a research topic without rewriting the name and roll number at all.

The chapter distinguishes four forms:

  • Single inheritance — one derived class from one base class.
  • Multiple inheritance — one derived class from two or more base classes.
  • Hierarchical inheritance — several derived classes from one base class, and those in turn acting as parents.
  • Multilevel inheritance — a derived class from another derived class, forming a chain.

Its value is reuse with a single point of change: fix a fault once in the base class and every derived class benefits.

short.q: Describe how encapsulation is achieved in OOP.
short.a:
Encapsulation — wrapping data and the functions that work on it into one unit and hiding the inner details — is achieved in three steps.

1. Put the data and the methods in one class. The class is the unit of encapsulation: member data holds the state, member functions operate on it, and both are declared together.

2. Restrict access. The class marks each member private, protected or public. Data is normally made private, so it cannot be read or written from outside the class at all; methods that the outside world is allowed to use are made public; and protected members are visible to the class and to classes derived from it. This is the act of data hiding.

3. Provide a controlled public interface. Because the data is private, the only way to reach it is through public methods — conventionally called getters and setters — which can validate what they are given before storing it.

In practice:

  • declare the fields private;
  • expose public methods such as getBalance() and deposit(amount);
  • let those methods reject anything invalid, so the object's state is always sensible;
  • change the internals freely afterwards, because no outside code depends on them.

That last point is the real prize: encapsulation buys the freedom to rewrite the inside of a class without breaking the programs that use it.

short.q: Summarize how polymorphism enhances flexibility in programming.
short.a:
Polymorphism means "one interface, many forms". The same call is written once and each object answers it in its own way, so the code that uses the objects does not have to know which kind of object it is holding.

That flexibility pays off in several ways:

  • Less conditional code. Without polymorphism, handling several kinds of object means a long if/switch asking "what type is this?" and calling a different function in each branch. With it, one call — shape.area() — is enough, and the right version runs by itself.
  • New types without new code. A program that draws shapes can be extended with a Triangle class, and the drawing loop is not touched: it already calls draw() on everything it is given.
  • Shorter, clearer programs. The intent is expressed once instead of being repeated for every case.
  • Genuine reuse. One piece of general code — sorting, drawing, saving — works with any object that honours the interface, including ones written years later.
  • Easier maintenance. A change to how one type behaves is made inside that class, not in every branch of a conditional spread through the program.

In short, polymorphism lets the program be written in terms of what things do rather than what things are, which is what makes it possible to extend a system without rewriting it.

short.q: Explain the concept of data-abstraction.
short.a:
Data abstraction is the principle of showing only the essential characteristics of an object and hiding the details that do not matter to the user. It answers the question "what does this thing do?" and deliberately buries "how does it do it?". Abstraction is about design — choosing which of an object's properties are relevant — whereas encapsulation is the mechanism that then hides the rest.

There are two levels:

  • Data abstraction — the data is described by its meaning rather than by how it is stored. A Stack offers push() and pop(); nobody using it needs to know whether the elements live in an array or a linked list.
  • Control (or procedural) abstraction — the sequence of steps is hidden behind a call. sort() sorts; the algorithm is not the caller's concern.

A familiar non-programming example is driving a car: the driver uses the pedal, the wheel and the gears — the abstract interface — while the workings of the engine, the brakes and the fuel injection stay hidden. In OOP, abstraction is realised with abstract classes and interfaces, which state what must be done and leave each concrete class to decide how.

Its benefits are that it reduces complexity, keeps the programmer working at the level of the problem, lets the hidden implementation be improved later, and prevents outside code from depending on details that were always meant to change.

short.q: What is OOP? List the application of OOP.
short.a:
Object-Oriented Programming (OOP) is a programming model in which a program is built as a collection of objects — self-contained units that combine data with the functions that operate on it — rather than as a list of instructions. Objects are created from classes, which act as templates, and the model rests on encapsulation, inheritance, polymorphism and abstraction.

Applications of OOP:

  • Graphical user interfaces — windows, buttons and menus are naturally objects that respond to events. This is where OOP first took hold.
  • Games and simulations — each character, vehicle or particle is an object with its own state and behaviour.
  • Computer graphics, CAD and multimedia — shapes, layers and images are objects that know how to draw themselves.
  • Business and enterprise software — customers, orders, invoices and accounts map directly onto objects, and frameworks such as .NET and Java EE are built on them.
  • Databases — object-oriented and object-relational databases store objects rather than rows.
  • Web development — server-side frameworks (Laravel, Django, Rails) and front-end code use classes for models, controllers and components.
  • Mobile apps — Android (Java/Kotlin) and iOS (Swift) are object-oriented throughout.
  • Scientific modelling and AI — agents, neural-network layers and physical entities are modelled as objects.
  • Operating systems and embedded/real-time systems — devices and tasks are represented as objects.

short.q: What are the advantages and disadvantages of OOP?
short.a:
Advantages of OOP:

  • Reuse through inheritance. A new class reuses what already exists, so code is written once rather than copied.
  • Modularity. Each class is a self-contained unit that can be written, tested and fixed on its own; a fault is traced to one class.
  • Data security through encapsulation. Private data can only be reached through the object's own methods, which validate what they are given.
  • Easier maintenance and modification. The inside of a class can be rewritten without touching the code that uses it.
  • Lower development cost. Reuse, standard libraries and clearer structure shorten the work.
  • Productivity. Working with objects is closer to how people think about a problem than working with raw data and procedures.
  • Flexibility through polymorphism. One interface serves many types, so software is extended without being rewritten.
  • Suits real problems. Most real systems are naturally described as things that interact, not as a straight sequence of steps.
  • Parallel development. Teams work on separate classes at the same time.

Disadvantages:

  • Harder to learn. Classes, inheritance and polymorphism take real effort to master; the chapter itself lists this as the main drawback.
  • Larger, slower programs. Objects carry overhead, and OOP programs tend to be bigger and to run more slowly than their procedural equivalents.
  • More thinking up front. Designing the class hierarchy well takes analysis; a bad design is expensive to undo.
  • Not suited to every problem. A short, simple task is clearer written procedurally.
  • Over-engineering. The flexibility invites unnecessary layers of inheritance and abstraction.
  • Debugging across objects. Following behaviour through a chain of inherited and overridden methods is harder than reading a straight-line program.

short.q: What is procedural oriented programming? Explain.
short.a:
Procedural (procedure-oriented) programming is the older, conventional approach in which a program is a sequence of instructions that operate on data. The problem is broken into functions or procedures, and the data is held separately and passed from one function to the next. Languages such as C, Pascal, Fortran and COBOL follow it.

Its characteristics are:

  • Emphasis on algorithms and procedures — "what steps do we follow?" rather than "what things are involved?".
  • Data is separate from the functions and is usually global or passed around, so any part of the program can change it.
  • Top-down design — the main task is divided into subtasks.
  • Sequence, selection and repetition are the only control structures.
  • Data moves freely through the system, which is convenient for small programs and dangerous for large ones.
  • Reuse is limited to calling functions again; there is no inheritance or polymorphism.

The approach is simple, efficient and well suited to small or medium problems, which is why it is still taught first and why C remains important. Its weakness is scale: as the program grows, the data is touched from too many places, so a change in one place breaks another, and the whole thing becomes hard to maintain — the problem OOP was invented to solve.

short.q: Explain the features/characteristics of OOPs.
short.a:
The characteristics (features) that distinguish object-oriented programming:
  • Class. A user-defined template that describes the data and the behaviour of the objects made from it.
  • Object. An instance of a class — the real thing, with its own values, that exists in memory. It is the basic run-time unit of the program.
  • Encapsulation. Data and the functions that work on it are bound together in one unit and the internals are hidden from outside.
  • Data hiding. The mechanism behind encapsulation: members declared private cannot be reached from outside the class, which protects them from accidental or deliberate misuse.
  • Inheritance. A new class reuses, extends and refines the attributes and behaviour of an existing one — single, multiple, hierarchical and multilevel.
  • Polymorphism. One interface with many implementations: the same call behaves according to the object it is made on.
  • Abstraction. Only the essential features are shown; the complexity stays hidden behind a simple interface.
  • Modularity. The program is a set of independent classes that can be written, compiled and tested separately.
  • Message passing. Objects do not reach into each other; they communicate by calling one another's methods.
  • Dynamic binding. Which method actually runs is decided while the program is running, which is what makes polymorphism possible.
  • Extensibility and reuse. New classes are added without changing the existing ones, and existing classes are reused through inheritance.

long.q: What is object-oriented programming? How is it different from procedural-oriented programming?
long.a:
Object-oriented programming organises a program around objects — units that combine data with the functions that operate on that data — created from classes, and built on encapsulation, inheritance, polymorphism and abstraction.

Procedure-oriented programming organises a program around procedures (functions): the problem is broken into a sequence of steps, and the data is held separately and passed from one function to the next.

PointObject-oriented programming Procedure-oriented programming
Basic unit The object — data and functions together. The function or procedure.
Emphasis On data, and on what things are. On algorithms, and on what steps to follow.
Data and functions Bound together and hidden inside the object. Separate; data moves from function to function.
Access to data Controlled — private data is reached only through the object's own methods. Unrestricted — functions and data are visible to the whole program.
Approach Bottom-up: build the objects, then assemble them. Top-down: divide the main task into subtasks.
Reuse Through inheritance — a new class reuses an old one. By calling the same function again.
Adding a new feature Add a new class; existing code is untouched. Often means rewriting functions that share the data.
Security of data Strong — encapsulation and data hiding. Weak — global data is open to everything.
Flexibility Polymorphism: one interface, many behaviours. Limited; behaviour is fixed in the function.
Suited to Large, long-lived systems that will keep changing. Small to medium problems with a clear sequence of steps.
Size and speed Larger programs, some run-time overhead. Smaller and faster.
Difficulty Harder to learn and to design well. Simpler to learn; easier to read for a short program.
Examples C++, Java, C#, Python, Smalltalk. C, Pascal, Fortran, COBOL.

The difference in one sentence. Procedural programming asks "what must the computer do, step by step?"; object-oriented programming asks "what things are involved, and what can each of them do?" — and the second question scales far better.

long.q: Explain the different characteristics of Object-Oriented Programming (OOP).
long.a:
The characteristics that define object-oriented programming:

1. Class. A user-defined template describing the data (member data) and the operations (member functions) of the objects made from it. It is a logical description and occupies no memory of its own.

2. Object. An instance of a class. Objects are the real entities that exist while the program runs; each has its own state and identity, and objects communicate by passing messages to one another — that is, by calling each other's methods.

3. Encapsulation. The binding of data and the functions that operate on it into a single unit, with the internal representation hidden. The object is a black box: what goes on inside is nobody else's business.

4. Data hiding. The mechanism that makes encapsulation real. Members declared private are invisible from outside the class, so data can be reached only through the public methods — which protects it from accidental corruption and from deliberate misuse.

5. Inheritance. The property that lets a new class reuse the attributes and behaviour of an existing one, so common code is written once. The chapter names four kinds: single (one base, one derived), multiple (several bases), hierarchical (several derived from one base, which in turn become bases) and multilevel (a chain of derived classes).

6. Polymorphism. "Many forms". One interface has several implementations, and which one runs is chosen according to the object — so one call serves many types.

7. Abstraction. Representing the essential features while hiding the complexity. The user of an object sees what it does, not how.

8. Modularity. The system is a collection of independent, self-contained classes, each of which can be written, compiled, tested and reused on its own.

9. Message passing. Objects do not read each other's data; they request action by invoking a method, which is how the parts of the system stay independent.

10. Dynamic binding. The method to run is chosen while the program is running rather than when it is compiled, which is what allows polymorphism to work.

11. Reuse and extensibility. Existing classes are reused through inheritance and new ones are added without changing what already works.

Together these give OOP its reputation for software that is easier to maintain, extend and reuse — and its reputation for being harder to learn and for producing larger programs.

long.q: Compared to procedure-oriented programming, what advantages does event-driven programming offer?
long.a:
Procedure-oriented programming decides the order of events in advance: the program is a sequence of instructions, and it runs from beginning to end along a path the programmer chose.

Event-driven programming is structured around events — things the user or the system does. The program starts, builds its interface, and then waits. When an event happens — a click, a key press, a window being resized, a timer expiring, data arriving — the corresponding handler runs. The order in which things happen is decided by the user, not by the programmer.

The advantages it offers:

  • The user is in control. People do not work in a fixed order; they click whatever they want, whenever they want. Event-driven programs allow that, where a procedure-oriented one insists on its own sequence.
  • A natural fit for graphical interfaces. Windows, buttons, menus and text boxes are inherently event-driven — an event-driven program matches how a GUI actually behaves, whereas forcing one into a procedural sequence means writing your own loop to ask "what did the user do now?".
  • Responsiveness. The program is always listening. It does not block waiting for input in a fixed place, so it can keep the display updated and react to several things at once.
  • Modularity of handlers. Each event is handled by its own small piece of code, which can be written and tested independently — the same benefit object-oriented design gives, applied to behaviour.
  • Easier to extend. Supporting a new event means adding a new handler; the existing flow is not disturbed.
  • Reuse of interface components. A button carries its own click behaviour wherever it is placed.
  • Matches real-world systems. Most real systems — booking systems, monitoring systems, servers — react to whatever arrives rather than following a script.

The trade-offs are honesty worth stating: the flow of control is harder to follow, because it is not written down in one place; programs can become hard to debug when handlers interact through shared state; and careless handlers make an interface feel unresponsive. Modern applications combine the two — an event-driven shell around procedures that do the actual work.

long.q: Explain the Class, object and encapsulation.
long.a:
Class. A class is the template or blueprint from which objects are made. It declares the data the object will hold — its member data or attributes — and the operations it can perform, its member functions or methods. The class is a logical construct: it exists once in the source code and occupies no memory for data. For example, a Student class might declare name, roll and marks as data and display() and grade() as methods. Every student object then has the same shape, with its own values.

Object. An object is an instance of a class — the real entity that exists in memory while the program runs. Where the class is the cookie cutter, the object is the cookie. Student ram; creates one student and Student sita; another; each has its own name, roll and marks, and changing one does not affect the other. An object has three things: state (the current values of its data), behaviour (what its methods do) and identity (it is distinguishable from every other object even if the values happen to match).

Encapsulation. Encapsulation is the binding of that data and those methods into one unit, together with the hiding of the internal details. The object is a sealed box with a small labelled panel on the outside. Its data is made private, so nothing outside the class can read or change it directly, and the only way in is through its public methods.

How the three fit together. The class defines what an object will be; the object is one realisation of it; and encapsulation decides what the rest of the program is allowed to see of either. A bank account makes the point plainly: the BankAccount class declares a balance and the methods deposit(), withdraw() and getBalance(); each customer's account is a separate object with its own balance; and because the balance is private, withdraw() can refuse a withdrawal larger than the balance — so the account can never be put into an impossible state. That is the whole payoff: the class gives the shape, the object holds the values, and encapsulation guarantees the values stay valid.

mcq.q: Which statement is incorrect about the object-oriented approach?
options: Emphasis is on data rather than procedure.
Data is hidden and cannot be accessed.
It supports abstract data but not the class.
mcq.teacher_note: A class IS the central abstract data type of OOP, so 'supports abstract data but not the class' is the incorrect statement.

mcq.q: Which is not a feature of OOP in general definitions?
mcq.teacher_note: The printed key is (b) Efficient code, and this chapter backs it up: §5.3 lists as a disadvantage that object-oriented programs are larger and slower than other programs and demand more system resources. Reusability (a) and modularity (c) are genuine OOP features, and duplicate/redundant data (d) is what inheritance exists to eliminate — so by the chapter's own logic, efficiency is the thing OOP does not claim.

mcq.q: Under … Inheritance, there is a derived class with only one base class.
mcq.teacher_note: One base class → single inheritance. (This question is repeated as MCQ 16 with the same answer.)

mcq.q: Which feature of OOPs derives the class from another class?
mcq.teacher_note: Inheritance is the only feature that builds one class out of another.

mcq.q: Child class is derived from base class in …
mcq.teacher_note: Base class = parent; derived/child class = what inheritance produces.

mcq.q: Which concept allows you to reuse the written code in OOPs?
mcq.teacher_note: Inheritance is the reuse mechanism; the class is the container that makes reuse possible.

mcq.q: In OOPs, public, private and protected are?
mcq.teacher_note: These three keywords set the visibility of members — they are access modifiers (access specifiers).

mcq.q: Which of the following concepts in object-oriented programming refers to binding data and function into a single unit?
mcq.teacher_note: Wrapping data + functions into one unit = encapsulation. Abstraction is showing only the essential features.

mcq.q: OOP stands for …
mcq.teacher_note: Object-Oriented Programming.

mcq.q: … is a concept or thing with defined boundaries that is relevant to the problem we are dealing with.
mcq.teacher_note: This is the book's own definition of an object (§5.2.1, feature 1).

mcq.q: … is a collection or group of similar objects that have the same properties, common behavior, and relationships.
mcq.teacher_note: The book's own definition of a class (§5.2.1, feature 2).

mcq.q: … is a property that allows the reuse of an existing class to build a new class.
mcq.teacher_note: The book's own definition of inheritance (§5.2.1, feature 3).

mcq.q: … is the process that allows selective hiding of data and functions in a class.
mcq.teacher_note: The book's own definition of encapsulation (§5.2.1, feature 4).

mcq.q: … enables the same function to behave differently on different classes.
mcq.teacher_note: The book's own definition of polymorphism (§5.2.1, feature 5).

mcq.q: … is the process of identifying properties and methods related to a particular entity as relevant to the application.
mcq.teacher_note: The book's own definition of data abstraction (§5.2.1, feature 6).

mcq.q: Under … Inheritance, there is a derived class with only one base class.
mcq.teacher_note: Printed twice in the book (MCQ 3 and MCQ 16); the answer is single both times.

mcq.q: In … paradigm, programs are written as a collection of classes and objects.
mcq.teacher_note: Classes and objects are the vocabulary of the object-oriented paradigm only.

mcq.q: … is a programming paradigm based upon the concept of procedure calls, in which statements are structured into procedures (also known as subroutines or functions).
mcq.teacher_note: Procedures/subroutines/functions = the procedural paradigm.

mcq.q: Which OOP feature allows a class to inherit properties and behavior from another class?
mcq.teacher_note: Inheritance again — it is the only feature that transfers properties between classes.

mcq.q: In an Object-Oriented Language, a single unit that encapsulates both data and function is termed as …
mcq.teacher_note: The object is the single unit that holds both; the class is the template it is made from.

key_terms.meaning: An approach to solving problems with a programming language — the strategy a language follows. The three main kinds are procedural, structural and object-oriented.
A paradigm built on procedure calls, where statements are structured into procedures (subroutines or functions). Examples: Fortran, C, COBOL.
A paradigm that improves clarity and quality through structured control flow — selection, repetition, block structures and subroutines — instead of go-to jumps.
A paradigm in which a program is a collection of classes and objects and all computation is performed on objects; emphasis is on data rather than procedure.
A programming model that uses objects to design applications and programs, drawing on modularity, polymorphism, inheritance and encapsulation.
A concept or thing with defined boundaries relevant to the problem; a particular instance of a class that stores data and its associated functions.
A collection or group of similar objects that share the same properties, behaviour and relationships; the template from which objects are created.
A single object created from a class. Objects are referred to as instances of their class.
The data contained inside an object.
A function belonging to an object; it has access to the data stored in that object and is the only way to reach that data.
Wrapping data and the functions that operate on it into a single unit, so that only essential details are exposed and the rest stay hidden.
Keeping an object's data private so that it can be reached only through its member functions, protecting it from accidental or intentional misuse.
The property that lets a new class (derived class) reuse the attributes and behaviour of an existing class (base class) with little or no modification.
The pre-existing class whose attributes and behaviour are inherited.
The new class formed by inheriting from a base class.
One derived class created from a single base class.
One derived class created from two or more base classes.
Several derived classes created from one base class, with those children in turn acting as parents.
A derived class created from another derived class, forming a chain of inheritance.
The ability of the same function or operator to behave differently in different classes — from 'poly' (many) and 'morph' (form).
Representing the essential features of an entity while hiding the background details; identifying only the properties and methods relevant to the application.
A programmer-defined data type that can be manipulated like a system-defined data type.
The way objects communicate in OOP — by calling one another's member functions.
The OOP style of development: build and test the small objects first, then combine them into the whole program.
The structured-programming style: solve the high-level logic first, then break it into smaller functions.
Providing access to an object only through its messages while keeping the internal details private.
The OOP benefit that a class written once can be reused by other objects and by other programmers.
A keyword — public, private or protected — that sets the visibility of a class member.
A program whose flow is decided by events such as clicks and key presses; in this chapter it is used as a synonym for an OOP program.
A language in which a program is a collection of instructions executed sequentially, organised into functions. Examples: C, FORTRAN, COBOL.

quick_revision.title: Paradigms
points: A paradigm is the strategy a programming language follows to solve problems.
Procedural — statements structured into procedures (subroutines/functions): Fortran, C, COBOL.
Structural — selection, repetition, blocks and subroutines instead of go-to: Algol 60, PL/I, Pascal, C.
Object-oriented — a program is a collection of classes and objects; emphasis on data, not procedure: C++, Java, C#, Ruby.

quick_revision.title: The six features of OOP
points: Object — a thing with defined boundaries; a particular instance of a class.
Class — a group of similar objects sharing properties, behaviour and relationships.
Inheritance — reusing an existing class to build a new one (single, multiple, hierarchical, multilevel).
Encapsulation — data + functions wrapped in one unit, with the details hidden.
Polymorphism — the same function behaving differently in different classes.
Data abstraction — showing only the essential features, hiding the background.

quick_revision.title: Object vs class
points: A class is the template; an object is one instance of it.
A class is written once; many objects can be made from it.
Data inside an object is reached only through member functions — that is data hiding.
Objects talk to each other by message passing: calling one another's member functions.

quick_revision.title: Advantages and disadvantages
points: Advantages: complexity managed, secure programs via data hiding, user-defined types via classes, redundant code removed via inheritance, message passing, easy to add data/functions.
Disadvantages: wasteful for small projects, programs are larger, heavy planning is needed up front, slower and more resource-hungry.

quick_revision.title: OOP vs structured programming
points: OOP is bottom-up; structured programming is top-down.
OOP's main ideas are class and object; structured programming's main idea is the function.
OOP hides data; structured programming has no hiding mechanism (globals are open to all).
OOP: C++, Java, VB.Net, C#. Structured: C, FORTRAN, COBOL.

quick_revision.title: Applications of OOP
points: Expert systems and artificial intelligence.
Management information systems and decision support systems.
Object-oriented databases.
Computer games, mobile applications and internet-based applications.
Designing user interfaces and security systems, plus computer-based training and education.

teaching_plan.activity: Open with the question 'what is a paradigm?' and take the three paradigms straight from the book. Note openly that the book prints nearly the same paragraph for procedural and structural, then give students the one-line distinction. Move to the concept of OOP: data + function in one unit, member function, encapsulation and data hiding. Draw the OOP paradigm figure on the board and walk through the nine main concepts.
Object and class. Use the class figure to show one template and many instances, then relate it to reusability and abstract data types. Drill the pair: class = template, object = instance.
Teach inheritance from the base/derived class idea and the animal-and-vehicle examples. Then draw all four types in sequence, using each figure, and close with the at-a-glance comparison table.

Encapsulation (wrapping up + information hiding), polymorphism (the + operator on numbers vs strings, draw() in Circle vs Square) and data abstraction (the switchboard example). Contrast encapsulation with abstraction explicitly — students mix them up.

Nine advantages and four disadvantages, the eleven application areas, then the twelve-point OOP vs structured programming table as board revision. Finish with Exercise 5: solve the 12 short and 4 long questions orally or in pairs, then run the 20-question MCQ self-test.
