learning_objectives: State the concept of a software project, software development process, and SDLC.
Compare between system analyst and software engineer.
State the concept of system design.
Show the relation between software and quality.
Explain the software development model.

blocks.text: A program is a sequence of instructions. An instruction is a command given to the computer to perform a certain specified operation on given data. A set of programs written for a computer to perform a particular task is called software — or the logical components, or set of procedures, routines or instructions, are called software. It is a group of commands that tells the computer what to do and how to do it.
A well-defined task, which is a collection of several operations done in order to achieve a goal (for example, software development and delivery).

The complete procedure of software development from preliminary study or survey (also called requirement gathering), followed by feasibility study, investigation and fact recording for properly carrying out the system study — which is again followed by system analysis of the proposed system, system design, system testing, system implementation and system maintenance — carried out according to the execution methodologies, in a specified period of time, to achieve the intended software product.

Software is an intangible product and its development is a new field in this world. Most software products are tailor-made to fit a client's requirements. As current technology advances so frequently and rapidly, the application of a particular product may not be applicable to another one. Due to such various constraints there is a risk in software development; hence it is essential to manage software projects efficiently.
The triple constraints

The triple constraints for software projects show the essentiality for a software organisation to deliver a quality product, keeping the cost within the client's budget range and within the given time.

items: Budget / cost
Time
Scope

blocks.title: Remember
blocks.text: These three constraints are tied to each other — change one and the other two move. This is the single most quoted idea in software project management.

Defines a sequence of tasks that must be carried out to build new software. It groups the development activities into a sequence of phases. A phase in sequence can only commence once the previous phase has been completed. A report is produced at the end of each phase, describing what has been achieved and outlining the plan for the next phase.

Once a problem or opportunity for new software is recognised, a request for developing a new one is forwarded for approval. If approved, a study is conducted to ensure that the proposed system is feasible. When it is feasible, the system requirements are specified, followed by a phase of system design, development, conversion, testing, debugging, implementation, system maintenance, and finally reviews for new software.

Recycling of development activities may occur in the software if it still requires modification or redevelopment. It is also important to take precautions to ensure that all user requirements are satisfied at the completion of the software. This means that it is necessary to include a quality assurance mechanism in the software development process. Quality assurance is a process to ensure the development of quality products; this mechanism includes validation and verification.

An organised way to develop a software/system. System Development Phase, or System Development Life Cycle, or Software Development Life Cycle (SDLC) is a methodology used to develop, maintain and replace software/information systems.

It is a systematic process of developing any software. It helps in establishing a system, or software, or project, or plan. It gives an overall list of processes and sub-processes required for developing a system. SDLC starts when management or development personnel feel that new software, or an improvement in the existing software, is required.
Importance and the Necessity of SDLC

SDLC should result in high-quality software that meets customer expectations, reaches completion within time and cost estimates, works effectively and efficiently in the current and planned Information and Communication Technology (ICT) infrastructure, and is cost-effective to enhance and maintain.

items: It helps to determine the needs of the user.
It supports constant communication between the developer and the user.
SDLC helps for easy identification of missing requirements.
It ensures that the software meets the needs of its users.
It supports proper analysis and design of the software.
It ensures proper development and testing.
Proper documentation support for future upgrades and maintenance.
It provides flexibility for adding features even after the software is developed.

blocks.text: SDLC Phases

items: System Study or Preliminary Investigation and Feasibility Study.
System Analysis or Determination of System Requirements.
System Design.
System Development or Development of Software.
System Testing.
System Implementation.
System Maintenance and Reviews or Evaluation.

blocks.caption: Figure: Stages of system development life cycle.

blocks.text: This is the first step of SDLC. This phase is also called the Preliminary Investigation or Need Analysis Phase. This phase is basically concerned with determining whether or not the new software/system should be developed. During this phase the development team focuses on completing three tasks:

items: Survey the system by collecting the inputs from various sources.
Analyse the current system (manual or automated) in depth and develop possible solutions to the problem.
Select the best solution and define its function with a feasibility study.

blocks.text: This phase begins when the need is identified for a new or modified software/system. During this phase the system analyst thoroughly studies the organisation's current procedures and the software used to perform organisational tasks. In system study, the first challenge is to define the problem accurately. With the problem accurately defined, the organisation can decide whether to undertake the software or not. When the decision is made to proceed, the system analyst investigates the current software and its limitations.

At the end of this phase the team of system analysts concludes which new software is to be adopted. Then the detailed plans and schedules are drafted for making the new system, through a feasibility study.
Feasibility Study

The determination of whether or not a software/system or project is worth doing. The process followed in making this determination is called a feasibility study. So, a feasibility study is to determine whether the whole process of system analysis leading to computerisation would be worthwhile for the organisation or not.

It is a post-phase of system study. A feasibility study is conducted once the system goal is set. The feasibility study is basically the test of the proposed system in its workability, meeting user's requirements, effective use of resources, and cost-effectiveness. The main goal of the feasibility study is not to solve the problem but to achieve the possibility of the system. In the process of the feasibility study, the cost/benefits analysis is estimated with greater accuracy.
Need of Feasibility Study

items: It determines whether the system meets the goal of the clients or not.
It determines the strengths and limitations before starting to develop the system.
It focuses on the boundary of the system's outline.
It suggests new opportunities through the investigation process.
It enhances the probability of success by addressing and justifying the factors that can affect the system prior to development.
It provides quality information for decision-making.
It helps to increase investment in the system.
It provides documentation of the investigated system.
It allows new technologies and development areas for faster processing, more storage, and lower costs than ever before.
It helps in obtaining funds from financial institutions and other sources.

blocks.text: Types of Feasibility Study

An important outcome of the system study or preliminary investigation is the determination of whether the system requested is feasible or not. That requires the need for a precise feasibility study. In conducting it, the system analyst will usually consider eight distinct but interrelated types of feasibility.
1. Technical Feasibility

The system analyst identifies the existing computer systems (hardware and software) of the concerned department and determines whether these technical resources are sufficient for the proposed system. If they are not sufficient, the analyst suggests the configuration of the computer systems that are required. The system analyst generally pursues two or three different configurations which satisfy the main technical requirements but which represent different costs. During technical feasibility, financial resources and budget are also considered.

items: It determines whether the technology needed for a system is available or not.
It determines how the technology can be well used within the system.
It identifies the correct personnel and the correct equipment for the system, including hardware and software systems.

blocks.title: Note
blocks.text: Out of all types of feasibility, technical feasibility is generally the most difficult to determine.
2. Economical Feasibility

Economical feasibility is the most important study: it determines the cost and benefits of the proposed system and compares them with the budget. The cost of the system should not outweigh the budget. The cost of the system includes the cost of hardware, software, development and implementation. To ensure that the new system will certainly lead to benefits, a cost-benefit analysis is carried out.

items: It concerns the return of investments in the system/project.
It determines whether the system or project is affordable or not.
It identifies the financial benefits and cost-benefit analysis associated with that system.
It determines whether the system's goals can be achieved within the allocated fund.

blocks.text: 3. Operational Feasibility

When the system is both economically and technically feasible, the next step is to determine whether it is operationally feasible. During the operational feasibility study it is determined whether the system will operate in the way that the user wants. Operational feasibility depends upon human resources for the development and implementation of the system. It is considered whether qualified and experienced manpower is available. User involvement is more required in determining the operational feasibility. This study is carried out by a small group of people who are familiar with information system techniques, who understand the parts of the business relevant to the system, and who are skilled in system analysis and design processes.

items: It determines the general skills, training and capabilities of the existing personnel.
It concerns the organisational structures, the business problems and their solutions.
It identifies how the system will fit in the current operations.

It is mainly related to human, organisational and political aspects. Generally the project will not be rejected simply because of operational infeasibility, but such considerations are likely to critically affect the nature and scope of the eventual recommendations.

blocks.title: Note
blocks.text: Feasibility studies like technical, economic and operational are the most important. In addition, feasibility studies like social, management, legal and contractual, time (schedule) and behavioural can also be performed to evaluate the proposed system effectively.
4. Social Feasibility

Social feasibility is a determination of whether a proposed system will be acceptable to the people or not. This determination typically examines the probability of the system being accepted by the group directly affected by the proposed system change. It determines the impact of the system on the employees. The result of the study is a report recommending whether to proceed with other phases or not. If the answer is yes, then project planning is done, which establishes the high-level plan, schedule, or system/project goals.

blocks.title: Worked example
blocks.text: Suppose the system will result in the loss of 1200 jobs — or alternatively would create 1200 posts that could not be filled. Either of these two extremes is undesirable and would result in a recommendation to prevent the project from the beginning. Social feasibility covers more than just human issues: there could be a cost to the environment, a cost to society, a cost to company culture. It is essential to consider the social cost of a proposed system or project.
5. Management Feasibility

It is a determination of whether a proposed system will be acceptable to management or not. If management does not accept a system or project and gives negligible support to it, the system analyst will tend to view the system or project as a non-feasible one.
6. Legal and Contractual Feasibility

Legal feasibility is a determination of whether a proposed system infringes on known Acts, Statutes, as well as any pending legislation. Although in some instances the system or project might appear sound, on closer investigation it may be found to infringe on several legal areas.

items: It concerns the legal and contractual outcome of the system in an organisation.
Legal effects like taxation, copyright, patent, trademarks and labour laws are considered.
Contractual effects like software and hardware ownership and the licence agreement are considered.

blocks.text: 7. Time (Schedule) Feasibility
Time feasibility is a determination of whether a proposed system can be implemented fully within a stipulated time frame or not. If a project takes too much time it is likely to be rejected.

items: It concerns the time constraints for the system accomplishment.
It concerns system or project deadlines and the time frame for system completion.

blocks.text: 8. Behavioral Feasibility
Behavioral feasibility includes a study of organisational behavior.

items: It concerns the behavioral approach of the management staff and workers within the system in the organisation.
It concerns fear of loss of job and lost identity, displacement of the manpower, and fear of technology.

blocks.caption: The eight types of feasibility at a glance
head: Type
The question it answers
rows: Do we have the hardware, software and people to build it?
Do the benefits outweigh the cost, and is it within budget?
Will it work the way the users want it to?
Will the people affected accept it?
Does it break any Act, licence or contract?
Can it be finished in the stipulated time?
How will people react to it — fear of job loss, fear of technology?

blocks.text: The eight feasibility types are a guaranteed 8-mark question. The mnemonic to write on the board: Technical, Economical, Operational, Social, Management, Legal, Time, Behavioral — and always add that the first three are the most important.

System analysis is an important activity that takes place when the new information system is being changed. It follows the feasibility study and involves a detailed study of the current system, leading to specifications of a new system. It is a central part of the whole of system development. System analysis is a detailed study of various operations performed by a system and their relationships within and outside the system. During system analysis, data are collected from the various available sources by using tools such as interviews, on-site observation, questionnaires, sampling, research and documentation.
Using the following steps, it becomes easy to draw the exact boundary of the new system under consideration:

items: Keeping in view the problems and new requirements.
Find out the pros and cons including new areas of the system.

blocks.text: All procedures and requirements must be analysed and documented. System analysis includes sub-dividing the complex process involving the entire system, identification of data store, and manual processes. Finally, system analysis determines the shape, form, strength, capability, and even the life of the system.

This phase is the most creative and challenging phase of SDLC. This phase is concerned with the design of the final system. The design of an information system produces the details that clearly describe how a system will meet the requirements identified during system analysis. System specialists often refer to this stage as logical design, in contrast to the process of developing program software, which is referred to as a physical design.

During this phase the designer must design all the aspects of the system, from the input and output screen to reports, databases and processes of computing. The designer must provide the physical specifics of the system designed, either as a model or as detailed documentation, to guide those who will develop the new system.

Many system design tools are available to help teams through the steps of system design. Some of them are algorithm, flowchart, pseudo code, context diagram, DFD (Data Flow Diagram), decision table, decision tree, E-R (Entity-Relationship) diagram, prototyping, and CASE (Computer-Aided Software Engineering) tool. Designers are responsible for providing programmers with complete and clearly outlined software specifications.

sections.title: System Development or Development of Software

blocks.text: During the development phase the developers play a key role, creating or customising the system. After designing the new system, the defined procedures are transformed into the physical system. In this phase technical writers also work with the developers to develop the technical documents for the system. The technical documentation includes information about system features, the flow of the system, the design, and the layout of the necessary components. The major goal of this phase is to translate the problem studied in the system analysis and design phase into the proper physical system. At the end of this phase the system is ready for testing.

The programmer is also responsible for documenting the program, providing an explanation of how and why a certain procedure is coded in specific ways. Documentation is essential to test the program and carry on maintenance once the application has been installed.

Testing is an integral part of phases 4 (System Development) and 6 (System Implementation). After developing all the components of the system, a test plan should be developed and all the testing must be done according to that schedule. A test schedule may contain the following steps:

items: Test unit specification.
Features to be tested.
Approach used for testing.
Test deliverables.
Schedule.
Personnel allocation.

blocks.text: According to the test plan, every component of the system must be thoroughly checked. Errors are corrected so that there is no difference between the actual output and the desired output. This phase is the costliest, most time-consuming and most complex. It is the process of verifying that the system fulfils the objective of development. Using the test data, the following testing process is carried out:
1. Unit testing

It is the process of testing the individual component of the system after the component is developed but before the components are combined together to form a complete system. Since the program is one of the important components of the system, it needs to be tested. When the programs have been coded, compiled and brought to working conditions, they must be individually tested with the prepared test data. Any undesirable happening must be noted and debugged (error corrections). This testing process is performed by the developer.
2. Integration testing

Integration is the process of combining all the individual components together to form a complete system. Integration testing is the process of testing the individual components of the system after all the individual components are combined together. This testing process is also performed by the developer.

This process is important as it helps to identify and remove any errors which arise during the integration process, as well as those which are not visible during unit testing. An individual component of a system operating without any error may not operate as before after it is integrated with other components of the system. Integration testing can help to identify and rectify those errors.
3. System test

It is the process of testing the complete system after all the components of the system are combined together. After carrying out the unit test of each component of the system, an integration test is performed, and then the system test is done. At this stage the test is performed on the complete system using actual data. At each stage of the execution, the results or output of the system are analysed. If the expected output is not obtained, the errors in the particular components are identified, fixed, and further tested for the expected output. This testing process is performed by the developer too.

blocks.caption: Black box testing vs white box testing
head: Black box test (functional test)
White box test (glass box test)
rows: The internal code of the program is tested.
The structure of the program is tested.
Called black-box testing because the test cases are totally hidden from the general users.
Called white-box testing because the test cases are totally visible to the general users and they can also make test cases.

blocks.text: 4. User acceptance testing

It is the process of testing the complete system by the user to identify whether the newly developed system meets the user's requirement or not. This testing process is performed by the targeted user for whom the system is developed, before the system is implemented. Users use actual data to evaluate the system which they will be using in the day-to-day operation of the system.

blocks.caption: The four testing processes at a glance
head: Testing
Who performs it
What is tested
rows: One component, on its own, before integration.
The components after they have been combined.
The complete system, using actual data.
The complete system, against the user's requirements, before implementation.

blocks.text: The way of carrying out a developed system into working condition. It involves testing, debugging, loading or distributing the developed software to user sites, and training user personnel. Implementation activities include initial user support such as the finalisation of documentation, training programs, and ongoing user assistance.

It is not always a simple process — even the major well-designed systems can fail if the implementation is not well managed. It is the stage of a system or project during which theory is turned into practice. The users move from the older system to the new system to perform work. The process of moving from the old system to the new system is called System Conversion. System developers must handle this process carefully to avoid losing or corrupting data while the system is in operation. There are four ways of system conversion:

items: Direct conversion: all users must stop the old system and immediately the new system comes into existence. This option is fast, but it can put disruptive pressure on support, and users may take time to adopt this system.

Parallel conversion: all users continue to use the old system as well as the new system, making a comparative analysis between the two systems. The output and the performance of both systems are verified after entering the inputs. If the users are satisfied then they switch over to the new system.
Phased conversion: all users start using the new system component by component. This option works only for systems that have subsystems.

Pilot conversion: the system is first used by a small unit of the organisation; they test it and, once satisfied, that component comes into operation. Again, the same process is repeated for another component of the system. This process is continuously performed till the whole system is implemented. Since each component of the system is tested, satisfied and implemented, this approach takes more time than the direct, parallel and phased conversions. This is the best and most reliable conversion of the system, because each component is checked before the system is operated fully.

blocks.caption: The four conversion strategies
head: Strategy
How it works
Risk / cost
rows: Old system stops, new system starts immediately.
Both systems run together and their outputs are compared.
The new system is introduced component by component.
Only works for systems with subsystems.
One small unit tries it first, then it spreads component by component.
Slowest, but the best and most reliable.

sections.title: System Maintenance, Reviews and the System Analyst

blocks.text: System Maintenance

The correcting and upgrading process of the system. Maintenance is necessary to eliminate errors in the working system during its working life and to tune the system to any variations in its working environment.

Proper testing and documentation should significantly reduce the frequency and extent of the required maintenance. System maintenance involves training sessions, documentation of the system, and support after the sale. When a system is operating in an organisation, users sometimes encounter problems and often think of ways to perform its functions correctly. In this phase the system developer makes the required changes according to the specification. These changes are necessary to keep the system running and useful.

It has been seen that there are always some errors found in the system that must be noted and corrected. It also means the review of the system from time to time. If a major change to a system is needed, a new project may have to be set up to carry out the change — and the new system or project will proceed through all the above life cycle phases. The amount of time and effort devoted to maintenance depends on the performance of the previous phases of the life cycle. The importance of maintenance is to continue to bring the new system to standards — and the success of a newly developed system lies on it, to a large extent.

blocks.title: Maintenance is classified as
items: Corrective maintenance: repairing processing or performance failures, or making alterations because of previously ill-defined problems.
Adaptive maintenance: changing the program functions as and when a need arises, to correct a problem or upgrade the performance of the system.
Perfective maintenance: enhancing the performance or modifying the program to make it even more perfect.

blocks.text: The greatest amount of maintenance work is for user enhancement and improved documentation of the system for better efficiency. Maintenance covers a wide range of activities including correcting coding and design errors, updating documentation and test data, and upgrading user support. Many activities classified as maintenance actually fall under enhancements. Maintenance means restoring something to its original position. Unlike hardware, software does not wear out; it is corrected. Maintenance is expensive. One way to reduce maintenance costs is through maintenance management and software modification audits — maintenance management should be of due importance, as it affects the system to a large extent and any negligence may lead to disastrous results.
System Review

The last phase of the system development or implementation process is the system review. This is usually carried out by a group consisting of a representative from the client departments, internal audit, the system analyst and data processing. Its basic purpose is to see whether the system has met the objectives set for it or not. It is the final phase of SDLC.
System Analyst
A computer specialist person who is involved in analysing, designing, implementing and evaluating computer-based information systems to support the decision-making and operations of an organisation.
Role and Responsibilities / Duties of the System Analyst

The system analyst is involved in conducting system study and analysing the system. S/he studies the existing system by conducting interviews with the users, and may also employ other methods such as observation of system activities and going through the documents of the organisation. The system analyst should have high communication skills and writing ability. The roles are:

items: Defining requirement: understanding user's requirements by interviewing users, finding out what information is being used in a current system, how it is used, and what their expectations are towards the proposed system.

Prioritising requirement by consensus: each user in the organisation has some special information needs, and it may not be possible to satisfy the needs of everyone because of the lack of computing capabilities and availability of programmers. Thus there is a need to set priorities among the requirements of various users. This responsibility requires good interpersonal relations — s/he must be able to convince all the users about the soundness of group discussion and obtain their cooperation.

Gathering data, facts and opinions of users: having determined the information needs and their priority, the system analyst must develop the system with the active and willing cooperation of all the users.

Analysis and evaluation: the system analyst analyses the working of the current information system in the organisation, then sifts through the facts and opinions gathered and finds the best characteristics of a new or modified system.

Solving problems: a system analyst must study the problem in depth and suggest an alternate solution to the management. The relative difficulties in implementing each of the alternatives and the benefits of each must be considered, so that a manager can pick what analysts consider the best solution.

Drawing up specification: a key job of a system analyst is to obtain the functional specification of the system to be designed in a form which can be understood by users. The specification must be non-technical so that users and managers can understand it; it must be precise and detailed so that it can be used by the system implementer; and it must also take account of expansion into the near future.

Designing system: once the specification is accepted, the system analyst designs the system. The design must be understandable to the system implementers and it must be modular to accommodate changes easily.

Evaluating system: a system analyst must evaluate a system after it has been in use for a reasonable period of time. The time at which evaluation is to be done, how it is to be done, and whose comments are to be gathered and used must be decided by the system analyst.

blocks.text: Desirable Characteristics / Qualities / Attributes of a System Analyst

A system analyst is a person responsible for the analysis, design and implementation of a system on the computer. The development of a computer information system is a difficult task, which requires a significant amount of time, people and money. The people involved can be broadly classified into technical and non-technical. System analysts should be good at problem solving; s/he has to know about business operations and have a strong background in a relevant area of the computer system. In order to be a successful system analyst, s/he must possess the following characteristics:

items: Knowledge of organisation: a system analyst must understand the way in which various functions of an organisation work; the management structure and the relationship among the departments; its day-to-day operations for which the system is being developed; and the policy and principles of the organisation.

Technical knowledge: a system analyst should be well trained in relevant areas of computer science, thoroughly familiar with the capabilities and limitations of hardware and software products, and must know enough programming ideas and techniques to be able to design a system which can be implemented.

Interpersonal communication skill: effective communication is vital to the success of any system. The system analyst is the medium through which communication should flow smoothly. S/he must be able to talk intelligently with high-level management, technical staff, non-technical users, programmers and operators, and is required to influence people to change their minds and attitudes and to motivate them to work in a group.

Character and ethics: the nature of the job requires a strong character and sense of ethics. Ethics is the personal character quality in which an individual understands the difference between “right” and “wrong” and acts accordingly. In short, a successful system analyst must be professional — resourceful, inventive and creative.

Problem-solving skill: systems are developed to solve problems, so system analysts must have wide experience in solving them. The objective is achieved by defining the problem, analysing the problem, considering many alternatives, evaluating many alternatives, and choosing the best alternative.

System analysis and design skills: the system analyst needs thorough and ongoing training in system analysis and design. These skills can be conveniently factored into three subsets — concepts or principles, tools, and techniques.

blocks.text: The eight duties and six qualities of a system analyst are asked together as a long-answer question. Tell students to write the eight duties as a numbered list and the six qualities as a second numbered list — the examiner marks the lists, not the prose.
System analysts and software engineers are both concerned about the development of software/systems. However, their core roles are different.

blocks.caption: System analyst vs software engineer
head: System Analyst
Software Engineer
rows: System analysts are responsible for determining how a business computer system is serving the needs of the company, and what can be done to make those systems and procedures more effective.
Software engineering is concerned about designing and developing engineering-specified software of the highest quality.
A system analyst explores and documents requirements.
A software engineer designs software to meet requirements.
A system analyst is more responsible for documenting the progress of a project for quality control and relaying information about the end users' preferences to the engineer or programmer.
A software engineer's responsibilities lie with developing and programming the software. In some cases the terms software engineer and programmer or developer are interchangeable.
System analysts need to work with a big amount of data — scrape it, visualise it, or make software to work with it.
Software engineers work on building new software (desktop, web or cloud, mobile, etc.) or adding new features to already existing software.
A systems analyst does more problem research and plans solutions, and makes software and system recommendations to solve these problems.

A software engineer develops their product to show the result. They need to understand software architecture, the OS core, memory handling and the computing environment, and build the gaps within any software system's limitations — even how the user interface interacts.
A person working as a system analyst is more experienced and hence more paid than a software engineer.
A person working as a software engineer is less experienced and hence less paid than a system analyst.

blocks.text: Collection of requirements is one of the core functions of system analysis. System analysts must collect information about the current system and how users would like to improve their performance with the new information system. Understanding the user's requirement better will help the system developing team deliver a proper system to the end users in limited time and budget. During system analysis, data are collected from the various available sources by using different methods; some of them are:

items: Interview: interviews of stakeholders and users are critical to developing great software. Without understanding the goals and expectations of the users and stakeholders, we are very unlikely to satisfy them. We also have to recognise the perspective of each interviewee, so that we can properly weigh and address their inputs.

Survey / Questionnaire: when collecting information from many people — too many to interview within budget and time constraints — a survey or questionnaire can be used. The survey can force users to select from choices, rate something, or have open-ended questions allowing free-form responses.

On-site Observation: by observing users and the work process, an analyst can identify a process flow, steps, pain points and opportunities for improvement. Observations can be passive or active (asking questions while observing). Passive observation is better for getting feedback on a prototype (to refine requirements), whereas active observation is more effective at getting an understanding of an existing business process. Either approach can be used.
Brainstorming: used in requirement gathering to get as many ideas as possible from a group of people. Generally used to identify possible solutions to problems and clarify details of opportunities.
Document Analysis: reviewing the documentation of an existing system can help when creating requirement documents, as well as driving gap analysis for scoping migration projects.

Focus Group: a focus group is a gathering of people who are representative of the users or customers of a product, to get feedback. The feedback can be gathered about needs, opportunities and problems to identify requirements, or can be gathered to validate and refine already elicited requirements.

Prototyping: a relatively modern technique for gathering requirements. In this approach you gather preliminary requirements that you use to build an initial version of the solution — a prototype. You show this to the client, who then gives you additional requirements.
Requirement Workshops: workshops can be very effective for gathering requirements. More structured than a brainstorming session, involved parties collaborate to document requirements.

blocks.text: The system design tool is used by system analysts for representing and facilitating comprehension of complex processes and procedures. Some of these tools are: algorithm, flowchart, pseudo code, context diagram, Data Flow Diagram (DFD), decision table, decision tree, E-R (Entity-Relationship) diagram, prototyping and CASE tool.
Algorithm

The finite set of step-by-step instructions that solve a particular program. It is used to explain the working process of the program using simple stepwise English and mathematical statements. Once the problem is clearly stated, it is broken down into a number of steps, which are written as a sequential procedure to solve a problem — to process input to achieve the desired output.

blocks.title: Where the word comes from
blocks.text: The word algorithm arrives from the name of the Persian mathematician Abu Jafar Mohammad ibn Musa al-Khwarizmi (845 A.D.).
An algorithm is a finite set of instructions that are followed to accomplish a particular task. In addition, all algorithms must satisfy the following criteria:

items: Input: it can receive either one or more inputs.
Output: it produces at least one output.
Definiteness: each instruction must be clear and unambiguous.
Finiteness: the algorithm must terminate after a finite number of steps.
Effectiveness: each step must be basic, so that it is simple, easier to understand and implement.

blocks.text: The algorithm should have the following properties:

items: It should have an input with a START statement.
The steps mentioned in an algorithm should be executable by the computer.
Each and every instruction should be in simple English language and mathematical statements.
The number of steps should be finite.
It should not depend on a particular computer language or computer.
The algorithm should give an output after executing the finite number of steps, and it must END or STOP.

blocks.text:
/* Example 1: multiply two numbers (a, b) and show their product */
Step 1: START.
Step 2: Input numbers; a and b.
Step 3: Multiply a and b and store in c (i.e., c = a*b).
Step 4: Display or Print the value of c.
Step 5: STOP.

/* Example 2: input a number and decide whether it is even or odd */
Step 1: START.
Step 2: Input a number n.
Step 3: Calculate n mod 2 and store in x (i.e., x = n mod 2).
Step 4: if x equals 0, then display the number n is even.
Step 5: if x does not equal 0, i.e. 1, then display the number is odd.
Step 6: END.

/* Example 3: calculate the sum of natural numbers up to 100 */
Step 1: START.
Step 2: Set i = 1 and sum = 0.
Step 3: Calculate sum = sum + i.
Step 4: Calculate i = i + 1.
Step 5: Repeat steps 3 and 4 till i <= 100.
Step 6: Print sum.
Step 7: STOP.
Flowchart
A diagrammatic representation that illustrates the sequence of operations to be performed to arrive at the solution or algorithm.
There are mainly two types of flowcharts: (1) program flowchart and (2) system flowchart.
1. Program Flowchart

A program flowchart is a pictorial representation of the steps involved in solving a particular procedure or program. It is another system design tool used to check the flow of logic running in a program. It also shows the logical sequence in which the steps are performed. It is a detailed diagram showing how individual processing steps will be performed within the computer to convert input data into the desired result.

blocks.caption: Symbols of a program flowchart with their function and meaning
head: S.No.
Symbol
Function
Meaning
rows: Oval indicates START and STOP of a program.
Parallelogram indicates an Input or Output operation of a program.
Rectangle indicates the processing of data, or the editing or calculating of data.
Diamond is used to specify a condition. It is used to check logical conditions. It has one entry and two exit points, which are true and false.
Circle indicates a data flow from one page of the flowchart to another page.
Arrows indicate all the directions of data flow which have to be followed for solving a problem.
An unclosed rectangle with broken lines can be used to include any comments for better documentation, clarity, and in the case of explanatory notes.

blocks.caption: Figure: Different examples of flowchart — the product of two numbers, and the largest of three numbers.
More flowchart examples — printing a name ten times, the sum and average of the first 20 natural numbers, the Fibonacci series up to 10 terms, and the sum of even numbers from 1 to 60.
Two more flowchart examples — the factorial of a number n, and the multiplication table of an entered number.

blocks.text: 2. System Flowchart

A system flowchart plays a vital role in system analysis. It graphically illustrates the elements and characteristics of a system and expresses its structure and relationships in terms of flowchart symbols. A system flowchart is a diagram that shows a broad overview of the data flow and sequence of operations in a system.

blocks.caption: Figure: Symbols of system flowchart with their functions.
Figure: A system flowchart for a payroll processing system.
Differences between system flowchart and program flowchart
head: S.N.
System Flowchart
Program Flowchart
rows: It gives a broad overview of the overall system.
It gives a specific view of the control flow of a program.
It shows the data flow of a system.
It shows the instruction flow of a program.
It has many categories like E-R diagram, DFD, context diagram, etc.
System flowchart is designed by the system designer.
Program flowchart is designed by the programmer.
Since there exist different kinds of symbols, one must have good knowledge to understand the system flowchart.
Since there are limited symbols, it is easy to understand even for normal people.

blocks.text: Pseudo Code

It is a tool used to formulate the processing steps of a program. A pseudo-code uses English phrases to describe the processing steps of a program or module. The logical control instructions within a structured design are emphasised in a pseudo-code. Even an algorithm is commonly written using pseudo-code.

The term pseudo refers to 'artificial' and code usually refers to a computer program or something written in a programming language. So it is a language similar to a real programming language. An important feature of pseudo-code is that it is not forced to follow the strict rules imposed by the programming language. The only requirement is that the pseudo-code is clear and unmistakable in sequence or statement, like in any major high-level language.

/* Example 1: determine whether the entered number n is positive or negative */
Input a number (n)
if n > 0
   then n is positive
else if n < 0
   then n is negative
else
   n is neither positive nor negative

/* Example 2: display all the natural numbers from 1 to 100 */
i = 1
repeat
{
   display i
   i = i + 1
} until i <= 100
Context Diagram
A zero-level Data Flow Diagram (DFD) which expresses the scope of an organisational system, its system boundaries, the external entities that interact with the system, and the information flow.

The context diagram doesn't have a data store. The symbol represents the entire information system, and we express it as process 0. Then we place the external entities around the perimeter of the page and use data flows to connect the entities to the central process. Data stores in a context diagram are not shown, because data stores are internal to the system.

blocks.caption: Figure: Context diagram of a Library Membership System.

blocks.text: Data Flow Diagram (DFD)

The most commonly used way of documenting the process of the current and required system. A DFD is a pictorial representation showing the flow of data into, around, and out of a system. The graphical representation of a system's data and how the processes transform the data is known as a Data Flow Diagram.

Unlike flowcharts, a DFD does not give detailed descriptions of modules, but graphically describes the system's data and how the data interact with the system. A DFD uses four basic symbols that represent a process, a data flow, a data store and an external entity. Several different versions of DFD symbols exist, but they all serve the same purpose.

blocks.caption: Figure: Symbol set of DFD with each symbol's name and function.

blocks.text: A Data Flow Diagram shows how data moves through an information system but does not show program logic or process steps. It also shows the relationships between the data and external entities such as students and schools outside the system.

blocks.caption: Figure: DFD of a Library Membership System.

blocks.title: The four elements of a DFD
items: External entities: they represent the source of data as input to the system. These are represented by rectangles.

Data-store: data stores represent stores of data within the system — for example computer files or databases. An open-ended box (unclosed rectangle) represents a data store, i.e. data at rest or a temporary repository of data.
Process: a process transforms the input data into output data. Circles stand for a process that converts data into information.

Data flow: labeled arrows represent the movement of data from one component to the other. A labeled arrow identifies data flow, i.e. data in motion. Labeled arrows are generally shown as one-way direction signs only.

blocks.text: E-R (Entity Relationship) Diagram

The E-R model, or E-R diagram, grew out of the exercise of using commercially available DBMS, which were based on hierarchical and network approaches. E-R is a generalisation of these models. Although it has some means of describing the physical database, it is basically used in the design of a logical database model. This analysis is then used to organise data as a relation, normalising relations and finally obtaining a relational database model.

The E-R model is based on a perception of a real world that consists of a collection of basic objects, called entities, and relationships among these objects. An E-R diagram is a graphical representation of different entities and their relationships — it is a graphical representation of the database. The overall logical structure of a database can be expressed graphically by an E-R diagram, which is built up from the following components:

items: Rectangle: it represents the entity and contains the objects used in a relational database.
Oval or ellipse: it represents the attributes of entities. Attributes specify the properties of entities.
Diamond: it represents the relationship among entities. It connects entities and represents meaningful dependencies between them.
Line: it is used to link attributes to entity sets and entity sets to the relationship, and vice versa.

blocks.title: Note
blocks.text: Details of the E-R diagram are provided in Unit 1 (Database Management System).
Decision Table

A table that allows an analyst to identify the exact course of actions for given conditions. It provides clear-cut decisions, leading to a good program design. A decision table generally consists of two parts: (a) condition and (b) action.

A decision table is a precise model of logic. Like if-then-else and switch-case statements, a decision table associates conditions with actions to perform. But unlike the control structures found in traditional programming languages, the decision table can associate many independent conditions with several actions in an elegant way.

blocks.title: The discount policy example
blocks.text: Suppose Asmita Publication decides to set up a Book Consumer Club (BCC). Members of the BCC are entitled to special discounts on the purchase of books. The discount policy is: members of BCC are always entitled to a discount of 12% on all their purchases; however, if any purchase exceeds Rs. 12000, the member is entitled to a discount of 18%; non-members aren't normally given any discount, but if their purchase exceeds Rs. 12000, a discount of 6% is given.

blocks.text: Decision Tree

A decision tree is another way of presenting a potentially confusing situation in a clear, concise and unmistakable manner; it can be used in decision making or analysis. It helps a system analyst to study the relationship between conditions and actions. It looks like a tree with branches.
This decision tree does not work for complex system analysis, but a simple decision tree can be easily understood by non-technical users.

blocks.text: A field of study and practice that describes the desirable attributes of software products.
There are two main approaches to software quality: defect management and quality attributes.
Defect Management

A software defect can be regarded as any failure to address end-user requirements. Common defects include missed or misunderstood requirements and errors in design, functional logic, data relationships, process timing, validity checking, and coding errors. The software defect management approach is based on counting and managing defects. Defects are commonly categorised by severity, and the numbers in each category are used for planning. More mature software development organisations use tools such as defect leakage matrices (for counting the number of defects that pass through development phases prior to detection) and control charts, to measure and improve development process capability.
Quality Attributes

This approach to software quality is best exemplified by fixed quality models, such as ISO/IEC 25010:2011. This standard describes a hierarchy of eight quality characteristics, each composed of sub-characteristics:

items: Functional suitability
Reliability
Operability
Performance efficiency
Security
Compatibility
Maintainability
Transferability

blocks.text: The software can be considered good software if it contains the following qualities:

items: The software should be correct — it should not contain errors.
It should be easy to understand.
It should be easy to maintain and update.
It should be reliable.
It should be flexible — able to operate with a wide range of possibilities.
It should have an easier user interface.
It should be portable.
It should be efficient in terms of processing and memory utilisation.

blocks.text: The Software Development Life Cycle (SDLC) is a systematic process of developing any software system; it is a part of software engineering. The Institute of Electrical and Electronic Engineers (IEEE) defines it as “the period that starts when the product is conceived and ends when the software is no longer available for use”.

The computer system is complex and often links multiple traditional systems potentially supplied by different software vendors. To manage this level of complexity, a number of SDLC models have been developed — “waterfall”, “spiral” and “prototyping”.

blocks.caption: Figure: Different types of SDLC model.

blocks.text: Each system or project must select an SDLC process that makes the most sense for that system or project, on the basis of corporate culture, willingness to take risks, application area, volatility of requirements, and the extent to which the requirements are well understood. There are different models developed by different developers, and each of them uses different techniques and steps. Some of the SDLC models are:

items: Waterfall Model
Prototype Model
Spiral Model
Agile Development Approach

blocks.text: 6.8.1 Waterfall Model

The waterfall model is a popular version of the SDLC model for software engineering. It is often considered the classic approach to the SDLC. It describes a development method that is linear and sequential. The waterfall model has distinct goals for each phase of development.

blocks.title: The waterfall image
blocks.text: Imagine a waterfall on the cliff of a steep mountain. Once the water has flowed over the edge of the cliff and has begun its journey down the side of the mountain, it cannot turn back. It is the same with waterfall development: once a phase of development is completed, the development proceeds to the next phase and there is no turning back.
It starts with identifying the problem and ends up, in a downhill structure, with a working and fully implemented system. The waterfall model is considered the “parent” of the whole SDLC model.

blocks.caption: Figure: The waterfall model.

blocks.text: The waterfall model is seen as flowing steadily downwards through the phases of initial investigation, requirement analysis, software design, development, test and deploy, and post-deployment review. Thus the waterfall model maintains that one should move to a phase only when its preceding phase is completed and perfected. Phases of development in the waterfall model are thus discrete, and there is no jumping back and forth or overlap between them.

This model is the parent of the incremental model and is not used nowadays. When the feedback and learning loop is incorporated into this model and the project is broken down into discrete phases that build on one another, we get the incremental model.
Advantages of Waterfall Model

items: It allows for departmentalisation and managerial control.
A schedule can be set with deadlines for each stage of development and a product can proceed through the development process.
Development moves from concept, through design, implementation, testing, installation, troubleshooting, and ends up with operation and maintenance.
Each phase of development proceeds in strict order, without any overlapping or iterative steps.

blocks.text: Disadvantages of Waterfall Model

items: It does not allow for much reflection or revision.
Once an application is in the testing stage, it is very difficult to go back and change something that was not well thought out in the concept stage.

blocks.text: 6.8.2 Prototyping Model

Prototyping is the construction of the 'model' of a system. It is a working model or a reference model to show the functionality of the system to the users. In the process of prototyping, a small prototype (model) is designed so that the user can experience the system and figure out the faults and problems in it. The system analyst looks upon the feedback of the user and improves the model of the system until the user is satisfied. Thus this process is iterative in nature.

Prototyping is an attractive idea for complicated and large systems for which there is no manual process or existing system that can support determining requirements. This might be needed for novel systems where it is not clear that the constraints can be met to implement the requirements.

blocks.caption: Figure: Prototyping model.

blocks.text: The basic idea is that instead of freezing the requirements before a design or coding can proceed, a throwaway prototype is built to understand the requirements. This prototype is developed based on the currently known requirements. Quick Design and Building Prototype undergo design, coding and testing — but each of these phases is not done very formally or thoroughly. By using this prototype, the customer can get an “actual feel” of the system, since the interactions with the prototype enable the Customer evaluation to better understand the requirements of the desired system using the Refining block. If any changes take place in the prototype system, then enter it again in the Quick Design; otherwise enter in the Engineering Product.

blocks.title: On cost
blocks.text: This prototyping is twice as expensive as other models. However, some argue that prototyping need not be very costly and can actually reduce the overall development cost. The prototype is usually not a complete system — the goal is to provide a system with overall functionality. The cost of testing and writing detailed documents is reduced, and the experience of developing the prototype is very useful when developing the final system.
Advantages of Prototyping Model

items: It provides a better system to users, as users have a natural tendency to change their mind in specifying requirements, and this method supports that tendency.
In this methodology a working model of the system is provided, so the users get a better understanding of the system being developed.
Errors can be detected much earlier, as the system is made side by side.
Quicker user feedback is available, leading to better solutions.

blocks.text: Disadvantages of Prototyping Model

items: It leads to an implementing-and-repairing way of building systems.
Practically, this methodology may increase the complexity of the system, as the scope of the system may expand beyond the original plans.

blocks.text: 6.8.3 Agile Development Approach

The ability to create and respond to change. The agile software development model was mainly intended for helping developers build a project which can adapt to transforming requests quickly. The most important endeavour of the agile method is to make easy and rapid project achievements, by eliminating activities which may not be crucial for that specific project.
Four core values of agile software development

items: Individual and team interactions over processes and tools
Working software over comprehensive documentation
Customer collaboration over contract negotiation
Responding to change over following a plan

blocks.text: Five stages in the agile development approach

items: Exploration — explore the environment in which the problem can and should be approached with agile development, and assemble the team
Planning
Iteration to the first release
Productionizing
Maintenance

blocks.text: 6.8.4 Spiral Model

The spiral model, also known as the spiral lifecycle model, is a system development life cycle (SDLC) model used in information technology (IT). This is a software development process combining the features of the prototyping model and the waterfall model. The spiral model is a recent model, favoured for large, expensive and complicated systems or projects. As the name suggests, the activities in this model can be organised like a spiral that has many cycles. The structure of the spiral development model consists of four quadrants:

items: Quadrant 1 — Analysis: determine objectives, alternatives and constraints.
Quadrant 2 — Evaluation: evaluate alternatives, identify and resolve risks.
Quadrant 3 — Development: develop and verify the next-level product.
Quadrant 4 — Planning: plan the next phases.

blocks.caption: Figure: Spiral model — the four quadrants.

blocks.text: Each cycle in the spiral begins with the identification of objectives for that cycle, the different alternatives that are possible for achieving the objectives, and the imposed constraints — in the first quadrant. The next step is system evaluation as the second quadrant; system development and system planning are the third and fourth quadrants; and then analysis of the system again in sequence if new requirements are identified or the system requires modification and next-phase planning.

The second quadrant evaluates the different alternatives based on the objectives and constraints, and also involves identifying the uncertainties and risks involved. The third quadrant develops strategies that resolve the uncertainties and risks — this step may involve activities such as benchmarking, simulation and prototyping. Next, the software is developed keeping in mind the risk associated. Finally, the next stage is planned. An important feature of this model is that each cycle of the spiral is completed by a review, which covers all the products developed during that cycle, including plans for the next cycle. The spiral model works for developed as well as enhancement systems or projects.
Advantages of Spiral Model

items: Its estimates (i.e. budget, schedule) get more realistic as work progresses, because important issues are discovered earlier.
It is more able to cope with the changes that software development generally entails.
Software engineers (who can get restless with protracted design processes) can get their hands in and start working on a system or project earlier.

blocks.text: Disadvantages of Spiral Model

items: It is highly customised, limiting re-usability.
It is applied differently for each application.
It has a risk of not being completed within the allocated budget or time.

blocks.text: The process of collecting, organising, storing and maintaining a complete record of the system and other documents used or prepared during the different phases of the life cycle of the system.

The system cannot be considered complete until it is properly documented. In fact, documentation is an ongoing process, which starts in the definition phase of the system and continues until its implementation and operation phase. Moreover, documentation is a process which never ends throughout the life of the system — it has to be carried out from time to time as and when the system is modified during its maintenance phase.
Proper documentation of the system is necessary for the following reasons:

items: It solves the problem of the indispensability of an individual. Even if the person who designed or developed the system leaves the organisation, the documented knowledge remains with the organisation, which can be used for the continuity of that software.

It makes the system easier to modify and maintain in the future. The key to maintenance is proper and dynamic documentation; it is easier to understand the concept of a system from the documented records. A system flowchart, a program flowchart, or comments within the system prove to be very helpful in this regard.

It helps in restarting a system development which was postponed. The job need not be started from scratch, and the old ideas may still be easily recapitulated from the available documents, which avoids duplication of work and saves a lot of time and effort.

blocks.text: The three commonly used forms of documentation are the system manual, the program manual and the user manual.
System Manual

A good system must be supported with a standard system manual. It contains all the detailed technical details of the system, which can be mainly used for upgrading and maintenance of the system. It contains the following information:

items: A statement of the problem, clearly defining the objectives of developing the system and its usefulness to various categories of users.
A description of the system, specifying the scope of the problem, the environment in which it functions, its limitations, its input requirement, and the form and type of output required.
The specific tools required, along with their description and purpose.
A detailed diagram of the system flowchart and the program flowchart.
A source listing of all the full details of any modifications made since its development.
The specification of all input and output media required for the operation of the system.
The structure and description of test data and test results, and the storage dumps used to debug the system.

blocks.text: Program Manual

The program manual contains the details about the program used in the system. It contains program analysis, its design including algorithm, flowchart, DFD and input/output screens. It is prepared with a view to providing technical details about the program to the technical persons, which can be used in the future to upgrade or maintain the software. It contains the following information:

items: Problem definition and the objective of developing the program.
Program analysis reports of the program.
Program design reports including algorithm, flowchart, DFD, E-R diagram, input/output screens.
Output and test results of the program.
Upgrade or maintenance history, if any modification of the program is made.

blocks.text: User Manual

A good system must be supported with a good user manual to ensure the smooth running of the system. This document is prepared with the view of providing the way of operating the system to the user. It contains the following information:

items: Set up and operational details of each system.
Loading and unloading procedures.
Problems which could arise, their meaning, reply and operational action.
Special checks (if any) and security measures.

blocks.text: It is very important that the work of the programmer in producing a finished program is fully documented. The documentation will include a statement of the problem, pseudo-code, algorithms, flowcharts, source codes, test data and results. Producing these documents should be done as part of each stage in programming — if this is done, the documentation will aid the maintenance of the program during its lifetime.
