short.q: Highlight the importance of the first two stages of SDLC.
short.a:
The SDLC begins with system study (preliminary investigation) and feasibility study, and these two decide whether the project should exist at all.

System study. The first contact with the problem. The analyst finds out what the users actually need, what the present system does, where it fails, and what a new system would have to achieve. It sets the scope and states the objectives, so nobody later disagrees about what was being built.

Feasibility study. The test of whether the proposal is worth doing — technically possible, affordable, workable by the people who will use it, and acceptable to the organisation. It answers "should we go ahead?" with evidence.

Why they matter most:

  • They are cheap, and everything after them is not. Abandoning an unworkable idea during the study costs a few days; abandoning it after implementation can cost more than the system was worth.
  • Most failures are requirement failures. Building the wrong system perfectly is the most common way a project fails, and both stages exist to prevent it.
  • They fix the budget and the schedule. Cost, time and scope are agreed here, and the triple constraints of the project are set by them.
  • They define what "finished" means. Without agreed objectives there is nothing to test the result against.
  • They decide the shape of everything else. Analysis, design, testing and implementation all start from what these two stages establish.

short.q: What are system analysis and design? Describe briefly.
short.a:
System analysis is the detailed study of what the present system does and what the new one must do. The analyst gathers requirements — by interviewing users, sending questionnaires, observing the work, and reading existing documents and forms — and then studies the operations, their relationships and the data that flows between them. The output is a specification of what the new system must achieve; no decision is made about how it will be built.

System design is deciding how it will be built. It turns the specification into a blueprint: the logical design describes how the system will meet the requirements — data structures, database design, inputs, outputs, processes and the modules — and the physical design develops the actual program software, files, screens and reports from it.

In short, analysis defines the problem and design defines the solution. Analysis comes first, and skipping it is the classic cause of a system that works perfectly and is of no use to anybody.

short.q: What is a feasibility study? Why is it important in the system analysis phase? Explain.
short.a:
A feasibility study is the test of a proposed system for workability: whether it can be built with the technology available, whether it meets the users' requirements, whether it uses resources effectively, and whether the benefits justify the cost. It is carried out during the system analysis phase, right after the preliminary investigation, and it produces a report recommending whether to proceed.

Why it is important at that point:

  • It is the go/no-go decision. The study is the first point at which the organisation commits real money, and it exists to stop the project if the answer is no.
  • It catches impossible requirements early. A requirement the technology cannot meet, or that costs more than it returns, is far cheaper to drop on paper than after design has started.
  • It sets the budget and the schedule. The cost-benefit analysis done here is what the rest of the project is measured against.
  • It compares the alternatives. Usually there is more than one way to meet the need, and the study chooses between them on evidence rather than enthusiasm.
  • It protects against the triple constraints failing. Cost, time and scope are checked against each other before any of them is committed.
  • It brings the users in early. Operational feasibility asks whether the people who will use the system can and will, which is where many projects quietly fail.

short.q: What do you mean by feasibility study? Why is it necessary before designing a system?
short.a:
A feasibility study is a systematic investigation of a proposed system to decide whether it is worth building. It tests the proposal for workability — can it be done? — for meeting the users' requirements, for the effective use of resources, and for cost-effectiveness. The four levels usually examined are technical, economic, operational and social feasibility.

Why it is necessary before designing a system:

  • Design is expensive; the study is not. Once design begins, the project consumes money, time and people. The study is the last cheap chance to say no.
  • It stops the wrong system being built. Design answers "how"; if "what" and "whether" were never settled, design simply builds the wrong thing efficiently.
  • Design needs a defined problem. A designer cannot choose between alternatives without knowing the constraints, and those constraints come out of the study.
  • It prevents a redesign later. Discovering in the design phase that the technology does not exist, or that the cost cannot be met, means going back to the beginning.
  • It gives the decision-makers evidence. Management commits funds on the strength of the feasibility report.
  • It surfaces the risks. Technical difficulty, staff resistance and schedule pressure are identified while there is still time to plan around them.

The rule of thumb is that the later a fault is found, the more it costs to correct — so the study is the cheapest insurance a project can buy.

short.q: Explain different stages of the system development life cycle with a clear figure.
short.a:
The System Development Life Cycle (SDLC) is the organised sequence of phases through which a system is planned, built, used and eventually replaced. The stages, in order:

1. System study (preliminary investigation / need analysis). Identify the problem, find out what the users need, define the scope and the objectives, and decide whether a new system is warranted at all.

2. Feasibility study. Test the proposal for technical, economic, operational and social feasibility and produce a report recommending whether to proceed.

3. System analysis. Study the present system in detail, gather the requirements, and produce the specification of what the new system must do.

4. System design. Produce the blueprint — logical design (how the system will meet the requirements: database, inputs, outputs, processes) and physical design (the programs, files, screens and reports).

5. System development (coding). Write the programs, build the database, create the files, and unit-test each component.

6. System testing. Test the components together and then the system as a whole against the requirements, using test data and, ideally, real users.

7. System implementation. Install the system, convert the data, train the users, and cut over — directly, in parallel, or in phases.

8. System maintenance. Keep it running: correct faults, adapt it to changes in the environment or the law, and improve it. Periodic reviews decide whether to enhance or eventually replace it.

Diagram (description). Drawn as a cycle running clockwise: Preliminary investigation → Feasibility study → System analysis → System design → Development → Testing → Implementation → Maintenance, with an arrow from Maintenance back to Preliminary investigation — because maintaining a system eventually raises the need for a new one, and the life cycle begins again.

short.q: What is system testing? Explain different types of testing techniques during the system development.
short.a:
System testing is the phase in which the completed system is executed with real and deliberately awkward data to find the difference between what it does and what it was specified to do. Its purpose is not to prove the software works but to find where it does not, before the users do.

The testing techniques used during system development:

  • Unit testing. Each component — a function, a module, a class — is tested on its own before it is combined with anything else. It finds faults at the smallest, cheapest level.
  • Integration testing. The components are combined and tested together, to find the faults that only appear at the joins: wrong parameters, mismatched data formats, bad interfaces.
  • System testing. The complete system is tested as a whole against the requirements, checking that the inputs, processes, outputs, performance and security are all correct.
  • Acceptance testing. The users test the system with their own data and their own scenarios, and either accept it or send it back. This is the test that decides whether the system goes live.
  • Alpha and beta testing. Alpha testing is done in-house by the developers' own organisation; beta testing is done by a selected group of real users in their own environment.
  • Regression testing. After a change or a fix, the previously passing tests are re-run to make sure nothing else was broken.
  • Black-box testing. Testing from the specification, looking only at inputs and outputs — the internal code is not considered.
  • White-box testing. Testing from the code: every branch, loop and statement is exercised.
  • Top-down and bottom-up testing. Testing from the top levels of the design downwards, or from the lowest modules upwards.
  • Performance, stress, security and usability testing — checking the system under load, under attack, and in the hands of real people.

short.q: What is the documentation? Explain the importance of documentation in program designing.
short.a:
Documentation is the written record that describes a system: what it does, how it is built, how it is operated and how it is maintained. It includes the user manual, the technical or system documentation (design, data dictionary, program specifications), the operating instructions, and the record of every change made.

Why it matters in program designing:

  • It records the design decisions. A design that exists only in the programmer's head is lost the day they leave, and the system becomes unmaintainable.
  • It makes maintenance possible. Maintenance is the longest and most expensive phase of the life cycle, and whoever does it needs to know how the system works.
  • It is the reference for the requirements. Testing and acceptance are checked against the specification, so the specification has to be written down.
  • It helps the users. A user manual is what turns a working system into a usable one, and it cuts the training and support burden.
  • It supports communication. Analysts, designers, programmers, users and management all work from the same written description instead of from memory.
  • It is needed for audit and control. Organisations must be able to show what their systems do and how the data is handled.
  • It eases change. With current documentation, a change can be planned against the design; without it, every change is a guess.
  • It protects the investment. The documentation, not the code, is what lets the system outlive the people who built it.

long.q: Describe the role of system analysts in each step of the software development process.
long.a:
A system analyst studies an organisation's needs, works out what a system must do, and sees it through to a working reality — acting as the bridge between the users, who know the problem, and the programmers, who know the technology. Their role in each step of the software development process:

1. System study / preliminary investigation. Meet the users, recognise that a problem exists, find out what the present system does and where it fails, and define the scope and objectives of a new one. The analyst produces the initial request and decides whether the matter is worth pursuing.

2. Feasibility study. Examine the proposal for technical, economic, operational and social feasibility, carry out the cost-benefit analysis, compare the alternatives, and write the report that recommends whether to proceed.

3. System analysis. Gather the requirements in detail — interviews, questionnaires, observation, documents — study the operations and their relationships, and write the specification of what the new system must do. This is the analyst's central task.

4. System design. Turn the specification into a blueprint: work with the designers on the logical design (data structures, database, inputs, outputs, processes) and confirm that it meets the requirements, then review the physical design.

5. Development (coding). Stay available to the programmers to explain the requirements, clarify ambiguities, check that what is being built still matches the specification, and control changes.

6. Testing. Plan the tests from the requirements, prepare the test data, take part in system testing, and organise the users' acceptance testing.

7. Implementation. Plan the cut-over, arrange the data conversion, run the training, and support the users through the first days of live running.

8. Maintenance and review. Monitor how the system performs in use, collect the users' complaints and requests, judge which changes are worth making, and take part in the periodic review that decides whether to enhance or replace the system.

Throughout all of it the analyst is the translator and the referee: translating between what the users want and what the system does, and refereeing between what is wanted, what is affordable and what is possible.

long.q: Who is a system analyst? Highlight the characteristics of a good analyst.
long.a:
A system analyst is the person who studies an organisation's information needs, determines what a system must do, and guides it from the first idea to a working installation. They are the link between the users, who understand the business but not the technology, and the programmers, who understand the technology but not the business — so they must be comfortable on both sides.

Characteristics of a good analyst

  • Good communication. They must be able to interview a user who cannot express the problem technically, and then explain the result to a programmer who does not know the business. Listening is the larger half of this.
  • Analytical and problem-solving ability. They have to break a messy situation into its parts, see the real problem behind the symptoms, and reason about alternatives.
  • Knowledge of the business. Understanding how the organisation actually works — not how the manual says it works — is what makes a specification realistic.
  • Technical knowledge. Enough understanding of hardware, software, databases and networks to know what is feasible and to talk to the designers as an equal.
  • Interpersonal skills and patience. Users are often busy, defensive about the present system, or afraid of the new one; the analyst has to work with all of that.
  • Open-mindedness and impartiality. They must look for the best solution rather than the one they happen to like, and be willing to report that a favourite project is not worth doing.
  • Attention to detail. A requirement missed in the specification becomes a fault in the system.
  • Organisation and discipline. They manage many sources of information, keep the documentation current, and keep the project to its scope.
  • Ability to work under pressure. Deadlines, competing users and changing requirements are normal.
  • Integrity and confidentiality. The analyst sees how the organisation really runs, including its payroll, its problems and its plans.
  • Willingness to keep learning. Technology and the business both move, and a method learned five years ago may no longer apply.

long.q: What is a feasibility study? Explain the different types/levels of the feasibility study.
long.a:
A feasibility study is the test of a proposed system to decide whether it is worth building. It examines whether the system can be built with the technology available, whether it meets the users' requirements, whether it uses resources effectively, and whether the benefits justify the cost — and it ends with a report recommending whether to proceed.

The types, or levels, of feasibility study:

1. Technical feasibility. Can it be built? Are the hardware, the software, the network and the technical skills actually available, and can the necessary volumes and response times be met? It also asks whether the technology is mature enough and whether it can be integrated with what exists. This is usually the most difficult type to judge, because it requires estimating what has never been done before.

2. Economic feasibility. Is it worth the money? The costs — development, hardware, software, training, running — are weighed against the benefits, both those that can be counted (fewer staff, less stock) and those that cannot (better decisions, faster service). This is carried out as a cost-benefit analysis and is generally considered the most important of the four.

3. Operational feasibility. Will it work in practice, and will the people use it? It examines whether the system will operate in the way the users want, whether the organisation has the human resources to run it, whether management will support it, and how it will change the way people work.

4. Social feasibility. Will it be accepted? It examines the effect of the system on the people affected by it, on the culture of the organisation, and on society — including questions such as whether it will cost jobs, whether it is fair, and whether it respects privacy.

Some texts add legal feasibility (does it comply with the law and with data-protection rules?), schedule feasibility (can it be delivered in time to be useful?) and behavioural feasibility (how people will actually react to it). A sound study examines all of them, because a system can be technically brilliant, affordable and on time, and still fail because the people who have to use it will not have it.

long.q: Define feasibility study. Why is a feasibility study important in the system development process? Explain.
long.a:
A feasibility study is a systematic investigation carried out early in the system development life cycle to decide whether a proposed system is worth building. It tests the proposal for workability, for meeting the users' requirements, for the effective use of resources and for cost-effectiveness, and it produces a report that recommends whether to proceed, modify or abandon the idea.

Why it matters in the system development process:

  • It is the go/no-go decision. It is the point at which the organisation decides whether to commit real money, and its whole purpose is to make that decision on evidence.
  • Faults cost more the later they are found. An idea abandoned during the study costs a few days; the same idea abandoned after implementation can cost more than the system was worth. The study is the cheapest insurance available.
  • It prevents the wrong system being built well. The most common way a project fails is not technical — it is that the system did not do what was needed. The study is where the requirements are checked against reality.
  • It sets the triple constraints. Budget, time and scope are fixed here, and everything afterwards is measured against them.
  • It compares the alternatives. There is almost always more than one way to meet a need; the study chooses between them rather than letting the first idea win by default.
  • It identifies the risks. Technical difficulty, cost overruns, staff resistance and schedule pressure are all surfaced while there is still time to plan around them.
  • It brings the users in at the start. Operational feasibility asks whether the people will use it — and a system nobody uses has no benefit at all.
  • It gives management the evidence to commit funds. A request backed by a cost-benefit analysis is a decision; one backed by enthusiasm is a gamble.
  • It defines the problem before design begins. Design answers "how"; the study settles "what" and "whether", without which design has nothing to aim at.

long.q: State the steps involved in the system development cycle in chronological order.
long.a:
The steps of the system development life cycle, in chronological order:

1. System study — preliminary investigation or need analysis. Recognise the problem, study the present system, find out what the users need, and define the scope and the objectives of the proposed system.

2. Feasibility study. Test the proposal for technical, economic, operational and social feasibility, carry out the cost-benefit analysis, and report whether the project should go ahead.

3. System analysis. Gather the requirements in detail and study the operations and their relationships, producing the specification of what the new system must do.

4. System design. Decide how it will be done: the logical design (data structures, database, inputs, outputs, processes), then the physical design (programs, files, screens, reports).

5. System development — coding. Write the programs, build the database and the files, and test each component as it is finished.

6. System testing. Combine the components, test the complete system against the requirements with test data, and have the users carry out acceptance testing.

7. System implementation. Install the system, convert the data, train the users, and cut over — directly, in parallel or in phases.

8. System maintenance. Keep the system running: correct faults, adapt it to changes in the environment, and improve it.

9. Review. Periodically review the system to decide whether it should be enhanced, re-engineered or replaced — at which point the cycle begins again, which is why it is called a life cycle.

Each phase produces a report or a document before the next begins, and the gate between phases is what stops a project carrying a mistake forward.

long.q: Why is documentation essential in developing a system? Explain its types in detail.
long.a:
Why documentation is essential. Documentation is the written record of a system — what it does, how it is built, how it is operated and how it is maintained. Without it a system is a black box that only its author understands, and the moment that person leaves, the system is unmaintainable.

  • Maintenance depends on it. Maintenance is the longest and most expensive phase of the life cycle; the person doing it needs to know the design, not guess it.
  • It records the design decisions and the reasons for them. Knowing why something was done a particular way is often more valuable than knowing what.
  • It is the contract with the users. Testing and acceptance are checked against the written requirements, so the requirements must be written.
  • It lets people change. Staff come and go; documentation is what keeps the knowledge in the organisation.
  • It supports training and cuts support costs. A user manual answers the question before it is asked.
  • It is needed for control and audit. An organisation must be able to show what its systems do and how data is handled.
  • It protects the investment. The documentation is what lets a system outlive the people who built it.

Types of documentation

1. User documentation. Written for the people who use the system: the user manual, the operating instructions, the on-screen help, the error messages and their meanings, and a tutorial. Non-technical, task-oriented.

2. System (technical) documentation. Written for the people who build and maintain it: the requirements specification, the feasibility report, the data-flow diagrams, the E-R diagrams, the data dictionary, the program specifications, the source-code comments, the test plan and the test results. This is the record of the design itself.

3. Operations documentation. Written for the people who run it: how to start and stop the system, the backup and recovery procedures, the batch schedules, and what to do when something fails.

4. Maintenance documentation. The change log, the record of problems and how they were fixed, and the history of every release — so the next maintainer can see what has already been tried.

Documentation must be written as the system is built rather than afterwards. Documentation written at the end is always out of date before it is finished, and documenting a system nobody has time to read is as useless as not documenting it at all.

long.q: Explain the Waterfall Model, Prototyping and Spiral Model.
long.a:
A software development model (process model) describes how the phases of the life cycle are arranged and how one leads to the next. Three of the best-known are the waterfall, prototyping and spiral models.

1. The Waterfall model

The oldest and simplest model. Each phase — requirements, design, implementation, testing, deployment, maintenance — is completed and signed off before the next begins, and the progress flows steadily downwards like a waterfall.

Advantages: simple to understand and to manage; each phase has a defined start, a defined end and a defined deliverable, so progress is easy to measure; and it forces discipline — requirements and design are settled before coding starts.

Disadvantages: it assumes the requirements can be stated completely and correctly at the beginning, which is rarely true; there is no working software until late in the project; going back a phase is difficult and expensive; and it suits only projects where the requirements really are stable and well understood.

2. The Prototyping model

Instead of specifying everything first, a working prototype — a partial, quickly built version — is put in front of the users early. They try it, say what is wrong with it, and it is refined; the cycle repeats until the prototype is accepted, and only then is the final system built properly (or, in evolutionary prototyping, the prototype is grown into it).

Advantages: the users see something real instead of reading a specification, so requirements are discovered rather than guessed; misunderstandings surface immediately; the result fits what people actually want; and the risk of building the wrong system falls sharply.

Disadvantages: the users may mistake the prototype for the finished system and expect it to be delivered; the constant changes can make the design messy; it is harder to estimate cost and time; and there is a temptation to keep refining for ever.

3. The Spiral model

Proposed by Barry Boehm, the spiral combines the discipline of the waterfall with the iteration of prototyping and adds explicit risk analysis. Development proceeds in a series of loops; each loop passes through four quadrants — determine the objectives and alternatives, identify and resolve the risks, develop and test the next version, and plan the following loop. Each turn of the spiral produces a more complete version of the system.

Advantages: risk is examined at every turn instead of being discovered late; change is expected and accommodated; the users see progress regularly; and it suits large, expensive, high-risk projects.

Disadvantages: it is complex to manage, needs people who can actually do risk analysis, and the number of loops is not known in advance — so cost and time are hard to estimate. It is not worth the overhead for a small project.

In short: the waterfall is the simplest and suits a well-understood problem; prototyping is the way to discover requirements that nobody can state; and the spiral is the answer when the risk of getting it wrong is high.

mcq.q: The … determines whether the project should go forward.
mcq.teacher_note: A feasibility assessment decides go / no-go. Opportunity identification comes earlier, evaluation later.

mcq.q: Which of the following feasibility studies is concerned with cost benefit analysis?
mcq.teacher_note: Economic (economical) feasibility compares cost against benefit and the budget — the book calls it the most important study.

mcq.q: During which phase of the SDLC are system specifications documented?
mcq.teacher_note: Specifications are written down while the requirements are being gathered and analysed, i.e. in planning and requirements analysis. Design then produces the details that meet those documented requirements.

mcq.q: Conducting feasibility analysis is done in which phase of SDLC?
mcq.teacher_note: Feasibility belongs to the very first phase — system study / preliminary investigation, which is the planning phase.

mcq.q: What is the significance of the Planning phase in the SDLC?
options: It defines the project schedule and budget.
It outlines the technical specifications of the system.
It identifies project risks and mitigation strategies.
It designs the user interface and system architecture.
mcq.teacher_note: The key says (c) risks and mitigation — remember that the planning phase is also where the schedule and budget (the triple constraints) are set.

mcq.q: What is the last step in the software development lifecycle as given below?
mcq.teacher_note: Errata: the book prints the options as a, b, d, d (there is no 'c') and the key as d. Read by position, 'd' = Preliminary investigation and analysis, which is in fact the FIRST phase of SDLC; the option that fits the question is System testing. Flag this to students.

mcq.q: Which phase of the SDLC involves training end-users and preparing the system for deployment?
mcq.teacher_note: Implementation includes training user personnel, finalising documentation and ongoing user assistance.

mcq.q: Which phase of the System Life Cycle involves deploying the system and making sure it runs as expected?
mcq.teacher_note: Putting the developed system into working condition = system implementation.

mcq.q: What does the term “QA” stand for in the software development process?
mcq.teacher_note: QA = Quality Assurance — the process that ensures the development of quality products, and it includes validation and verification.

mcq.q: A set of programs written for a computer to perform a particular task is called …
mcq.teacher_note: Software is the logical component; hardware is the physical machine.

mcq.q: … defines a sequence of tasks that must be carried out to build new software.
mcq.teacher_note: This is the chapter's own opening definition of the software development process (§6.2).

mcq.q: SDLC stands for …
mcq.teacher_note: Software/System Development Life Cycle.

mcq.q: … is also called a Preliminary Investigation or Need Analysis Phase.
mcq.teacher_note: System study is the first step of SDLC and carries both of those alternative names.

mcq.q: … is to determine whether the whole process of system analysis leading to computerization would be worthwhile for the organization or not.
mcq.teacher_note: The chapter's own definition of a feasibility study (§6.3.1).

mcq.q: … is the process of testing the individual component of the system after the component is developed but before the components are combined together to form a complete system?
mcq.teacher_note: Before combining → unit testing. After combining → integration testing. Complete system → system testing. By the user → user acceptance testing.

mcq.q: The way of carrying out a developed system into working condition is called …
mcq.teacher_note: Errata: the key prints (d) system maintenance, but the chapter's own definition is “The way of carrying out a developed system into working condition is called system implementation” — which is option (c). Correcting and upgrading is maintenance (that is MCQ 17).

mcq.q: Correcting and upgrading the process of the system is called …
mcq.teacher_note: Correcting + upgrading = system maintenance (the chapter's own definition in §6.3.7). Note the contrast with MCQ 16: implementation puts it into working condition.

mcq.q: … is involved in conducting system study and analyzing the system.
mcq.teacher_note: The chapter lists this as the first role of the system analyst.

mcq.q: DFD stands for …
mcq.teacher_note: Data Flow Diagram — one of the system design tools in §6.6.

mcq.q: Which model of SDLC is characterized by a linear progression of phases from requirements gathering to maintenance?
mcq.teacher_note: Linear and sequential with no turning back = the waterfall model, the “parent” of all SDLC models.

key_terms.meaning: A sequence of instructions; an instruction is a command given to the computer to perform a specified operation on given data.
A set of programs written for a computer to perform a particular task — the logical components of a computer system.
A well-defined task that is a collection of several operations done in order to achieve a goal.

The complete procedure of software development, from requirement gathering through feasibility study, analysis, design, testing, implementation and maintenance, carried out in a specified time to achieve the intended product.
Budget/cost, time and scope — the three constraints of a software project, which are tied to each other.
A sequence of tasks that must be carried out to build new software, grouped into phases; each phase produces a report before the next begins.
A process to ensure the development of quality products; it includes validation and verification.
Software/System Development Life Cycle — an organised way to develop, maintain and replace software/information systems.
The first phase of SDLC, also called preliminary investigation or need analysis, which decides whether a new system should be developed.
The test of a proposed system for workability, meeting user requirements, effective use of resources and cost-effectiveness; it decides whether the project is worth doing.
Whether the technology, hardware, software and personnel needed for the system are available. It is the most difficult type to determine.
Whether the cost and benefits of the system fit the budget — the most important feasibility study, carried out as a cost-benefit analysis.
Whether the system will operate in the way the user wants, given the available human resources.
Whether the proposed system will be acceptable to the people affected by it, including its cost to society and to company culture.
A detailed study of the operations performed by a system and their relationships, leading to the specification of a new system.
The system design phase, which describes how the system will meet the requirements.
The process of developing the program software from the logical design.
Testing an individual component on its own, before the components are combined.
Testing the components after they have been combined into a complete system.
Testing the complete system with actual data after all the components have been combined.
Testing the complete system by the target user, before implementation, to check it meets their requirements.
Functional testing in which the test cases are hidden from the general users.
Glass box testing in which the structure of the program is tested and the test cases are visible to the users.
The way of carrying out a developed system into working condition — testing, debugging, loading, distributing and training.
The process of moving from the old system to the new one: direct, parallel, phased or pilot.
Repairing processing or performance failures, or making alterations because of previously ill-defined problems.
Changing program functions as the need arises, to correct a problem or upgrade performance.
Enhancing performance or modifying the program to make it even more perfect.
The final phase of SDLC, carried out by a group representing the client, internal audit, the analyst and data processing, to see whether the system met its objectives.
A computer specialist involved in analysing, designing, implementing and evaluating computer-based information systems.
A professional concerned with designing and developing specified software of the highest quality; sometimes used interchangeably with programmer or developer.
A finite set of step-by-step instructions that solve a particular problem, written in simple English and mathematical statements.
A diagrammatic representation that illustrates the sequence of operations to be performed to arrive at a solution.
A pictorial representation of the steps in a particular program, designed by the programmer.
A diagram showing a broad overview of the data flow and sequence of operations in a system, designed by the system designer.
English phrases used to describe the processing steps of a program; not bound by the strict rules of a programming language.
A zero-level DFD showing the whole system as process 0 with the external entities around it; it has no data store.
A pictorial representation of the flow of data into, around and out of a system, using external entities, processes, data stores and data flows.
A graphical representation of entities, their attributes and the relationships between them; used to design a logical database model.
A table associating conditions with the actions to perform — a precise model of logic made of a condition part and an action part.
A tree-shaped diagram that shows the relationship between conditions and actions in a clear, unmistakable way.
The field of study and practice that describes the desirable attributes of software products; approached through defect management and quality attributes.
Any failure to address end-user requirements — missed or misunderstood requirements, design or coding errors, and so on.
A linear and sequential SDLC model in which each phase must be completed before the next begins; considered the “parent” of all SDLC models.
An iterative model in which a throwaway prototype is built, shown to the customer and refined until the requirements are understood.
An approach based on creating and responding to change, valuing individuals and interactions, working software, customer collaboration and responding to change.
A model combining prototyping and waterfall, organised as cycles through four quadrants — analysis, evaluation, development and planning — each ending with a review.
The ongoing process of collecting, organising, storing and maintaining a complete record of the system across all phases of its life cycle.
The document holding all the technical details of the system, used for upgrading and maintenance.
The document holding the analysis, design, algorithm, flowchart, DFD and test results of a program.
The document that tells the user how to set up and operate the system, and what to do about problems.
Computer-Aided Software Engineering tool — one of the system design tools listed in §6.6.

quick_revision.title: Projects, processes and the life cycle
points: Software = a set of programs; a project = a task with a goal; a software project = the whole development procedure within a fixed time.
The triple constraints are budget/cost, time and scope — and they are tied to each other.
The software development process groups activities into phases; a phase can start only after the previous one finishes and each phase ends with a report.
SDLC has seven phases: study, analysis, design, development, testing, implementation, maintenance and review.

quick_revision.title: System study and feasibility
points: System study (preliminary investigation / need analysis) asks: should we build it at all?
A feasibility study decides whether the project is worth doing — its goal is the possibility of the system, not the solution.
Eight types: technical, economical, operational, social, management, legal and contractual, time (schedule), behavioral.
Technical is the most difficult to determine; economical is the most important.

quick_revision.title: The seven phases in one line each
points: Study — survey, analyse the current system, select the best solution.
Analysis — detailed study of operations, producing the specification of the new system.
Design — the most creative phase; logical design, using algorithm, flowchart, DFD, E-R and so on.
Development — the design is translated into the physical system; documentation is written.
Testing — unit, integration, system and user acceptance; the costliest and most complex phase.
Implementation — into working condition; conversion can be direct, parallel, phased or pilot (pilot is the best and most reliable).
Maintenance and review — corrective, adaptive and perfective maintenance; the system review is the final phase.

quick_revision.title: Testing
points: Unit testing — one component, before integration; done by the developer.
Integration testing — after the components are combined; done by the developer.
System test — the complete system with actual data; done by the developer.
User acceptance testing — by the target user, before implementation.
Black box = functional, test cases hidden. White box = structural, test cases visible.

quick_revision.title: Design tools
points: Algorithm — finite, definite, effective, with input and at least one output.
Flowchart — program flowchart (instruction flow, by the programmer) vs system flowchart (data flow, by the designer).
Pseudo code — English phrases describing processing steps, not bound by language rules.
Context diagram — zero-level DFD, the system as process 0, no data store.
DFD — external entity (rectangle), process (circle), data store (open-ended box), data flow (labeled arrow).
E-R diagram — rectangle = entity, oval = attribute, diamond = relationship, line = link.
Decision table and decision tree — the discount policy: member above Rs 12000 = 18%, member = 12%, non-member above Rs 12000 = 6%, otherwise 0%.

quick_revision.title: Quality and models
points: Software quality has two approaches: defect management and quality attributes (ISO/IEC 25010:2011 lists eight characteristics).
Waterfall — linear and sequential, no turning back; the “parent” of all models.
Prototyping — iterative, a throwaway model refined by customer evaluation; about twice as expensive.
Agile — four core values and five stages (exploration, planning, iteration to first release, productionizing, maintenance).
Spiral — four quadrants (analysis, evaluation, development, planning) with a review at the end of every cycle.

quick_revision.title: Documentation
points: Documentation is an ongoing process that never ends while the system lives.
Three reasons: it removes dependence on one individual, it makes modification and maintenance easier, and it lets a postponed project restart without starting from scratch.
System manual — all technical details for upgrading and maintenance.
Program manual — analysis, design, algorithm, flowchart, DFD, test results and maintenance history.
User manual — set up, operation, loading/unloading, problems and their meaning, checks and security.

teaching_plan.activity: Define program, software, project and software project; then the triple constraints. Move to the software development process (phases, reports, quality assurance) and the SDLC definition, its importance and the seven phases. Close by walking the SDLC stages figure on the board.

System study's three tasks, then the feasibility study: definition, the ten reasons to conduct one, and all eight types with the at-a-glance table. The 1200-jobs example makes social feasibility stick.
System analysis, system design (logical vs physical, the design-tool list), and system development. Emphasise that documentation starts here, not at the end.
The six-step test schedule, then the four testing processes with the 'who does it' table, plus black box vs white box. Draw the testing pyramid: unit → integration → system → acceptance.
Implementation and the four conversion strategies with the risk/cost table; then maintenance (corrective, adaptive, perfective), the point that software does not wear out, and the system review.

The system analyst's definition, eight duties and six desirable qualities — the standard long-answer question. Then the analyst vs software engineer table, and the eight requirement-collection methods.

Algorithm criteria and properties with the three worked examples; then the program-flowchart symbol table, the three example figure sheets and the system-flowchart symbols. Have students draw one flowchart of their own.

teaching_plan.topic: 6.6 — system flowchart, pseudo code and DFD
teaching_plan.activity: The payroll system flowchart and the system-vs-program flowchart table; pseudo code with two examples; then the context diagram and the DFD symbol set and library example.

E-R components (cross-reference Unit 1), then the discount-policy example worked as both a decision table and a decision tree. Finish with software quality: defect management and the eight ISO characteristics.
The four SDLC models with their figures, advantages and disadvantages, then the at-a-glance comparison table. Close with documentation: the three reasons, and the system, program and user manuals.
Solve the 7 short and 7 long questions, then run the 20-question MCQ self-test. Go through the two errata notes (MCQ 6 and MCQ 16) explicitly so students are not caught out in the exam.

blocks.text: The branch of computer science concerned with designing intelligent computer systems. That computer system shows the characteristics of intelligence in human behavior — understanding natural languages, learning, reasoning, drilling, and solving problems. Artificial Intelligence is a branch of science that deals with helping machines find solutions to complex problems in more human activities.
AI is generally associated with Computer Science, but it has many important links with other fields such as maths, psychology, linguistics, cognition, biology, neuroscience and philosophy.

blocks.caption: The fields that contribute to Artificial Intelligence — computer vision, robotics, programming, gaming, music, technology, medical science and communication.

blocks.text: AI is usually defined as the science of making computers do things that require intelligence when done by humans. AI is the study of how to make computers do things which, at the moment, people do better.
Components of AI

Different disciplines contributed their ideas, viewpoint and techniques to plan the foundation of AI; these act as the components of AI. The major components are learning, reasoning, problem-solving, perception and language understanding.
a. Learning

The learning process involves memorising individual items including various problem-solving techniques, vocabularies and foreign languages. Through this learning process, AI programs can record all actions or moves that lead to positive results, enabling them to leverage this knowledge should similar problems arise in the future. AI systems learn from data and examples; the key learning approaches are:

items: Supervised Learning: it utilises labeled data to train models.
Unsupervised Learning: it identifies patterns without labeled data.
Reinforcement Learning: it involves learning through interaction with an environment.

blocks.text: b. Reasoning

Reasoning is carried out based on a strict rule of validity to perform specified tasks. It can be deductive or inductive. Deductive reasoning guarantees the truth of the conclusion based on the truth of the premises. Inductive reasoning, on the other hand, supports the conclusion but it cannot be fully dependent on the premises.
c. Problem Solving

AI addresses various problems using problem-solving methods, mainly divided into two types: special-purpose and general-purpose methods. General-purpose methods are applicable to a wide range of problems and involve step-by-step reduction of the difference between the current state and the goal state. Special-purpose methods are customised to solve specific types of problems.
d. Perception

Perception is the ability to understand and interpret information. This involves recognising different datasets, such as images, text or sound, and knowing how to process that data. When AI systems perceive data, they need to provide valuable insights. For example, a natural language processor (NLP) allows AI to understand human language.
e. Language Understanding

Language understanding in AI involves understanding and generating natural language. Techniques like natural language understanding, machine translation and text generation enable effective interaction with language. Example: virtual assistants understand and respond to spoken commands.
Uses / Applications of AI

The potential applications of Artificial Intelligence are abundant. They stretch from the military, for autonomous control and target identification, to the entertainment industry, for computer games and robotic pets. Big establishments dealing with huge amounts of information — such as hospitals, banks, industries and insurances — can use AI to predict customer behaviour and detect trends.

items: Game playing: General game playing (GGP) and General video game playing (GVGP) are concepts and designs for artificial intelligence programs to successfully play plenty of games. For video games, game rules have to be either learned over multiple repetitions by artificial players or predefined manually in a domain-specific language and sent in advance to the artificial players. For instance, in the GGP of chess, computers are programmed to play using a specially designed algorithm; it was considered a necessary landmark on the way to Artificial General Intelligence. The first commercial practice of general game-playing technology was Zillions of Games in 1998.

Speech recognition: the input is given to the computer in the form of vibrations produced by the sound, with the help of an analog-to-digital converter that converts those vibrations into digital format. Then a set of complex algorithms runs on that data to recognise the speech and return text as a result. Depending on the goal, the end result may vary: Google Voice typing converts spoken words into suitable text format, while personal assistants like Siri and Google Assistant take the sound as input and convert it into both voice and text format.

Understanding natural language: natural language understanding is a branch of AI that uses computer software to take input in the form of sentences using text or speech. It simply reduces the gap between humans and computers, allowing them to interact easily with each other.
Computer vision: a field of AI which enables the computer and its systems to get input in the form of digital images and videos and take action based on the provided input.

Expert systems: a computer system that mimics, or even surpasses, the decision-making ability of a human expert. It is generally designed to solve complex problems by surfing through bodies of knowledge, and is divided into two subsystems — the knowledge base (which represents facts and rules) and the inference engine (which applies the rules to the known facts to deduce new facts).

Robotics: AI in robotics is the ability of the computer or the robot to perform multiple tasks performed by humans which require human intelligence and discernment. It gives robots a computer vision to navigate, sense and calculate their reaction accordingly. For example, robotic packaging uses various forms of AI for quicker and accurate packaging at a lower price; likewise Sophia, marked as a “social robot”, is successfully able to mimic social behavior and induce feelings of love in humans.

Theorem proving: proving theorems requires high intelligence, as many practical problems can be cast in terms of theorems. If knowledge is expressed by logic, proving a theorem is reasoning. It uses various AI techniques such as heuristic search.

Symbolic mathematics: refers to the manipulation of formulas rather than doing arithmetic on numeric values. It is often used in conjunction with ordinary scientific computation as a generator of programs used to actually do the calculations.

blocks.text: Robotics

The branch of technology that deals with the design, construction, operation and application of robots. It is a discipline overlapping artificial intelligence and mechanical engineering. It is concerned with building robot programmable devices consisting of mechanical actuators and sensory organs that are linked to a computer.

blocks.caption: Robotics — where artificial intelligence meets mechanical engineering.

blocks.text: The mechanical structure might involve manipulators, as in industrial robotics, or might concern the movement of the robot as a vehicle, as in mobile robotics. Robotics research is used in artificial intelligence as a framework for exploring key problems and techniques through a well-defined application.

items: Robotics is the branch of technology that deals with the design, construction, operation and application of robots.
It is a discipline overlapping artificial intelligence and mechanical engineering.
It is concerned with building robots — programmable devices consisting of mechanical actuators and sensory organs that are linked to a computer.
Robots are being used in applications like industry, scientific research, military applications, intelligent home applications and health services.

blocks.text: The use of various services, such as software development platforms, servers, storage and software, over the Internet, often referred to as the “cloud”. It is defined as a type of computing that relies on sharing computing resources rather than having local servers or personal devices to handle applications.

In cloud computing the word cloud is used to represent “the Internet”, so the phrase cloud computing means “a type of Internet-based computing”, where different services — such as servers, storage and applications — are delivered to an organisation's computers and devices through the Internet. Cloud computing allows application software to be operated using internet-enabled devices.

blocks.caption: Cloud computing — services delivered over the Internet instead of from local servers.

blocks.text: Types of Clouds

blocks.caption: Public, private and hybrid cloud
head: Type
Description
rows: Made available to the general public or a large industry group.
The computing environment resides within the boundaries of an organisation and is used exclusively for the organisational benefits.

The combination of both public and private cloud. With this cloud, organisations might run non-core applications in a public cloud while maintaining core applications and sensitive data in a private cloud.

blocks.text: Service Models of Cloud Computing
The service model defines the services provided through the cloud. The service models of cloud computing are:

items: IaaS (Infrastructure as a Service): in this service, computing infrastructural components like server hardware, storage, bandwidth and other fundamental computing resources are provided through the cloud.
SaaS (Software as a Service): this service includes complete software on the cloud. Users can access software hosted on the cloud without installing it on their own computer.

PaaS (Platform as a Service): it allows the user to rent virtualized servers and associated services used to run existing applications, or to design, develop, test, deploy and host applications. It provides clients with access to the basic operating software and optional services to develop and use software applications, without the need to buy and manage the underlying computing infrastructure.

blocks.caption: IaaS (Infrastructure as a Service) — server hardware, storage and bandwidth provided through the cloud.
IaaS, PaaS and SaaS at a glance
head: Model
You get
You still manage
rows: Server hardware, storage, bandwidth and other fundamental computing resources.
The operating system, the applications and the data.
Virtualised servers and the basic operating software, to design, develop, test, deploy and host applications.
Complete software, hosted on the cloud and accessed without installing it.
Nothing but your own use of the software.

blocks.text: Advantages of Cloud Computing

items: Cost-efficient: it is probably the most efficient method to use, maintain and upgrade.
Almost unlimited storage: storing information in the cloud gives us almost unlimited storage capacity.
Backup and recovery: since all the data is stored in the cloud, backing it up and restoring it is relatively much easier than storing the same on a physical device.
Automatic software integration: in the cloud, software integration usually occurs automatically. It also allows us to customise the options with great ease.
Easy access to information: once the user is registered in the cloud, the user can access the information from anywhere there is an Internet connection.
Quick deployment: once the method of functioning is selected, the entire system can be fully functional in a matter of a few minutes.

blocks.text: Disadvantages of Cloud Computing

items: Technical issues: this technology is always prone to outages and other technical issues. Even the best cloud service providers run into this kind of trouble, despite keeping up high standards of maintenance.
Security in the cloud: storing all the sensitive information with a third-party cloud service provider could potentially put the company at great risk.
Prone to attack: storing information in the cloud could make the company vulnerable to external threats and attacks.

blocks.text: Complex and large data sets that have to be processed and analysed to uncover valuable information that can benefit businesses and organisations.

items: It refers to a massive amount of data that keeps on growing exponentially with time.
It is so voluminous that it cannot be processed or analysed using conventional data processing techniques.
It includes data mining, data storage, data analysis, data sharing and data visualization.
The term is an all-comprehensive one, including data, data frameworks, along with the tools and techniques used to process and analyze the data.

blocks.title: Gartner's definition
blocks.text: “Big data is high-volume, velocity and variety information assets that demand cost-effective, innovative forms of information processing for enhanced insight and decision making.”
Types of Big Data
Big data can be classified as structured, unstructured and semi-structured.

items: Structured: data that can be processed, stored and retrieved in a fixed format. It refers to highly organised information that can be readily and seamlessly stored and accessed from a database by simple search engine algorithms.
Unstructured: data that lacks any specific form or structure whatsoever. This makes it very difficult and time-consuming to process and analyse.

Semi-structured: data containing both of the formats mentioned above, that is, structured and unstructured data. To be precise, it refers to data that, although it has not been classified under a particular repository (database), yet contains vital information or tags that segregate individual elements within the data.

blocks.text: Characteristics of Big Data — the Seven Vs

blocks.caption: The Seven Vs of Big Data — Volume, Velocity, Variety, Veracity, Value, Variability and Visualization.

items: Variety: the variety of data gathered from multiple sources; it can be structured, unstructured or semi-structured.
Velocity: the speed at which data is being created in real time. It also comprises the rate of change, the linking of incoming data sets at varying speeds, and activity bursts.
Volume: huge ‘volumes’ of data generated daily from various sources like social media platforms, business processes, machines, networks, human interactions, etc.
Veracity: the reliability or trustworthiness of the data. Due to the large volume of data, there is uncertainty about the validity and accurateness of data.
Value: the worth, in business value, of the collected data.
Variability: the inconsistency of big data, and how the big data can be used and formatted.
Visualization: in today's world visualization is essential — large volumes of complex data can be visualized using graphical representations far more effectively than using reports and Excel sheets.

blocks.title: Exam hint
blocks.text: Many textbooks list only the three Vs (Volume, Velocity, Variety) or the four Vs (adding Veracity). This chapter lists seven — always write all seven, and mention that the four Vs asked about in MCQ 5 are Volume, Velocity, Variety and Veracity.
Application Areas of Big Data

items: Healthcare or the medical sector
Academia
Banking
Manufacturing
Information Technology (IT)
Retail business
Transportation

blocks.text: Advantages of Big Data Processing

items: Businesses can utilise outside intelligence while taking decisions.
Improved customer service.
Early identification of risk to the product/services, if any.
Better operational efficiency.
Big data analysis derives innovative solutions; it helps in understanding and targeting customers, and helps in optimising business processes.

blocks.text: Disadvantages of Big Data Processing

items: Traditional storage can cost a lot of money to store big data.
Big data analysis is not useful in the short run — it needs to be analysed over a longer duration to leverage its benefits.
Big data analysis results are sometimes misleading.

blocks.text: A term that expresses computer-based simulated environments which can be perceived as in the real world, as well as in unreal worlds.

The virtual reality environments are primarily concerned with the visual experiences, displayed either on a computer screen or through special stereoscopic displays; but some simulations include additional sensory information, such as sound through speakers or headphones. Virtual reality creates such a realistic artificial environment that the user really pretends what s/he should feel as in the real world. Today VR technology is applied to advanced fields of medicine, engineering, education, design, training and entertainment.

It can be used in scientific research laboratories, so that scientists can easily research a specific topic.
It can be used in entertainment like games and movies, to make the gaming experience more real and to allow individuals to experience adventures under extreme conditions.
It can be used in driving schools, as it gives a real look at roads and traffic.

items: Virtual reality creates a realistic world.
It enables users to explore places.
Through virtual reality, users can experiment with an artificial environment.
Virtual reality makes education easier and more comfortable.

blocks.text: Disadvantages of Virtual Reality

It consists of complex technology.
In a virtual reality environment we can't move by ourselves as we do in the real world.

blocks.text: e-Commerce

A process of buying and selling, or exchanging products, services and information using electronic media. There are many definitions for electronic commerce that include elements of electronic transactions and the buying and selling of goods and services online.

e-Commerce is a modern business methodology that addresses the needs of organisations, merchants and consumers to cut costs while improving the quality of manufactured goods and services and increasing the speed of service delivery. More commonly, e-commerce is associated with the buying and selling of information, products and services via computer networks. The main platforms of e-commerce remain the Internet, e-mail, fax and telephone orders.

blocks.caption: e-Commerce — buying and selling over electronic media.

blocks.text: Classification of e-Commerce
Classifications of e-Commerce by the nature of the transaction are:

blocks.caption: The four e-Commerce models
head: Type
Description
rows: Sells products or services to other businesses. e.g., www.freemarkets.com
Sells products or services directly to consumers. e.g., www.amazon.com, www.yahoo.com
The consumer fixes a price on their own, which businesses accept or decline. e.g., www.priceline.com
A consumer sells directly to other consumers. e.g., www.ebay.com

blocks.text: Advantages of e-Commerce

items: It enables more individuals to work at home and to do less travelling for shopping, resulting in less traffic on the roads and lower air pollution.
It allows some merchandise to be sold at lower prices, benefiting less affluent people.
It enables people in Third World countries and rural areas to enjoy products and services which otherwise are not available to them.
It facilitates the delivery of public services at a reduced cost, increases effectiveness and/or improves quality.
It enables consumers to shop or do other transactions 24 hours a day, all year round, from almost any location.
It provides consumers with more selections or choices.
It provides consumers with less expensive products and services, by allowing them to shop in many places and conduct quick comparisons.
It allows quick delivery of products and services, especially with digitized products.
Consumers can receive relevant and detailed information in seconds, rather than in days or weeks of walk-around searching for a product.
It makes it possible to participate in virtual auctions.
It allows consumers to interact with other consumers in electronic communities, exchange ideas and compare price tags.
It facilitates competition, as a result of substantial discounts.
It expands the marketplace to national and international markets.
It decreases the cost of creating, processing, distributing, storing and retrieving paper-based information.

blocks.text: Disadvantages of e-Commerce

items: Businesses often calculate return on investment numbers before committing to any new technology. Costs, which are a function of technology, can change dramatically during even short-lived e-commerce implementation projects.
Many companies have had trouble recruiting and retaining employees with the technological, design and business process skills needed to create an effective e-commerce presence.
There is difficulty in integrating existing databases and transaction-processing software designed for traditional commerce into the software that enables e-commerce.
Many businesses face cultural and legal impediments to e-commerce.
Some consumers are still fearful of sending their credit card numbers over the Internet.
Consumers are simply resistant to change and are uncomfortable viewing merchandise on a computer screen rather than in person.

blocks.text: e-Medicine
An online clinical medical knowledge database, which is an approach to providing health care service to a large number of people spread across different locations.

It is mainly beneficial for people in rural areas with limited or no medical facilities. e-Medicine is targeted to provide high-quality healthcare service; it minimises the time and cost required for treatment. e-Medicine usually contains up-to-date, searchable, peer-reviewed medical journals, online physician reference textbooks, and a complete article database on medical specialties. This Internet medical library and clinical knowledge base are available to physicians, medical students, nurses, other health professionals and patients.

With the use of e-Medicine, doctors and patients who are physically apart can connect, so that patients can share their problem with the doctor and the doctor can suggest treatment or any test required.

blocks.caption: e-Medicine — health care delivered to people in different locations.

blocks.text: e-Governance
The use of information and communication technology (ICT) to enhance the access to and delivery of government services, to benefit citizens, business partners and employees.

It transforms the traditional government using ICT to make it clear, effective and accountable. However, it doesn't mean that putting more computers on the desks of government officials is e-governance — e-Governance is more than just a government website on the Internet. Political, social, economic and technological aspects determine e-governance.

It establishes a relationship between government officials and citizens by: providing greater access to government information and services by making the government accessible online; promoting citizen participation by enabling citizens to interact more conveniently with government officials, such as by requesting a government service and filing required documents through the website; increasing government accountability by making its operations more transparent, thereby reducing the opportunities for corruption; and supporting development goals by providing business, rural and traditionally underserved communities with information, opportunities and communications capabilities.

blocks.caption: e-Governance — ICT used to deliver government services to citizens, businesses and employees.

blocks.text: Objectives of e-Governance

items: E-Governance refers to the provision of online public services to citizens and businesses.
Services for citizens include registration to government services such as health care, education or employment benefits.

For businesses, e-Governance services can take the form of online alerts for public procurements or funding opportunities, as well as information and support on the applicable legislation in a given sector.
E-Governance helps to cut down administrative costs, speed up procedures and therefore increase efficiency and reactivity.

Creating trust and transparency of successful delivery of e-Governance service.

Network security and protection against viruses, spam, unwanted attacks, etc.
Online privacy.
All the citizens may not have access to computing resources.

blocks.text: A generic term describing one's ability to use technology while moving, as opposed to portable, which is only practical for use while deployed in a stationary configuration. A mobile computing device is created using mobile components, such as mobile hardware and software. Mobile computing devices are portable devices capable of operating, executing, providing services and applications like a computing device. It is a computing device used in transit — users can access data and information from wherever they are.
Many types of mobile computers have been introduced since the 1990s, including the wearable computer, PDA, enterprise digital assistant, smartphone, UMPC (Ultra-mobile PC) and Tablet PC.

blocks.caption: Mobile computing — technology that can be used while moving.

blocks.text: Features of a Mobile Computing Device

items: It is a portable device that can be used during mobility.
It has limited processing and storage capability.
It includes mobile communication, mobile hardware and mobile software.

It usually contains a touch screen for providing input. It contains an on-screen or virtual keyboard for providing text inputs; however, an external keyboard can be connected using the USB port, infrared or Bluetooth.
It contains a camera, speaker and microphone.
It contains handwriting-recognising software.
Most mobile computing devices contain a memory card slot to expand the storage capacity.
It has wireless connectivity such as Bluetooth and Wi-Fi to connect to the Internet or to other computing devices, as well as a wired connection through the USB port.
Most mobile computing devices can synchronise their data with applications on users' computers.

blocks.text: The network of physical devices, vehicles, home appliances and other items embedded with electronics, software, sensors, actuators and connectivity, which enables these things to connect, collect and exchange data.

The Internet of Things (IoT) is a system of interrelated computing devices, mechanical and digital machines, objects, animals or people that are provided with unique identifiers (UIDs) and the ability to transfer data over a network without requiring human-to-human or human-to-computer interaction.
By combining these connected devices with automated systems, it is possible to “gather information, analyse it and create an action” to help someone with a particular task or learn from a process.

A thing in the internet of things can be a person with a heart monitor implant, an animal with a biochip transponder, an automobile that has built-in sensors to alert the driver when the tyre pressure is low, or any other natural or man-made object that can be assigned an Internet Protocol (IP) address and can transfer data over a network.

blocks.caption: Figure: IoT — everyday objects connected and exchanging data over a network.

blocks.text: Advantages of IoT

items: It automates tasks and helps to improve the quality of a business's services, reducing the need for human intervention.
It helps to operate business operations more efficiently, and to better understand customers so as to deliver enhanced customer service.
It supports improved decision-making and increases the value of the business.
It has the ability to access information from anywhere at any time on any device.
It provides improved communication between connected electronic devices.
Transferring data packets over a connected network saves time, effort and money.

blocks.text: Disadvantages of IoT

Organisations may eventually have to deal with massive numbers — maybe even millions — of IoT devices, and collecting and managing the data from all those devices will be challenging.
If there's a bug in the system, every connected device will likely become corrupted.
Since there's no international standard of compatibility for IoT, it's difficult for devices from different manufacturers to communicate with each other.

blocks.text: Learning, teaching or understanding about a topic with the help of Information and Communication Technology. e-Learning allows us to learn anywhere and usually at any time, as long as we have a properly configured computer, networks, devices, etc. e-Learning can be CD-ROM-based, Network-based, Intranet-based or Internet-based.
