short.q: What is e-Commerce? Explain its role to enhance the digital economy.
short.a:
e-Commerce (electronic commerce) is buying and selling goods, services and information over the internet, together with the payments, the delivery arrangements and the customer service that go with them. It includes online shops, online banking, ticketing, auctions and digital downloads.

Its role in enhancing the digital economy:

  • It makes the market national and then global. A shop in Kathmandu can sell to a customer anywhere, so a small business is no longer limited to the people who walk past its door.
  • It lowers the cost of doing business. No showroom rent, fewer staff, less paper — and the savings can be passed on as lower prices.
  • It creates new work. Web development, digital marketing, logistics, customer support, content creation and data analysis all grow around it.
  • It drives digital payments. e-Commerce pushes people into online banking, mobile wallets, QR payments and cards, which brings transactions into the recorded economy and widens financial inclusion.
  • It generates data. Every transaction leaves a trail that can be analysed to understand demand, price properly and target what customers actually want.
  • It pulls other sectors online. Logistics, warehousing, banking, telecommunications and advertising all have to modernise to serve it.
  • It enables new business models. Marketplaces, subscription services, the gig economy and the platform economy all rest on e-commerce infrastructure.
  • It brings the informal economy into the formal one. Digital payments leave records, which widens the tax base and makes credit available to businesses that previously had no accounts.

short.q: Write the impact of e-Commerce technology in our society.
short.a:
The impact of e-commerce technology on society has been broad and mostly, though not entirely, positive.

Positive impacts:

  • Convenience. Shopping, banking and paying bills at any hour from anywhere, without travelling or queueing.
  • Wider choice and lower prices. Buyers compare products and prices across many sellers in minutes, which forces prices down.
  • Opportunity for small and rural businesses. A weaver in a village can sell directly to a customer in the city or abroad without a shop or a middleman.
  • Employment. New jobs in technology, delivery, warehousing, digital marketing and customer service.
  • Financial inclusion. Mobile wallets and online payments bring people without bank accounts into the cashless economy.
  • Less travelling. Fewer trips to shops means less traffic, less fuel and less pollution.
  • Better information. Reviews, ratings and product details let people choose with their eyes open.
  • Work from home. Many online businesses are run entirely from home.

Negative impacts:

  • Traditional shops suffer. Small physical retailers struggle to match online prices, and high streets lose trade.
  • Fraud and loss of privacy. Card fraud, phishing, fake websites and the harvesting of personal data.
  • Consumer risk. Goods arrive late, damaged, or not at all; returning them is harder than in a shop.
  • Over-consumption and waste. Easy buying encourages impulse purchases and a great deal of packaging waste.
  • A digital divide. People without internet access, a device or digital skills are left behind.
  • Fewer face-to-face interactions. Shopping was a social activity for many people, and it is less so now.

short.q: Classify e-Commerce according to the nature of the transaction.
short.a:
e-Commerce is classified by who is on each side of the transaction. The usual categories:
TypeWho sells to whomExample
B2C — Business to Consumer A business sells to an individual shopper. Amazon, Daraz, an airline's booking site
B2B — Business to Business One business sells to another, usually in bulk. A wholesaler supplying a retailer; Alibaba
C2C — Consumer to Consumer Individuals sell to each other, usually through a platform. eBay, Facebook Marketplace, classified sites
C2B — Consumer to Business An individual offers something and businesses bid for it. A photographer licensing a photo; freelance marketplaces
B2G — Business to Government A business supplies goods or services to a government body. A company tendering for a public contract
G2C — Government to Citizen Government provides services, and takes payments, online. Online tax filing, applying for a passport, paying a fine
G2B — Government to Business Government provides information and services to businesses. Company registration, tender portals

By the nature of the goods it is also divided into direct e-commerce, where the whole transaction happens online because the product is digital (software, music, e-books, tickets), and indirect e-commerce, where the order and the payment are online but the goods must still be delivered physically.

short.q: Explain the merit and demerit of e-Commerce in detail.
short.a:
Merits of e-Commerce.

  • Convenience. Open at any hour, reachable from anywhere, with no travelling and no queueing.
  • Global reach. A seller can reach customers in any country, and a buyer can buy from one.
  • Lower costs. No showroom, fewer staff and less paperwork mean lower prices for the buyer and better margins for the seller.
  • Wider choice. The buyer compares many sellers and products in minutes.
  • Faster transactions. Ordering, payment and confirmation happen immediately.
  • Less paper. Catalogues, invoices and receipts are digital.
  • Personalisation. What a customer has looked at and bought can be used to suggest what they may want next.
  • New opportunities. Small and home-based businesses reach a market they could never have afforded to reach before.
  • Information. Reviews, ratings and detailed specifications help people choose well.

Demerits of e-Commerce.

  • No physical inspection. A buyer cannot touch, try on or test the goods; what arrives may not match the picture.
  • Delivery delay and risk. Goods can be late, damaged or lost, and returning them is a chore.
  • Security and fraud. Card fraud, phishing, fake websites and identity theft.
  • Loss of privacy. Every purchase, search and click is collected, profiled and often sold.
  • Limited personal contact. No salesperson to ask, and no social side to shopping.
  • Dependence on technology. No internet, no power or no device means no shopping.
  • The digital divide. People without access, money or skills are excluded from the savings and the choice.
  • Harm to local shops. Small physical retailers lose trade, and money leaves the local economy.
  • Legal uncertainty. Consumer protection, taxation and jurisdiction across borders are still unsettled.
  • Over-consumption and waste. Easy buying encourages impulse buying and generates packaging waste.

long.q: In your opinion what has been the greatest breakthrough in computer technology in the recent year and why?
long.a:
A reasonable answer, argued rather than merely listed, is that the greatest breakthrough of recent years has been the coming together of cloud computing and artificial intelligence. Cloud computing made enormous computing power and storage available to anyone with an internet connection, for the cost of a monthly bill instead of a capital purchase; artificial intelligence turned that raw power into something that can see, read, write and reason. Neither would have mattered much without the other: AI needs computing power it could never have afforded on its own, and the cloud needs something worth renting the capacity for.

Why this one, rather than the others:

  • It changed who can build things. Before the cloud, starting anything computationally serious meant buying servers. Now a student, a hospital or a company in a developing country rents the same capability as a large corporation, and anyone with an internet connection can use a model that would have been a research project a few years ago. That democratisation is the part with the widest consequences.
  • It is not one technology but a platform for all the others. Big data, the Internet of Things, robotics, virtual reality and e-medicine all run on the cloud, and AI is now being added to every one of them. A breakthrough that makes other breakthroughs cheaper outranks a breakthrough that stands alone.
  • It reached ordinary people. Smartphones put the internet in everyone's pocket, but AI is what made that device useful — voice recognition, translation, navigation, photography, recommendation and now assistance with writing, learning and diagnosis. Millions of people use it daily without thinking of it as computer science.
  • It has changed what computers do. Every previous advance made people faster at telling the machine what to do. AI is the first to let the machine work out part of the answer for itself — to summarise, translate, recognise a tumour in a scan, or find the fault in a piece of code.

Other candidates, honestly weighed. Smartphones and mobile computing put the internet in more hands than anything else, but they are the delivery mechanism as much as the breakthrough. The Internet of Things connects machines to the network, but mostly feeds the cloud and AI. Vaccine and genomics work driven by computing has saved the most lives, and was made possible by the same two technologies.

The honest caveat is that this is a judgement, not a measurement — the greatest breakthrough is whichever one changed most of what people can do, and by that test the cloud plus AI is the answer I would defend. It has to be used carefully, though: it raises real questions about privacy, bias, jobs and who controls the infrastructure, and a technology that powerful needs to be governed rather than merely adopted.

long.q: What are the key challenges of implementing e-governance in developing countries?
long.a:
e-Governance is the use of information and communication technology to deliver government services, information and decision-making to citizens and businesses online. Its promise is real, but implementing it in a developing country is unusually hard.

The main challenges:

  • Poor infrastructure. Unreliable electricity, limited internet outside the cities, and slow and expensive connectivity. A service that is online in Kathmandu may not exist at all in a rural district.
  • The digital divide. Many citizens have no device, no connection, and — just as important — no digital skills. Without literacy and training, an online service simply excludes the people who most need it.
  • Low digital literacy. Knowing how to fill in an online form, attach a document and track an application cannot be assumed.
  • Cost. Building and maintaining the systems competes with more immediate needs such as schools, roads and hospitals, and the benefits take years to show.
  • Lack of skilled people. Government departments struggle to recruit and keep IT staff at public-sector salaries.
  • Resistance to change. Officials may see transparency as a threat to their authority or to their income, and paper-based routines are deeply established.
  • Corruption and vested interests. e-Governance removes the discretion that corruption depends on, so the people who benefit from the present system have a reason to slow the new one down.
  • No interoperability. Departments built their own systems at different times, they do not talk to each other, and the citizen is asked for the same document repeatedly.
  • Legal vacuum. Without laws on electronic signatures, data protection, cybercrime and the legal validity of digital records, online services cannot be trusted or enforced.
  • Language and localisation. Services delivered only in English exclude most of the population.
  • Security and privacy. Centralised citizen data is a valuable target, and a breach would destroy trust in the whole project.
  • Sustainability. Donor-funded pilots work well and then stop when the funding ends, because nobody budgeted to run them.
  • Citizen trust. People who have been let down before will not use an online service until it has proved itself.

What works, in practice, is to start with the services that people use most and understand best — certificates, licences, tax, exam results — provide assisted access in offices and libraries, publish in the local language, pass the enabling laws first, and keep a paper route open for those who need it. e-Governance succeeds when it makes an existing service simpler, not when it moves an existing obstacle onto a website.

long.q: Describe the terms e-Learning, e-Governance, and e-Medicine.
long.a:
e-Learning is learning that is delivered, supported and assessed through electronic media — usually the internet — instead of in a classroom. It covers recorded and live online lessons, learning management systems that hold the material and the assignments, digital textbooks and libraries, educational apps, simulations, and video-conferenced classes.

Benefits: it is available at any time and from anywhere, so a student is not bound by a timetable or a location; it lets each learner go at their own pace, repeating what was not understood; it reaches rural and remote students who have no access to good teachers; it costs less than building classrooms; and it produces records of progress that a teacher can act on.

Limits: it needs a device, a connection and the self-discipline to work alone; it weakens the social side of education; practical and laboratory subjects are hard to teach through a screen; and without a teacher's encouragement many students give up.

e-Governance is the use of information and communication technology by government to deliver services and information to citizens and businesses, to make its own operations more efficient, and to involve people in decision-making. Examples are online tax filing and payment, applying for a passport or a driving licence, company registration, public tenders, land records, and publishing budgets and decisions for anyone to see.

Benefits: services are available round the clock without queuing; removing the official's discretion removes the opportunity for bribery; published data makes government accountable; and money is saved on paper, buildings and staff.

Limits: it excludes people without access or skills, it needs laws on electronic records and data protection, and a service moved onto a badly designed website can be worse than the counter it replaced.

e-Medicine (telemedicine) is the delivery of health care at a distance through telecommunications: a consultation by video call, a scan or an X-ray sent to a specialist in another city for an opinion, remote monitoring of a patient's heart or blood sugar by their own doctor, electronic prescriptions, and digital health records.

Benefits: a specialist's advice reaches a patient who is days away from the nearest hospital; patients in remote areas get diagnosed and treated early; travel costs and waiting times fall; and a specialist can supervise many more patients than by travelling.

Limits: an examination through a screen cannot replace hands-on examination; it depends on a reliable connection; patient confidentiality must be protected; and the law is often unclear about where a doctor is licensed to practise when the patient is in another district or country.

long.q: What is e-governance? List out the objectives of E-governance.
long.a:
e-Governance is the application of information and communication technology by government to deliver services, exchange information, carry out transactions and involve citizens in decision-making. It covers the relationships between government and citizens, between government and businesses, and between one part of government and another.

Its objectives:

  • Better service delivery. Services available at any hour, from anywhere, without queuing or repeated visits.
  • Transparency. Publishing budgets, decisions, tenders and expenditure so that citizens can see what their government is doing.
  • Reduced corruption. When a rule is applied by a computer and the record is kept, the discretion that bribery depends on disappears.
  • Accountability. Every transaction is time-stamped and traceable to the official who handled it.
  • Efficiency and cost reduction. Less paper, fewer buildings, fewer staff per transaction, and faster processing.
  • Citizen participation. Online consultation, petitions, feedback and voting give people a say between elections.
  • Empowerment through information. Publishing rights, entitlements, schemes and procedures lets people claim what is theirs.
  • Reduced burden on citizens. One portal instead of a dozen offices; the data is given once rather than re-typed at every counter.
  • Better internal coordination. Departments share data instead of each keeping its own paper file.
  • Bridging the rural-urban gap. A service delivered online is available in a village as much as in the capital.
  • Economic development. Faster company registration, easier tax compliance and open public data make it easier to do business.
  • Environmental benefit. Less paper and less travelling to government offices.

long.q: What is e-Business? List out the objectives of e-Business.
long.a:
e-Business (electronic business) is the conduct of business processes over the internet. It is broader than e-commerce: e-commerce is the buying and selling, while e-business covers everything a company does electronically — buying from suppliers, managing inventory, running the accounts, recruiting, marketing, customer service and internal communication. All e-commerce is e-business, but not all e-business is e-commerce.

Its objectives:

  • Operational efficiency. Automating ordering, invoicing, payroll and inventory removes the paperwork and the delay, and cuts the cost of each transaction.
  • Reduced costs. Less paper, less postage, smaller premises, fewer staff on routine work, and cheaper purchasing through online comparison.
  • Global reach. The business is open to customers and suppliers everywhere, at any hour, without opening a branch.
  • Faster processes. Quotes, orders, payments and confirmations happen in minutes rather than days.
  • Better customer service. Order tracking, online support, self-service accounts and quick answers to questions.
  • Stronger supply-chain management. Suppliers see demand as it happens, so stock is ordered when it is needed instead of being guessed at.
  • Better decisions. Every transaction leaves data, and analysing it shows which products sell, which customers are profitable and where the money is going.
  • Competitive advantage. A business that answers faster, costs less and knows its customers better wins against one that does not.
  • New revenue and new models. Subscriptions, digital products, marketplaces and platform services become possible.
  • Flexible working. Staff can work from anywhere, which widens the pool of people the business can employ.
  • Improved communication. Inside the firm through intranets and collaboration tools, and outside it through e-mail, social media and the website.
  • Faster time to market. A new product is announced and sold the same day.

long.q: What is Cloud Computing and robotics?
long.a:
Cloud computing is the delivery of computing services — servers, storage, databases, networking, software and analytics — over the internet, from data centres owned by a provider, instead of from a computer or a server the user owns. The user rents capacity and pays for what is used; the provider buys and maintains the hardware. The usual service models are IaaS (raw infrastructure: virtual machines and storage), PaaS (a platform on which to build and run applications) and SaaS (complete software used through a browser, such as webmail), and the deployment models are public, private and hybrid cloud.

Advantages: no large upfront purchase; capacity grows and shrinks with demand; data is reachable from anywhere; backups and disaster recovery are handled by the provider; and software updates itself. Risks: dependence on an internet connection and on the provider's continuing good health, anxiety about where the data physically is and who can see it, and ongoing subscription costs that eventually exceed the cost of buying outright.

Gmail and Google Drive, Netflix, online banking and the photo library on a phone are all cloud services.

Robotics is the branch of technology concerned with the design, construction, operation and use of robots — machines that can be programmed to carry out tasks automatically or semi-automatically. It sits across mechanical engineering, electronics and computer science, and overlaps heavily with artificial intelligence: a robot senses its surroundings with sensors, reasons about what it senses, and acts through motors and actuators.

Uses: manufacturing — welding, painting and assembling cars; medicine — surgery carried out with a precision a hand cannot match, and rehabilitation; exploration — space probes and deep-sea vehicles; agriculture — harvesting and spraying; logistics — warehouse robots and delivery; the military — bomb disposal and reconnaissance; and the home — vacuum cleaners and lawnmowers.

Benefits: robots work continuously without tiring, they are more precise and more consistent than people, and they do work that is dangerous, dirty or repetitive. Concerns: the cost, the loss of jobs to automation, the difficulty of making a robot cope with an unexpected situation, and the question of who is responsible when one causes harm.

The two are converging: cloud robotics lets a robot offload its heavy computation to the cloud, so a cheap robot can share an expensive brain.

long.q: Define the term “e-Learning” and Virtual reality.
long.a:
e-Learning is learning delivered, supported and assessed electronically — usually over the internet — rather than in a classroom. It includes video lessons and live online classes, learning management systems that hold the material and the assignments, digital textbooks and libraries, quizzes marked automatically, educational apps, and simulations and virtual laboratories.

Advantages: it is available anywhere and at any time, so a student is not tied to a timetable or a place; each learner works at their own pace and can replay what they did not follow; it reaches students in rural areas who have no access to good teachers; it costs less than classrooms and printed books; it offers far more choice of courses; and it records progress so a teacher can see exactly where a student is struggling.

Disadvantages: it needs a device, a connection and the discipline to work alone; it lacks the social life of a classroom and the immediate help of a teacher; practical, laboratory and clinical subjects are hard to teach through a screen; screen fatigue is real; and without someone to encourage them many students never finish.

Virtual reality (VR) is a computer-generated, simulated environment that a person can enter and interact with, usually by wearing a head-mounted display and holding controllers. It produces the feeling of actually being somewhere else by tracking the head and hands and updating the view in real time, and it blocks out the real world while it does so. Augmented reality (AR) is the related idea of overlaying computer images on the real world rather than replacing it.

Uses of VR: training pilots in flight simulators and surgeons in operating theatres, where a mistake costs nothing; education, letting students walk through ancient Rome or inside a molecule; medicine, for treating phobias and for pain management; architecture and engineering, walking a client through a building that has not been built; gaming and entertainment; tourism, visiting a place before booking; and therapy and rehabilitation.

Advantages: it makes the impossible safe and cheap — practising surgery or firefighting without risk; it makes abstract ideas concrete; and it engages people in a way a book cannot. Disadvantages: the equipment is expensive; some users suffer motion sickness and eye strain; prolonged use can be isolating; and a convincing simulation is not the same as the real thing.

The two combine naturally: e-learning provides the material, and virtual reality provides the experience that cannot be put into a book.

long.q: Explain “e-Commerce” and “m-Commerce”.
long.a:
e-Commerce is buying and selling goods, services and information over the internet, along with the payment, the delivery and the customer service that surround the sale. It covers online shops, online banking, ticketing, auctions and digital downloads, and it is classified by who is trading: business to consumer (B2C), business to business (B2B), consumer to consumer (C2C), consumer to business (C2B), and the government variants.

Advantages: shopping at any hour from anywhere, a much wider choice, prices that are easy to compare, lower costs for the seller, and a market that is national or global rather than local.

Disadvantages: the goods cannot be examined before buying, delivery takes time and can go wrong, there are real risks of fraud and intrusion into privacy, and the buyer needs a device and a connection.

m-Commerce (mobile commerce) is the same activity carried out on a mobile device — a phone or a tablet — over a wireless network. It is e-commerce specialised to the device in your pocket: mobile banking and wallets, QR-code payments, in-app purchases, ordering food or a ride, and buying airtime.

Advantages of m-commerce: the device is always with the user and switched on, so buying can happen anywhere at any moment; the phone's location enables services that a desktop cannot offer, such as finding the nearest shop or tracking a delivery; payments are made by scanning a QR code or tapping, which is quicker than entering card details; and it reaches people who have a phone but never owned a computer, which is why it has grown fastest in developing countries.

Disadvantages: the small screen makes browsing and comparing harder; typing on a phone is slower and more error-prone; the connection can drop; the battery runs out; and a phone is easier to lose or steal, which makes security and authentication more important.

e-Commercem-Commerce
Any internet-enabled transaction, on any device. Transactions carried out specifically on a mobile device.
Usually done on a desktop or laptop at a fixed place. Done anywhere, at any time — the device is always carried.
Not tied to the user's location. Location-based services are possible.
Bigger screen, easier typing and comparison. Small screen, slower typing.
Paid by card, bank transfer or cash on delivery. Paid by mobile wallet, QR code, or added to the phone bill.
Reaches people with computers and internet at home. Reaches people who have only a phone — a much larger group.

m-Commerce is therefore best understood not as a rival to e-commerce but as its mobile form — and in much of the world it is the form that most people meet first.

mcq.q: Which of the following characteristics defines "Big Data"?
options: Data that can be easily managed with traditional database systems.
Data with low velocity and variety.
Data with a volume that exceeds the capacity of traditional data management tools.
Data that is always structured and well-organized.
mcq.teacher_note: Big Data is defined by being too voluminous for conventional processing tools — and it is often unstructured, not always structured.

mcq.q: What is the primary benefit of using the IoT in industrial settings (Industrial IoT or IIoT)?
mcq.teacher_note: In industry, IoT is about efficiency and automation — it reduces cost by cutting human intervention and saving time, effort and money.

mcq.q: Which type of AI system uses pre-defined rules and knowledge to make decisions?
mcq.teacher_note: An expert system has a knowledge base of facts and rules plus an inference engine — it is the rule-based one. Deep learning and reinforcement learning learn from data instead.

mcq.q: Which AI technique aims to imitate the way the human brain processes information?
mcq.teacher_note: Neural networks are modelled on the brain's interconnected neurons.

mcq.q: What are the four V's that best define Big Data?
mcq.teacher_note: Volume, Velocity, Variety, Veracity. Note that this chapter's own §7.3 lists SEVEN Vs — the extra three are Value, Variability and Visualization.

mcq.q: What type of communication technology is commonly used in IoT devices?
mcq.teacher_note: IoT devices use all of these — Wi-Fi, Bluetooth and Zigbee — depending on range and power needs.

mcq.q: … is the part of computer science concerned with designing intelligent computer systems.
mcq.teacher_note: This is the chapter's own opening definition of AI (§7.1).

mcq.q: … is the branch of technology that deals with the design, construction, operation, and application of robots.
mcq.teacher_note: The chapter's own definition of robotics (§7.1).

mcq.q: … is the use of various services, such as software development platforms, servers, storage, and software, over the Internet.
mcq.teacher_note: The chapter's own definition of cloud computing (§7.2).

mcq.q: SaaS stands for…
mcq.teacher_note: SaaS = Software as a Service — complete software hosted on the cloud.

mcq.q: IaaS stands for…
mcq.teacher_note: IaaS = Infrastructure as a Service — server hardware, storage and bandwidth.

mcq.q: PaaS stands for…
mcq.teacher_note: Errata: the printed key says (b) “program as a service”, which is wrong — PaaS is Platform as a Service (option a), as §7.2 states. Note the book's own pattern in MCQ 10 (SaaS = software as a service, key a) and MCQ 11 (IaaS = infrastructure as a service, key b); the answer here is (a).

mcq.q: … is a term that expresses computer-based simulated environments which can be perceived as in the real world, as well as in unreal worlds.
mcq.teacher_note: The chapter's own definition of virtual reality (§7.4).

mcq.q: … is a process of buying and selling or exchanging products, services, and information using electronic media.
mcq.teacher_note: The chapter's own definition of e-Commerce (§7.5).

mcq.q: IoT stands for…
mcq.teacher_note: Internet of Things.

mcq.q: IP stands for…
mcq.teacher_note: Internet Protocol — every “thing” in the IoT is assigned an IP address so it can transfer data over a network.

mcq.q: What type of protocol is utilised to enable internet connectivity on mobile devices?
mcq.teacher_note: Mobile IP keeps a device reachable as it moves between networks. TCP/IP is the general Internet suite, WAP is an old mobile browsing standard, and HTTP is the web's transfer protocol.

mcq.q: What does the term “virtual” refer to in the context of Virtual reality?
options: Physical reality that can be touched and experienced physically
Simulated or artificial environment that is created using computer technology.
Augmented reality experiences through wearable devices.
mcq.teacher_note: “Virtual” = simulated or artificial, created with computer technology — the opposite of physical reality.

mcq.q: Which of the following best describes social media?
options: A system for tracking online purchases
A way to order food delivery
A platform for sharing cat memes
mcq.teacher_note: None of the four options matches the chapter's own definition (creating and sharing information, ideas and interests via virtual communities and networks). The printed key is (d), so treat this as a deliberately light-hearted item — in an exam, write the chapter's definition.

mcq.q: What term refers to the process of analyzing …?
mcq.teacher_note: Errata: the book's question is truncated — it reads “What term refers to the process of analyzing” with no object — and two of the four options are both labelled (c). The printed key is (a) Data mining. Data mining is the process of analysing large data sets to find patterns.

key_terms.meaning: The branch of computer science concerned with designing intelligent computer systems that show the characteristics of human intelligence.
A machine-learning approach that uses labelled data to train models.
A machine-learning approach that identifies patterns in data without labelled examples.
Learning through interaction with an environment, rewarded for positive results.
A computer system that mimics or surpasses a human expert's decision-making, built from a knowledge base (facts and rules) and an inference engine.
The field of AI that lets computers take digital images and videos as input and act on them.
The branch of technology dealing with the design, construction, operation and application of robots — overlapping AI and mechanical engineering.
Using services such as servers, storage, platforms and software over the Internet instead of on local servers or personal devices.
A cloud made available to the general public or a large industry group.
A cloud environment that resides within one organisation and is used exclusively for its benefit.
A combination of public and private cloud — non-core applications in the public cloud, core and sensitive data in the private cloud.
Infrastructure as a Service — server hardware, storage, bandwidth and other fundamental computing resources provided through the cloud.
Software as a Service — complete software hosted on the cloud and used without installing it.
Platform as a Service — virtualised servers and the basic operating software for running, developing, testing, deploying and hosting applications.
Complex and large data sets that must be processed and analysed to uncover valuable information; too voluminous for conventional processing tools.
Data that can be processed, stored and retrieved in a fixed format.
Data that lacks any specific form or structure, making it hard and slow to process.
Data containing both structured and unstructured elements, with tags that segregate individual elements.
The characteristics of Big Data: Volume, Velocity, Variety, Veracity, Value, Variability and Visualization.
The reliability or trustworthiness of data.
A computer-based simulated environment that can be perceived as if it were the real world, or an unreal world.
Buying, selling or exchanging products, services and information using electronic media, usually computer networks.
Business to Business — selling to other businesses; Business to Consumer — selling directly to consumers.
Consumer to Business — the consumer fixes the price and the business accepts or declines; Consumer to Consumer — consumers sell directly to each other.
An online clinical medical knowledge database used to provide health care to people spread across different locations.
Using ICT to enhance the access to and delivery of government services for citizens, business partners and employees.
The gap between those who have ICT knowledge and access to computing resources and those who do not — a key e-governance challenge in developing countries.
Using technology while moving, with portable devices that can operate, execute and provide services in transit.
The network of physical devices, vehicles and appliances embedded with electronics, software, sensors and connectivity so they can connect, collect and exchange data.
The identity given to each thing in the IoT so it can transfer data over a network without human interaction.
Learning or teaching a topic with the help of Information and Communication Technology, anywhere and at any time.
Mobile commerce — buying and selling goods and services through wireless handheld devices such as phones and PDAs.
Computer-based technology for creating and sharing information, ideas, interests and other forms of expression through virtual communities and networks.
Crime carried out using computers or the Internet; listed as a disadvantage of social media.

quick_revision.title: Artificial Intelligence and robotics
points: AI = the branch of computer science that designs intelligent computer systems.
Five components: learning, reasoning, problem solving, perception, language understanding.
Learning comes in three flavours: supervised (labelled data), unsupervised (patterns) and reinforcement (interaction).
Eight applications: game playing, speech recognition, natural language understanding, computer vision, expert systems, robotics, theorem proving and symbolic mathematics.
Robotics overlaps AI and mechanical engineering; robots are used in industry, research, the military, intelligent homes and health services.

quick_revision.title: Cloud computing
points: Cloud = the Internet; cloud computing shares computing resources instead of using local servers or personal devices.
Three deployment types: public, private and hybrid.
Three service models: IaaS (infrastructure), PaaS (platform) and SaaS (software).
Advantages: cost-efficient, almost unlimited storage, easy backup and recovery, automatic software integration, access from anywhere, quick deployment.
Disadvantages: technical issues and outages, security risk with a third party, and vulnerability to attack.

quick_revision.title: Big Data
points: Big Data = data sets too large and complex for conventional processing tools.
Three types: structured (fixed format), unstructured (no form) and semi-structured (both, with tags).
Seven Vs: Volume, Velocity, Variety, Veracity, Value, Variability, Visualization.
Applied in healthcare, academia, banking, manufacturing, IT, retail and transportation.
Advantages: outside intelligence for decisions, better customer service, early risk identification, better efficiency, innovative solutions.
Disadvantages: expensive traditional storage, not useful in the short run, results can be misleading.

quick_revision.title: Virtual reality
points: VR = computer-based simulated environments perceived as real or unreal, mainly visual, sometimes with sound.
Used in medical studies, research labs, entertainment, driving schools and military training.
Advantages: realistic world, explore places, experiment with an artificial environment, easier education.
Disadvantages: expensive equipment, complex technology, you cannot move by yourself as in the real world.

quick_revision.title: e-Commerce, e-Medicine, e-Governance
points: e-Commerce = buying and selling through electronic media; main platforms are the Internet, e-mail, fax and telephone orders.
Four models: B2B, B2C, C2B (the consumer fixes the price) and C2C.
e-Medicine = an online clinical knowledge database bringing health care to people in different locations, mainly rural areas.
e-Governance = ICT used to deliver government services; it is more than just a government website.
e-Governance challenges in Nepal: high-speed infrastructure, trust and transparency, the digital divide, network security, online privacy, and access to computing resources.

quick_revision.title: Mobile computing, IoT, e-Learning, m-Commerce, social media
points: Mobile computing = technology used while moving; devices have limited processing and storage, touch screens, cameras, wireless connectivity and GPS.
IoT = a network of physical things with UIDs and IP addresses that exchange data without human interaction.
e-Learning = learning through ICT, anywhere and any time; it can be CD-ROM, network, intranet or Internet based.
m-Commerce = buying and selling through wireless handheld devices; it affects financial services, telecoms, service/retail and information services.

Social media = creating and sharing information through virtual communities — advantages are fast communication and worldwide sharing, disadvantages are cyber-crime, wasted time, fraud, rumours and lost privacy.

teaching_plan.activity: Open with the question 'can a machine think?'. Give the definition of AI, show the fields diagram, then teach the five components — with supervised, unsupervised and reinforcement learning spelled out. Finish with the eight applications.
Robotics: definition, industrial vs mobile robotics, and the five bullet points on where robots are used. Then revise AI as a whole with the component list.
Definition, the three cloud types, and the three service models with the 'you get / you still manage' table. Then the six advantages and three disadvantages.

Definition and Gartner's definition, the three types, then the Seven Vs figure with all seven explained. Contrast with the three-V and four-V versions other books use. Close with application areas, advantages and disadvantages.

Virtual reality: definition, five application areas, four advantages and three disadvantages. Then e-Commerce: definition, the four transaction models with the examples table, the fourteen advantages and six disadvantages.
e-Medicine and who it helps, then e-Governance: definition, what it is NOT, the four relationships it builds, the Nepali portal examples, the five objectives and the six challenges.

Mobile computing: definition, the twelve features, ten advantages and five disadvantages. Then IoT: definition, unique identifiers, the 'thing' examples, and the six advantages and four disadvantages.

e-Learning (with the Covid-19 note), m-Commerce and the four industries it affects, then social media with its five advantages and five disadvantages. Finish with Exercise 7 — 4 short and 8 long questions — and the 20-question MCQ self-test, going through the two errata notes.
